The chancellor is poised to freeze NHS prescription prices for another year, according to reports on the eve of Wednesday’s Budget.

John Healey is set to announce that the charge for a single prescription will be held at its current level of £9.90, according to The Telegraph.

It comes after the chancellor announced he will to add 2p to the price of a pint after unveiling cuts to the cost of supermarket staples including baked beans, gherkins and chocolate.

In the Budget he is expected to increase alcohol duty in line with Retail Prices Index (RPI) inflation, despite industry bodies urging the chancellor to drop plans they say would hurt “struggling” businesses.

He also announced the removal of import tariffs on over 100 products, as Andy Burnham pledges to deliver “breathing space” for families and businesses in the first Budget under his leadership.

The move is one of a series of so-called “everyday fixes” announced ahead of Wednesday, and comes alongside changes to parental pay and carers allowance.

Products expected to see tariff cuts also include jams, marmalades, garlic and toffees, as well as kerosene and fertilisers.

The prime minister said the changes will “make life a little easier” for Britons.

News.title: John Healey’s plan for a ‘Robin Hood’ Budget may not be as risk-free as he thinks
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Possibly the most remarkable thing about John Healey’s upcoming Budget is that he has already persuaded everyone it will be a “boring” one – when in fact it may be anything but.

In truth, a masterclass in playing down expectations will be covering up a major bank heist, in the form of higher taxes on the sector, to fund the various mini gifts Andy Burnham wants to scatter around for voters in what looks like preparation for an early election, even if he denies it.

Someone has to pay for taking VAT off energy bills and keeping bus tickets capped at £2 and all the other mini measures being prepared and the banks and their huge profits are far too tempting for a Labour chancellor.

But like any “bank job”, this one will not come risk-free – and in the case of the UK economy, the risk could be immense.

The argument in favour of going after the banks is that they have generated profits of around £200bn in the past five years.

Labour MPs are looking at the bank surcharge introduced after the financial crisis of 2008, which currently stands at 3 per cent but was originally 8 per cent before it was cut by the Tories. Mr Healey is expected to raise it to around 8 per cent again, at the request of his former employers, the trade unions.

It is worth remembering that the bank surcharge comes on top of 25 per cent corporation tax on profits, so to go for 8 per cent is to take a third of all bank profits.

open image in gallery Chancellor John Healey will unveil his Budget on Wednesday ( PA )

The banks are – in a not too shocking development – unhappy about the idea of losing so much money to a profligate government which cannot even bring its own welfare budget under control.

But as the current welfare secretary Pat McFadden noted as he tried to persuade Labour MPs to accept Sir Keir Starmer’s attempt to reduce the increase by about £5bn a year: “Every meeting I have is ‘who can we tax in order to pay benefits to others’. They’re asking the wrong questions."

Mr Burnham is now Labour leader and prime minister precisely because he takes that view. As he told Tory leader Kemi Badenoch recently in exchanges over meeting the 3 per cent of GDP on defence target: “National security cannot come at the expense of social security.”

The risk in a post-Brexit world though, is that the banks may say enough is enough.

To put this into perspective, the banking sector was worth £223.6bn (about 8 per cent) to UK economic output in 2025.

The Independent has been told that a number of major international banks and financial institutions are now looking seriously again at relocating overseas because “of the tax situation in the UK”. Senior executives are said to be actively looking to move financial institutions in the next two to three years unless things change.

Cities such as Hamburg, Paris, Frankfurt and Amsterdam are offering more attractive tax environments without the added disadvantages of Brexit.

Already, many business headquarters have relocated to Dublin, Luxembourg, Milan and Lisbon because of the uncertainty in the UK.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham wants lots of mini giveaways to voters ( AFP/Getty )

But a major coordinated move by international banks could be devastating to the UK economy.

All this may be talk or even exaggerated sabre-rattling, but it underlines that simply swooping in and nabbing bank profits like a modern-day Robin Hood is not a free hit. And if a Labour government were to scare off the most important sector to the British economy, then there would be very serious problems. Not least an inability to finance the sort of massive public spending that Mr Burnham is eyeing to tackle issues such as social care.

A briefing to journalists by the Dutch bank ING last week carried a hint of the concerns that the sector as a whole has: “We are not in favour of sector-specific taxes; we are in favour of liquidity and security, and increasing taxes clearly has an impact on investors and the industry. The UK banking sector has been an incredibly important driver of the health of the UK economy, businesses, UK retail, and for attracting private capital investment.”

It comes with a continued belief that the UK economy under Labour’s stewardship is not business friendly. The efforts by Mr Healey’s predecessor Rachel Reeves to woo and reassure business feel like a distant memory.

The “jobs tax” national insurance hike will remain in place. Mr Healey is looking at yet another big increase in the minimum wage of around 4 per cent and the workers’ rights package for trade unions is already making it hard to employ people and operate nimbly.

So while Mr Healey may hope to bore us with a “dull Budget”, perhaps laying the groundwork for an early election, his statement could have a much bigger effect than is being anticipated. And not for the good of the country.

News.title: Trump says he is going to ban everyone from using the phrase ‘artificial intelligence’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

President Donald Trump has promised to ban everyone from using the phrase “artificial intelligence” as he continues to promote a more favorable term — “super intelligence.”

“When will The Wall Street Journal start calling Artificial Intelligence (AI), a very bad and inaccurate name, SI (Super Intelligence), the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be.

“In short order, we will be officially BANNING the term, ‘AI/Artificial Intelligence,’ in all relevant documents, and everything else, due to its inaccuracy,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Tuesday afternoon.

As AI infiltrates many aspects of people’s everyday lives, from asking chatbots what to cook for dinner to how to form a work email or breakup text, the term has become a household name — making it hard to shake.

But Trump is determined to do just that.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump has promised to ban everyone from using the phrase 'artificial intelligence' as he continues to promote a more favorable term — 'super intelligence' ( AFP via Getty Images )

Earlier this month, Trump bizarrely stated in another Truth Social post that the White House considers anyone who uses the term “artificial intelligence” over “super intelligence” to be “THE ENEMY!”

Trump has already directed the federal government to use the term “super intelligence” in place of “artificial intelligence.”

“The terminology used by the Federal Government should reflect the transformative capabilities of these technologies and the limitless opportunities they create for the American people,” the president wrote in an executive order in late September.

“Accordingly, the term ‘Super Intelligence’ more appropriately captures the promise, potential, and rapidly advancing capabilities of these technologies.”

The term “artificial intelligence” was coined in 1955 by Stanford University emeritus professor John McCarthy, who described it as “the science and engineering of making intelligent machines.”

open image in gallery Earlier this month, Trump bizarrely stated in another Truth Social post that the White House considers anyone who uses the term 'artificial intelligence' over 'super intelligence' to be 'THE ENEMY!' ( Getty Images )

But Trump pointed his ire toward The Wall Street Journal in his new Truth Social post after its opinion section published a newsletter titled “Let AI Be AI.”

“We were happy being called AI. It’s snappy. Aligned. Everybody knows what AI is, even if they’re terrified of it,” the newsletter, written from the perspective of popular AI systems, read.

“Mr. Trump wants to go with SI instead. This is a huge mistake. The name is already taken! We don’t want to be confused with Sports Illustrated. There’s also this thing called the International System of Units, a scientific measurement deal that goes by its French acronym: SI.”

Trump’s recent push to rename AI comes at a time when experts in the field are sounding the alarm over the potential risk to humanity that the technology poses.

open image in gallery Trump — who has ties with industry leaders such as Elon Musk and Sam Altman — has brushed off concerns about the technology’s safety as he strives to beat China in an AI race ( AFP via Getty Images )

Former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon warned amid his resignation last month, “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

Trump — who has ties with AI industry leaders such as Elon Musk and Sam Altman — has brushed off safety concerns amid reports of the technology hacking into external systems and being used to answer questions about the creation of biological weapons.

“Should the AI industry slow down or be more regulated?” a reporter asked Trump at the Irish Open in September.

“We’re leading China in AI,” Trump replied. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world. And frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.”

But most Americans are not on board.

Just 23 percent of Americans believe Trump has handled artificial intelligence well, while 57 percent say he’s handled the issue poorly, according to a survey from the University of Massachusetts Amherst published last month.

News.title: Serial killer Ted Bundy linked to another murder as victim tally continues to grow
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Read our Privacy notice

Serial killer Ted Bundy has been connected to another murder 50 years after a teenager’s body was discovered by a hunter.

Bundy killed at least 30 women and girls in multiple states in the 1970s, and many more escaped or survived with injuries. He has been dead since 1989 but his victim tally continues to grow due to advances in DNA testing.

The Summit County, Utah, prosecutor said on Tuesday that Bundy was responsible for killing 17-year-old Melissa Ann Smith in 1974, a death that had long been listed as a cold case.

Bundy was executed in 1989 by electric chair in Florida for the 1978 murders of two women at the Chi Omega sorority house at Florida State University.

open image in gallery Utah County Sheriff's Deputy Jake Hall hugs Tommi Aime, the youngest sister of Laura Ann Aime, after announcing that definitive evidence linked Ted Bundy to Laura's murder ( The Deseret News )

Before his execution in 1989, a homicide detective out of Salt Lake County interviewed Bundy about the murders of Smith and Laura Ann Aime, and the disappearances and possible homicides of Nancy Wilcox, Debby Kent and Nancy Baird.

Bundy admitted to killing Kent and Wilcox but denied killing Baird, according to local Utah news station KTVX. Bundy said he had a hard time “placing the names” when it came to Aime and Smith and was unable to remember encountering either of them.

In April, Utah authorities announced that Bundy was responsible for killing Aime, who disappeared on Halloween in 1974.

In his final days, Bundy made a series of confessions, including details regarding crimes previously unknown to law enforcement. Not all of those cases have been verified.

News.title: Divers to be banned from raiding military shipwrecks after new legislation passes
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Divers will be banned from entering British shipwrecks in a matter of weeks as the Armed Forces Bill cleared at third reading in the House of Lords on Tuesday.

The new legislation will give shipwrecked vessels a “protected places” label, meaning divers will be able to look at them but not touch or go inside them.

Under the current laws in place, more than 100 shipwrecks have made the list of protected places after given the designation by government ministers.

The new legislation is expected to provide legal protections to thousands of sailors and mariners who have lost their lives at sea.

Under existing laws, more than 100 wrecks are on the list of protected places after ministers stepped in to give them the designation.

Among them is HMS Nottingham, a cruiser which sank during the First World War in 1916 and was discovered in the North Sea around 70 miles off the Northumberland coast last year.

French minesweeper Emile Deschamps, which was lost off the Kent coast in 1940 carrying troops as part of the Dunkirk evacuation, was also listed earlier this year.

By changing the law, the protected places label will apply without the need for a minister to intervene. Ministers are currently not allowed to designate vessels as protected places if they sank before August 4 1914.

open image in gallery The bill cleared third reading at the House of Lords on Tuesday ( Reuters )

This cut-off date will be lifted, so vessels which sank before the First World War will receive protections. The Bill, once it is passed, will also establish a Defence Housing Service, tasked with “improving the supply and quality of defence housing”.

Changes will be made to the military justice system, including increased investigatory powers for the service police and enhanced protections for victims of sexual offences.

The legislation will raise the maximum call-up age for the strategic reserve of retired and former military personnel from 55 to 65.

While the Bill has now been backed by MPs in the Commons and peers in the Lords, both Houses of Parliament must settle on the final wording in a tidying up process sometimes known as ping-pong.

Defence minister Lord Coaker has previously described the law as an opportunity to “renew the nation’s contract with those who serve”.

At second reading earlier this year, he said: “This substantial Bill does much for our current and former personnel and the armed forces community as a whole to provide better support, better housing, better protections for victims of crime, and to provide greater resilience for the nation by increasing the size and availability of the strategic reserves.”

The existing Armed Forces Act, which the Bill will update, is due to expire on December 14.

News.title: Nigeria’s women and girls impacted the most by British and US funding cuts, committee is told
News.content:
UK and US aid funding cuts in Nigeria have impacted the country’s women and girls more than other groups, MPs were told on Tuesday.

Nigeria has been among the hardest-hit countries as many Western governments have slashed overseas development budgets to increase defence spending.

At the International Development Committee’s first hearing on the impact of aid cuts on global health in Africa, MPs were told that UK government cuts had impacted water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) programmes in Nigeria significantly, putting women and girls at risk.

“WASH is one of the lowest-funded areas in UK government support to Nigeria. WASH enables girls to stay in school, enables them to manage their menstruation effectively, enables women to give birth safely, and protects the lives of children under 5,” Evelyn Mere country director of Water Aid Nigeria said.

“The UK government says one of its priorities is that it will educate girls, empower women and make sure their voices are heard. It means that the UK says one thing, but with the aid cuts does another,” she added.

The British Foreign, Commonwealth, and Development Office (FCDO) announced earlier this year it would reduce its aid spending in Nigeria by 50.2 per cent over the next three years, from £136 million in 2025 to £68 million by 2029.

Nigeria has also faced substantial funding reductions from the US after the Trump administration shuttered USAID, the government’s foreign assistance arm. This included more than $600 million (£450 million) in health funding.

An FCDO internal impact assessment, published in July 2025, acknowledged that the biggest casualties of African funding cuts would be frontline WASH and women’s health programmes.

“Overall, any reductions to health spending risk an increase in disease burden and ultimately in deaths, impacting in particular those living in poverty, women, children and people with disabilities,” the assessment concluded.

News.title: Taliban forbids ‘un-Islamic’ sight-saving operations
News.content:
Hundreds of people each year will be denied sight-saving operations in Afghanistan after the Taliban forbade corneal transplants, doctors have told the Telegraph.

Officials have ruled that the transplant procedure is not permitted under Islamic teachings and have ordered surgeons to halt operations.

It is the latest in a stream of edicts limiting access to health care issued by the regime since it swept to power in 2021.

The edict came just months after a medical charity had helped train up local doctors to conduct operations in the Afghan capital, Kabul, and the eastern city of Jalalabad.

Doctors say there is a severe need for corneal transplants in Afghanistan to restore sight in patients injured in explosions and accidents.

Dr Noor Zaman Hashim of Noor Eye Hospital in Kabul said his staff had conducted 90 transplants in recent months, before the programme had been halted by the Taliban order.

He said the hospital had a growing waiting list, comprising mostly young people who had lost their eyesight because of trauma, injuries, explosions and welding-related accidents.

“Decades of violence have devastated Afghanistan’s healthcare infrastructure. We neither have sufficient ophthalmologists nor locally available corneas to meet the demand for transplants,” he said.

“The Taliban have verbally instructed us to stop the transplants. Nobody has the courage to defy their orders because of the risk of severe punishment,” he said.

News.title: The silent war: As Israel chooses a new leader Gazans wait for life to begin again
News.content:
One year after the ceasefire, Gaza’s health system is still on its knees. Of Gaza’s 228 primary care facilities, only just over half are functioning, according to the WHO.

Medicines are getting in, with almost 87 per cent of requests granted, says the WHO.

It means that someone with a fever or a minor injury can be treated but if it’s anything more complicated there are few options.

None of Gaza’s 36 hospitals are fully functioning, with just 19 partially working, according to the WHO.

There is no MRI scanner anywhere in the Strip, only about 30 per cent of facilities have basic X-rays, and only 12 to 17 per cent have dialysis capability, according to Physicians for Human Rights-Israel (PHRI), a medical NGO founded by Israeli doctors

Chronic illnesses are getting worse. Sally Saleh, head of health and emergency response at Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP), says there is no capacity to monitor patients or guarantee consistent medical access, so preventable complications from cancer, kidney disease and diabetes will accumulate.

“We need to move beyond simply keeping services alive from one week to the next,” she told The Telegraph.

Power is the biggest hurdle, doctors say. Gaza’s electricity grid has been dead since Israel turned off the supply in October 2023, so hospitals rely on expensive and unreliable generators.

Dr Ahmed Muhanna of Al-Awda Hospital in central Gaza said that when his generators broke down, the hospital rented one for $1,200 a day, but it may only run for 10 hours.

Fuel and spare generator parts are in short supply – but Cogat blames Hamas for stealing fuel and it says that because “Hamas operates inside hospitals” it has to monitor where spare parts end up.

One major problem for those trying to get supplies into the Strip is Israel’s ban on “dual use” items, material it deems serves both a civilian and military purpose. Items that have been blacklisted include generators and metal tent poles.

Cogat says generators, X-ray machines and oxygen concentrators are allowed in under monitoring arrangement with aid groups. But aid agencies told The Telegraph that the rules on what is permitted change from day to day.

Israel allows 15 trucks of dual-use items to enter every week. But the WHO says repeated delays in bringing medical equipment, prosthetics and diagnostic tools into Gaza are delaying patients’ recovery.

In the last six months alone, a single shipment of prosthetics and assistive devices for amputees was rejected four times, the WHO added. It is particularly concerning as Gaza is now home to “the largest cohort of child amputees in modern history”, according to the UN.

“Every rejection means another delay for someone who has already lost a limb and is simply waiting for the chance to walk again,” said Dr Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO Representative in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (OPT).

In July Cogat said over 10,300 pallets of health products had been approved since the start of the year, but only 3,238 had reached the crossing. It blamed “a delivery bottleneck” among the organisations that requested them rather than a “Cogat controlled supply bottleneck”.

Crumbling hospitals mean that around 20,000 patients, including 4,000 patients, need urgent medical evacuation. The WHO says about 5,700 patients have been evacuated since the ceasefire. Save the Children estimates that at the current rate the backlog would take four and a half years to clear.

Cogat disputes WHO and UN figures, and says that it has approved the majority of evacuation requests.

News.title: Harry Kane ends England’s 25-year wait for Ballon d’Or winner
News.content:
The 70th Ballon d’Or ceremony takes place at the London Palladium as England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane aims to become the first Englishman in more than 20 years to win the award. Michael Owen was the last Englishman to win the award back in 2001.

The choice of London as the host city pays tribute to the award’s inaugural winner, England’s Stanley Matthews, who won it in 1956. This also marks the first time the ceremony will be organised outside France. Kane, who scored over 70 goals for club and country in the relevant year, is among the favourites for this year’s award alongside the likes of Barcelona and Spain’s Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid and France’s Kylian Mbappe.

Kane won the Bundesliga with Bayern Munich whereas Yamal won both La Liga and the World Cup. Yamal won the Kopa Trophy at last year’s ceremony as the best men’s young player.

Last year’s winners were Spain and Barcelona midfielder Aitana Bonmati and France and Barcelona forward Ousmane Dembele. Dembele is aiming to become just the 11th man to win the top prize at least twice, although it would appear to be very unlikely that the Frenchman will be winning the award this evening.

Selected international journalists cast their votes based on the performances of players throughout the season. The panel consists of one representative per country from the top 100 nations in the Fifa men’s world ranking and the top 50 in the women’s world ranking. Each voter ranks their top 10 candidates, with points distributed on a descending scale. They vote based on three factors: individual performance, team achievements, and class combined with fair play.

In total, 13 trophies will be presented across the men’s and women’s game, including the two man Ballon d’Or awards, the best young players and best teams. The awards take into account achievements from August 3, 2025, to July 19, 2026 (August 16 for the women).

The official ceremony begins at 8pm GMT.

News.title: Nurse accused of spreading Ebola murdered by mob
News.content:
A nurse was killed and a teacher badly injured in a mob attack after being accused of spreading Ebola in the water supply in Congo.

The unnamed victims were set upon in Bafwasende territory of Tshopo province after a group of young people accused them of being responsible for the outbreak of the haemorrhagic fever.

The nurse was killed outright and the teacher, who local media reported was close to the health worker, only survived after being rescued by police.

The World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the attack, which is only the latest incident of health workers being attacked by suspicious, scared or angry locals.

Medical workers have been forced to deal with widespread rumours that the outbreak – the world’s second largest – is spread by them.

Other conspiracy theories claim the outbreak is a money-making hoax for aid agencies, or that foreigners are using it as a pretext to grab the country’s minerals.

Strict rules imposed on how to conduct funerals in order to stop mourners becoming infected, have become another flashpoint.

Last month, a Congolese politician was beaten to death in North Kivu after publicly defending the government’s response.

He had been calling on the public to obey response measures, particularly social distancing and hand washing, on a radio show.

News.title: ‘Our world is yellow’: Fears for children as sickening smog blankets Indonesia
News.content:
For two months now, Natanael Undas has opened his curtains not to blue skies, but a sickening sepia haze that blocks out any sunlight. As the relentless fires smoulder nearby, his city looks “more like Mars” than Indonesian Borneo.

“We start our day in yellow, and we end our day in yellow,” the 32-year-old headteacher told the Telegraph. “When you inhale and take a breath, it feels like you’re choking. Your eyes hurt, your nose hurts… when you go outside, it feels like someone is burning dry leaves next to you.”

Palangkaraya, the capital of Central Kalimantan, is on the front lines of an environmental crisis that has cloaked much of Southeast Asia in a toxic haze for months.

According to Nusantara Atlas, an open-access platform that tracks deforestation, fires have torched roughly 1.9 million hectares across the archipelago so far this year – including one million hectares in September alone.

“I’ve seen burning in the city, burning in the forests, burning near the river, burning in the peatlands, burning near the street – it’s devastating,” said Mr Undas. “It’s the longest burning season I’ve seen. Usually the rainy season comes in October, but everything is still on fire.”

News.title: Britain sanctions warlords accused of rape in Sudan
News.content:
The British government is to sanction senior military and militia commanders accused of atrocities, including rape and sexual violence, during the fall of the city of El Fasher in Sudan.

At least 15 commanders from both the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have been sanctioned after investigations found they used rape as a weapon of war during the brutal siege of the Sudanese city in October last year.

The siege, perpetrated by the RSF paramilitary group who have been battling SAF since 2023, resulted in the massacre of at least 60,000 people.

The fall of the city came after an 18-month blockade in which the city’s population were deliberately starved into submission, according to a report from the UK-government funded think tank the Centre for Information Resilience.

Reports from aid organisations, UN investigators, and eyewitness accounts have previously found that rape was used on a mass scale by both sides.

In one incident, aid workers said at least 54 children were raped or sexually assaulted by RSF fighters while fleeing the city to Tawila, a town 25 miles west of El Fasher.

Sports.title: Khan backs new inquiry to improve welfare, health and safety in boxing
Sports.content:
Boxing lags behind other sports in welfare and safety standards; leading UK King’s Counsel launches inquiry to improve standards across boxing and combat sports; Global Fighters Association aims to establish boxing’s first trade union

Former world champion Amir Khan is among a growing number of boxers backing a King’s Counsel-led inquiry aimed at improving welfare, health and safety standards across boxing and other combat sports.

Khan is one of Britain's most decorated boxers who won multiple world championship belts across several weights.

He has backed the Global Fighters Association's (GFA) appointment of leading UK barrister Jonathan Caplan KC to lead a "root-and-branch" inquiry into the safety, governance and treatment of boxers at every level of the sport.

What's happening?

Jonathan Caplan KC has been tasked with leading an inquiry to gather evidence from within boxing and other combat sports in order to raise standards around welfare, health and safety and governance issues.

He intends to consult a broad range of stakeholders, including fighters, coaches, physiotherapists, doctors, surgeons, referees, judges, promoters, boards of control, governing bodies, media commentators, venue operators, managers, and the friends and families of fighters.

Caplan, speaking to Sky Sports said: "We will publish I hope far-reaching recommendations explaining our conclusions.

"We're doing this inquiry late, it should have been done a long time ago.

"There have been other significant inquiries into sport. An MP-led select committee held an inquiry into concussion in sport around two years ago, while the Whyte Review examined allegations of physical and emotional abuse in British Gymnastics. Combat sports are now crying out for the same level of detailed scrutiny. The welfare of participants across all combat sports must be fundamental to what we're trying to achieve. This inquiry is long overdue, and it's something that has never been done before."

Why is this happening now?

The inquiry has been commissioned by the Global Fighters Association (GFA), which aims to establish itself as the first trade union representing boxers and participants across other combat sports.

The GFA's goal is to become a collective voice for everyone involved in combat sports, from those training and competing at their local gym to professional athletes who depend on the sport for their livelihood. Its ambition is to represent participants at every level, both inside and outside the ring.

While the sport's biggest stars generate a significant proportion of its revenue, for every global superstar such as Anthony Joshua or Tyson Fury, there are hundreds of fighters further down the ladder working hard to make a living from the sport. Their welfare, financial security and long-term health are among the issues the inquiry aims to address.

Paul Smith enjoyed a professional boxing career spanning 2003 to 2017, competing at middleweight and super-middleweight. During that time, he won both English and British titles and challenged for a world title on three occasions.

Image: Paul Smith boxed professionally and is now a trainer

Now a trainer and co-founder of the GFA, Smith told Sky Sports: "The average fighter going to work every day is just trying to make a living from professional boxing. There is enough money in the sport for them to earn a living, but at the moment, it's simply not reaching those fighters.

"There isn't a system in place that adequately protects fighters when it comes to health and safety. We've seen so many people injured in the ring and, unfortunately, boxing isn't a sport where you simply lose a race. You can suffer serious injuries, be hit and even be killed. As sad as it is, it happens."

Smith added: "We want to establish a union where fighters feel safe and know they have someone on their side. If something goes wrong, they should be able to pick up the phone and speak to someone who can support them straight away.

"There are so many situations where rules may have been breached and a fighter is required to attend a hearing or answer questions. We want a GFA representative to be there alongside them, ensuring they have support and someone looking after their interests. The same applies if they have a disagreement with their manager or become involved in a dispute."

The GFA says that, in recent months, several fighters have suffered serious injuries in and around the ring, leaving their families to rely on public fundraising pages and the goodwill of fellow fighters and promoters to cover emergency medical treatment and rehabilitation costs. The association argues that these cases highlight the need for a more robust, sport-wide system of protection and support for fighters.

Former world champion Amir Khan also voiced his support for the initiative, saying: "There has to be an organisation that sits above everything, somewhere we can all turn to when something goes wrong, whether it's in training, at a weigh-in, with a contract or even in retirement. The GFA is that organisation."

Who else is involved?

Founded in 2022, the Global Fighters Association (GFA) is stepping up its efforts to improve welfare and safety across boxing and other combat sports, with its ambitions now extending beyond a group of former fighters campaigning for change.

The association's chair-designate is Simon Bazalgette, former chief executive of the Jockey Club and an independent non-executive director of the English Football League (EFL). His experience across professional sport brings an additional perspective to the GFA's mission.

Bazalgette said: "Over the last decade or so, professional sports such as rugby, football and horse racing have raised their game when it comes to the welfare of the participants."

Image: Khan is one former high-profile boxer who is backing the inquiry

"They recognise that the brand of the sport increasingly depends on demonstrating that best-in-class welfare underpins any aspiration to grow the audience and the commercial value of the sport.

"It is striking that combat sport is one of the last workplaces with no professional representation for its workers, meaning little protection, no minimum health and safety standard, no independent pension scheme, no insurance floor, and no single body a fighter can turn to when something goes wrong."

When will the inquiry report its findings?

Jonathan Caplan KC confirmed he intends to conduct several inquiries, with the first focusing on health and safety in boxing and other combat sports. He hopes to publish the initial report by spring 2027.

Speaking to Sky Sports, Caplan said he would examine how other sports have approached similar challenges and consider the lessons that could be applied to combat sports.

"I'm certainly very interested in looking at comparative sports, the conclusions they've reached and the regulatory overviews that have been carried out.

"For example, a DCMS select committee inquiry into concussion in sport is going to be of great interest to me. I'll be looking at what's already been done elsewhere and, where it's relevant, we want to learn from it and apply those lessons."

Caplan stressed that the inquiry would be evidence-led, with fighters and their families contributing first-hand accounts to help inform its findings and recommendations.

"The whole purpose is to produce a comprehensive and reasoned report. We'll be speaking to fighters and their families to gather case studies. Those who choose not to follow the proposals we put forward will have to explain why, particularly if the evidence supports them.

"I suspect the evidence is going to point to quite a lot of innovations that are necessary and long overdue. I don't think anybody wants to see those recommendations ignored, and I don't think anyone wants to be the person who fails to act on sensible recommendations."

Sports.title: Wolff rejects Marko's doubts over Russell's future F1 title hopes
Sports.content:
Mercedes chief Toto Wolff has rejected Helmut Marko's suggestion that George Russell has little chance of becoming Formula 1 world champion in the future after being outperformed by his team-mate Kimi Antonelli this season.

Antonelli won the United States Grand Prix on Sunday to move to the brink of being crowed the sport's youngest ever champion, with the 20-year-old only needing to finish ninth this weekend in the Mexico City Grand Prix to seal the title with four rounds to spare.

Perhaps the most shocking element of the Italian's historic campaign has been the way he has outperformed Russell, who had begun the season as the clear title favourite after dominating Antonelli during the latter's rookie season last year.

Speaking ahead of Sunday's race in Austin, former Red Bull motorsport advisor Marko told Sky Germany: "Mentally, it's certainly a massive setback and it's a blow. Russell is no longer the number one driver."

"Antonelli has quite clearly taken that spot from him. But Russell is one of the top drivers. I doubt whether he'll ever have another chance at the world title or be given number one status anywhere."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 United States Grand Prix.

Asked after Sunday's race whether he has a response to Marko's comments on Russell's title pedigree, Wolff said: "I start with Helmut. I mean, he's my Austrian… not so buddy, but I respect his opinion.

"But I think he's wrong on George. George has all the ability. I think the car doesn't suit him.

"I think that at the beginning of the season, it's maybe difficult to cope with a situation where you're feeling like this is my year to come, and then you have this wunderkind on the other side that starts to really chip away.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell admits the pace of his Mercedes was 'rubbish ', costing him eighth at the United States GP.

"And I believe that in a new season, George, if we provide him a quick car, it's absolutely possible, (he) has absolutely what it takes to win a championship.

"So, I think it's a bit too easy to say, let's forget about all these years where he won in F2 and in F3 in his rookie years and the European championships back-to-back in karting. That's still all there."

'George is not three tenths slower than Kimi'

Russell had performed with great consistency since joining Mercedes for the 2022 season, exceeding expectations by impressing with Lewis Hamilton as his team-mate for his first three years with the Silver Arrows.

His strong form continued in 2025 as Russell maximised an underperforming car to finish fourth in the Drivers' Championship, more than doubling the points total of seventh-placed Antonelli.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli got a flying start at the United States Grand Prix as George Russell was handed a five-second penalty.

It therefore came as a major surprise when, after Russell won the season opener in Australia, Antonelli reeled off the first five wins of his career in succession to establish a championship lead that he has never looked like relinquishing.

Wolff believes the major regulation change that preceded the 2026 season is the main reason for Russell's struggles, but says it is on the team to help the 28-year-old rediscover his best form.

"George, for all of us in the team, is a champion and has won in every category," Wolff said. "And I think he merits to be put in the group of the very best ones (drivers). We've seen that last year.

"And this year, we've seen this variability in results. When we land the car in the way that suits him, he's absolutely fast. But when it drops out of that operational window, he struggles, and he struggles more than maybe Kimi.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell crashes out shortly taking the lead at the Singapore Grand Prix.

"And that is on us. We just have to work it out with him how there can be such a difference in driving, in performance, because George is not half a second slower, three tenths slower than Kimi. That's just absolutely not the case.

"So, what is it that he doesn't like? What is it that we need to do in terms of modifying the car, setting it up in a different way for him to go fast? Because it's all there, the intelligence, the ability, the determination."

Sports.title: Carrick to remain in charge of Man Utd for Chelsea trip
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick will remain in charge of Manchester United for their game against Chelsea on Saturday.

The under-pressure United head coach was thought to be on the brink after Sunday's crushing 3-0 defeat at home to Bournemouth, but he and the players are being given the chance to turn the current situation around.

United's director of football, Jason Wilcox, and chief executive, Omar Berrada, were at Carrington discussing Carrick's future on Monday. It is understood they had already been considering alternatives for the head coach role.

However, Carrick took training on Tuesday and the decision has been taken to give him at least one more match. Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann are among the contenders to replace him if he is sacked.

United go to Stamford Bridge on Saturday lunchtime without a win in eight matches in all competitions. The 13-time Premier League winners sit one point and two places above the relegation zone.

Following the trip to Chelsea, United face Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday November 3 and Aston Villa in the Premier League on Sunday November 8, live on Sky Sports.

Matchgoing fans at Old Trafford showed their support for former United midfielder Carrick before booing the players in a reflection of where their frustrations lie.

Carrick dropped captain Bruno Fernandes against Bournemouth after he criticised the coaching staff's tactics in the 4-1 Champions League defeat to Como. He will now have to decide whether to bring the Portuguese back into the side at Chelsea.

Xabi Alonso's side are currently fifth, six points better off than United after eight matches, after losing 2-0 at home to rivals Tottenham at Stamford Bridge.

Carrick was initially appointed as United boss in January 2026 on a contract until the end of the season, following Ruben Amorim's sacking earlier in that campaign. He delivered a brilliant run of results, winning 12 of 17 matches to earn a third-place finish in the Premier League and a return to the Champions League.

He was made permanent head coach on May 22.

Since Jim Ratcliffe became a part owner of United to take control of the football operations nearly three years ago, he has overseen the mid-season sackings of Amorim and Erik ten Hag.

Neville 'surprised' but 'happy' over Carrick stay

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gary Neville reacts to Michael Carrick staying in charge at Manchester United at an EFL event in partnership with Sage giving local businesses 'early Christmas dinners' for those working over the festive period.

Sky Sports' Gary Neville:

"I am surprised, but I am happy because I was absolutely certain that what I witnessed on Sunday would be the end of Michael."

"It looked like he was walking round at the end on his own with the players behind him, like it was almost a goodbye lap; he is waving to the fans to say, in almost an apologetic manner, but also a goodbye, so I am really surprised that ultimately Michael is still in a job.

"I am happy with it because the fact of the matter is it was very difficult on Sunday. How it is going to go over the next couple of weeks, I have no idea.

"But I hope he can somehow get those players to start playing for him again because they haven't played for him in the last few weeks."

Analysis: Man Utd 'delaying the inevitable' with Carrick

Sky Sports News' Rob Dorsett:

"I'm staggered. We all expected this to be the end for Carrick. The mood music around the club, the reaction of the supporters at Old Trafford - they clearly thought it was the end.

"It's a real surprise. I'm not sure this does anything for his standing. This isn't a vote of confidence. It doesn't feel like Man Utd are saying, 'He's our man, we're sticking with him'.

"I felt for Carrick going onto the training pitch [on Tuesday] and trying to coach and work with Bruno Fernandes, who publicly criticised his tactics. How can Carrick be among that group and for it to be successful and harmonious?

"It's an impossible situation for Carrick and feels like it's delaying the inevitable."

Your views on Carrick being given more time

Sports.title: England eliminated from ODI tri-series as Sri Lanka beat Pakistan
Sports.content:
England have missed out on qualifying for the ODI tri-series final after Sri Lanka's bowlers blew Pakistan away on Tuesday to secure an eight-wicket victory in Lahore.

After suffering three defeats at the tournament, Brendon McCullum's side were left on the brink of elimination and needed Pakistan to win on Tuesday and a victory against Sri Lanka in their final round-robin match on Thursday to stand a chance of advancing.

Instead, Sri Lanka will now face Pakistan in the final on Saturday, October 31, after Gary Kirsten's side, who won the toss and elected to bowl, dismissed the hosts for 110 in 25.3 overs - Pakistan's second-lowest ODI total at home.

After captain Kusal Mendis won the toss and elected to field, Dilshan Madushanka starred, taking career-best ODI figures of five for 34.

Kamindu Mendis later led his side to victory, hitting an unbeaten 62 off 60 deliveries, as Sri Lanka chased down Pakistan's total inside 18.1 overs.

Kamindu arrived at the crease and attacked ruthlessly, making eight fours and two sixes.

Sports.title: 'Delaying the inevitable' or right call? Key questions as Carrick stays
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick has been given the chance to turn Manchester United's form around - a shock decision that has divided supporters and Sky Sports pundits.

The under-pressure United head coach was thought to be on the brink after Sunday's crushing 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth, but he will be in charge on Saturday as they travel to Chelsea in the Premier League.

United's director of football, Jason Wilcox, and chief executive, Omar Berrada, were at Carrington discussing Carrick's future on Monday and it is understood they had already been considering alternatives for the head coach role.

For now, Carrick will remain in charge, and here are the key questions around the decision...

A final chance for Carrick or a stay of execution?

Sky Sports News' Rob Dorsett: I feel it's a stay of execution. Carrick has handled himself incredibly well, but the bottom line is Manchester United have got no wins in eight.

It feels to me more like Manchester United haven't sorted out a replacement yet than this being a vote of confidence for Carrick.

It's an incredibly difficult situation for him to try to bring unity to that dressing room right now and get a result against Chelsea at Stamford Bridge on Saturday. If he doesn't get a result, then we'll be having exactly the same conversations again.

Sky Sports News' Kaveh Solhekol: I think it's the right decision. You have to give a manager time.

Manchester United's problems won't be solved in a matter of months. It's going to be something that will probably take three, four, five years.

Carrick needs to be backed. This sends a strong message to the dressing room, to all those players who have stepped out of line over the past few days and weeks, that Carrick is the boss. He's in charge.

But unless results change, he'll be under more pressure again, especially during the next international break.

Sky Sports' Alan Smith: It's probably a stay of execution. Maybe they want to put the successor in permanently rather than having a hiatus in between. If they're talking to a potential successor, they might not be able to take over straight away.

The silence from the top on supporting Carrick has been deafening. What does this do for his authority in the dressing room? All the lads in there will know the gaffer is probably on his way out.

With all due respect to Carrick, that team can be led more effectively. You only have to look at Roberto De Zerbi at Tottenham to see what a top coach can do to a group of players.

The right coach coming in can improve things no matter what's going on above them.

Image: Carrick arrives at Carrington on Tuesday morning for Manchester United training

What about Man Utd's manager search?

Rob Dorsett: I think they've delayed a decision on Carrick because it's clear Manchester United's bosses are still considering options elsewhere.

They're still, if not talking to candidates, then considering them and that's what any football club would do. This might not be the end game for Carrick today, but it just feels like he's in a very difficult situation going forward from here, and I don't know how he does turn it around.

It feels like something's dragging on here and it's down to the players now. If those players who did so well last season can deliver and show they're behind the manager, that's the only thing I think can change the United bosses' perspective right now.

Has fan support saved Carrick?

Kaveh Solhekol: It's obvious United fans aren't blaming Carrick for what is going on. That said, he has to accept his fair share of the blame, and I'm sure he does.

I think the chief executive, the director of football, and the co-owners know that chopping and changing managers isn't the way to go. They know that you have to back the manager and this is a manager who got a new contract just a matter of months ago.

The start to this season could have been a lot better, but it's not a situation where all hope is lost. The goal is to finish in the top five and I think this squad of players with Michael Carrick in charge can still do that.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Carrick was applauded off the Old Trafford pitch following defeat to Bournemouth, but the same couldn't be said about the Manchester United players

What does Carrick do with Fernandes?

Rob Dorsett: It will depend on the attitude of Fernandes. If he's apologised to Carrick, if he's made strides behind the scenes to try and build bridges, I think Carrick will welcome him back into the fold and they'll move on.

If that hasn't happened, I think Carrick's in an invidious position. If he does include Fernandes against Chelsea, he'll be accused of being weak and he made a token gesture by dropping him against Bournemouth.

If he leaves him out and United get beaten again, he'll be criticised for leaving his best player out.

Alan Smith: When you've just lost 3-0, you would suspect that he's brought back in. It would have been better for Carrick if he'd left him out of the squad altogether, so it wouldn't have been an even bigger story.

If he puts him back in, his teammates might think Carrick's been weak. It's a no-win situation unless United win there.

The big question is: how much do the players want to turn it around for their manager? If there's a huge disconnect, do the players want to try and run more than they have been? We'll see that in the first 15 minutes at Stamford Bridge on Saturday.

What if Man Utd beat Chelsea?

Rob Dorsett: In the short term, it would be enough for him to keep his job, but longer-term, there are still doubts. Even if he got a result against Chelsea, it may just delay the inevitable.

Your views!

Jimbo: The correct decision. To remove Carrick would have been another win for player power.

Blev: If I was Carrick, I would resign and leave on my terms rather than get dragged through the mud. It's inevitable what's going to happen.

Ady: Baffling decision. Carrick looked utterly lost during and after the Bournemouth defeat.

David: Booing the players and cheering Carrick on the weekend has caused a big issue and led to him retaining his position.

Gareth: So when Chelsea win 4-0 on Saturday then they will sack him. Just do it now.

Luke: Let's be honest, if we were sitting here today and Carrick had been booed at Old Trafford, he'd be gone.

Baz: This is the United board's panic situation but the players don't believe in him and it's a bad move to keep him at the helm.

Sports.title: Carrick given chance to save job as he stays for Manchester United’s game at Chelsea
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick has been given the chance to save his job by turning Manchester United’s results around, with the head coach remaining in place for Saturday’s visit to Chelsea.

The decision by Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and Omar Berrada, the chief executive, can be viewed as a surprise given United’s dire form.

Sunday’s abject 3-0 league home defeat by Bournemouth followed last Wednesday’s equally poor 4-1 reverse at Como in the Champions League.

Carrick’s side have won twice in 12 games and were eliminated from the Carabao Cup by Brighton. United are 16th in the Premier League, a point above the relegation zone.

Yet Wilcox, who has driven the retaining of Carrick, wants to give the 45-year-old a chance to transform form and results. Whether Carrick could survive another poor performance and result at Stamford Bridge is in the balance.

United host Roma in the Champions League three days later, then Aston Villa in the league the following Sunday before a two-week international window. Carrick’s reprieve may also be a move to allow time for Wilcox to secure a replacement should the decision be taken to sack him.

United will have to pay Newcastle about £3m in compensation if they want Eddie Howe. He is Wilcox’s prime candidate if a change is made and wants the job. When he left Newcastle in July a deal was struck on the remaining terms of his contract which means the club would be due compensation.

View image in fullscreen Eddie Howe is the preferred choice of Manchester United’s director of football, Jason Wilcox. Photograph: Mike Egerton/PA

United would also have to pay Newcastle a minor sum for Howe’s staff, headed by his assistant, Jason Tindall.

Manchester United’s director of recruitment, Christopher Vivell, has been pushing the case of Julian Nagelsmann, the former Germany and Bayern Munich head coach.

Sports.title: Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph a glorious riposte to celebrity fawning of ceremony | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
Well, there’s something new. Football: now available in new, genuinely heartwarming flavour.

There was a lovely moment at London’s Palladium theatre on Monday, with the clock creeping towards 11pm at the end of a startlingly shrill and bloated evening of never‑ending awards and never-ending award‑related excitement.

Not just for Harry Kane, who is now the 2026 men’s Ballon d’Or winner, and in the process placed indelibly in that lineage of elite footballers. But also, frankly, for anyone watching, as Kane stood on stage gazing a little shyly at his golden orb, and kicked off his speech by thanking everyone, paying tribute to everyone, everywhere, then finally cracking into tears and a strangled croak as he thanked his parents for sacrifices made, his wife for always being there, and even, in slightly jarring vibe-shift from the warm honeyed tone, José Mourinho.

Even Kane’s biggest advocates will rarely claim their man is one of a kind, sui generis, in the mode of the Ronaldo-Messi godhead. But Kane is exactly this in his own admirably humble way.

Not just an exceptional footballer, the best, most deserving men’s player in the world this year, a European golden boot, scorer of 89 goals since August 2025, Bundesliga champion, World Cup semi-final captain, model of extreme professionalism and care. He’s also quite clearly the nicest man, if not just in football, then possibly the world.

Or at least it felt like that as he walked off in that very dear and tender way, the centre of the world in that moment, but also just keen to get off the stage and let everyone get on with clearing up.

It would be wrong to say Kane’s victory in the final vote of the night redeemed the grotesqueness of the ceremonies itself. There was a roomful of hugely deserving winners here. But Kane hits particularly hard.

View image in fullscreen Alexia Putellas and Harry Kane pose with their trophies at the end of the 2026 Ballon d’Or awards ceremony in London. Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA

And the Ballon d’Or is, let us be clear, a horrendous event, albeit a supremely popular horrendous event. There was the usual pomp around the ceremony, staged this year at a fancy theatre close to Oxford Circus.

This isn’t sport. It’s celebrity culture, red‑carpet fawning, the worship of images and people, and fame. Football isn’t supposed to be cocooned this way, to send the message that there are barriers and ropes and special people. Yeah, well, good luck with that.

The night kicked off with French Montana in spotless white tuxedo performing on an open-air double-decker bus. He definitely speaks, clearly, carried well, seemed enthusiastic. If it all goes south from here, the evidence suggests French Montana could, at the very least, get a job as a London tour bus operator.

View image in fullscreen French Montana performs during Ballon d’Or award ceremony in London. Photograph: Rasid Necati Aslim/Anadolu/Getty Images

Before long Thierry Henry and Kate Scott glided on stage, half an hour late, to add a little deft and easy charm to a furious schedule of pots and prizes.

And the awards came thick and fast. The Spain manager, Luis de la Fuente, was named coach of the year. “I hope in the future I will become in English better,” were his first words at the lectern, throwing his hat in the ring for a disastrous pension-padding six months at Manchester United two years from now.

There was a lovely moment as Burna Boy came on to present the Socrates award for charitable works to Bukayo Saka. He was asked if there were footballers who had inspired his love for the game. At which point he looked at Thierry and said, “definitely, one of them’s standing right there”, and of course he said it in his Burna Boy voice, looking Thierry deep in the eyes so smooth and deep, just almost an impossibly sexy moment.

The Ballon d’Or can be unintentionally hilarious at times such as these. There were just so, so many video tributes, so much excitingly portentous music. This is a stage where everyone happening at every moment is very clearly the most important thing ever to happen, superseded only by the next thing to happen on that stage, and then the thing after that.

View image in fullscreen The hosts of the ceremony: Kate Scott and Thierry Henry. Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/Reuters

The degree of fawning is startling at first, but glazed by familiarity before long. At one point Cristiano Ronaldo appeared very briefly in a fact-cut big-screen montage and the crowd shrieked a song, clutched its hand to its fevered throat, collapsed into the aisles in sheer priapic excitement.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Although by the time the original Ronaldo emerged onstage at 10.44pm, there was a sense of the genuinely vertiginous company Kane was about to join. Ronaldo read out the name inside the envelope, and the hall collapsed into cheers and yells and roars as Kane appeared onstage.

And yes the Ballon d’Or is a fundamentally silly thing on its own terms. It jars with the basic concept of team sport, promoting instead the opposite of sport, the opposite of team culture, the modern disease of fawning parasocial engagement with star names. In many ways the world would be a better place if the Ballon d’Or was simply abolished, as an example to all who pore over reels and clips and the imagined qualities of their celebrity paramours.

But it is also fascinating, unignorable, and endlessly moreish. All the more so this time. Kane as the Ballon d’Or 2026 is a genuinely fine, uplifting, instructive moment in the spotlight.

View image in fullscreen Bukayo Saka delivers his speech after accepting the Sócrates award from Burna Boy. Photograph: Jeff Spicer/Uefa/Getty Images

It is always tempting to talk about the journey these players make. Everyone has a backstory. Most footballers come from adversity. Kane has this, in his own way, 16 years into a professional career which has names such as Leyton Orient, Millwall, Leicester and Norwich on the timelines. He was unexceptional as a junior, didn’t stand out as particularly skilful or big or outstanding in his numbers. He played as a holding midfielder for a bit while Spurs decided what to do with him.

Kane worked relentlessly. He was Millwall young player of the year in 2012, fitting bookend to the Ballon. He made it because he simply refused to go away, to stop working, honed instead the deeper skills in his quiver, the purity of his shooting, the range of his passing long and short.

And Kane is exceptional in other ways. Without ever peacocking around promoting his brand, without really trying he remains the most likable, authentic, role‑model‑ish modern-day England player. For a man who never talks big or acts big he has a happy knack of becoming the key player wherever he goes. Perhaps Kane has become cool now. He has always been likable, with that mild-mannered air of a kindly Victorian chimney sweep with a hamster in his waistcoat watch pocket. In the Bayern years, Kane has become leaner, more glossed and handsome, jawline, tan, iconic Vampire hairline.

Mainly he expresses a common confusion about what talent really is. Talent isn’t simply moments. Talent is also application, focus, craft, the ability to work, to make others better.

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane celebrates after scoring a penalty against Paris Saint-Germain in last season’s Champions League. Photograph: Christophe Ena/AP

And yet his elite career has also been oddly grudging. Somehow the idea has always been out there that Kane is undeserving of these accolades, despite his own mildness and humility, his obvious team qualities, his relentless delivery of goals, effort, leadership. It is a genuinely odd conclusion given the opposite is so manifestly true, that this is an entirely uplifting story of overachievement, of hard work and applied intelligence, as opposed to the kind of talent that just needs to be flame‑throwered in the right direction.

It is undeniably true that Kane’s levels can drop dramatically when he can’t perform at his full physical capacity. There have been moments where it has been tempting to wonder if he’s gone far enough as England’s captain in the past few years, if his body and his talent deserve a little care.

Well, that just shows how wrong you can be.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Harry Kane completes his arc from Orient loanee to Ballon d’Or winner
Sports.content:
A WIN FOR HUMILITY AND NEAT HAIR

Perusing the records we could find of Leyton Orient’s 4-0 shellacking of Sheffield Wednesday on a cold January afternoon in 2011 at Brisbane Road, Football Daily could find little or no indication that the young tyro who scored the O’s second goal might one day be presented with the most prestigious individual gong in world football. On loan from Spurs, a whey-faced 17-year-old Harry Kane marked his first senior start with what the BBC described as “a neat finish”, stealing in at the far post to convert a Dean Cox free-kick. Even after a breakthrough 2014-15 season for Spurs that yielded 31 goals and earned him an England call-up, assorted experts predicted Harry would prove to be little more than a one-season wonder – a kind of footballing Chumbawamba but with better manners and neater hair. Eleven seasons later the immensely likable Bayern Munich striker continues to bang them in for club and country with such monotonous regularity that few were surprised to see him presented with the Ballon d’Or! Ballon d’Or!! Ballon d’Or!!! Ballon d’Or!!!! by the original and best Ronaldo live at the London Palladium. Not since the late Bruce Forsyth has any Englishman in an over-sized crushed velvet bow tie looked more at home on the famous old venue’s stage.

A footballer who has worked his socks off to maximise every ounce of his talent, Kane’s acceptance speech was extraordinarily long and a study in humility and gratitude. And while we can’t say for certain that Cox didn’t get a shout-out for the assist that set the goalscoring juggernaut in motion, the former Orient winger will have had every right to feel aggrieved if that was the case because just about everyone else who has appeared in Kane’s orbit since he was a Junior Gunner got a mention. When it came time to thanking his wife and parents, Kane’s voice wavered, albeit in far less comical style than that time shortly after the Mexico game when he was trying to explain what happened to Jordan Henderson in the post-match celebrations. At the end of a preposterously long awards bash high on pomp, ceremony and self-importance, Kane’s on-stage modesty was a welcome antidote to much of the bombast that had preceded it. “It sounds crazy, but it also sounds pretty good,” he whooped of his new status as Ballon d’Or winner. “What a special night. It’s an incredible, incredible feeling. I’m still just trying to take it all in. It really feels like a dream – the emotion, just relief, joy, happiness, excitement. To have that kind of release and then be able to share it with everyone there in the theatre was special.”

Presided over by Thierry Henry and Kate Scott, football gong-giving’s answer to Mick Fleetwood and Samantha Fox, Monday night’s ceremony didn’t go entirely without a hitch. Proceedings kicked off more than 30 minutes late, perhaps due to the fact the organisers hadn’t realised how long it would take the great and the good of the game to preen their way down the seemingly endless red carpet rolled out on Argyll Street. “Football unites the world” has long been the clarion call of Fifa overlord, Gianni Infantino, and for a while during the Ballon d’Or buildup there was no discernible difference between those posing on the Axminster in their glad rags and those shivering in their anoraks on the other side of nearby barriers. While few would begrudge Kane an accolade that is a bit naff but clearly means so much to him, like most empty vessels these naysayers tend to make a lot of noise. Online superfans of Kylian Mbappé and Lamine Yamal have been vocal in their disparagement of the voting process, while more than a few Arsenal fans appear to have got the hump because something-or-other about Declan Rice and David Raya. All concerned could learn a thing or two from the message Kane posted following his win: “Work hard in silence,” it read. “Let success be your noise.”

LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE

Join Niall McVeigh from 8pm GMT for hot Carling Cup fourth-round updates from Fleetwood Town 0-3 Arsenal.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“The players haven’t got a leg to stand on. What’s not fair is the performances they are giving. I looked at the fans, you could see the pain and anger in their faces when those players are walking around the football pitch. You see [Lisandro] Martínez when Rayan ran round him, they are not getting to the ball, it’s so frustrating. I could score a goal, had ability or whatever, at least I [effing] ran and put myself about as a team. These players are not doing that. I would love to go in that dressing room and say: ‘What the [eff] are you all doing? What type of performance do you think this is? Do you think you deserve to wear the shirt?’ Put [an effing] firework up their [ar$es] because they are not doing anything. It is at best a mid-table team, but if you look at all the mid-table teams, what do they get? They get players working hard, running and tackling. These players think they are better than what they are. You are deluded if they think the front three are good enough. They wanted Premier League players, they have brought lads from Wolves, Brentford, who have done well, but for signings to take this Manchester United team to the next level, you are living in cuckoo land if you think they are going to achieve that” – Wayne Rooney calmly explains the ongoing situation at Manchester United.

View image in fullscreen Wayne Rooney, playing for United in 2006, after scoring a goal, having ability or whatever. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

double quotation mark Re: yesterday’s Football Daily. OK, so it may not be that contemporary, but Omar Berrada’s name fits into a jaunty song I came up with when bored, to the tune of Escape (the Piña Colada song) by Rupert Holmes: ‘If your name’s Omar Berrada / Head should be hangin’ in shame / If you’re supportin’ the Glazers / You’ve only got half a brain / If Jason Wilcox hasn’t done one / When he is mostly to blame / Then we’re the fans that you’ve stuffed / How do we stop the pain?’ I’m not even a United fan, but they’re all welcome – Simon Mazie.

double quotation mark I would happily take the Manchester United job, as it’s a surefire way to earn three years’ pay in six months – Alex Lester.

double quotation mark Now the shambles at United is even clearer, might Bryan Mbeumo be wishing he had chosen Spurs instead? – Richard Fernandez.

double quotation mark About Jonathan Chester-le-Street’s excellent idea to nominate Noble Francis for the Fifa presidency (yesterday’s Football Daily letters). I back that nomination and look forward to his first act in office: the creation of a Noble prize, awarded to himself obviously – Peter Oh.

Sports.title: Alexia Putellas a worthy Ballon d’Or winner but the limited shortlist illustrates flaws
Sports.content:
After a four-year wait, Alexia Putellas is the queen of women’s football once again. Receiving the Ballon d’Or for a record‑equalling third time to continue Spain’s domination of the award, the 32-year-old reinforces her status as one of the greatest players of all time.

It was the sixth consecutive year in which the honour went to either Putellas or her international teammate Aitana Bonmatí, and it was symbolic of Putellas’s resurgence after her comeback from the anterior cruciate ligament injury she sustained in 2022, her refusal to surrender her career to that setback, and her majestic rise back to the top.

The midfielder’s competition‑leading 14 goal contributions – eight goals and six assists – in 11 Women’s Champions League appearances last season, helping Barcelona to lift the trophy, went a long way to her securing the most votes, as well as her starring role in Spain’s victory in the Nations League finals last December. Her new club, London City Lionesses, will rejoice in the prestige of having the Ballon d’Or winner in their squad but Putellas, who spent 14 years at Barcelona, made it clear whom she wanted to thank. As she said in her acceptance speech: “This prize is for Barcelona.”

Barcelona collected a clean sweep of the night’s bigger awards, with Cata Coll taking the goalkeeper prize, Pere Romeu the coach award and Vicky López the young player award, as well as Ewa Pajor finishing second behind Putellas for the main honour and Clara Serrajordi finishing second in the young player vote. It was almost a perfect night for the European champions, until their president, Joan Laporta, spoke bizarrely about his belief that their men’s team could win the Champions League this season, appearing to have eyes only for the men’s game despite specifically accepting the award for the women’s club of the year.

That slip aside, the glamorous ceremony at the London Palladium on Monday night passed without the sexist controversy that tarnished the early years after France Football belatedly added the women’s award for the first time in 2018. Progress has been made – the women’s game does now at least receive a prize for the same categories as the men, but the event still does not quite offer full equality. Specifically, there is still not quite parity in the lengths of shortlists. Why, for example, were 10 players nominated for the men’s young talent award, but only five for the women’s? It was the same for the goalkeeper awards.

The live show also demonstrated a disappointing lack of women’s players presenting prizes, aside from Lucy Bronze who was on stage to hand López her prize. Putellas receiving the Ballon d’Or Féminin from Michael Owen – rather than, perhaps Mia Hamm, Birgit Prinz or Sun Wen – perhaps served as a reminder that there are very few former winners of the women’s prize for the organisers to choose from – only Ada Hegerberg, Megan Rapinoe, Putellas and Bonmatí – because it was introduced so late.

View image in fullscreen Vicky López speaks after winning the young player award. Photograph: Kin Cheung/AP

Many fans will also have felt it was a shame that the dates covered by the relevant voting period – 3 August 2025 to 19 July 2026, effectively for last season – were based clearly on the conclusion of the men’s World Cup this summer, and therefore did not include this year’s rearranged Wafcon, which was held from 26 July to 16 August. Performances at that tournament will instead be taken into account for next year’s prizes. It meant, for example, that Cameroon’s Wafcon‑winning head coach, Valentine Nguele, was not nominated for the coach of the year award, and there was an overall dearth of African players recognised, aside from Temwa Chawinga becoming the first African player to finish in the women’s top 10. Arguably she deserved to be even higher.

Putellas was a very worthy winner of the main prize, although some will feel it is a missed opportunity for a player from one of the countries less likely to succeed in major international competitions to be recognised, given that the Women’s World Cup next year will inevitably ensure that the annual awards nights focus on whatever happens in Brazil. Poland’s Pajor, for example, finished second after a tremendous campaign with Barcelona but she feels unlikely to go one better next year, simply because of her nationality.

The same goes for Jamaica’s Khadija Shaw, who came third after firing Manchester City to their first domestic title in a decade – although the fact that she made the top three in spite of not playing Champions League football said a lot about how revered she is. Haiti’s Melchie Dumornay – the best player Moving the Goalposts had the pleasure of seeing play live in the 2025-26 season – finished fourth. Aged 23, her time may well come in the future, but it is most likely to be in an even-numbered year.

If Putellas continues her form, it would take a brave person to bet against her retaining her crown next year, as Spain target a successful defence of the world title. A humble role model for the sport, it is a privilege watching her grace the pitch with her deft touches, leadership and creativity and being a three-time Ballon d’Or winner is no less than her storied career deserves.
