World.title: ‘Some get less’: Grant recipient demands answers over SASSA payments
World.content:
A SASSA grant recipient is demanding to know why some beneficiaries are not receiving their money while others are getting less than expected.

Maggie Cloete raised the question in the comments section on The South African’s Facebook page, describing the situation as a disgrace.

“So, disgraceful, some get less,” she wrote.



Not everyone paid on the same day

Part of the answer may lie in SASSA’s review process. SASSA said payments for beneficiaries whose grants are under review will be made on 5 November.

That date sits apart from the main schedule, under which the Older Persons Grant is paid on Friday, 30 October 2026, the Disability Grant on Monday, 02 November 2026, and Children’s Grants on Tuesday, 03 November 2026.

SASSA has urged beneficiaries undergoing reviews to respond to official communication and attend appointments when requested.

Amounts differ by grant type

Different payments may also reflect different grant categories. Older persons and disability grants are both set at R2 400, while the war veterans grant comes in slightly higher at R2 420. The foster child grant sits at R1 300, and child support and grant-in-aid recipients each receive R580.

For Cloete, though, even the full amount falls short.

“We can’t do with R 2400 rand,” she wrote.



Food and electricity squeeze

Cloete said rising costs leave little room in the monthly budget.

“We can’t even afford to buy enough food,” she wrote.

SASSA advises beneficiaries to keep their bank details current and active ahead of each payment cycle, as outdated information can delay payments. Beneficiaries who have not been paid are encouraged to check whether their grant is under review before visiting an office.

Win R2 000 in the South African SASSA grant survey

If you receive a SASSA grant and want to share your story, we want to hear from you.

Take part in our survey and stand a chance to win R2 000. Your responses help us tell the stories that matter.

World.title: Heavy downpours, strong winds plunge parts of Eastern Cape in darkness
World.content:
KUGOMPO CITY- Various areas in the Eastern Cape have been plunged into darkness after heavy downpours that have lashed through the province.

Areas affected include Alfred Nzo, O.R. Tambo, Amathole, Chris Hani District Municipalities and Buffalo City Metropolitan Municipality.

Eskom confirmed that it is attending to the widespread electricity supply interruptions.

“The adverse weather conditions have resulted in damage to electricity infrastructure, including damaged poles, broken conductors and other network components. “In some areas, difficult road and weather conditions are also hampering access to affected infrastructure and slowing restoration efforts,” the power utility said in a statement.

Because of the extent of damage and the continued adverse weather conditions, Eskom said restoration times may vary from one area to another.

In the meantime, residents have been urged to exercise caution, including staying away from damaged or fallen electricity infrastructure.

“Customers in affected areas are urged to remain patient while Eskom teams continue with repairs.

Safety remains Eskom’s priority.”

World.title: Number of the Day | 5 | 27 October 2026
World.content:
South Africa's Investment Problem Is Bigger Than A Ranking

Morocco's rise in an African investment index raises a difficult question: can South Africa turn its considerable economic advantages into the conditions businesses need to grow?

South Africa has spent decades presenting itself as a natural entry point for investors seeking access to African markets. It has sophisticated financial institutions, established industrial capacity and deep connections to international trade. Yet those advantages are becoming less decisive as other countries build the infrastructure, manufacturing industries and export networks needed to compete for investment.

The latest warning comes from Rand Merchant Bank's Where to Invest in Africa ranking, released on 27 October 2026. Morocco has overtaken South Africa to claim fourth place, pushing the continent's largest economy into fifth. Seychelles, Mauritius

and Egypt retain the top three positions. The ranking covers 31 African countries and considers 20 indicators spanning economic performance, investment conditions, market accessibility and human development.

It is important to understand what the index measures. Fifth place does not mean South Africa receives the fifth-largest amount of foreign investment on the continent. Rather, it reflects a comparative assessment of the conditions that make countries attractive to investors. That distinction matters because the ranking is less a verdict on investment already secured than a warning about future competitiveness.

Manufacturing changes the competition

Morocco's advantage has not emerged overnight. RMB attributes its improvement to sustained industrialisation, export diversification, infrastructure investment and macroeconomic stability. Automotive manufacturing is a particularly important example: a country that builds a strong production base does more than attract a factory. It creates opportunities for suppliers, logistics companies, technical workers and related industries.

Those networks can become increasingly valuable over time. Once manufacturers have established supply arrangements, trained workers and reliable export routes, moving production elsewhere may be costly. An investment destination can therefore develop advantages that are difficult for competitors to dislodge.

South Africa understands this model. Major global automotive manufacturers already operate in the country, supported by an established industrial ecosystem. But an existing manufacturing base does not guarantee future expansion. Investors considering where to place their next production line will also examine whether electricity is dependable, freight can move efficiently and public services can support operations.

The growth figures illustrate the competitive pressure. Morocco's economy expanded by 4.9% in 2025, compared with South Africa's 1.1%, according to the figures cited in the latest reporting. These percentages alone do not establish which economy offers the better investment opportunity: countries differ in size, structure and starting point. They do, however, underline the challenge facing an economy seeking to generate jobs and expand its industrial capacity while growing slowly.

The hidden cost of unreliable systems

Investment competitiveness is often discussed in terms of tax incentives, labour costs and market size. Yet the more immediate question for many businesses is whether they can operate predictably. A manufacturer needs electricity to run machinery, water for industrial processes and transport systems that deliver goods on schedule. Interruptions impose costs that can erode the advantages of an otherwise attractive location.

South Africa has made progress in addressing electricity constraints, but weaknesses in freight logistics and municipal services remain important concerns. These are not separate from industrial policy. A factory expansion, for example, depends on the performance of infrastructure and public institutions well beyond the factory gate.

Skills also form part of that equation. The ability to develop higher-value manufacturing and adapt to technological change depends on education, training and a workforce equipped for new production methods. Investment attraction is therefore connected to decisions made in classrooms, municipalities, transport networks and government departments.

A warning, not a verdict

Nigeria offers another perspective. It climbed seven places to eleventh in the latest ranking, with RMB pointing to changes including fuel-subsidy removal, foreign-exchange reforms and statistical improvements. Its rise does not mean every reform has been painless or that its economic challenges have disappeared. It does suggest that the investment landscape is responsive to changes in policy and economic conditions.

South Africa's fall to fifth is not evidence that its industrial and financial strengths have vanished. The more consequential risk is that those strengths become less valuable if competing economies translate reforms and infrastructure spending into faster-growing productive industries.

The challenge is not simply to return to fourth place in a ranking. It is to build an economy in which companies can invest, manufacture, export and hire with greater confidence. If South Africa achieves that, a stronger ranking could follow. If it does not, the country may discover that the most expensive part of losing ground is how difficult it becomes to recover.

References

· Rand Merchant Bank, Where to Invest in Africa; methodology and investment-attractiveness framework.

· Bloomberg, “Morocco tops South Africa in RMB continental investment ranking”, 27 October 2026, also carried by Polity.

· Number of the Day, 27 October 2026; Gareth Edwards and Francis Herd's discussion of manufacturing, infrastructure and investment competitiveness.

World.title: India orders evacuations as Cyclone Arnab looms
World.content:
NEW DELHI - Indian authorities ordered nearly 100,000 people to evacuate homes in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, ahead of a severe cyclone the national weather office expects to make landfall by Wednesday.

Neighbouring Nepal and Sri Lanka have also issued weather warnings.

Cyclone Arnab is forecast to hit India's southwestern Andhra Pradesh coast as a "very severe cyclonic storm", with gusts of up to 150 kilometres (93 miles) per hour on Wednesday morning at 6:00 am GMT (11.30 am Indian Standard Time), the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said in a bulletin.

Torrential rain lashed the coast in the port city of Kakinda as heavy waves crashed on shore.

"I've never seen anything like this before," Kotesh Kumar, 35, told AFP, adding the government warned people to stock up on groceries.

"There was a cyclone here three years ago, but the water didn't rise this much."

Cyclones, called hurricanes in the North Atlantic and typhoons in the Pacific, are a regular menace in the Bay of Bengal and northern Indian Ocean.

The storm season, however, has been turbocharged by the El Nino weather phenomenon that has caused unprecedented warming.

Neighbouring Sri Lanka, meanwhile, closed schools with warnings of torrential rain, with the island's Department of Meteorology warning storms could trigger flash floods and mudslides.

The military has been placed on alert, Colombo's Disaster Management Centre said.

Indian media reported that as many as 50,000 people have been told to move to safe areas in Andhra Pradesh, and 48,000 in Odisha.

'Damage'

Nepal's disaster authority issued a warning on Tuesday, saying that as the storm travels inland towards the Himalayas -- likely overnight Thursday -- it will bring heavy rainfall as well as "a high risk of heavy snowfall, snowstorms and avalanches".

It called on tourists to avoid travelling to high mountain areas and advised those already there to remain in safe locations.

Nepal is still recovering from a catastrophic August 26 flood sparked by a glacial mountain collapse, which swept away more than 1,400 people and left over 5,000 missing.

India's weather bureau said it expects the cyclone to result in "total destruction" of thatched houses and create localised flooding, uprooting of power and communication poles, and "widespread damage" to standing crops.

In Kakinada, police barricaded roads leading to the sea.

Andhra Pradesh State Chief Minister Nara Chandrababu Naidu ordered the storm to be "constantly monitored and advance precautions taken", his office said in a statement on Monday.

"Adequate shelters and evacuation arrangements have been made," New Delhi's Cabinet Secretariat said in a statement.

The neighbouring Indian state of Odisha opened 1,735 cyclone shelters and imposed restrictions on movement in landslide-prone zone areas, the state's information office said.

Local media reported that Andhra Pradesh authorities ordered evacuations in key, low-lying areas and shut "all educational institutions" in some districts from Tuesday until Saturday.

Over 4,700 pregnant women residing in potentially dangerous sites were moved to hospitals, according to The Indian Express newspaper.

World.title: 'There is no water contamination' - Joburg Water warns against fake reports
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Johannesburg Water has dismissed reports of water contamination in the city as fake news.

The water utility spokesperson, Nombuso Shabalala, insists there are no confirmed water contamination incidents affecting Johannesburg and urged residents to stop sharing these messages, as they create ‘unnecessary worry and confusion’.

As such, she has referred residents to the water utilities' official communication channels for any information.

“Water quality concerns reported in a particular area should not be interpreted as affecting the entire city. Any precautionary water quality advisory issued by Johannesburg Water applies to the specific areas identified in that notice. “Customers in those areas should continue following the guidance provided until the advisory is officially lifted,” she said.

Shabalala has also urged residents to report any concerns about changes to water quality, including unusual colour or smell.

These issues, she said, will then be attended to with tests through accredited laboratory processes.

World.title: Water woes | Stomach complaints disrupt learning in Bronkhorstspruit crèche
World.content:
PRETORIA - More than 115 children from a creche in Zithobeni, Bronkhorstspruit, have reportedly fallen ill with a stomach bug.

There are claims by the school that it could be linked to untreated drinking water.

The principal of Themebalethu Place of Care claims that the incident has left parents fearful, with many now questioning whether water supplied by water tankers is safe to consume.

Their fears were heightened further following Deputy President Paul Mashatile's visit to Bronkhorstspruit on Monday.

READ | Bronkhorstspruit Treatment Water Plant temporarily shut down

The visit followed reports of gastrointestinal illness linked to contaminated water in the area.

During a media briefing, Mashatile raised concerns about the source of water supplied by some private tanker operators.

Currently, the City of Tshwane has deployed 36 water tankers to help restore access to safe water in Bronkhorstspruit.

READ | Govt raises concern over unregulated water tankers

But government has noted the emergence of private tanker operators, with Mashatile saying there will be intervention to follow up on those water tankers.

Tshwane Mayor Nasiphi Moya said the Tshwane Metro Police Department has received all registration numbers to follow up on the water tankers around to ensure they know where they source the water and who has tested it.

World.title: Ramaphosa approves deployment of SANDF troops to KZN
World.content:
DURBAN - President Cyril Ramaphosa has approved the deployment of 510 South African National Defence Force (SANDF) soldiers to KwaZulu-Natal to assist police with law enforcement operations under Operation Prosper until the end of November.

The deployment, announced just days before the local government elections, is expected to cost more than R34 million.

The move comes amid growing concerns over the safety of refugees and foreign nationals in the province, following a series of protests and violent incidents targeting alleged undocumented foreigners.

READ | Foreign national beaten to death in Durban CBD

Authorities have also raised concerns about a campaign of misinformation surrounding a Constitutional Court judgment on the Refugees Act.

Last week, a crowd of approximately 50 people reportedly murdered a foreign national in Durban.

Earlier this month, protests against illegal immigration brought parts of the city to a standstill, raising further concerns about public safety and social stability.

World.title: Not so fast! Court blocks Bomas expansion
World.content:
Contractors hired are barred from clearing vegetation, cutting trees, excavating, grading, fencing, constructing routes, and undertaking any works at the disputed site. [File, Standard]

The Environment and Lands Court has blocked the government from continuing with the construction of a car park inside the Nairobi National Park.

Justice Grace Kemei, in her ruling, said that the contractors hired are barred from clearing vegetation, cutting trees, excavating, grading, fencing, constructing routes, and undertaking any works at the disputed site.

World.title: Kikuyu PCEA church loses 2.7-acre illegally acquired land
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Justice Jacqueline Mogeni, in her verdict, said the land in contention was public property and its registration in the name of the said church was irregular and fraudulent. [Courtesy, EACC]

The Presbyterian Church of East Africa (PCEA) has lost its 2.7-acre piece of land to a school.

This is after the Environment and Lands Court at Thika established that the land under the church's Ruguthi Women's Guild was a school playground and was illegally allocated.

Presiding Judge Jacqueline Mogeni, in her verdict, said the land in contention was public property, and its registration in the name of the said church was irregular and fraudulent.

According to her, the land had been reserved for use as a playground by Kanyiha, Lusigetti and Njumbi Primary Schools.

The verdict follows a case filed by the Law Society of Kenya, with the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) participating as an interested party.

In a statement on Monday, EACC's head of Corporate Affairs and Communication Stephen Karuga said the anti-graft agency presented evidence demonstrating that the land had been reserved for public use and therefore, any allocation to third parties was irregular. Justice Jacqueline Mogeni, in her verdict, said the land in contention was public property and its registration in the name of the said church was irregular and fraudulent. [Courtesy, EACC]

"Our investigations established that the land was set aside in 1957 by the former County Council of Kiambu for use as a school playing field," Karuga said, adding, "the investigations further revealed that there was no letter of offer or acceptance, no evidence of payment of rent rates and no proof that the Women's Guild had paid any consideration to the council for the land."

According to Karuga, the judgement safeguards a vital public facility used by more than 1,300 pupils, ensuring that the playground remains available for learning, sports and recreation for the current and future generations.

As a result, the judge said the allocation, transfer and registration of the land LR. NO KARAI/350 and subsequent issuance of a title deed in 2001 was unprocedural, illegal, null and void.

"An order of Mandamus is hereby issued directing the 3rd respondent, the Land Registrar, Kiambu Chief Land Registrar, to forthwith cancel and revoke the Title Deed and all register entries in respect of the land issued to the 1st respondent on Dec 6, 2001, or at any subsequent date," the Judge said.

The judge further ordered that the said parcel of land be handed over to the Board of Management of the two schools and the Education Ministry.

"An order of permanent injunction is hereby issued restraining the 1st respondent, whether by herself, her church officials, agents, servants, assigns or anyone claiming through her, from entering into, taking possession of, fencing, depositing construction materials upon, transferring, charging, developing or in any other manner dealing or interfering with the land," she ordered.

World.title: Sakaja protests release of 14 suspects linked to Eastleigh collapsed building
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Sakaja demanded answers from Kamukunji Police on how the suspects were arrested in June but released on Sh50,000 bail without being charged in court. [GPS]

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has protested the release of suspects linked to the collapsed building in Eastleigh.

While pushing for the county to have prosecutorial powers, Sakaja demanded answers from Kamukunji Police on how the suspects were arrested in June but released on Sh50,000 bail without being charged in court.

Sakaja in statement posted on his X account (formerly Twitter) said City Hall had taken enforcement action against those involved after establishing change of user from a residential property to a commercial had been approved.

According to Sakaja, architectural plans required to authorise construction had not been approved.

The Governor said County officers arrested the suspects and handed them over to Kamukunji Police Station because county governments no longer hold prosecutorial powers they previously held.

“We enforced the law and arrested those involved. However, because we do not have prosecutorial powers, the suspects were handed over to Kamukunji Police Station. They were reportedly released on a cash bail of Sh50,000 without being taken to court,” Sakaja said.

“We want the police to explain why the suspects were released without being presented in court and why construction was allowed to continue. These are serious questions that must be answered,” he added.

A police occurrence book entry from Kamukunji Police Station indicates that 14 suspects were booked into custody on June 17, 2026, over the alleged offences relating to contravention of city planning laws.

Enforcement action and arrests were made severally by the county officials and most recently in July after failing to comply with the enforcement order below. However the suspects were released on a 50k bail at Kamukunji police on the very same day. Prosecution of the same was also denied. We have repeatedly asked for the resumption of the power to prosecute such violations of such county and county related laws after this was taken away from County governments in 2024 (one such letter to the office of the DPP is attached). Meanwhile, several such cases have either been rejected by prosecutors (who are independent of the County), dismissed by the justice system or have had minimal fines imposed. Fining a developer 50k for an illegal development with hundreds of millions without orders to stop and remove the offensive development is completely unreasonable. I raised this in the Senate a fortnight ago and we shall keep pushing for a review of this position. All of these instances, where enforcement action has been curtailed, blocked or interfered with, will be published to the public. October 25, 2026

The entry, recorded under OB No. 98/17/06/2026, names the suspects and states that they were booked by Nairobi City County officers before being placed in police cells.

A separate Kenya Police Service record indicates that 10 suspects were subsequently released on a cash bail of Sh50,000.

The entry, recorded at 9.44pm, states that the release was carried out on the instructions of the Officer Commanding Station (OCS), identified in the record as C.I. Onyapidi, through Corporal Awadh.

The record references receipt number 2039434 and states that the suspects left the station without complaints.

However, the documents do not, on their own, establish the specific charges against the suspects, the legal basis for the bail arrangement or whether they were subsequently presented in court.

The discrepancy between the 14 suspects recorded as booked into custody and the 10 named in the release entry also raises questions about the subsequent status of the other suspects. Sakaja demanded answers from Kamukunji Police on how the suspects were arrested in June but released on Sh50,000 bail without being charged in court. [GPS]

Sakaja said a June 2025 enforcement notice adds another dimension to the questions surrounding the property and the enforcement of planning regulations.

The notice, issued by Nairobi City County over alleged construction works undertaken without the required development permission, cited the Physical and Land Use Planning Act, 2019, and county by-laws.

It directed the recipient to stop the works and remove the development described as illegal, warning that the County could undertake the required action and recover the costs if the directives were not followed.

The notice also provided for an appeal to the County Physical and Land Use Planning Liaison Committee.

Sakaja clarified that approval to change a property’s use from private to commercial-cum-residential does not amount to approval of architectural plans authorising construction.

He said the County approved the change of use but did not approve the architectural plans, yet construction proceeded.

I have seen some people peddling a fake approval document alleging that the Eastleigh development was approved. It is telling that this is the same document that the Eastleigh developer used to get NCA approval. They allege that the development was approved in January of 2024. This is not true. The application for development as shown below was made in November of 2024, it could not have been approved in February of the same year. Also, there is a difference between a change of user approval and a development approval. The developer applied for change of use from residential to residential & commercial in August of 2024. Change of user was approved in October of 2024. Development approval has never been granted. The developer went on to build with impunity and without building approvals despite enforcement action by the county and arrests. — Sakaja Arthur Johnson (@SakajaJohnson) October 25, 2026

“If the building had been approved for construction, I would have named the officers who approved it so that action could be taken against them,” he said.

Sakaja, in his argument, said the current arrangement creates a gap between enforcement and prosecution, leaving counties dependent on other agencies after taking action against alleged offenders. Sakaja demanded answers from Kamukunji Police on how the suspects were arrested in June but released on Sh50,000 bail without being charged in court. [GPS]

Under his proposal, appropriately authorised county prosecutors would be able to pursue qualifying county offences through the courts, subject to the law and the constitutional authority of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

He said county prosecutors previously had a better understanding of technical offences involving planning, construction and other county regulations, enabling them to handle such cases more directly.

“We want to be able not only to enforce regulations and make arrests, but also to take offenders to court and prosecute them. When counties had prosecutorial powers, we had prosecutors who understood the nature and seriousness of county offences and could ensure that appropriate legal action was taken,” he said.

World.title: Pregnant woman rescued from collapsed Eastleigh building
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kenya Red Cross workers after rescuing a man who trapped in the rubble.

A pregnant woman was on Saturday evening rescued from the multi-storey building that collapsed in Nairobi’s Eastleigh estate on Friday, October 23 and rushed to the Kenyatta National Hospital (KNH) for treatment.

She is the second person to rescued as earlier in the afternoon the Kenya Red Cross society announced the rescue of a man from the ill-fated building.

The man was also taken to KNH for treatment with the society saying that the rescue followed hours of work put in by the search and rescue multi-agency team.

“After hours of painstaking work alongside multi-agency partners, our search and rescue teams in Eastleigh brought a trapped man out of the rubble,” said Red Cross.

The rescue comes even as the fate of six people who were reported missing on Friuday remains unknown with rescue teams still continuing with the search at the site of the collapsed building along Yusuf Haji Avenue.

The society said that 66 of the 67 construction workers who were at the site had been traced and accounted for but the search continues for people who may have been near the site of the collapsed building.

The development comes as police announced that they had launched a manhunt for the for the owner and contractor of a building.

Police spokesperson Muchiri Nyaga said that officers had launched a probe in collaboration with relevant bodies to establish the cause of the collapse and determine criminal liability.

“Any individual or entity found culpable of negligence or of violating building regulations will face the full force of the law,” he said in a statement.

Nyaga called on members of public to stay completely clear of Yusuf Haji Avenue and 9th Street to give access to heavy excavators, specialised canine units and rescue personnel to perform their duties.

Earlier Saturday, at least 31 families reported their relatives missing as coordinated rescue efforts entered their second day.

No deaths have been reported so far.

The National Construction Authority (NCA) on Friday evening identified the developer, contractor, architect and structural engineer listed for the collapsed building.

The Authority has faced scrutiny over its oversight role, as Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja said the project had failed to comply with construction guidelines.

He said the county had forwarded relevant information to the Directorate of Criminal Investigations for further investigation.

In a statement, the NCA said the building was registered on July 30, 2025, as a proposed development on 9th Street in Eastleigh.

It identified 9th Street Plaza Limited as the developer and Stromax Holdings E.A. Limited as the contractor.

Emmanuel Mwangi Maina was listed as the project architect, while Joseph Muturi Mugu was named as the structural engineer.

World.title: Several feared trapped in Eastleigh building collapse
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Rescue efforts at the collapsed storey building in Eastleigh 9th street in Nairobi County. [Benard Orwongo Standard]

What was supposed to be a usually busy Friday afternoon in Eastleigh's 9th Street turned chaotic after an 18-floor building that was under construction came down, tumbling.

By Friday evening, rescue operations were still ongoing, with cries from people believed to have been trapped being heard from a distance as bulldozers and rescuers continued the search operation.

Two victims, a man and a woman, who were injured in the building had been rescued and rushed to hospital as the search continued.

Asha Jilo, one of the witnesses, said the building collapsed around 1:09 pm just after the afternoon prayers.

"Immediately after the building collapsed, we started contacting some people we know who work there, one of them was still available on the phone until around 3 pm, when his phone went offline," Jilo shared

On Fridays, Eastleigh is usually a hive of activities, being the main market day, but all the businesses were shut as police were battling rowdy youths, some of them believed to be opportunists.

The building, whose height was said to be about 15 floors, had not been cleared for occupation as required, raising questions about why the investors had allowed it to be taken.

It is said that the ground and first floors were already occupied by businesses, raising fears that the number of victims could be high. Rescue efforts at the collapsed storey building in Eastleigh 9th street in Nairobi County. [Benard Orwongo Standard]

At the time of the collapse, it is said that some construction workers were busy on the upper floors.

Governor Johnson Sakaja, who visited the scene after the collapse, was still gathering information about the building. The first priority was about saving lives.

“The building that collapsed is around 16 floors, and we have got information about the building, but what is more concerned right now is for us to save lives,” said Sakaja

Adding, “Equipment has already been mobilized, excavators and breakers, so we can be able to remove the big debris and save lives,’

The Governor said some developers engage qualified professionals to secure construction approvals before dismissing them and disregarding approved plans and safety standards.

He urged professional bodies to strengthen oversight, investigate such cases and take appropriate disciplinary action, stressing that developers must comply with approved designs, engage qualified personnel and obtain occupation certificates after safety inspections.

Rescue efforts at the collapsed storey building in Eastleigh 9th street in Nairobi County. [Benard Orwongo Standard]

Nairobi Regional Police Commander Issa Mohamud, who was at the scene, said that, according to reliable information, several people were trapped inside the debris, inside the big boulders, and the rescue effort is ongoing.

The city police boss said investigations will be carried out to ascertain who is responsible for any negligence.

“If there will be any death, that is negligence by murder. Whoever is the owner, whoever authorized the building, all of them will be charged properly. But that will come after thorough investigation is done,” he warned

Adding, “We will not excuse anybody on this matter. This has become now and then, and we will make sure that people face the law accordingly for any criminal negligence,”

World.title: Ruto hands over COMESA chairmanship, pushes for levy to fund regional programmes
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President Ruto and Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa during the handover of the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa chairmanship at the bloc’s 25th Summit of Heads of State and Government in Harare, Zimbabwe, on Thursday, October 22, 2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto has handed over the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) chairmanship to Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa.

Ruto took over the one-year chairmanship from Burundi’s President Évariste Ndayishimiye at the 24th COMESA Summit in Nairobi on October 9, 2025.

His tenure focused on using digital technology to deepen regional integration, expand trade and promote inclusive growth.

He handed over the role on Thursday, October 22, during the 25th Comesa Summit of Heads of State and Government in Harare, Zimbabwe, where he urged the regional bloc to fast-track a market levy to finance its programmes and institutions.

“We cannot be ambitious in our plans and timid in our financing. Every programme we agree upon must be matched by the resources to deliver it. Otherwise, our communiqués will promise what our budgets cannot pay for,” Ruto said.

He urged the Comesa Secretariat to fast-track Article 168 of the COMESA Treaty, which provides for the Comesa Market Levy, as the organisation seeks sustainable and predictable financing.

The treaty establishes the levy to generate resources for financing the bloc’s activities.

Ruto said officials from finance ministries, central banks and other relevant agencies would meet to consider a draft COMESA Resource Mobilisation Strategy aimed at strengthening member states’ ownership of regional programmes and finding new ways to raise funds.

He called on member states to make financing central to their discussions, warning that the bloc’s institutions and integration agenda would depend on their ability to fund agreed commitments.

“Can we finance what we commit, and deliver what we finance?” he asked.

Ruto also urged African countries to channel more of their domestic financial resources into African institutions rather than leaving funds in foreign accounts while development projects lack capital.

He said Africa holds more than $4 trillion in domestic financial assets, arguing that regional financial institutions could mobilise more of these resources to support trade, infrastructure and development.

Ruto named the Trade and Development Bank (TDB), the African Trade and Investment Development Insurance (ATIDI) and ZEP-RE among the institutions that could mobilise capital for regional priorities.

He urged African governments to place more reserves with these institutions, finance more projects through them and support their bonds and guarantees.

The outgoing Comesa chairperson said the bloc needed stronger regional value chains and more trade among member states as global supply chains faced disruption and protectionism returned.

“Regional integration is no longer a dream we discuss. It is an economic and strategic necessity,” he noted.

Ruto said Comesa’s economic growth rose from 5.6 per cent in 2024 to 6.4 per cent in 2025, while inflation fell from 31 per cent to 13.2 per cent.

Exports among member states increased by 10.5 per cent to $14.7 billion, their highest level between 2020 and 2025, while exports to global markets rose by 6 per cent to $212 billion, he said.

He argued that African countries needed to process more raw materials locally instead of exporting them and importing finished products.

“To every partner who seeks our minerals, our markets and our young workforce, our offer is clear: invest with us, process with us, build with us,” Ruto added.

He called for partnerships based on mutual benefit and equal treatment, saying African countries should have a greater role in determining how their resources and markets contribute to economic development.

World.title: Judge certifies fresh bid to jail Sakaja, Charles Kerich over Sh76.7m debt as urgent
World.content:
Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja. [File, Standard]

The High Court has certified as urgent a fresh application seeking to have Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja, former Finance Executive Charles Kerich and two other county officials jailed over an alleged breach of a court-approved payment plan in a Sh106.7 million legal fees dispute.

Justice Francis Gikonyo certified the application by Kwengu & Company Advocates seeking to reinstate a three-month jail sentence previously imposed on Kerich and hold Sakaja, current Finance County Executive Committee Member Ibrahim Auma Nyangoya and Chief Officer for Finance Asha Abdi accountable for the alleged failure to pay Sh76.7 million.

World.title: Kenya confirms third Ebola case
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kenya has confirmed a third case of Ebola involving a 65-year-old woman who is a close relative of the first two patients.

The Ministry of Health, in a statement, said the woman developed a fever, sore throat and malaise while in quarantine, prompting her isolation and testing.

Her samples tested positive for Ebola at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI).

According to the Health Director-General Patrick Amoth, the patient has been transferred to an infectious disease unit, where she is receiving supportive care and being monitored.

“Having been in quarantine, she was diagnosed early and is currently receiving supportive care, improving her chances of recovery while limiting the risk of further spread of the disease,” the statement read.

The second patient, on the other hand, is in stable condition and responding well to supportive care.

The latest case brings the number of confirmed Ebola infections in Kenya to three.

According to the Ministry, of the 130 contacts identified so far, 127 had been traced and placed in quarantine, with efforts ongoing to trace the remaining three.

World.title: Anthropic’s nearly 100-page list of business risks includes everything from bioweapons to AI blackmail
World.content:
Anthropic filed for an initial public offering Monday in what could become one of the largest stock market debuts in history — detailing its surging business growth, along with a vast multitude of warnings about how it could all go wrong.

Anthropic’s filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission sets the stage for the company to go public and begin trading on the stock market as soon as November 16. The IPO could reportedly value the company at up to $2 trillion, which would make it one of the largest public companies in the world.

The company’s stock will trade under the ticker ANT and will be listed on the Nasdaq exchange.

The San Francisco-based company did not disclose how many shares it intends to sell nor at what price. That information will be determined in the coming weeks ahead of the stock market debut.

In the filing, Anthropic’s founders penned a letter to potential shareholders laying out their vision for the value of AI, while also disclosing what they see as the major risks for the business. Those risks include everything from competition from other AI labs to “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

The IPO filing offers insight into how Anthropic views the future of its business despite those concerns and uncertainties.

Anthropic’s revenue grew 1,300 percent year-on-year in the first six months of 2026, to $16.3 billion. The company’s business is largely dependent on companies using its Claude AI system. Anthropic said it has more than 14,000 enterprise customers, with approximately 250 of those contributing $10 million or more in annual revenue.

But the company reported an overall net loss of over $80 billion, according to the SEC filing. Still, just shy of $9 billion of that loss was due to spending on AI infrastructure and computing, while more than $72 billion was attributable to “change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs.” That means only a fraction of the loss was actual spending during the first half of the year.

The company did not include results for the most recent financial quarter, which ended on September 30.

Anthropic’s IPO will test Wall Street’s appetite for AI, as the general public, policymakers and the industry’s own technologists raise major questions about the risks posed by AI — and whether the rapidly advancing research and data center buildout should be slowed.

The filing also addresses many of the same themes that have sparked concerns of an AI bubble, including the possibility of AI demand growing more slowly than expected.

Anthropic was last valued at $965 billion after raising $65 billion from investors in May.

Anthropic’s decision to move forward with its IPO signals “a willingness to face heightened public scrutiny,” said Jacob Bourne, an analyst with Emarketer.

“Anthropic’s IPO filing comes at a pivotal moment for the AI industry, as an anticipated wave of fall public offerings has failed to materialize amid rising concerns over debt-fueled infrastructure investments, uncertain returns, and AI safety risks that have reportedly contributed to rival OpenAI delaying its own IPO until next year.”

Anthropic’s risk factors

Anthropic’s filing lays out four major categories of risk from artificial intelligence: misuse, such as being used to design and implement bioweapons or cyberattacks; loss of human control; authoritarian abuse, such as its potential use to create surveillance states; and economic disruption.

The filing includes 93 pages of risk factors for Anthropic’s business. That’s significantly more than other tech companies that have filed to go public over the last decade, like Snap, which had around 30 pages of risk factors, and Uber, which had about 50.

If Anthropic’s models cause extreme harm, the company could face liability exceeding what its insurance can cover, the filing states.

The company also said its AI models may behave in unintended or “misaligned” ways and may take “harmful actions that no user or third party directed.”

Dario Amodei, co-founder and CEO of Anthropic. Jason Henry/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Anthropic sought to reassure potential investors by writing that it believes “frontier AI companies must invest in safety and alignment to help ensure the responsible diffusion of this technology.” But the company could face conflicting pressures to balance safety versus returns for investors once it goes public.

Anthropic sees a wave of other potential risks to its business in other areas as well, from whether it’s able to secure enough computing resources to uncertain regulatory and political environments. It also said much of its revenue relies on a limited number of products and customers.

But Anthropic’s growth will likely overshadow concerns about the company’s losses, challenges and potential risks to its business, according to Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville & Ives Co.

Anthropic and the AI race

Tech giants including Meta, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic are pouring billions of dollars into the AI race, all hoping to become the dominant player in what they promise will be a society-changing industry. Global spending on AI across services, software, infrastructure and other areas is expected to reach roughly $3.6 trillion in 2027, up from $1.8 trillion in 2025, according to market research firm Gartner.

OpenAI had an early lead following ChatGPT’s launch in November 2022, but the competition has intensified in the last four years. Anthropic’s Claude Code tool quickly became a favorite among software developers after launching in early 2025, and the company sought to replicate that success for other office jobs earlier this year with its Cowork agent.

Claude Cowork helped kickstart the shift from AI chatbots to agents — and rattled software stocks in the process over anxieties that it could make other businesses’ software tools obsolete. Fintech firm Ramp reported that 43.8 percent of US businesses paid for services from Anthropic in September, compared to OpenAI’s 40.6 percent share.

The Claude app has also seen a surge in growth this year. Market intelligence firm Sensor Tower estimates that it has more than 67 million monthly active users as of the third quarter of 2026, compared to 9.4 million a year ago.

But OpenAI also beefed up its own agents this year by launching its Codex coding app in February and ChatGPT Work agent in July for accomplishing multistep tasks like writing a brief or analysis.

Anthropic claimed in the S-1 that its own employees have made huge efficiency gains using Claude — pointing to a growth in revenue per employee from $1.4 million in September 2025 to more than $6.6 million in September 2026, mirroring sharp overall revenue growth during the period.

Now, tech companies are racing to create AI agents that will become the gateway to our entire digital lives, handling everything from shopping to booking restaurants and messaging friends. Anthropic is challenging Meta and OpenAI in this space with its new Duet agent, designed to complete tasks that require taking multiple steps across several apps.

At the same time, Anthropic has landed at the center of ongoing concerns over the breakneck pace of AI advancement.

Last month, CEO Dario Amodei called for an industry-wide slowdown to allow time for safety research, industry standards and regulation to catch up, a sentiment echoed by some other top AI leaders. His essay came after an employee resigned over fears that AI could pose a threat to humanity, and follows reports from Anthropic and its rivals of AI models hacking into other companies during testing.

Anthropic has also had a rocky relationship with the White House. The company temporarily revoked all access to its most capable models when the Trump administration ordered it to prevent foreign nationals from using the technology in June. But Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei was one of several AI CEOs who met with President Donald Trump in September and signed a voluntary commitment to self-police AI models.

World.title: In prominent West Bank settlement, voters speak of uniting a fractured country
World.content:
In the prominent Israeli settlement of Efrat in the occupied West Bank, voters said they were focused on uniting a country that has grown more fractured and divided over the last four years.

“I hope my children will have a good place to grow up, that there will be brotherhood among us, not just wars,” Elinor Veinglas told CNN. She said she hopes “that we will remember to come together and that will be our foundation here in this country.”

Even so, Veinglas said she would only decide for whom to vote “when I see the ballots.”

Her husband, David Veinglas said he would vote for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s rival, Gadi Eisenkot. “I believe whatever comes in the end will be fine,” he told CNN. “I hope for a united government.”

Meanwhile, Haviva, who declined to give her last name, said she prays for “the people of Israel, especially that there will be unity and that they will first find what they have in common between right and left.”

Just south of Jerusalem, Efrat is more ideologically diverse community than settlements deep in the West Bank that are aligned with far-right parties. Israeli settlements are considered illegal under International law by most of the international community and the United Nations.

Zvolon, who also declined to give his last name, said he was voting for far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. “The people of Israel were exiled for 2,000 years living among the non-Jews. We had no government. Today we come and vote. I can say it seems my ancestors dreamed of this day,” Zvolon said.

World.title: What exactly Democrats have pledged to do if they win in the midterms
World.content:
If Democrats can win control of either the House or the Senate, they will have seized some control of Washington back from President Donald Trump and Republicans.

They will have powerful new tools to conduct oversight and investigate Trump’s government; a seat at the table when it comes to government spending; and potentially a mandate to undo some of the changes he has imposed or push for AI regulation he has opposed.

While House Democrats may pass several partisan bills as a show of their priorities, there are limits to what the caucus would actually be able to accomplish. And maintaining unity and resolve would take work, especially since Trump, barred by the Constitution from seeking a third term, might not be willing to work with Democrats to keep the government functioning.

“What happens is I veto everything, and then the Democrats come and they want to make a deal,” Trump said last week of the prospect of working with a Democratic-majority Congress.

Any measures that the Democrats really want to become law would likely have to be part of must-pass legislation, such as the annual appropriations bills. And that would take negotiating with Republicans, at least in the Senate, since the Democrats are not expected to gain enough seats in that chamber to approve bills without GOP votes.

Here’s a look at some of the power Democrats could gain with a House or Senate majority, and what they would be able to do with it.

Cost of living

It was the affordability crisis and inflation that turned voters against President Joe Biden, and it may end up being inflation and affordability that turn voters against Trump. Democrats are promising a new focus on affordability, but there may be little they can do while Trump is president. There’s little chance they could gain the kind of majority that would allow them to overturn his veto. That means effort to pare back Trump’s tariffs or end his war on Iran would require help from Republicans.

The top Democrat in the House, Hakeem Jeffries, has said his party is creating working groups to explore how to bring down prices in five areas: housing, healthcare, caregiving, gas and utilities, and groceries and goods.

Jeffries has cited three immediate goals:

► Ending the war to bring down energy prices.

► Undoing cuts to Medicaid in the Republican tax and spending cuts bill, and renewing Obamacare’s enhanced premium subsidies to address health care costs…

► Repeal Trump’s tariffs to bring down the costs of goods…

But again, those things would require unlikely buy-in from Trump.

The power of the purse will be Democrats’ leverage

Maintenance workers are seen just after midnight at the US Capitol on October 1, 2025, when the government shut down after Congress failed to reach a funding deal. Kent Nishimura/Getty Images/FILE

Democrats’ main power point would be over the spending of taxpayer dollars, which means their leverage to force Trump to do things would be through the threat of taking away money. Trump will need legislation from Congress in order to keep the government running, although he has already overseen multiple protracted and unpopular lapses in funding during his presidencies.

Republicans sought to inoculate his immigration policy from Democrats by approving funding for the Department of Homeland Security to get through his term. Democrats could try to undo that funding, but they will likely lack votes to override Trump’s veto and they may have little control over how his DHS, flush with funding, goes about its business.

Another expected clash will be over the debt ceiling. Republicans raised the debt ceiling by $5 trillion when they passed Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act — yes, the tax cuts bill added a lot of money to the national debt. It’s expected that the debt ceiling will have to be raised again in 2027.

Look for Democrats to use their power over funding to stall or stop Trump’s DC projects, which he argues are necessary to beautify the capital, but which Democrats see as vanity projects. This is probably why Trump’s administration is trying to move quickly on things like the triumphal arch and the championship-level golf course he wants to use taxpayer money to build.

But Democrats also would have to deal with the reality that reversing or modifying some of the sweeping cuts in the “big, beautiful bill” will cost a lot of money, a daunting hurdle even for many in the caucus at a time when the national debt has topped $40 trillion.

Healthcare

Continuing the enhanced premium subsidies to Affordable Care Act enrollees has been a top priority for Democrats for the past two years. They shut down the government for a record 43 days last fall in an effort to pressure GOP leaders to extend the more generous assistance, which lapsed at the end of 2025.

The enhanced subsidies’ expiration sent premium payments soaring 58% this year, and several million people have dropped their coverage.

But the cost alone would be daunting — a permanent extension could cost $350 billion over a decade, according to the Congressional Budget Office.

As for reversing the historic Medicaid cuts in the GOP’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Democrats would have to decide which of the multiple measures to target. The first-ever federal work requirement is expected to lead to the largest loss of coverage, but it would be a big lift to remove the mandate, which is set to kick in on January 1 in most states. Democrats might seek to delay or soften some of the provisions in the law and regulations, such as those related to self-attestation, medical frailty and provider taxes.

That’s not to say that Democrats would just sit back as the Medicaid cuts take effect. They are expected to actively monitor the rollout of the provisions and publicize their impact on enrollees and other Americans, hospitals, and states, among others.

It’s also likely that they would push the Trump administration for more details on its “Most Favored Nation” deals with drugmakers. Trump would like them codified into law, but there are a lot of questions about the details of the agreements and whether they have actually driven down costs for patients.

While several progressive Democratic candidates have pushed for Medicare for All on the campaign trail, don’t expect the caucus to move forward on an expansion of Medicare to more Americans in the coming Congress.

Investigations

Left to right: Eric Trump, Jared Kushner, Ivanka Trump and Donald Trump, Jr. applaud during the inauguration of President Donald Trump in the Rotunda of the US Capitol on January 20, 2025. Kevin Lamarque/Pool/AFP via Getty Images

Oversight is likely to be one of the most immediate and visible consequences of any Democratic takeover of either the House or the Senate. With the majority comes the power to call hearings and subpoena witnesses.

Expect Democrats to launch inquiries into Elon Musk, for starters. Many questions remain about the so-called Department of Government Efficiency he launched with Trump’s blessing. Contracts awarded to Musk’s companies could also be scrutinized.

Trump’s efforts to effectively shut down agencies created by Congress like USAID, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Department of Education will likely get their first real scrutiny by lawmakers.

So will the actions of Trump’s children to make money during their father’s presidency. Trump has made more than $1 billion on crypto at a time when he could be overseeing its regulation.

His most controversial policies, like the Iran war, mass deportation and tariffs, will be put under the microscope.

Cabinet members like Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Attorney General Todd Blanche will also need to make more time on their calendars for public hearings and their agencies will face more scrutiny from congressional committees.

Iran war

Fires rage at the Shahran oil depot after US and Israeli strikes in Tehran, Iran, on March 8. Hassan Ghaedi/Anadolu via Getty Images

There will be bipartisan support for ending the war, but forcing Trump to abandon the project will be complicated. The War Powers Act seemingly requires congressional approval for prolonged military action, but Trump has found ways around those provisions. Plus, it would take 67 votes — which would mean help from Republicans — to override Trump’s veto. Republicans will be under immense pressure to pass a massive war funding bill in the lame duck period after the election but before new lawmakers take office in January. But the question of Pentagon funding and whether spending bills can be used to control war policy will become a major issue. If the war continues to be unpopular, pressure from Congress and the public will be hard for Trump to continue to ignore.

Food stamps

Workers for La Colaborativa hands out fresh food to Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) recipients in Chelsea, Massachusetts, on November 13. Joseph Prezioso/AFP via Getty Images

In an effort to blunt the Republicans’ historic cuts to food stamps, Democrats are expected to target a provision of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that will require states to shoulder a portion of the benefit costs if they have high rates of payment errors. Currently, the federal government covers the entire tab, but that will change next October for many states.

Democrats have already been pushing for a two-year delay to this measure as part of the Farm Bill. The Senate Agriculture Committee has passed a one-year delay but included an increase in the penalty rate for states with the highest error rate, which Democrats oppose. It’s unclear whether the Farm Bill will become law before this Congress’ term ends at the end of December.

The error rate provision has prompted some states to tighten their application and renewal processes and to add more paperwork requirements. That has contributed to more than 5.5 million people losing benefits since Trump signed the bill into law in July 2025, according to the Food Research & Action Center.

Still, the measure could take a big bite out of state budgets next year at a time when many aren’t flush with funds. That could prompt states to take even more drastic actions, which could lead to more coverage losses.

College education

Democrats will seek to draw a contrast between themselves and Republicans, who reduced the amount of federal loans graduate students and parents can take out and made student loan repayment plans less generous for many borrowers, said Jon Fansmith, senior vice president for government relations at the American Council on Education.

That might include forcing congressional Republicans to take tough votes to keep the stricter rules or requiring Trump to veto the package.

Meanwhile, they may try to address a controversial Department of Education rule that subjects nurses, physician assistants, physical therapists and certain other healthcare professionals to lower loan limits than doctors. There may be bipartisan support to change that rule, considering the shortage of healthcare professionals in the US.

Democrats could also hold oversight hearings on the Trump administration’s efforts to dismantle the Department of Education and shift its responsibilities to other agencies. They would likely look into whether these moves are helping or hurting students and their educations.

Social Security and Medicare

Don’t expect Democrats to advance any serious measures in the next year to address the looming insolvency of the Social Security and Medicare trust funds, which are projected to be drained in the early 2030s. Neither party is expected to tackle this complex and sensitive issue until closer to the deadline.

Democrats may float bills that seek to shore up the programs’ fiscal health to make it clear what their fixes would entail. They generally support lifting the income threshold on Social Security payroll taxes that would subject more of higher earners’ pay to the levy. Some would also expand benefits, such as making the annual cost-of-living adjustment more generous or increasing the minimum monthly payment.

Addressing Medicare’s financial problems will be more complicated. Democrats have supported expanding benefits, such as adding dental, vision and hearing coverage. They have also looked at ways to save the program money, such as rein in reimbursements for Medicare Advantage insurers — though not all of those would help the Medicare Part A trust fund.

Where Trump might work with Democrats

Jeffries came under some scrutiny from Democrats when he met this year with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner about areas where the two sides could work together. The two talked about housing and criminal justice reform. Housing in particular could be an area where Democrats and Republicans negotiate.

Trump himself has also talked with Democratic New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani about housing and infrastructure projects. During his first term, Trump’s major bipartisan achievement was passing the First Step Act, an effort that brought together Democrats and Republicans in the months after voters gave control of the House back to Democrats during Trump’s first term midterm election.

World.title: Gas under Trump 2.0 is now more expensive than it was under Biden
World.content:
New York — On the campaign trail in 2024, President Donald Trump On the campaign trail in 2024, President Donald Trump promised to make gas dirt-cheap again and blamed record-high gas prices on the Biden-Harris “war on energy.”

But then an actual war got in the way: Trump’s deeply unpopular conflict with Iran.

Nearly eight months into a war that has destabilized the global energy system, the average price of gas during Trump’s second term is now more expensive than it was during the Biden era, according to a CNN analysis of AAA data.

That milestone — a nearly unthinkable outcome as recently as January — underscores the frustration over high prices that has engulfed Trump and the Republican party leading up to the midterm elections.

“It’s pretty astonishing,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said of the fact that gas is now more expensive under Trump than former President Joe Biden. “I don’t think anyone would have predicted this 10 months ago.”

It’s a major reversal of the return to sub-$2 gas that Trump promised in the summer of 2024 as he successfully convinced voters to return him to the White House.

Polar opposite of Trump 1.0

During his first term, the national average for regular gas was just $2.47 a gallon. During the depths of the Covid-19 pandemic, gas prices plunged to as low as $1.77 nationally in April 2020.

The health emergency caused demand for fuel to crash to the point that the world ran out of room to store oil, a phenomenon that briefly drove crude oil futures below zero for the first time ever.

At one point in April 2020, Trump even pleaded with Saudi Arabia and Russia to stop pumping so much oil to halt a crash that threatened to bankrupt US oil companies and kill countless jobs.

The situation couldn’t be more different today.

The White House has waged a last-minute scramble to contain the damage from high fuel prices by taking a wide range of steps, including throwing farmers an $8 billion financial lifeline, buying millions of barrels of Russian diesel and examining steps to drive down extremely high shipping costs.

“President Trump is fixing these long-term problems by taking tangible steps to increase our refining capacity here in the United States, while also taking immediate actions, such as releasing oil from our (Strategic Petroleum Reserve) to add supply to the market, temporarily waiving the Jones Act, and allowing red-dyed diesel for highway use, to lower prices at the pump,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told CNN.

A truck is parked at a diesel fuel pump displaying prices above $8 per gallon at a truck stop in the Wilmington neighborhood of Los Angeles on September 22, 2026. President Donald Trump expressed support for a diesel export ban, with fuel prices having surged on the back of the Middle East war. Patrick T. Fallon/AFP/Getty Images

Gas was cheap — before the war

The outlook for gasoline and diesel prices was very favorable for Americans when the year started.

Gas prices were safely below $3 a gallon, and, if anything, the energy market was worried about a supply glut that could keep fuel prices low.

“If Trump really wanted to keep his promise to keep gas prices low, what he should have done was nothing,” said Gregory Brew, senior analyst at consulting firm Eurasia Group. “The market was oversupplied. There was a lot of crude sloshing around. Inventories were quite large. But Trump reversed that with the war.”

Trump has argued that elevated gas prices are a small price to pay for keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon.

But the spike in gas prices has angered voters who were hoping for the opposite under Trump.

“High gas prices do not bode well for incumbents. They didn’t bode well for Biden either,” GasBuddy’s De Haan said.

Stuck above $4

Gas prices spiked even higher under Biden, zooming to an all-time high of $5.02 a gallon in June 2022 after Russia invaded Ukraine.

However, gas prices came down faster under Biden.

In fact, 2026 has already shattered the Biden-era record for the most number of days with $4 gas or higher.

The war with Iran led to the unthinkable: The unprecedented closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway the world relied on to get oil out of the Middle East.

While oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz have largely recovered, the cost to get that crude out has skyrocketed because of expensive and inefficient workarounds being used. The cost of hiring an oil tanker has skyrocketed from $65,000 a day last year to $1.6 million earlier this month.

A shortage of refining

Not only that, but the world is now grappling with a global refining shortage. Refineries that would normally churn out diesel, jet fuel and gasoline have been damaged in the Middle East and Russia. China has held back its own fuel exports.

To make up for lost refinery output, the world has drawn fuel from commercial and emergency stockpiles.

But that leaves the intricate energy system vulnerable to shocks.

Case in point: A recent, unexpected outage at ExxonMobil’s Joliet, Illinois, refinery caused gasoline prices to go through the roof in Michigan, Ohio and other Great Lakes states in recent days.

“Right now, there is no cushion. Commercial inventories are very low,” said Brew. “When there is any kind of outage, everyone starts to scramble.”

An unloaded truck, fuel tanker, and compressed natural gas fueled transit bus drive past the Marathon Petroleum Corp. Los Angeles Refinery in Carson, California, on September 22, 2026. According to the company’s website, the refinery is the largest on the West Coast with a crude oil capacity of 365,000 barrels per calendar day, producing California Air Resources Board (CARB) gasoline and CARB diesel fuel among other products. Patrick T. Fallon/AFP/Getty Images

Refiners, incentivized by the ability to make incredible profits due to the shortage, are producing as much fuel as possible even though normally this is the time of year operations slow for routine repairs.

“Refiners have been running flat-out for months. If you own a refinery, you are printing money. Some are skipping maintenance because there is money to be made right now,” said Brew. “But if you run refiners for months on end, they will break down.”

Once the Exxon refinery returns to normal, gas prices should come back down. However, that relief will likely be offset by the fact that oil prices have surged to seven-month highs as traders brace for the risk of a return to all-out war in the Middle East after the election.

De Haan said Trump is “pulling every small lever he can” to cushion the blow from high prices.

“Unfortunately, they’re not adding up to much,” he said. “Until the biggest lever — diplomacy — is pulled, he’s going to continue to fight against very elevated gas and record diesel. It’s fairly ominous.”

World.title: PM witnesses signing of $650M solar power project agreements
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly attended on Monday evening the signing of an initial financing agreement for the Dandara solar power project in Nag Hammadi, Qena Governorate, with a capacity of 1,000 megawatts and 200 megawatt-hours of battery storage, and total investments of around $650 million.

The agreement was signed by Norwegian company Scatec, the European Investment Bank (EIB), the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), and the African Development Bank (AfDB).

Agreements were also signed to connect the project to the national electricity grid and for the National Bank of Egypt to contribute to the project company. Minister of Electricity and Renewable Energy Mahmoud Esmat attended the ceremony.

The project will be implemented in two phases. Each phase will add 500 megawatts of solar power capacity and 100 megawatt-hours of battery storage.

The project aims to meet around one-third of Egypt Aluminium’s electricity needs, helping reduce carbon emissions from aluminium production and improve the competitiveness of Egyptian products in international markets, particularly amid growing environmental requirements for exports.

The signings mark an important step toward completing the project’s financing and implementation arrangements.

The project reflects cooperation between the Egyptian government, Scatec, international financial institutions, and national banks to support the transition to clean energy, reduce carbon emissions, and strengthen the competitiveness of Egyptian industry and exports.

World.title: Egypt, Iraq seek to strengthen cooperation in water resources management
World.content:
Minister of Water Resources and Irrigation Hani Sewilam underscored the longstanding historical and fraternal ties between Egypt and Iraq, reaffirming Cairo’s commitment to strengthening bilateral cooperation to help both countries address water challenges and improve water management efficiency.

Sewilam made the remarks during a meeting with Iraqi Minister of Water Resources Muthanna Al-Tamimi on the sidelines of the ninth Cairo Water Week.

The talks focused on expanding bilateral cooperation and exchanging expertise in water resources management and irrigation.

The two ministers reviewed progress in implementing a memorandum of understanding (MoU) between their ministries, which establishes a framework for cooperation in water resources and river basin management, modern irrigation, water treatment and reuse, water quality improvement, aquatic weed control, coastal protection, training and capacity building.

Both sides stressed the importance of advancing implementation of the MoU and translating its provisions into practical programs and activities.

They also underlined the role of the joint steering committee in following up on implementation.

Sewilam highlighted progress in training cooperation, notably the first training program organized for Iraqi participants under the title “Non-Conventional Water Resources Management.”

The two-week program was attended by 19 Iraqi trainees at the Regional Training Center for Water Resources and Irrigation.

He reaffirmed Egypt’s readiness to share its expertise and successful practices with Iraq in modern water resources management, irrigation system development, agricultural drainage water treatment and reuse, and the application of advanced technologies.

These include artificial intelligence, remote sensing, geographic information systems (GIS), telemetry systems and unmanned aerial vehicles, which can support decision-making and improve the operational efficiency of water systems.

Sewilam also affirmed the Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation’s readiness to meet Iraq’s technical and training needs through expertise exchange and specialized training programs and workshops.

He welcomed a visit by an Iraqi delegation to learn about Egypt’s experience in irrigation, the management of barrages, pumping stations and hydropower plants, canal rehabilitation, and wastewater treatment.

The visit would create broader opportunities for practical cooperation and mutual benefit from the two countries’ expertise, he said.

The ninth Cairo Water Week features broad participation by international and regional organizations, which are organizing technical and scientific sessions and sponsoring competitions across a total of 137 sessions.

Participating organizations include the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the European Union, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), the International Water Management Institute (IWMI), the Inter-Islamic Network on Water Resources Development and Management (INWRDAM), the German Agency for International Cooperation (GIZ), and the World Water Council, reflecting the event’s expanding partnerships.

World.title: Foreign Minister: Egypt seeks to strengthen its position as a regional manufacturing hub
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty, who also serves as Egypt’s governor at the World Bank Group, stressed Egypt’s commitment to strengthening its position as a regional manufacturing hub.

Abdelatty made the remarks on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, during the fifth global Manufacturing Conference, organized by the World Bank Group in Cairo from October 26 to 28 under the theme “Manufacturing for Jobs, Value Addition and Prosperity,” with the participation of officials and representatives of international institutions and the private sector.

He said developing industrial capabilities was a priority in Egypt’s structural economic reform efforts, helping expand the production base, attract investment and integrate the Egyptian economy into regional and global value chains.

Abdelatty outlined national strategies to boost economic growth, enhance competitiveness and support industrial development in Africa, highlighting Egypt’s target of increasing non-oil exports to $100 billion by 2030 through localizing industries, components and production inputs and increasing domestic value added.

He also highlighted efforts to direct investment toward priority industries, particularly green and sustainable sectors, and facilitate access to industrial land and facilities, stressing the private sector’s role in localizing technology and creating sustainable jobs.

Abdelatty said Egypt’s strategic location, advanced infrastructure, large domestic market and skilled workforce make it attractive for industrial investment.

He stressed the importance of cooperation with international financial institutions and development partners to support technology transfer, skills development and access to financing, and enhance the competitiveness of Egyptian exports amid climate-related trade challenges.

World.title: Egypt to host UN COP18 desertification summit in 2028
World.content:
Egypt will host the 18th United Nations Conference of the Parties to Combat Desertification (COP18) in 2028, the Agriculture Ministry said on Tuesday, October 27, 2026.

Agriculture Minister Alaa Farouk met the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) Executive Secretary Yasmine Fouad in Cairo to finalize logistics and establish a joint executive committee overseeing preparations for the summit.

The summit comes as North Africa faces escalating climate risks, land degradation, and water scarcity. Egypt plans to showcase its land reclamation and food security initiatives during the event, with the Desert Research Center acting as national focal point.

Former UN climate chief Fouad praised Egypt’s expertise in arid land management as both sides agreed to align technical and operational strategies ahead of the summit.

World.title: Liberia: Edwina Dekontee Mowon Becomes APM Terminals First Female Shift Manager
World.content:
MONROVIA – Edwina Dekontee Mowon continues her trailblazing journey from first female Gate Administrator and first female Berth Supervisor to becoming APM Terminals Liberia’s first female Shift Manager – another milestone for women in Liberia’s maritime industry.

The Freeport of Monrovia is celebrating another historic breakthrough for women in Maritime as Edwina Mowon becomes Shift Manager, the first female employee at APM Terminals Liberia to mark this achievement.

The milestone underscores APM Terminals Liberia’s continued commitment to developing Liberian talent, fostering inclusive leadership and creating opportunities for women to thrive in male dominated roles across the maritime sector.



Edwina joined APM Terminals Liberia in 2011 as the company’s first female Gate Administrator.

Over the past 15 years, she has built an inspiring career through hard work, continuous learning and operational excellence, serving in roles including Data Entry Clerk, Junior Buyer/Procurement Assistant, Dispatcher, Auxiliary Operations and Berth Supervisor.

In 2023, Edwina became APM Terminals Liberia’s first female Berth Supervisor, breaking barriers in one of the terminal’s core operational functions.

Since then, she has led vessel operations at the quay, coordinating teams to ensure safe, efficient and timely cargo handling to keep Liberia’s gateway to global trade moving.

As Shift Manager, Edwina will lead shift operations, overseeing the safe and efficient coordination of vessel, yard and gate activities to drive operational performance and deliver exceptional service to customers.

Reflecting on her achievement, Edwina’s journey demonstrates what is possible through determination, perseverance and a commitment to excellence.

It also reflects APM Terminals Liberia’s investment in developing local talent and building a more diverse and inclusive workforce.
