World.title: Mnangagwa targets Russian investment at Moscow summit as war in Ukraine reshapes alliances
World.content:
President Emmerson Mnangagwa is in Moscow for the third Russia-Africa Summit, seeking to attract Russian investment in energy, mining, agriculture and digital technology, as Harare looks to offset the economic pressure of years of Western sanctions and deepen ties with a longstanding ally.

Mnangagwa arrived in the Russian capital on Monday for the two-day summit, which begins on October 28 and focuses on trade, investment, food security, artificial intelligence and nuclear energy.

He is also attending in his capacity as chairperson of the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA), a role that places regional trade integration at the centre of his engagements.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Chigwedere helps shape historic Dakar 2026 Olympics
World.content:
ZIMBABWEAN event management expert Farai Chigwedere is helping coordinate operations at Stade Abdoulaye Wade ahead of Dakar 2026, the first Olympic sporting event to be held on African soil. As Senegal prepares to welcome young athletes from around the world, Chigwedere (FC) discusses operational readiness, African expertise, volunteer development and the importance of turning a historic sporting occasion into lasting opportunities for the continent with NewsDay reporter Tendai Sauta (TS).

TS: Farai, welcome back to NewsDay.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: ZIFA endorses LM Zaka Girls Tourney
World.content:
ZIFA Masvingo Province chairperson Nabioth Magwizi, who was among the dignitaries at the inaugural LM Auctioneers Zaka Girls Soccer Festival, has endorsed the tournament and urged LM Auctioneers to keep backing girls’ football as the women’s game continues to develop.

The festival was held at St Joseph High School in Jerera on Saturday, with Air Force of Zimbabwe Commander Air Marshal John Nzvede as guest of honour. Magwizi thanked the sponsor for giving girls from Zaka an opportunity.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Binga school gets €210 000 infrastructure upgrade
World.content:
KAPALE Primary School in Binga District, Matabeleland North province has received a major facelift following a €210 000 infrastructure upgrade sponsored by ActionAid Zimbabwe.

The new infrastructure includes classroom blocks, disability- and girl-friendly toilet facilities, a 20kVA solar power system, 20 computers for the computer laboratory, a solar-powered borehole, and a perimeter fence.

Primary and Secondary Education permanent secretary Moses Mhike last week commissioned the infrastructure, deacribing it as a game changer.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Scottland sack Mapeza
World.content:
Defending league champions Scottland have parted ways with coach Norman Mapeza, dismissing the former Warriors head coach with immediate effect following the club’s exit from the CAF Champions League.

Although the club are yet to officially announce the decision, a reliable source within the camp confirmed Mapeza’s departure in the wake of Friday night’s demoralising defeat to Petro Atlético de Luanda. The loss brought an abrupt conclusion to Scottland’s continental ambitions, as they threw away a comfortable two-goal lead from the first leg to succumb 3-2 on aggregate in Luanda.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Malawi: Chawinga Makes History By Reaching Ballon d'Or Top 10
World.content:
Nairobi — Malawi international Temwa Chawinga has made history by becoming the first African woman to finish in the top 10 of the prestigious Ballon d'Or Féminin rankings.

The Kansas City Current forward secured 10th place in the global rankings announced in London, surpassing the previous best finish by an African woman, Nigeria's Asisat Oshoala, who reached 12th place.

The milestone highlights Chawinga's remarkable rise in women's football, following a series of outstanding performances for her club in the United States' National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) and Malawi's national team, the Scorchers.

Chawinga has established herself as one of the most dangerous attacking players in the game, combining blistering pace, clinical finishing and an exceptional ability to find the back of the net.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Her performances for Kansas City Current have earned her international recognition and strengthened her reputation as one of the leading forwards in women's football.

Her top-10 finish represents a significant breakthrough for African women's football, demonstrating the growing presence of players from the continent among the world's elite.

It is also a major moment for Malawi, whose footballing profile continues to rise through Chawinga's achievements on the international stage.

While Chawinga celebrated a historic milestone for Africa, the ceremony also recognised the achievements of Spain's Alexia Putellas, who claimed her third Ballon d'Or Féminin title.

Putellas further cemented her place among the game's most decorated players, joining compatriot Aitana Bonmatí in the exclusive group of three-time winners. Bonmatí, however, remains distinguished by having won the award three consecutive times.

Chawinga's recognition also reflects her growing influence in international football, particularly following Malawi's memorable campaign at the Women's Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON).

As captain of the Scorchers, she played a key role in the team's historic continental campaign, inspiring her teammates with her attacking threat, leadership and determination.

Her performances helped raise Malawi's profile and demonstrated the country's ability to compete against some of Africa's established footballing nations.

From her early career in Malawi to her success in China's women's football league and her subsequent rise in the NWSL, Chawinga has continued to break barriers and set new standards for African players.

Her achievement in the Ballon d'Or rankings is more than a personal accomplishment. It represents an important moment for Malawi and African women's football, offering inspiration to a new generation of players aspiring to compete at the highest level.

Close 

By securing a place among the world's top 10 female footballers, Chawinga has strengthened her standing on the global stage and added another landmark achievement to an already remarkable career.

Her historic finish is a powerful reminder of the talent emerging from Africa and the continent's growing influence in the global women's game.

World.title: Kenya: Specialised Rescue Team Deployed to Eastleigh Building Collapse
World.content:
Search and rescue operations continue at the site of the building collapse along Yusuf Haji Avenue, Eastleigh.

Nairobi — The Kenya Defence Forces (KDF) has deployed specialised rescue teams, canine units and equipment to support ongoing efforts to locate survivors following the collapse of a building along 9th Street in Eastleigh, Nairobi.

The military personnel have joined a multi-agency operation involving emergency responders, with the teams working to clear debris, access trapped sections of the building and rescue anyone who may still be alive beneath the rubble.

In a statement, the KDF said it had deployed specialised Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams, a Rapid Response Unit (RRU) from the Kenya Air Force and canine units to reinforce the search and rescue operation.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The teams are also using specialised vehicles and equipment to facilitate debris clearance and improve access to areas affected by the collapse.

The operation brings together the National Police Service, Kenya Red Cross Society, Nairobi County Fire Brigade, National Disaster Management Unit, National Disaster Operations Centre, Ministry of Health, St John Ambulance and other emergency responders.

The coordinated efforts have so far resulted in the recovery of six survivors, including two rescued during subsequent operations.

The two survivors were reported to be in stable condition and were referred to Kenyatta National Hospital for further medical attention and monitoring.

Rescue teams continued to cautiously clear the debris and examine the collapsed structure as they pursued leads on the possible presence of additional survivors.

Excavators and specialised equipment provided by the KDF, National Youth Service and Nairobi City County have been deployed to help remove the rubble and facilitate access to affected sections of the building.

The General Officer Commanding Central Command, Major General William Kamoiro, visited the scene to assess the progress of the rescue operation, engage emergency responders and express solidarity with families affected by the incident.

The KDF said its involvement reflected the military's commitment to supporting civilian authorities during humanitarian emergencies and disasters.

Beyond its primary responsibility of safeguarding the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity, the military provides specialised capabilities, personnel and logistical support during emergencies requiring rapid mobilisation.

The KDF deployment comes as the multi-agency rescue operation enters its fourth day following the collapse of the multi-storey building under construction along 9th Street in Eastleigh on Friday, October 23.

The building's ground floor and basement housed commercial premises that were occupied at the time of the incident, raising fears that traders and other members of the public could have been caught in the collapse.

Close 

The operation has been complicated by the extent of the structural damage, with engineers describing the collapse pattern as resembling a "pancake collapse", in which floors fall onto those below them. The arrangement of heavy concrete slabs and debris presents challenges for rescuers seeking to reach possible survivors without destabilising the remaining structure.

The disaster has also triggered investigations into the circumstances surrounding the collapse. The Engineers Board of Kenya has launched a probe into possible contributing factors and the role of professionals involved in the project, while the Directorate of Criminal Investigations has been directed to investigate possible wrongdoing.

World.title: Namibia: Health Ministry Halts Recruitment of New Staff
World.content:
The Ministry of Health and Social Services has halted the recruitment of new staff.

This leaves unemployed qualified nurses waiting for further employment opportunities until the next financial year, which begins in April 2027.

This was announced in a statement by the ministry's executive director, Penda Ithindi, who says the decision follows the government's limited financial position and adverse external economic developments affecting domestic revenue.

"Taking into account the expressed fiscal position of the country as a result of adverse external economic developments, which has a negative effect on domestic revenue, the Ministry of Health and Social Services wishes to reiterate that new staff recruitment is now halted," Ithindi says.



The ministry says N$259 million was allocated for the recruitment of health workers, including nurses, in the 2026/27 financial year.

Of this amount, N$241 million, inclusive of recruitment costs for positions that became vacant during the year, had been used.

By the end of September, about 1 770 health personnel had been recruited, including approximately 1 320 nurses.

The ministry says it had received guidance through the Ministry of Finance that the remaining recruitment would only resume in the next financial year, beginning in April 2027.

However, recruitment to fill positions that become vacant through retirement and other natural attrition will continue to be advertised and filled.

The announcement comes as the ministry responds to a collective petition concerning the unemployment of qualified enrolled nurses and the current recruitment process in Namibia.

The ministry says it recognises that nurses are critical to healthcare delivery, providing frontline services, basic care and clinical support.

During the 2025/26 mid-year budget review, the ministry received N$185 million, which it used to recruit 814 additional staff between December 2025 and March 2026.

These included 449 nurses, 134 medical officers and dentists, 103 allied health professionals and 107 administrative support staff.

According to the ministry, the recruited personnel were deployed to health facilities across the country, helping to ease pressure on services.

Ithindi says the recruitment enabled the introduction of 24-hour services at several clinics in the Khomas region, which the ministry saya further reduced long patient waiting times.

The ministry has addressed concerns around recruitment requirements.

"The tests administered by the Health Professional Council of Namibia are to ensure that qualifying nurses have demonstrated the capacity to execute their expected functions as this relates to safe-saving services which the nurses provide to the public," the statement reads.

World.title: Uganda: Two Bodies Recovered From Collapsed Entebbe Church Building
World.content:
Police say rescue operations are ongoing at Holy City Church, Brother Ronnie's Ministries, in Wakiso District as authorities investigate the collapse of a four-storey building extension.

Rescue teams have recovered two bodies from the rubble of a collapsed building under construction at Holy City Church in Bwerenga, Katabi Town Council, Wakiso District, although police have so far confirmed one death.

One of the deceased has been identified as a resident of Nansana Municipality (whose identity is being withheld on compassionate ground for now), according to information obtained by Nile Post.

A source who participated in the search and rescue operation on Monday evening told the Nile Post that two bodies had been retrieved from the debris following the collapse of the multi-storey structure.

Kampala Metropolitan Police spokesperson Rachael Kawala confirmed one person had died but said she was only on her way to the scene so she would be able to get the right information from the ground.



Police had earlier confirmed that approximately 22 people had been rescued and were being evacuated to Entebbe Grade B Hospital for medical attention.

The incident occurred at Holy City Church, which belongs to Pastor Ronnie Makabai of Brother Ronnies Ministries.

In a statement issued on Monday evening, police spokesperson Racheal Kawala said rescue operations were continuing as emergency teams searched for anyone who might still be trapped beneath the rubble.

"Rescue operations are ongoing, with approximately 22 people rescued so far," Kawala said.

Preliminary findings indicate that the collapsed structure was an extension of the main church building and had reached the fourth floor at the time of the incident.

The cause of the collapse had not been established by the time of publication, with police saying investigations were ongoing.

Emergency response teams have been working at the scene to search the debris, assist survivors and establish the full extent of the casualties.

Police had not publicly confirmed the reported recovery of the second body or provided a comprehensive account of the people affected by the collapse.

Nile Post will update this story as authorities release further information about the casualties and the circumstances surrounding the incident.

World.title: Uganda: Slow Poison - Idi Amin, Yoweri Museveni, and the Making of the Ugandan State
World.content:
book review

Slow Poison: Idi Amin, Yoweri Museveni, and the Making of the Ugandan State

By Mahmood Mamdani

Review by Uma Dhupelia-Mesthrie

Wits University Press, 2025, 338 pp., R380

The two protagonists of this book are Idi Amin, president of Uganda between 1971 and 1979, and Yoweri Museveni, the president from 1986 until now. Drawing on rich official and unofficial archival sources, including an unpublished biography of Amin by his son Jaffar, Mamdani provides a background to their lives before assuming the presidency, with insights into their personalities. The main focus though is on their terms as presidents and their legacy.

Mamdani’s assessment of Amin unsettles dominant public images of Amin, which became well established through a 1981 film, The Rise and Fall of Idi Amin, and which continued in the western media well into the 21st century. While he concedes that violence was a key part of Amin’s life and strategy to win power, he debunks the image of Amin as a cannibal, a man who kept severed heads of people in his fridge, who sacrificed his son and who was a monster equal to Hitler. All these were untrue and were just part of an anti-Amin propaganda campaign. Mamdani describes Amin as a “master of theatre” (p. 117) who deliberately embraced comedic performance for its shock value. While he may have come into power with Israeli and British support, once in office, he freed himself from their control. The reader is even drawn into admiring Amin for his mocking of the British government and its royal family.



Mamdani sees substance in Amin’s rule. For instance, his land tenure reform ensured all land was public land and provided protection for those who worked the soil. He responded to criticisms of excesses under his rule by appointing “one of the first truth commissions in the world” (p. 104). The commission investigated cases of disappeared people under his presidency. The public hearings, like that of the South African truth commission two decades later, gave ordinary Ugandans the opportunity to highlight the extent of abuse of power. Most importantly, Amin turned colonial legacy, which nurtured and fixed divisive tribal identities, on its head. He instead “shaped Uganda as a Black nation” (pp. 117-118). Mamdani reflects on Amin’s hero status in Uganda: “I have lost count of the number of times I have seen a poster on the back of a matatu (public taxi) in Kampala, with photos of Malcolm X, Muhammad Ali, Bob Marley, and Idi Amin, and no caption, because none seemed necessary” (p. 118).

At least three chapters are devoted to the expulsion of Asians in 1972.¹ We are given insight into why indigenous Africans in Uganda supported this. Many of these reasons are common to other countries in Africa with an Asian presence. Amin had personal experience of the “bad Asian” (p. 19) in his youth when he worked on a sugar plantation owned by one of the wealthiest Indian families. The dominant perception of Asians was that they were corrupt, exploited indigenous Africans, gave little back to the country, and did not embrace social integration. Their expulsion was central to Amin’s Africanisation project.

Yet other countries did not take such drastic action. White colonial and apartheid governments in South Africa, for example, offered repatriation or assisted emigration schemes from the late 19th century to the 1970s. These came with free passages to India with bonuses on surrender of domicile rights. In this way, South Africa got rid of at least 73,000 Indians with India’s co-operation between 1902 and 1940, when the scheme was most active (Dhupelia-Mesthrie, 2020). Except for noises made by the Economic Freedom Fighters, the ANC-led government in South Africa, while embracing black empowerment, has never contemplated the removal of its Indian population. Their contribution to the liberation struggle and their long-established South African identity precludes such a thought. Uganda, in contrast, denied Asians the right to Ugandan nationality.

A significant part of Mamdani’s discussion links Asian expulsions to the two expulsions that preceded it, after Amin fell out with the Israelis and the British soon after coming to power. The expulsion of Asians was also meant to embarrass and inconvenience Britain by leaving it the responsibility of resettling British Asians. Mamdani provides fascinating detail on how the Ugandan cabinet worked out procedures for the expulsion, the disposal of property and businesses, and the bureaucratic paperwork. Reading about the workings of the Departed Asians Property Custodian Board brings to mind the Group Areas Development Board in South Africa which, under the Group Areas Act, took control of the sale and acquisition of property of those who were disqualified from living in white group areas.

Mamdani and his family were among the expelled. While he provides very emotional details of his parents’ experience, Mamdani the academic dominates the discussion, and he makes some controversial conclusions. He concedes that the expulsion was “one big, well-organised theft” (p. 97) and that elites benefitted from the sale and expropriation of Asian property. At the same time, he is critical of prevalent narratives of Asian “victimhood” (despite them having to leave with just £50 and unable to take most of their personal possessions). While he argues that “there was no one Asian experience,” and that the greatest consequence of expulsion was a loss of “belonging” and the acquisition of a new status as “strangers” (pp. 94-95), his account, however, favours what he regards as a majority experience. Most Ugandan Asians, he argues, “experienced the expulsion as some kind of purgatory” (p. 94) from Ugandan conditions where access to economic opportunities had shrivelled. As evidence, we are given examples of how some families told him that life in Britain was better.

[Photo caption: Mahmood Mamdani, at a reading of Slow Poison: Idi Amin, Yoweri Museveni, and the Making of the Ugandan State. Photo: Instagram]

We are dependent on one individual’s account that Amin’s photograph was displayed alongside those of gods in the prayer rooms of several Asian homes in Britain. As for the fate of the wealthy Indian, we are provided with an example from a fictional narrative. The evidence we are given is slight and anecdotal. What is wrong with the expelled choosing to see themselves as victims? Most experienced oral historians would engage with why stories are narrated in a particular way rather than trying to prove them to be false or true. In this regard, it would have been appropriate for Mamdani to have engaged with the project led by Dolar Vasani to mark the 50th anniversary of the expulsion. This resulted in 24 podcasts of oral narratives and memoirs, providing accounts of their lives in Uganda, personal experiences of expulsion, life in transit camps, resettlement and racism in the new countries, which are also counterbalanced by stories of success post-expulsion.

Mamdani’s discussion is linked to his overall objective of rehabilitating Amin. He argues Amin was no Hitler and dismisses stories of robbery and rape. He argues that unlike, for example, in Rwanda in 1994 when Tutsis were killed en masse, Asians in Uganda were not killed.

Museveni fares very poorly in this book, deservedly so. The comparison with Amin leaves Amin in an even better light. Museveni the president bore no resemblance to the young man with vision that Mamdani had known. The governing principle of his presidency was how to build and retain power. Vision and desire for change and politics underpinned by morals and ethics were sacrificed. Museveni embraced tribalisation and ethnic divisions and “fragmented the nation” (p. 271). Museveni became a “Washington Poster Boy” (p. 272) with neo-liberalism and the International Monetary Fund determining what kind of changes could be made. Uganda became central to the American “War on Terror” (p. 253) on African soil. The most damning indictment of Museveni is revealed in the extent of corruption which the president sanctioned himself. The financial health of the nation was undermined by the prevalence of “ghost culture,” “ghost institutions,” “ghost soldiers,” and “ghost workers” (p. 248). There are echoes of independent South Africa in the Ugandan state’s purchase of poor quality, deficient arms and helicopters accompanied by significant embezzlement.

While many scholars of African history may focus on the story of the two presidents and the failed post-independence state, what makes this book particularly memorable is how the author’s memoir is woven into an academic study of power. While his grandparents may have come from India, Mamdani’s parents were African born. Although Kampala was home, the family also spent time in Dar es Salaam. Mamdani, however, was born in 1946 in Bombay, during the family’s brief sojourn there. In a strong expression of his African identity, Mamdani laments: “From the time I became politically conscious, I remember feeling resentful about being born in India. Why could I, too, not be born in Uganda, at least in East Africa, like everyone I knew” (p. 24). He lived in an exclusively Asian neighbourhood with a segregated school and social life. It was his years in America as a teenager and young adult that were the most transformative. First enrolling in engineering, he later switched to political science, and subjects such as history, economics, and philosophy opened new horizons for him. He became an activist and participated in several of the African-American civil rights movement campaigns and at Harvard he was drawn into the anti-Vietnam war movement.

He returned to Uganda in 1972, the very month that Idi Amin announced his intention to expel all Asians. Thus began a period of exile where he was employed at the University of Dar es Salaam. It is there that he joined and associated with political groupings that opposed Amin’s presidency. Once Amin was overthrown, Mamdani returned to Uganda and began a long association with Makerere University. In chapter 10 and more particularly chapter 11, Mamdani reflects on his teaching and research vision, which encompassed transformation of curricula and the nurturing of new African researchers free of dependency on external partners. To this end he was founding director of the Centre for Basic Research and, later in 2010, the Makerere Institute of Social Research. In a previous book, Scholars in the Market Place: the Dilemmas of Neo-Liberal Reform at Makerere University, 1989-2005 (Codesria, 2007), and in chapter 11, Mamdani repeats discussions on the deleterious effects of market-driven education and the influence of the World Bank.

Close 

In the very last paragraph of the book, Mamdani asks the questions “What lessons can we draw for intellectuals and academics on the margins of corridors of powers? What does it mean to be in conversation with those who are or will be in power and at the same time, keep a ‘safe distance’? Can one engage with power without being corrupted by it?” (p. 278). These are questions he faced in his relationship with Yoweri Museveni, whom he got to know fairly well in exile and after his return to Uganda. While Museveni was building up his military power in opposition to the presidency of Milton Obote, Mamdani chose “above ground” (p. 146) engagement. He and others strove to improve society through literacy programmes and by providing access to health facilities in rural areas. He declined an offer to join Museveni’s cabinet as a minister with responsibility for monitoring government institutions. This refusal came out of an understanding of power and how it works and the limits of individual influence. Later, he joined a commission on local government and made recommendations that were not to the president’s liking. It was “in the realm of practice” (p. 286) we are told we can find answers to his questions.

This is a book of quality which is expected of a giant scholar of Africa. It represents a sad story of a failed post-independence state, and all these failings cannot be blamed entirely on the colonial legacy. There is local culpability.

References

Dhupelia-Mesthrie, U. (2020). South Africa to India: Narratives of a Century of Repatriation (1871-1975). Matatu, 52(1), pp. 70-100.

World.title: Ethiopia: Drought, Food Shortages and Child Malnutrition Deepen Humanitarian Needs in Afar, Amhara and Tigray
World.content:
Addis Abeba — Drought, rising food prices, shortages of essential medicines and disruptions to health services are compounding humanitarian needs across northern Ethiopia's Afar, Amhara and Tigray regions, with displaced children particularly vulnerable to acute malnutrition, according to a humanitarian assessment document seen by Addis Standard.

The assessment, dated October 19 and covering developments between October 12 and 19, warns that the humanitarian consequences of escalating insecurity are unfolding against a backdrop of unmet needs left by the 2020-2022 northern Ethiopia conflict, subsequent episodes of fighting and displacement, and El Niño-related drought.

"Needs are likely to remain high," the assessment states, noting that the combined pressures have compounded existing humanitarian vulnerabilities across Tigray, Amhara and Afar.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

One of the clearest indicators of the crisis is the nutritional situation among displaced children in Tigray. Screening conducted in September and October in Laelay Adiabo, Axum and Adwa found that approximately 15% of around 11,800 children screened in internally displaced communities had moderate acute malnutrition.

The assessment cautions that information on the overall scale and severity of humanitarian needs remains fragmented. "At the time of writing, there is no needs assessment data available," it states, identifying rapid humanitarian needs assessments as a priority as access improves.

Food insecurity is being aggravated by crop failures, dwindling household resources and rising prices. In Raya Azebo woreda in southern Tigray, drought has devastated agricultural production, leaving households struggling to afford basic food.

More than 15,000 of the woreda's 26,000 hectares of farmland had reportedly been cultivated, but only around 400 hectares showed crop growth, according to the assessment. Approximately 10,000 hectares were not planted because of a lack of rainfall in May.

A farmer quoted in the assessment said households could no longer afford basic food as prices soared while agricultural production collapsed. Many had exhausted their savings after almost a year without a meaningful harvest. Livestock owners have also suffered as animal prices fell, buyers became scarce, and livestock died from a lack of fodder and disease.

Earlier this month, FEWS NET projected Crisis-level food insecurity outcomes, classified as IPC Phase 3, will persist until January 2027 in parts of southern and eastern Tigray and lowland areas along the Tekeze River catchment.

Health services under pressure

The crisis is also straining an already fragile healthcare system. Hospitals in Sheraro are reportedly struggling to maintain services amid insecurity, shortages of medical supplies and prolonged delays in salary payments to civil servants. The assessment says unpaid salaries have contributed to health workers leaving the area, further reducing the availability of care.

Transporting medical supplies through areas affected by fighting remains difficult, while insecurity is limiting civilians' ability to reach health facilities. Hospitals and other health facilities in Wukro and Adwa, as well as at Adigrat University, have reportedly been looted or vandalized.

A cholera outbreak in Wag Hamra zone in Amhara remains a concern, with humanitarian sources reporting limited availability of treatment supplies, including fluids. Mental health needs in conflict-affected parts of Afar also remain high, the assessment notes.

There have, however, been signs of improvement in humanitarian access to Tigray. An inter-agency convoy delivered essential supplies, including medicines, to northern Ethiopia on October 14, while the World Health Organization dispatched more than 71 tons of medical supplies. Hospitals in Tigray have also begun resuming operations.

The resumption of humanitarian flights to Mekelle and increased movement along the Semera-Abaala-Mekelle corridor have helped humanitarian organizations move personnel and supplies into the region. The International Committee of the Red Cross and the Ethiopian Red Cross Society also delivered essential equipment and medicines to hospitals in Shire, Maichew, Mekhoni and Alamata, as well as Chercher Health Centre.

Despite these developments, the assessment warns that access remains difficult or unsafe in areas experiencing active hostilities.

In Amhara, road blockages and insecurity continue to delay convoy movements, while humanitarian personnel have reportedly faced harassment, theft and demands for money.

Displacement and access to basic necessities

Displacement across Tigray, Afar and Amhara has largely remained within the same districts or zones, according to the assessment. However, the scale of new movements remains uncertain.

Civilians in rural parts of northwestern Tigray have reportedly moved toward Shire amid ongoing hostilities and heavy artillery fire. The assessment warns that new arrivals could intensify pressure on shelter and services in areas already hosting large internally displaced populations.

In Afar, an estimated 11,000 to 13,000 people may remain displaced, although the figures are difficult to verify. Some people previously displaced from areas including Abaala and Megale have reportedly returned home as security and humanitarian access improved.

Close 

In eastern Tigray, restrictions on movement and blocked roads have also disrupted access to food and essential goods. In Zala Anbesa, few supplies were reportedly reaching the town as of October 15, prices were rising sharply, and shops, restaurants and other businesses had closed, affecting both livelihoods and access to basic necessities.

The assessment warns that continued or intensified fighting could further undermine food security by restricting market supplies, prolonging shortages of cash and fuel, and driving up staple food prices.

Education has also been disrupted. Schools in Erob, Gulo Mekeda and Zala Anbesa in eastern Tigray remain closed, while the reported use of school facilities by armed actors in Tahtay Koraro has interrupted classes during the school year.

The full extent of the humanitarian crisis remains difficult to establish because of limited access, incomplete information and disrupted administrative structures. In Tigray, interruptions to the regional agriculture and disaster risk management institutions have also weakened local capacity to respond to drought.

The assessment concludes that improving humanitarian access must be accompanied by rapid needs assessments and stronger coordination to establish the scale of unmet needs and guide the response. It notes that the absence of functioning administrative structures continues to complicate humanitarian planning and coordination.

World.title: Uganda: Ebola - Uganda Orders 21-Day Quarantine for Citizens Returning From DR Congo
World.content:
The Ministry of Health said returning Ugandans with a history of travel to the DRC would bear the cost of their quarantine.

Uganda has ordered citizens returning from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to undergo a 21-day quarantine as authorities intensify measures to prevent further transmission of Ebola amid infections reported in Nigeria and Kenya.

According to a report by Al Jazeera, the Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi announced the measure at a news conference in Kampala, saying the government had strengthened surveillance at Entebbe International Airport and land border crossings.

The Ministry of Health said returning Ugandans with a history of travel to the DRC would bear the cost of their quarantine. Incoming travellers are also required to complete forms containing their contact details to facilitate follow-up by health authorities.



The measures come amid investigations into the source of Nigeria's first confirmed Ebola case in more than a decade and a possible connection between the Nigerian and Kenyan infections.

Uganda declared its Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak over in July after recording 20 infections and two deaths, according to the country's Ministry of Health. It maintains that it has no active Ebola infections.

However, the source of Nigeria's imported case remains under investigation, with conflicting accounts emerging about the infected woman's movements before she tested positive.

Dispute over Nigeria's Ebola case

Swiss authorities have said a Ugandan-born woman married to a Swiss diplomat contracted Ebola during a visit to Uganda in September.

Nigeria confirmed her infection on 20 October after she returned to Abuja on 3 October.

The 42-year-old woman developed symptoms days after arriving in the country and initially sought treatment at a private hospital, believing she had malaria, before being admitted to another facility.

PREMIUM TIMES previously reported that the woman had spent about two and a half weeks in Uganda before returning to Nigeria through Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, where she had a two-hour stopover.

At the briefing, Mr Baryomunsi questioned the conclusion that she contracted the virus in Uganda.

He said relatives who had previously visited the DRC had met the woman in a Kampala suburb, raising questions about whether investigators had adequately examined that possible route of exposure.

"We should speak science, not politics," he said.

Mr Baryomunsi said 60 people identified in Uganda following possible contact with the Kenyan patient had completed 21 days of monitoring and been discharged.

DRC outbreak

The current regional response follows a major Ebola outbreak in the DRC, where infections were first reported in May.

Close 

The WHO had recorded 9,704 cases and 4,687 deaths in the country as of 20 October.

The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a species of Ebola virus for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment.

Ebola spreads primarily through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated objects and surfaces.

The incubation period can last up to 21 days, making the identification and monitoring of contacts important to detecting infections before they lead to further transmission.

The WHO has called for stronger surveillance and cooperation between countries while advising against travel and trade restrictions on affected countries.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 27, 2026
World.content:
More Than 60 Killed In Attacks In Ethiopia

More than 60 people have been killed in a series of attacks targeting Christian communities in Ethiopia's Oromia region, according to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. The attacks occurred in three areas of the Shirka district, where at least 20 houses were reportedly burnt down, and five children were among those killed. One resident described the violence as an ambush, saying attackers surrounded the community from all sides. A church official called the incident a massacre, adding that security forces arrived but were unable to stop the assault. Many residents have since fled the area. A local official blamed a newly formed rebel coalition, the Alliance for Survival, which includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). The OLA has not commented on the latest allegations and previously denied responsibility for similar attacks. The Orthodox Church condemned the violence, saying attacks against Christians have increased and accusing authorities of failing to address repeated concerns about insecurity. A July 2026 report by the Ethiopian Human Rights Council recorded 458 deaths in attacks in the area over the previous four years, identifying local communities, particularly Orthodox Christians, as frequent targets. However, previous reports have also documented attacks against Muslims, with residents describing the violence as both ethnic and religious in nature.

Algeria Approves Troop Deployment To Niger

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Algeria is preparing to deploy troops to neighbouring Niger in its first foreign military deployment since sending forces to Egypt during the 1973 Arab-Israeli war. The proposed deployment follows a visit to Algiers by Niger's defence minister as the country seeks assistance in combating armed groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State. Algeria's parliament approved the deployment, with 148 of 174 senators voting in favour before the lower house also backed the move. Algeria has not yet announced the timing or number of troops, but they are expected to help secure energy infrastructure in northern Niger, near the Libyan border. The operation would mark the first use of a 2020 constitutional provision permitting overseas military deployments and a significant departure from Algeria's longstanding opposition to sending troops abroad. Algerian officials have stressed that the mission is intended to protect economic infrastructure rather than wage war. The country has significant economic interests in Niger, including a proposed gas pipeline that would transport Nigerian gas through Niger to Algeria.

UN Warns 3.6 Million in Uganda Facing Acute Food Insecurity as Crisis Worsens

About 3.6 million people in Uganda face high levels of acute food insecurity, and the number is projected to rise to 4.4 million between February and June 2027, according to the 2026 Integrated Food Security Phase Classification report. Refugees and communities in the Karamoja sub-region are expected to face the greatest burden as food shortages and malnutrition worsen. The report estimates that 465,900 children under five and 246,300 pregnant and breastfeeding women will require treatment for acute malnutrition between April 2026 and March 2027. The crisis is being driven by recurring climate shocks, declining agricultural production, crop and livestock pests and diseases, high food prices, deteriorating livelihoods and limited access to healthcare, clean water, sanitation and social protection. United Nations Resident Coordinator in Uganda Leonard Zulu called for urgent action to protect vulnerable households and strengthen food systems before conditions deteriorate further. Prime Minister Robinah Nabbanja urged the government, development partners and humanitarian agencies to invest in sustainable solutions that enable communities to produce their own food and reduce dependence on emergency assistance. The assessment, conducted across 60 districts between August and September 2026, was launched alongside a $50 million joint appeal by the United Nations and its partners to support emergency responses in Karamoja and early interventions in 37 districts and eight refugee settlements. The proposed response includes cash assistance, agricultural and livestock support, nutrition screening and treatment, healthcare, child protection, gender-based violence prevention, water and sanitation programmes, and disaster preparedness. The report warns that without sustained investment and coordinated action, vulnerable communities could face worsening hunger and malnutrition in the coming months.

Amnesty Warns Funding Crisis Could Shut Central African Republic War Crimes Court

Amnesty International has warned that suspected perpetrators of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Central African Republic (CAR), including senior officials, could escape justice if the country's Special Criminal Court (SCC) fails to secure urgent funding. In a report released in October 2026, the organisation said the court, inaugurated in 2018, has tried six cases and secured convictions against 19 people for war crimes and crimes against humanity, with reparations awarded to victims in one case. However, many survivors of atrocities committed during the 2003 coup and the 2012–2014 armed conflict are still waiting for those responsible to be prosecuted. The United States withdrew its funding in 2025, leaving more than US$4.15 million in unpaid commitments and plunging the court into an unprecedented financial crisis. The United Nations and European Union are now its only financial contributors, while funding shortages have forced staff reductions, including cuts to the witness protection unit, and prevented prosecutors from opening new investigations. Amnesty warned that the court could close when its mandate expires in October 2028 unless additional funding is secured.

Close 

Ukraine Allegedly Supporting Mali Militia

Ukraine is facing questions over its alleged involvement in supporting Tuareg fighters in northern Mali, a development that could extend its rivalry with Russia into Africa's Sahel region. A September 2026 CNN investigation reported that around 15 Ukrainian drone specialists were assisting Tuareg fighters, although DW said it had not independently verified the claims and Ukraine has not confirmed a specific operation. Analysts believe any involvement would fit Kyiv's broader strategy of weakening Russian influence internationally, particularly in countries where Moscow provides military support to governments. Mali's military authorities have increasingly relied on Russia for security assistance since taking power in coups in 2020 and 2021, with Russia's Africa Corps replacing the Wagner Group's role in 2025.

World.title: Haitian national charged with murdering estranged wife outside Walmart after green card marriage goes awry
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Haitian national Destino Jean Louis was charged with murder after he allegedly killed his wife outside a Pennsylvania Walmart store where she worked following the collapse of their marriage, according to court documents and a press release from the Montgomery County District Attorney's Office.

U.S. Marshals arrested Jean Louis on Friday morning in Philadelphia on charges related to overstaying his visa, which he had originally obtained through a now-terminated relief program for Haitian nationals. The district attorney's office then charged him in connection with the murder while he was in federal custody, authorities said.

"At 9 AM on Friday, October 23rd, Destino Jean Louis, 23, was arrested by [U.S. Marshals Service Philadelphia] on the 6600 block of N. 18th St for immigration violations. Louis, a Haitian national who overstayed his visa, was the prime suspect in the October 21st fatal shooting of a 45 year-old Walmart employee who had just left her shift," U.S. Marshals Service Philadelphia wrote in a Monday post on X.

ICE ARRESTS SOUTHWEST AIRLINES FLIGHT ATTENDANT IN NASHVILLE FOR ALLEGEDLY OVERSTAYING VISA SINCE 2021

Jean Louis' victim, identified by authorities as 45-year-old Latosha Ann Cooper, was his estranged wife who he had married in March. Investigators told Fox29 that immigration officials had determined the marriage to be not legitimate and was only for immigration purposes.

AMERICAN WOMAN MASTERMINDS $6 MILLION MARRIAGE FRAUD SCHEME, DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE SAYS

In July, Cooper withdrew her petition to sponsor Jean Louis' visa, according to documents reviewed by Fox29.

Jean Louis allegedly hid near a bush outside of the Walmart where Cooper worked, wearing a mask, and waited for her to end her night shift, according to Montgomery Country District Attorney Kevin Steele.

CALIFORNIA WOMAN CHASED, FATALLY SHOT BY ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT DOORDASH DRIVER WHO STALKED HER FOR MONTHS: DHS

"When Cooper left the store, he ran towards her and fatally shot her," according to court documents.

Court filings also revealed that Jean Louis, a former employee at the same Walmart who was terminated for immigration reasons, had previously physically assaulted Cooper and repeatedly contacted store staff to request Cooper's work schedule.

Prosecutors also determined from phone records that Jean Louis had taken multiple trips between his residence in Philadelphia and the Walmart location in Cheltenham the weeks leading up to the shooting, the documents stated.

Jean Louis is being charged with murder in the first degree, murder in the third degree, illegal alien use of a firearm, carrying a firearm without a license and possession of an instrument with intent to commit a crime, according to court documents.

Fox News Digital contacted the Montgomery County District Attorney's Office for further information.

World.title: Colts trade Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to Seahawks, the first of what could be multiple deadline moves
World.content:
The Indianapolis Colts appear to be waving a white flag on the 2026 season, with the first sign coming Tuesday when they traded perennial Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks.

The Seahawks are giving up a third-round pick in the 2027 draft and a fifth-round pick in the 2028 draft for Nelson — a 30-year-old anchor of the Indianapolis offensive line who has been selected to eight Pro Bowls in each of his previous eight seasons.

And this makes sense on multiple levels.

SEAHAWKS DOMINATE CHIEFS 20-3 AS SAM DARNOLD SILENCES CRITICS IN POTENTIAL SUPER BOWL PREVIEW

The Colts are struggling through a disappointing season where they find themselves with a 2-5 record and mired in a three-game losing skid. They've already fired general manager Chris Ballard and the next general manager will need draft capital to rebuild a veteran team that gave up multiple first-round picks last year at the trade deadline for cornerback Sauce Gardner.

The Seahawks, meanwhile, are coming off an impressive victory over the previously undefeated Kansas City Chiefs and are taking an opportunity to upgrade their offensive line as they try to defend their Super Bowl title.

With Nelson coming aboard, the club will likely move 2025 first-round pick Grey Zabel from left guard to right guard where he played in college at North Dakota State.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The Colts will not admit this is a garage sale. That would be frowned upon by the NFL.

But everyone knows. As recently as the weekend, the wife of running back Jonathan Taylor said her family is on "a Colts transaction watch," signaling Taylor and other players are aware of the current uncertain situation in Indianapolis.

OutKick and Fox News Digital included Nelson's name among the Colts players who could be trade targets before the Nov. 10 NFL trade deadline.

Nelson makes sense to trade because, while he is an outstanding player, he is also unsigned for 2027. So the Colts might have lost him in free agency.

The idea they could keep him now and still get a compensatory pick if they lost him in free agency is mitigated by the fact that comp pick would come in 2028. The higher draft pick Indy is getting in this trade comes in 2027.

Other names of Colts players OutKick and Fox News Digital have reported could be traded include:

RB Jonathan Taylor.

A couple of other Colts players who might be traded are WRs Josh Downs and Keenan Allen.

And all this comes with the understanding that everyone not named Tyler Warren is probably available in trade. Whether or not trades happen depends on interest from other teams and the price the Colts are willing to accept.

One more thing: Ed Dodds in currently the interim general manager in Indianapolis. He is in charge of the apparent deconstruction of the 2026 Colts.

World.title: Britain's sweeping new crackdown on 'anti-social' behavior sparks free speech backlash: 'Peak insanity'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The United Kingdom introduced new "Respect Orders" across England and Wales on Monday, giving authorities expanded powers to crack down on persistent "anti-social" behavior and drawing criticism from free-speech advocates concerned about potential government overreach.

The U.K. government’s order enables police and councils to take stronger "enforcement action" against "adult offenders" of persistent "anti-social" behavior, according to a government news release.

Under the new restrictions, U.K. courts could ban offenders from town centers or prohibit them from drinking in "public hotspots" like local parks, the announcement states. Courts can impose restrictions and requirements through a civil Respect Order, while individuals who breach an order without a reasonable excuse can face criminal prosecution, including potentially unlimited fines or imprisonment.

Under the legislation governing the Respect Orders, anti-social behavior is defined as conduct that has caused, or is likely to cause, harassment, alarm or distress to any person. The definition has prompted concerns from critics that the powers could be applied too broadly, although the law requires judicial approval before an order can be imposed.

UK PRIME MINISTER SAYS FOOTBALL FANS 'SINGLED OUT' BY ALCOHOL BAN NOT IMPOSED ON RUGBY MATCHES

"Unchecked, anti-social [behavior] blights our communities," Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said in a statement. "But it is not inevitable and I won’t accept it. For too long, we have lacked the powers we need to deal with this problem properly. From today, that changes: authorities will be able to take tough action against these offenders."

"This delivers on a commitment we made to the British people in our manifesto," Mahmood continued. "And, most importantly, those who make life a misery for others will now face the consequences of their actions."

Some offenders may be required to "tackle" the "root causes" of their behavior by participating in drug or alcohol treatment or anger-management programs, according to the announcement.

Violating a respect order is considered a criminal offense, giving police the power to arrest anyone on charges of violating the rules, per the press release. Those who defy an order could also face up to two years of jail time.

When reached for comment, the U.K. Cabinet Office referred Fox News Digital to the Home Office, which could not immediately be reached for comment.

Alan Mendoza, co-founder and executive director of U.K.-based think tank the Henry Jackson Society, told Fox News Digital on Tuesday that "vague" definitions under the government's respect orders could result in such enforcement actions being wrongfully "applied to lawful speech or protest."

"I think the breadth of these orders deserves scrutiny, particularly in the case of potentially unlimited fines," Mendoza explained. "The government has a legitimate duty to tackle genuinely antisocial behaviour, but the powers need to be tightly defined and proportionate. Vague or elastic definitions could allow measures intended for serious nuisance or harassment to be applied to lawful speech or protest. We have already seen similar after all with social media posts and police investigations that follow."

"There should be clear statutory limits, proper evidence requirements, judicial oversight and an effective right of appeal," he added. "Online criticism, however unwelcome, should not be treated as antisocial [behavior] simply because it is unpopular or embarrassing to those in authority."

UK POLICE APOLOGIZE TO 'FATHER TED' CREATOR GRAHAM LINEHAN FOR ARREST OVER TRANS SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS

Mendoza went on to say that the U.K. government "should be able to demonstrate that these powers are necessary and contain adequate safeguards against arbitrary or disproportionate use."

The orders notably replace civil injunctions for adult offenders and grant U.K. police more enforcement powers, "including the ability to arrest anyone who breaches an order," according to the announcement.

The new restrictions have drawn intense criticism across social media, with one X user claiming in a Monday post that the orders are "mental," while another X account referred to the rules as "peak insanity."

"Laugh all you want at what a joke England has become, but understand that the U.S. will follow right behind if Democrats ever take full power again," the Federalist CEO and co-founder Sean Davis wrote Monday in an X post.

Tech and free speech lawyer Preston Byrne similarly took to social media to criticize the orders, saying that U.K. residents should "keep in mind that one can cause 'harassment, alarm, or distress' in England and Wales by uttering a true statement of fact to someone who doesn't want to hear it, or by offering an honestly-held opinion or belief, spoken or written, which also offends."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

British political commentator Calvin Robinson wrote in a Monday X post responding to the orders that "this tyranny must end."

The U.K. has notably enacted a spate of laws restricting free speech in recent years, including the 2023 Online Safety Act, which gives the country's regulator the authority to impose major fines on digital platforms if they fail to comply with certain requirements.

The new restrictions come amid growing tensions across Europe, where protests and riots have rocked countries, most notably France.

World.title: Serbia’s student movement topples Vucic’s party after 14 years, but political agenda remains unclear
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Serbia’s longtime leader, President Aleksandar Vucic, conceded defeat Sunday to the student-led opposition in an election that sent shock waves throughout Europe and the Western Balkans.

"We do not have the final results yet, and many people will be surprised. Based on a stratified sample, it is clear that we have lost these elections. The student-led protest list has won," Vucic said in an address to the nation Sunday night.

The Student List victory brings an end to 14 years of Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party rule, in what many are saying is the biggest political shake-up in the Balkans since the toppling of Yugoslav dictator Slobodan Milosevic in 2000.

Observers say the Student List party's policies remain vague, which has some worried about Serbia's future.

Ana Brnabic, vice president of the main Board of the Serbian Progressive Party, told Fox News Digital that, "The election victory of the Student List recalls similar electoral triumphs in other countries. The Student List represents a classical anti-establishment movement: it had neither a program nor a coherent political ideology. In an essentially anarchic fashion, it opposed everything, claiming to fight for justice and against corruption."

ANTI‑CORRUPTION PROTESTS HIT EUROPEAN NATION AS CALLS FOR NEW ELECTIONS GROW

She added, "After 14 years of Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) rule, people may have wanted change. That is understandable and logical. But the grim consequences of this movement in power will soon become apparent."

Turnout reached 69 %, the highest this century, with more than 4.4 million people casting their ballots, according to Rasa Nedeljkov, head of the CRTA Election Observation Mission.

"This is by all means a historic victory and indeed a surprise to many. While it was clear from the beginning that the students will have an impressive result, very few expected a landslide," Helena Ivanov, associate fellow at the Henry Jackson Society, told Fox News Digital.

The Election Observation Mission reported that the Student List won 52.45 % of the vote and is projected to hold 138 of 250 seats in the National Assembly, an absolute majority, allowing it to form a government on its own.

Vucic won 39.2 % and is projected to hold 103 seats.

Supporters celebrated throughout Belgrade and across Serbia as it became clear the Student List won by a larger margin that caught many experts and observers by surprise.

Many claimed they were concerned about the possibility of violence escalating as polls began to close. Almost two hours after polling stations closed, Vucic addressed the nation, confirming his defeat and announcing the peaceful transfer of power.

FRANCE ROCKED BY STUDENT RIOTS AS HUNDREDS ARRESTED, VIOLENCE SPREADS NATIONWIDE

"The path to an electoral victory with such a decisive margin will undoubtedly earn its own chapter in the handbooks on how to topple an autocrat. Two years of unprecedented grassroots mobilization, creative organization and impeccable campaigning kept the student list two steps ahead of the regime. Vučić was left playing catch-up, and all his attempts to co-opt, demoralize and fragment the movement failed," Sinisa Vukovic, director of the Global Policy Program at the School of Advanced International Studies at Johns Hopkins University, told Fox News Digital.

The CRTA Election Observation Mission reported that the campaign was marked by the abuse of state resources, pressure on candidates and voters, attempts to bring the media under total government control, and attacks on independent election observers.

Tens of thousands of Serbians volunteered to run and monitor polling stations across the country, and the vote was mostly peaceful.

SERBIA, CAUGHT BETWEEN EUROPE AND RUSSIA, COULD MOVE ONE STEP CLOSER TO NORMALIZING RELATIONS WITH KOSOVO

Student led protests marched in the streets for two years after the deaths of 16 people following the collapse of a railway station in the town of Novi Sad in November 2024. People had taken to the streets, demanding justice for those killed and accountability for anyone responsible for the disaster.

The momentum of nearly two years of street demonstrations culminated in a nationwide movement ready for change. The political novices were able to rally the nation behind a simple message against corruption and state capture.

Serbs across the country embraced the Student List, who are viewed as fresh faces in politics and are not tied to Serbia’s traditional political opposition, which is perceived as ineffective and corrupt by a lot of the voters.

EXCLUSIVE: SERBIAN PRESIDENT VUČIĆ SAYS SUPPORT FOR US 'SURGED' UNDER TRUMP, INVITES HIM TO VISIT BELGRADE

Milos Jevtic, a 48-year-old professor with the Faculty of Organizational Sciences at the University of Belgrade, was among the many Student List candidates who won a seat in parliament.

Jevtic told Fox News Digital that their victory came from the values that the students have stood for from the very beginning: expertise, professionalism, responsibility, solidarity and unity.

"What is particularly important is that the students have never compromised on these values and principles. Of course, widespread public dissatisfaction also played a major role, along with a lack of trust in both the current regime and the opposition parties," Jevtic explained.

Jevtic said he believes the priorities for the new Student List-run government should be economic stability, fighting corruption, establishing the rule of law and strengthening institutions, much of what carried the student-led protests since 2024.

"The ultimate goal is to build a system in which institutions function in the interests of all citizens," Jevtic said.

On foreign policy, there is an expectation that there will be a certain degree of continuity with the Vucic administration in international relations, including maintaining good relations with neighboring European countries and all major international partners.

But Brnabic warned that "Serbia has lost meaningful political pluralism. After 35 years of a multiparty system, the country is effectively left with one established political party, SNS, while the rest of the political scene is dominated by largely unknown movements without a clear ideology. This is catastrophic for any parliamentary democracy."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

She added, "Secondly, nobody in Serbia knows where the country is heading. Are we firmly pro-EU? Will we maintain our ties with Russia? What about China? Will we continue to enhance our relations with the United States — which was a priority of Aleksandar Vucic? Will economic policy be more left-liberal or conservative? Are we heading towards a woke liberal society, or will we preserve our traditional Orthodox Christian values? There are no clear answers to any of these questions."

She concluded by noting, "We have also called for Parliament and all state institutions to be constituted as soon as possible, so that the country has functioning institutions on which people can rely. We will be a strong but constructive opposition. We call on the Student List’s representatives to end the intimidation and assume the responsibility entrusted to them by the voters."

World.title: Reporter caught in violent Paris protests recalls how 'all of a sudden, it exploded' after peaceful march
World.content:

A New York Post reporter caught in the chaos of violent protests in Paris recounted how a peaceful march of more than 100,000 people took a frightening turn.

World.title: Ilhan Omar's radical streamer ally rallies with embattled lawmaker after DC home raid

Far-left streamer Hasan Piker dodged his controversial past in an exchange with Fox News Digital on Tuesday, hours after teaming up with embattled Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on the campaign trail to co-host an event in her home state of Minnesota.

He also dismissed his disagreements with Democratic Party leaders after he called Republicans "terrorists" and Omar said the GOP is the "pedophile protection party" during the stream on Monday.

Omar's decision to embrace Piker on the campaign trail marks a potentially risky political alliance, coming on the back of a high-profile raid on her Washington, D.C., home amid two dueling investigations — one for alleged immigration fraud, which could threaten her political future and citizenship status, and the other for fishy financial disclosure statement discrepancies.

The lawmaker's appearance with Piker comes after Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed drew backlash from his own party for campaigning with the controversial Twitch streamer earlier this cycle.

HASAN PIKER LASHES OUT AT REPUBLICANS, CALLS THEM 'TERRORISTS' IN EVENT WITH ILHAN OMAR

Fox News Digital confronted Piker at the Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport heading out of Minnesota after the Monday livestream. He was pressed on the criticism stemming from Rep. Angie Craig, D-Minn., and Minnesota gubernatorial candidate Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., after the two condemned Piker’s comments and pushed back on Democrats’ choice to engage with him on the campaign trail.

"Well, Angie Craig lost, and I think Klobuchar is going to make for a great governor," Piker told Fox News Digital while walking to security.

Klobuchar condemned Piker’s past statements as "reckless and unacceptable," while Craig called his rhetoric "polarizing and dangerous" and directly called out Minnesota Democrats, like Omar and Fateh, for hosting Monday’s event with Piker as a "mistake."

When asked if the two Democratic lawmakers in Minnesota were right to call out the rhetoric, Piker wrote off their disagreements as "the beauty of democracy," while also throwing jabs at Fox News.

"I know this is probably going to come across as confusing, because you work for Fox News, but we sometimes disagree with our leadership in the Democratic Party," he said. "And sometimes our leadership disagrees with us."

"But at the end of the day," he continued, "that's the beauty of democracy."

HASAN PIKER ADMITS HE HAS 'DIALED DOWN' HIS OPINIONS AFTER PUBLIC AND DEMOCRATIC BACKLASH

The controversy over the Somali-born congresswoman deciding to sit down with Piker with just over one week until the 2026 midterms exposes a divide among Minnesota Democrats — is it justifiable to work with Piker in order to rally his large, young, progressive base to get out and vote despite his heavily condemned commentary?

Piker was asked on Tuesday about his previous comments on Jewish people and Israel after prominent Democrats joined Republicans who have called the streamer antisemitic. He suggested that Jewish Americans were inviting violence against themselves over their support for Israel. He has repeatedly stood by his comments against Israel over its ongoing war against Hamas in Gaza.

"Anti-Zionism is not antisemitism," Piker told Fox News Digital.

"I will always fight against antisemitism and I find all bigotry to be morally repugnant and completely unacceptable. But I also find it a real shame to constantly complain about people who are outspoken on the issue of Israel's genocide."

It was after Democrats, including House Minority Leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., began calling out Piker for his extreme comments that El-Sayed distanced himself after frequently making appearances side-by-side.

Another reason why Omar’s choice to engage with Piker has been questioned within the party.

Piker refused to comment on one issue though — his past comments claiming America "deserved 9/11."

"You made some comments on 9/11, do you still stand by them?" Fox News Digital asked Piker, at which point he ignored the question and walked through the line for security.

Both Piker and Omar attacked President Donald Trump during their event Monday night, with the Somali-born lawmaker ripping his "obsession" with Minnesotans. Piker, meanwhile, shamed Democrats for ceding on immigration arguments to Trump's agenda back in 2024.

REP ILHAN OMAR'S IMMIGRATION HISTORY FACES NEW SCRUTINY AS FEDERAL INVESTIGATORS SUBPOENA RELATIVES

"That's unacceptable. Migrants are not a national security threat. They are our neighbors. They are allies. They work alongside us. They are not the burden, but a benefit. They are what make this country strong, and they're what make it this country great," Piker insisted.

"Any Democrat that refuses to recognize that, in my opinion, is un-American," he concluded.

Omar is running for reelection and projected for a clear win, despite being under investigation by both Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and the Department of Justice (DOJ) for immigration fraud and questionable financial filings.
