World.title: How Aldi is pushing down grocery prices
World.content:
How Aldi is pushing down grocery prices

toggle caption i Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images North America

In the summer of 2020, I lived briefly in Ithaca, New York. It's the only time I've lived near Aldi, the grocery store known for low prices. I went twice, and I thought it was fine, but underwhelming. I appreciated the low prices, but it didn't have everything I needed. The store was small and a bit shabby.

I didn't know it yet, but those are the exact ingredients that have made Aldi the fastest-growing grocery chain in America. Per Bloomberg , Aldi plans to have more than 3,000 American locations by the end of 2028, which would be more than any other chain but Walmart. In 2024, Aldi generated some $29 billion in U.S. sales, which is more than Trader Joe's.

Sponsor Message

Aldi is a German company known for having low, low prices, and it deserves that reputation. Food reporter Deena Shanker told me that her experience comparison shopping over many months was that Aldi either matched Walmart on price or was a bit cheaper. Grocers like Wegmans and Kroger have announced defensive price reductions, and an analysis published in late 2023 of Lidl, another German grocer with a very similar model to Aldi's but fewer U.S. stores, found that grocery chains reduced their markups ~7 percent in areas where Lidl stores opened .

All to say: Aldi is disrupting the grocery business and actually lowering prices even as the cost of food—at restaurants and other grocery stores—goes up and up.

Maybe this sounds a bit humdrum. But I found it totally intriguing and perplexing, because…

Walmart and Costco's business models depend on low prices, too, and they can offer low prices by having huge stores, giant warehouses, and incredible economies of scale that allow them to pay less for Oreo's, baby carrots, and Jif peanut butter than other grocers. So how the heck is Aldi matching or beating them on price? When a company disrupts a longstanding industry, it's typically a startup enabled by new technology—like Netflix using online streaming to disrupt Blockbuster and video rental. But Aldi is not staffed by futuristic robots. Its stores just look like grocery stores, and Aldi was founded 80 years ago, in post-war Germany. So what's going on? One of the proudest achievements of America's capitalistic market economy is providing its citizens an abundance of increasingly affordable food. Somewhat famously, Soviet leader Boris Yeltsin toured a grocery store in Houston during the Cold War and was amazed that the average American enjoyed more variety than top Soviet politicians. From 1960 to 2019, Americans spent less and less of their income on food each year , even as they enjoyed more frequent restaurant meals, more sushi, and far better beer. But since the pandemic, food has become less affordable. Can American markets no longer provide cheap groceries? Did something break?

Sponsor Message

One necessary but not sufficient explanation for Aldi's low prices is that management is obsessed with efficiency and cutting unnecessary costs. There's no music in stores, because speakers (and licensing fees for muzak) cost money. The staff places products on shelves still in the cardboard boxes they were trucked in on, because artfully unpacking fruits, bread, and jerky sticks would mean higher labor costs. The shabbiness is intentional — it's the cost of cheaper groceries.

But other grocery chains are similarly obsessed with efficiency. Here's one of my favorite examples about Costco, courtesy of Zachary Crockett and The Hustle : "In another instance, reengineering a container of cashews from a circle to a square shape allowed Costco to stack more items in a single truck, reducing the number of shipments by 24,000 pallets per year. For shoppers, this meant cheaper nuts."

Instead, Aldi's disruptively low prices rely on two primary tactics:

Private label products: On Aldi shelves, you can find cookies that look a heck of a lot like Oreos and boxes of what sure seem like Ritz crackers. But they are "Benton's Chocolate Sandwich Cookies with Vanilla Filling" and "Savoritz Golden Round crackers." Both are made by Aldi, and therefore cost less, since Aldi doesn't have to pay Nabisco's markup and then add their own. More than 80 percent of Aldi products are these store-brand versions—aka private-label products or, in the case of look-alike Oreos, dupes . Limited selection: When the Albrecht brothers took over their family's grocery store in 1946, they had a small store and limited funds for stocking the shelves. But this became their secret sauce: Stocking a very limited selection of items — just essentials like rice and eggs, and just one of each rather than a variety of brands, sizes, and versions — allowed them to keep prices low. They could buy in bulk, which is cheaper, and by not stocking niche products that sit on shelves for weeks or days, they saved even more by avoiding spoilage and limiting shelf space, storage areas, and rent or real-estate costs. Even as the brothers grew rich, they kept stores small and selection limited. This is less convenient— shoppers often have to visit another grocery store to grab things like white pepper that Aldi doesn't stock. But what Aldi does stock is cheaper.

Sponsor Message

Aldi's low prices made their stores very attractive during periods like the Great Recession and today's inflationary era. The Great Recession, especially, enabled their current growth. But if all Aldi offered was bargain prices in shabby stores, customers might flee to Costco, Kroger, or Whole Foods when the economy recovered.

So another key to Aldi's success is that it's fun. Aldi has a famously chaotic-good middle aisle with rotating buys like fun toys, German spätzle, and advent calendars that contain 24 festive cheeses. And its U.S. stores have expanded their offerings (a bit) to attract higher-income customers: Aldi doesn't just have the cheapest apples, but the cheapest honey crisp apples. Not just super-duper cheap wine but well-priced "premium" wine.

Instead of being a sad place to shop when you're low on cash, Aldi has more flea-market energy: a place anyone might go to hunt for good deals and fun finds. Aldi is beloved; many customers are cult-like in their devotion . In some cases, customers line up for new store openings like early iPhone releases.

My main takeaway from researching and analyzing Aldi for several weeks (for an episode of Gastronomics !) is that there's always something new under the sun. American grocery stores are a mature market. They seem pretty stable equilibrium-y. But they are dynamic and always changing. Aldi didn't need futuristic tech to disrupt the industry; just a strategy developed 80 years ago, then tweaked for the American market. In healthy markets, there's always a way in for new competitors.

My other takeaway is greater appreciation for the famous business idiom: "There are only two ways to make money in business: One is to bundle; the other is to unbundle."

The clearest example of bundling and unbundling is probably television. Cable companies bundled hundreds of TV channels together and charged one high fee for all of them. Then streaming services like Netflix made money by unbundling television — by allowing people to pay for just Netflix. Which felt liberating! For a few years. But now customers are annoyed about subscribing to so many streaming services. So streamers are teaming up to form bundles, like getting Disney, Hulu, and HBO Max all for one reduced price. Now, to make money, you gotta bundle.

Sponsor Message

Even the person who coined the phrase about bundling and unbundling didn't think it's literally the only way to make money. Still, I often failed to see (un)bundling as a powerful framework outside of the media industry. Until I realized that Aldi is unbundling the grocery store.

For a long time, grocery stores got more bundled. People once went to the baker, the butcher, and the greengrocer. Then the super market put all those things under one roof. And then Walmart, Target, and Costco created superstores where you could buy groceries and clothes and big-screen TVs.

Now Aldi is reversing this process by unbundling the grocery store. Not only does Aldi not have the big-screen TVs and dupes of Lululemon hoodies and pants , it doesn't even have everything on your grocery list. Aldi unbundled the part of the grocery business it can do super cheaply, and it intentionally locates Aldi stores near competitor grocery stores so shoppers can easily go grab the last few things on their list (the rest of the bundle).

With this in mind, I've started seeing bundling and unbundling at work in more and more industries. If you look closely at your own, I suspect you will, too.

My third takeaway is that I just didn't live in Ithaca long enough to grok Aldi. If I'd been there longer, I bet I would have made Aldi part of a multi-store strategy. I get it now! Aldi, please come to Colorado (where I live)!

At the start of this post, I asked three questions inspired by Aldi's expansion. The first two, which are about how Aldi achieved a comparative advantage, I feel like I've answered.

The third was whether the American economy can still deliver a bounty of affordable food. I think the way Aldi's growth pressured competitors to keep prices low shows that grocers are not the right target of our ire over food prices. But grocery stores are just one slice of the food world.

World.title: Can Black voting power and Trump fatigue break Mississippi's red wall?
World.content:
Can Black voting power and Trump fatigue break Mississippi's red wall?

toggle caption i Stephen Fowler/NPR

COLUMBUS, Miss. — On paper, Mississippi's U.S. Senate race seems like the perfect place for a political upset this year, an assertion President Trump's Monday rally there seems to support.

It has the highest share of Black voters in the country, at close to 40%. It's a rural, agriculture-heavy state that is also among the poorest, so higher prices are felt harder.

But President Trump won the state by 23 points in 2024, and it's extremely racially polarized, meaning not enough white voters back Democrats for the party to win statewide.

In a midterm environment that has seen hundreds of millions of dollars poured into Senate races in conservative-heavy states like Iowa, Texas, Ohio and Alaska, and a last-minute flood of cash to Kansas, the Magnolia state has been left off of many peoples' radar — and largely out of campaign investments.

Sponsor Message

Scott Colom, a district attorney and the Democratic Senate nominee in Mississippi, told NPR that's a mistake.

"The reality is, Mississippi has never been a lost cause, we've been a betrayed cause," he said. "The Democratic Party has not been trying to win Mississippi. Let's stop kidding ourselves, right? They spent hundreds of millions of dollars in other states. They spent almost nothing in Mississippi."

Colom is challenging incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith, who blocked his nomination to be a federal judge during the Biden administration.

In the final weeks of the election, both parties have rushed to spend millions of dollars in Mississippi, as national polling shows a pathway where Democratic enthusiasm and elevated Black turnout, combined with fewer Republican base voters and defections from the party, has made deep red races deeply competitive this cycle.

'The moral compass of this country is gone'

toggle caption i Stephen Fowler/NPR

At a rally for Colom in his hometown high school gym Thursday, about a thousand people showed up to hear the candidate — joined by former Vice President Kamala Harris — give his closing message.

Many attendees expressed optimism for his campaign coupled with a vibe of feeling down about those in power, regardless of party affiliation – citing the war in Iran, rising fuel costs and dissatisfaction with Trump's second term.

Sponsor Message

That includes Celestine Rice, who said many people were realizing a need to focus on bringing change to the political system and representation.

"Before, we didn't realize how bad it was, but now it's obvious," she said. "The moral compass of this country is gone."

Rice said many people took for granted an era where it seemed the country used to be more focused on taking care of its citizens and now they see that "big money, it doesn't trickle down like they said."

The brunt of the Democratic money and manpower headed to Mississippi is driven by a growing number of those who argue the party's future runs through the South, including Harris, Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock and former transportation secretary Pete Buttigieg.

At the rally, Harris said political changes in the last year and a half were the result of "the most callous, corrupt and incompetent presidential administration we have ever experienced."

"We've been going through that range of emotions from anger to sadness to depression, all of that for a year and a half," she said. "Well guess what? We're 12 days out from an election. And it's time to turn that anger into action."

'Most radical Senate candidate'

toggle caption i Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

About a hundred miles up the road a few days later, Trump, Hyde-Smith and other Mississippi Republicans gathered in Corinth to motivate the party's base to show up and vote next Tuesday.

In a statement ahead of the rally, Hyde-Smith's campaign manager expressed confidence in her reelection bid.

"We are confident that Mississippians will once again send Cindy Hyde-Smith to the U.S. Senate," Jake Monssen said. "Senator Hyde-Smith and President Trump have built a strong working relationship, and she gladly accepted when President Trump offered to help rally voters and support her get-out-the-vote efforts.

"With so much at stake in this election, Mississippians deserve to hear directly from their President about the consequences of electing Democrats, the radical socialist policies being pushed by Scott Colom, and the importance of this election. Team Cindy looks forward to a successful, high-energy event in Corinth," he said.

Sponsor Message

Speaking ahead of the president, Hyde-Smith touted accomplishments from her time in office and said the choice facing voters "could not be clearer."

"We know what we're looking at: this is socialism versus capitalism, and we know that," she said. "Communism versus democracy, and big government versus the free market. It could not be higher stakes."

Hyde-Smith repeatedly reiterated that it was important for Republicans to get out and vote.

"Endorsements don't win elections, votes win elections," she said.

toggle caption i Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

For his part, Trump said his visit to Mississippi was because Hyde-Smith was in good shape in her matchup.

"Sometimes when you think somebody's doing so well, nobody votes," Trump said. "'Oh, Cindy's great, she's gonna do no problem, let's stay home.' And then bad things happen, Cindy. That's why I'm here, just get out and vote."

Over the last month, the Republican campaign strategy has been to highlight the investment and attention from national Democrats as proof Colom is too extreme for Mississippi — and have spent heavily on ads saying as much.

"Meet the most radical Senate candidate in our lifetime, Scott Colom," an ad titled "Most Radical" intones. "Twice nominated by Biden, beholden to the far left. As DA, violent crime doubled on his watch."

The Hyde-Smith campaign has spent more than $1.3 million on that ad, according to data from AdImpact.

But Democrats have spent more this month, about $5 million to the Republicans' $3.2 million, with a message that there's no daylight between the unpopular president and down ballot Republicans.

Colom thinks voters agree.

"I mean, the reality is if somebody's doing a good job, it's hard to beat them," he said. "If Cindy Hyde-Smith was focused on the voters, it'd be tough. But it's very clear the voters of Mississippi want to fire her."

Black voter turnout key

The race carries weight beyond Mississippi, or even control of the Senate. It's become a stand in for conversations about the power of Black voters in the South.

Sponsor Message

Many Southern Republican-led states have rushed to redraw Congressional maps that remove opportunities for Black voters to elect candidates of their choice after a Supreme Court ruling earlier this year rolled back part of the Voting Rights Act.

In Mississippi, Republicans have signaled a desire to redraw state legislative and judicial races after the midterms, and Colom said it could extend even further into local elections.

"What that tells us is you're trying to take away power from the voters and give it to the leaders," he said. "That's not how democracy is supposed to work. The voters have to pick the leaders, not the leaders pick the voters.

In a statewide race that can't be gerrymandered, and in an environment favorable to Democrats, history and math still prove to be a challenge. The last Democratic Senator from Mississippi came in the early 80s. The last successful Black statewide candidate was during Reconstruction.

Even during the 2018 blue wave, Cindy Hyde-Smith won a special election for this seat by roughly 7 points.

Still, there are many factors that have both parties anxiously awaiting results on Nov. 3, including a pervasive anti-incumbent streak that has shown up in polls and primaries this election cycle coupled with a significant increase in Black voter turnout in states that have early voting.

Ashley Kennedy Shelton, who runs a nonpartisan civic engagement group in Louisiana, told NPR earlier this month that people of all stripes have been expressing frustration and a desire for change.

"I think you're going to see voters truly show up, because folks are just tired," she said. "They're like: 'This doesn't work, and it hasn't been working for quite some time.' I think you're going to see it at the ballot box.

World.title: Polymarket has investigated 'dozens' of election-related cases
World.content:
Polymarket has investigated 'dozens' of election-related cases

toggle caption i Gabby Jones/AFP via Getty Images

Polymarket has investigated "dozens" of bets on its prediction markets related to the midterm election, according to the company's head of global intelligence and investigations, Shana Bautista.

At least two of these Polymarket investigations have been referred to its regulator, the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, according to a person who is familiar with the probes, but not authorized to speak publicly about them.

These investigations into election insider trading and manipulation come as prediction market Polymarket — and its chief competitor Kalshi — have exploded in popularity over the past year. But the fast-growing industry also faces significant legal challenges from states and political pushback from lawmakers who argue betting on the outcome of elections poses serious risks to the democratic process.

Sponsor Message

In April, Kalshi banned and fined a handful of political candidates from betting on themselves. A month later, NPR reported that campaign staffers had made "thousands" using insider polling information to bet on their own candidates on platforms like Polymarket and PredictIt.

Polymarket's Bautista — a former FBI official and cryptocurrency analyst — told NPR her team of 16 and a new election surveillance system are actively policing election bets ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.

"If you have information that you have a duty to protect, don't trade on it," Bautista said. "It's explicitly against our terms of use on both platforms, but also is against the law. If you decide that you are smarter and can do it, we will find you."

Bautista joined Polymarket in June. She oversees information gathered from both the U.S.-regulated version of Polymarket, which requires users to provide their real identities, and its bigger brother, Polymarket International, which is essentially unregulated and where trading can be done anonymously and with cryptocurrency. Despite this, Bautista said crypto trades are rarely completely anonymous.

"There's never been a case that we work where we haven't been able to identify, potentially, who these people are," Bautista said.

She said her election surveillance system pulls in "gigabytes" of data on each user from social media, Federal Election Commission data, cryptocurrency companies, banking partners, statistical models and other public information sources. If a user hits a certain number of internally-defined red flags, Bautista gets an alert on her phone.

Sponsor Message

"We're getting hundreds of alerts a day," Bautista said.

When asked about the specific detection criteria and thresholds, Bautista did not comment citing system security. But she said insider trading and market manipulation all look the same regardless of the financial market.

"We're looking at threat vectors and risk areas that have existed for decades in traditional markets," Bautista said. "But we recognize, too, that when it comes to prediction markets, we're seeing some of the old tried and known tactics, but being applied to a new vector through prediction markets."

Back in May, Kalshi, Polymarket's top rival, announced its own election surveillance system that also uses FEC data. Their system purportedly blocks any campaign staffer listed by the FEC from betting on an election. In July, Kalshi said it had blocked "dozens" of staffers from trading on elections, though at least one staffer told NPR they got around this. The staffer shared records of their recent trades and spoke to NPR on the condition of anonymity for fear of consequences for their future employment.

Prediction markets for elections are uniquely vulnerable to market manipulation and insider trading, said Rajiv Sethi, an economics professor at Barnard College at Columbia University, who has studied prediction markets for decades.

"[Election prediction markets] have the possibility of being a self-fulfilling prophecy," Sethi said. "Elections have the property that what one believes is going to happen can actually affect what happens if a candidate is thought to be losing momentum or the campaign is flagging."

Bautista said her Polymarket team and surveillance system is learning from past cases and putting their feet in the shoes of would-be insider traders and market manipulators.

"If I was worried about somebody trying to materially move an election market to make it look like one option was more likely to happen than the other and I identify a pattern where they're opening several different accounts and they're doing that in short bursts and I see device IDs consistent across different trades placed in short succession with new wallets across five or four different accounts," Bautista said. "If I were to work that case and then action that, the findings of that tactic go back into the process to create the detections."

Sponsor Message

As prediction markets have exploded in popularity over the last two years, the industry's federal regulator, the CFTC, has done little to police these new financial markets, largely leaving that work to the companies themselves.

World.title: Canada's new relationship with EU will be 'closer to membership' than ever, senior officials say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

European Union officials say the details and exact title of Canada's possible associate EU membership are still being internally debated — but the 27 countries are united in wanting the "closest possible association" with Canada.

Canada will host the EU at a summit in Montreal this week where the two sides are expected to announce new agreements on a number of key areas of co-operation, including trade, security and technology.

This year's meeting will be one of the "most important summits the European Union has ever held," one senior EU official said, speaking on background during a press briefing Tuesday morning in Brussels.

"It's building a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we've ever done before."

WATCH | Is Canada joining the EU? Is Canada becoming an ‘associate member’ of the European Union? | Duration 2:05 Associate membership? Strategic alliance? Whatever you want to call it, Prime Minister Mark Carney's push for deeper ties to Europe are well underway. The CBC’s Marina von Stackelberg breaks down some of the changes Canadians could see should Ottawa and Brussels formalize the agreement.

However, the process is just getting started, officials stressed.

"This is uncharted territory. This is also the work that will need to be done between now and the next summit," they said, which is expected to be held in 2027.

The officials acknowledged some member states have questions about what Canada's new role will actually mean.

"There is no questioning from the member state side on their ambition for this relationship," an official said.

Carney says summit launches year of talks

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen surprised many last month when she announced the EU would begin the process of making Canada its first "associate member," a status that does not exist within the bloc.

Prime Minister Mark Carney responded the next day during a speech to the European Parliament that Canada welcomed "the ambition" of associate membership, later telling reporters it was the substance of the relationship that mattered more than the name itself.

Speaking on Tuesday in Ottawa on his way into a cabinet meeting, Carney reiterated that stance, saying the two-day summit that begins Thursday would be the launch of formal discussions and negotiations over the next year.

WATCH | Carney speaks about the upcoming EU-Canada summit: EU agreement 'names or nomenclature' don't matter, says Carney | Duration closed caption 0:42 Prime Minister Mark Carney says what 'matters' at the EU summit set to take place later this week in Montreal is 'Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation so we can live our lives as we choose.'

"The good news is it doesn't matter about specific names or nomenclature," Carney said.

"What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians … and Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation, so we can live our lives as we choose."

Associate membership would be unique to Canada

There are many unanswered questions about what associate membership would require from Canada and what it would mean for the other European countries that have spent years trying to join the EU.

Officials said Tuesday this type of associate membership would be specific to Canada.

"We're embarking on the start of a journey, so let's not already now determine exactly how far we go," they said.

Officials would not say whether other countries had approached the EU looking to form a similar relationship as Canada's.

Carney has repeatedly stated that Canada is not seeking full EU membership, and often refers to the enhanced partnership as a "strategic alliance."

The prime minister has been aggressively seeking out stronger diplomatic and trade ties with other countries, including in Europe, as relations between the U.S. and Canada continue to suffer under the trade war, with U.S. President Donald Trump's escalating tariffs and ongoing threats to annex Canada.

World.title: Everyone’s going on — and off — GLP-1s. What’s that doing to your health?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

At a bridal shop in downtown Halifax, Beverley Smith is trying on wedding dresses, but there’s a catch: She's rapidly losing weight since starting a GLP-1.

The 32-year-old has already gone on and off several types of these popular medications to manage weight gain and other side-effects linked to polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), but decided to get serious about her health before getting married next summer.

She’s lost more than 30 pounds since starting the drug tirzepatide back in March, and says related symptoms — like joint pain — have improved as well.

Now she’s asking the same question as millions of GLP-1 users around the world: Is it possible to one day stop taking the drug that’s changed life for the better?

"When you are going off it … do you taper off of it or do you stop abruptly?" Smith wondered. "What is this really going to look like in the long term?"

As these blockbuster drugs explode in popularity, with more people using them off-label for short-term weight loss, scientists are also striving to find an answer.

"This is a real-world situation that needs to be studied," said Dr. Thomas Leung, a clinician-scientist at the University of Pennsylvania, who’s among the researchers doing exactly that.

WATCH | Researchers concerned about using GLP-1 for crash dieting: Researchers worried about use of GLP-1s for crash dieting | Duration 2:30 Traditionally, GLP-1s have been seen as long-term, even lifelong, medications used to manage diabetes or tackle obesity. But what about those interested in using them for short-term weight loss? There’s little research on how these drugs work in people without conditions like diabetes or obesity, and even less study on short-term 'crash' diets — but doctors do have evidence it's already having an impact.

Microdosing, drug cycling and more

GLP-1 drugs work by suppressing blood sugar, controlling appetite and slowing stomach emptying, all by mimicking their namesake hormone, glucagon-like peptide-1, which is released after you eat.

While these medications only became part of the zeitgeist in the last few years — driven by celebrity endorsements, before hitting the mainstream — they’ve been around for more than two decades.

The earliest forms were studied and approved to treat Type 2 diabetes. Later, options arrived for chronic weight management. What’s relatively new is the myriad ways people are using these medications, often with minimal medical supervision.

At a private appointment inside Kind Bridal in Halifax, Beverley Smith tries on a wedding dress and discusses alterations to accommodate her ongoing weight loss while using a GLP-1. (Hugo Levesque/CBC)

Many patients — or as some drugmakers now call them, "customers" — are treating GLP-1s like a yo-yo diet rather than taking them long term to manage chronic health conditions.

They’re ever easier to get through online pharmacies. And pill forms, versus injections, are becoming more accessible. (Though not yet available in Canada, there is a pill-based form of semaglutide for weight loss — the drug best known by the brand name Ozempic — already approved in the U.S. from drugmaker Novo Nordisk, alongside a pill version of orforglipron from Eli Lilly.)

Scroll through social media and it’s easy to find a range of short-term uses, from bodybuilders cycling through different types of GLP-1s (and steroids, too) alongside their gym routines to women "microdosing" the drugs off and on to manage menopausal weight gain to brides and grooms doing quick stints to lose weight before their wedding day.

One recent study from a Danish research team looked at the use of semaglutide for obesity and found roughly half of adults stopped treatment within just 12 months.

WATCH | How GLP-1s could treat dozens of conditions: Ozempic, other GLP-1 drugs may help with dozens of other conditions | Duration 2:04 A new study published in the journal Nature Medicine suggests that GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy could have a host of other potential benefits beyond treating obesity, including a reduction in drug and alcohol abuse and Alzheimer's disease.

Stop-and-start approach could hinder weight loss

It’s a trend Dr. Leung, the researcher from the University of Pennsylvania, noticed in his own social circle in recent years, as more of his friends and colleagues wanted to try GLP-1s just to drop a few pounds.

Some talked about wanting to shed weight before a vacation or to look good on Instagram or just to feel healthier. The common thread? A desire to go on the meds, then get off them as fast as possible.

"No one had really studied what happens when you model what human behaviour is, which is starting and stopping these drugs," Leung said. "So we’re like, OK, well, obviously you can’t test this in humans. But we can try to do this in mice."

Leung and his research team did exactly that , and found cycling overweight mice through GLP-1 use seemed to make the drugs less effective over time. Mice who started and stopped the drugs every two weeks struggled to lose weight compared to mice who stayed on GLP-1s for the entire months-long study.

Even after two months of consistent use at the end of the study period, the drug-cycling group remained 20 per cent heavier.

If that was happening to mice, Leung started to wonder: What’s actually happening inside the bodies of human patients stopping and starting these body-changing drugs?

WATCH | Is Ozempic the future of addiction treatment?: Ozempic: the future of addiction treatment? | Duration closed caption 1:55 From gambling and alcohol to pornography, Ozempic and GLP-1 drugs could soon be used to cure all manner of addictions. Watch The Ozempic Effect: Beyond the Waistline on CBC Gem.

'Buyer beware' when using GLP-1s off-label

Dr. Sean Wharton sees that regularly in his own patients at the Wharton Medical Clinic for weight and diabetes management in Burlington, Ont.

"People are using it off-label often. Maybe they heard about something on the internet or on Facebook. And if they're using it in this manner off-label, then it’s … buyer beware," he said.

"Because I don't know what type of negative aspects could potentially happen. There could be mainly positive and no negative aspects, but we don't exactly know yet."

Wharton stressed this growing class of drugs has clear benefits as a long-term treatment for obesity, which has a dangerous domino effect on other health issues, like inflammation and cardiovascular disease, when left untreated.

Research also suggests GLP-1s may help curb substance use disorders, cut the severity of sleep apnea or even reduce cancer risk .

Dr. Sean Wharton is an internal medicine specialist and clinical researcher in obesity medicine in Toronto. (Craig Chivers/CBC)

Yet increasingly, these drugs are moving from tested treatment into what Wharton calls the "aesthetic medicine space" for short-term use. And he says the benefits likely vanish when patients rush back off these drugs.

"If losing the weight was the reason why your metabolic condition — like your heart failure, your high blood pressure — got better, then regaining the weight usually means that that blood pressure is going to go back up."

Last year, one major research review concluded that the "magnitude and consistency" of these kinds of health effects "underscore the physiological consequences of [GLP-1] discontinuation."

A key need, according to that research team, was treatment guidelines to also address how to stop using the drugs.

What's the best way to go off these drugs?

GLP-1 pioneer Dr. Daniel Drucker agrees with that approach. In Toronto, he’s helping lead a randomized controlled trial — the gold standard of health-care research — to find out the best way for people to safely stop taking the drugs that he helped bring to the masses.

The research team, which includes Wharton and Drucker’s colleague and fellow endocrinologist Dr. Caroline Kramer, is recruiting patients for a 16-week-long study period where they’ll go through regular bloodwork and other metrics to gauge the impact of slowly tapering off a GLP-1 compared to abruptly stopping.

"We’re trying to answer a very simple question: If someone wants to know, can they come off the GLP-1 medicines, what is the best way to do it?" Drucker told CBC News inside a lab at Mount Sinai Hospital.

"Pharmaceutical companies are not good at studying how to stop their medicine," Drucker said, "but we need to answer that question."

GLP-1 researchers Dr. Caroline Kramer, left, and Dr. Daniel Drucker are studying the best way to stop using these blockbuster drugs through a trial based out of Mount Sinai Hospital in Toronto. (Lauren Pelley/CBC)

Drucker is among those who sees huge potential for GLP-1s as a way to reduce the dire impacts of obesity — a public health crisis so widespread that just this year, the World Health Organization released its first-ever guidelines to manage obesity starting from childhood.

But tackling long-term medical issues usually requires long-term treatment, he stressed. When you discontinue minoxidil for hair regrowth, for example, hair loss restarts. If you suddenly stop taking statins, cholesterol spikes fast. Why would GLP-1s be any different?

"There is a lot of stigma around staying on a medicine to control your body weight for long periods of time, but we would never have anyone question if they had MS or Crohn's or hypertension or high cholesterol," Drucker said.

"I could list at least 125 diseases where you take the medication for the rest of your life to control the disease, but for some reason with the GLP-1 medicine, people think, well, you should be able to do this yourself."

Short-term use may 'cause more harm than good'

Kramer said there really hasn’t been research to help show if the cardiovascular benefits of being on a GLP-1 can be maintained by gradually tapering off rather than quickly stopping.

The team will also be watching for symptoms and adverse events, given there can be a range of side-effects from common stomach upset to acute pancreatitis to rare reports of vision loss .

Kramer's advice for Canadians who want to do a short-term stint on a weight-loss drug before her team’s results come in?

"Patients who want to shed, like, three pounds because, ‘I have a wedding in two weeks’ … that is not what the medications were meant for," she said.

"If you are thinking of taking a medication without the proper assessment over a short term … it may cause more harm than good."

World.title: These midterm races will decide who controls U.S. Congress for the rest of Trump's presidency
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The most important elections in next Tuesday's U.S. midterms are in the handful of states and districts where polling suggests the Republicans and Democrats are locked in tight races.

The Democratic Party needs a net gain of just three seats to take control of the 435-member House of Representatives, a target that polling analysis suggests is well within reach.

The far more difficult task for Democrats will be wresting control of the Senate from U.S. President Donald Trump's Republican Party.

To achieve a 51-49 Senate majority, Democrats need a net gain of four seats. That requires flipping at least two states Trump won by double digits in 2024, such as Ohio, Iowa, Alaska, Texas or Kansas.

Here's a look at the pivotal races to watch in Tuesday's midterm elections.

Senate: Maine

U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican representing Maine, speaks with gun shop owner Rick LaChapelle at a campaign stop in Lewiston, Me. on Oct. 21. (Robert F. Bukaty/The Associated Press)

Candidates: (R) Sen. Susan Collins vs. (D) Troy Jackson

Collins has held this seat for 30 years, even though Maine has not voted for a Republican presidential candidate since 1988.

Collins has kept winning elections by persuading enough Democrats that she gets results for Maine in Washington. Most recently, she took credit for Trump's moves to exempt certain Canadian products used by Maine businesses from the crushing 50 per cent tariffs he'd imposed in late August.

The question is whether Maine voters will punish Collins for being a Republican this time or reward her for the occasions when she stood up to Trump.

Her Democratic Party opponent is a former logger turned politician from a small town in northern Maine. Jackson entered the race only in July after the original nominee, Graham Platner, stepped down amid allegations he had sexually assaulted a former partner.

Key issues: Trump's posture toward Canada has led to a sharp drop in Canadians crossing the border to visit Maine. His war in Iran triggered a 74 per cent jump in the price of furnace oil, which roughly half of all households in the state use to heat their homes.

Senate: Michigan

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is hoping to put U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada on the ballot in Michigan this November. (Sylvia Thomson/CBC News)

Candidates: (D) Abdul El-Sayed vs (R) Mike Rogers

This seat was thrown open by incumbent Democrat Gary Peters' decision not to seek re-election. If Democrats can't hold Michigan, their path to a Senate majority becomes significantly tougher.

El-Sayed is a medical doctor and staunch progressive who was born in the U.S. to Egyptian immigrant parents. Since winning the Democratic nomination in August, he has become a frequent target of Trump's attacks.

Trump launched an Islamophobic rant against El-Sayed during a rally Sunday in the border town of Port Huron, Mich. The president called him a "jihadist" and warned that a Democratic win would bring "hordes of jihadis to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror."

Rogers, a former FBI agent who served in the House for 14 years, has attempted to put some distance between himself and Trump on Canada-U.S. relations. He launched a new ad this month in which he said, "We need to end this tariff war now," while sitting in a sports bar with a Labatt beer.

Key issues: Trump's tariffs on Canadian products and the breakdown in trade talks are causing upheaval in the auto industry, Michigan's economic engine. Michigan residents have faced higher tariff costs per household than any other state, according to a recent study by the National Taxpayers Union Foundation.

Senate: Ohio

Trump listens as Republican Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio speaks at a campaign rally in Youngstown, Ohio on Oct. 12. (Gene J. Puskar/THe Associated Press)

Candidates: (R) Sen. Jon Husted vs (D) Sherrod Brown

Husted was appointed to the seat in 2025 to replace JD Vance when Vance became Trump's vice-president. Before that, Husted had a lengthy career in state politics, holding elected office since 2001.

Trump has recently commented frequently on the 59-year-old Husted's athletic physique, including at events outside of Ohio.

"I examined his ass," the president said at a rally in Kentucky on Oct. 17. " I then patted him on the shoulder, and it was like a piece of steel. I'm still recovering."

Brown has been in politics for more than 50 years, first elected to the state legislature just before his 22nd birthday. He held Ohio's other U.S. Senate seat from 2007 until losing his re-election bid in 2024.

Brown has long advocated targeted tariffs to protect U.S. manufacturing jobs but has consistently criticized Trump's sweeping tariffs, including those on Canadian goods, as ineffective and inflationary.

Key issues: Ohio is a often considered a bellwether state, so the issues top of mind for voters there mirror those resonating across the country: the rising cost of living and whether Trump's war against Iran and his tariffs are to blame. Concern over the spread of data centres is also emerging as a local issue that could affect the statewide race.

Senate: Texas

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, right, greets a supporter at a campaign rally in Allen, Tex. on Oct. 19. Paxton is the Republican candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, running against Democrat James Talarico. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Candidates: (R) Ken Paxton vs (D) James Talarico

Democrats haven't won a U.S. Senate election in Texas since 1988, the year before Talarico was born.

Yet polls suggest Trump himself has put the seat at risk by rejecting incumbent Sen. John Cornyn and endorsing Paxton — the state's scandal-ridden attorney general — as the Republican candidate.

A Republican loss in Texas would be the most significant midterm repudiation of Trump in the country. Paxton seems to realize the burden.

"I'm not exaggerating when I say if we lose Texas, we lose America," he told an Oct. 19 rally in Fort Worth.

In their campaign stump speeches, the rivals describe each another in extreme terms. Talarico calls Paxton "the most corrupt politician in Texas," while Paxton says a vote for Talarico is "a vote for every dangerous idea that Democrats across the country are putting forward right now."

Key issues: The Latino community accounts for roughly one in every five eligible voters in Texas. It supported Trump in record numbers in the 2024 presidential election, but Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) targeting thousands of non-criminals who've been in the U.S. for years could swing many of those voters toward Talarico.

Senate: Iowa

Iowa Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Ashley Hinson, right, speaks during a televised debate with Democratic nominee Josh Turek on Oct. 13 in Des Moines, Iowa. (Charlie Neibergall/The Associated Press)

Candidates: (R) Ashley Hinson vs (D) Josh Turek

Both parties believe they've nominated appealing candidates in the race to replace retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst.

Hinson was a TV reporter and anchor before winning a House seat in 2020. Turek is a three-time Paralympian in wheelchair basketball who was born with spina bifida after his father was exposed to Agent Orange in Vietnam.

Both candidates have tried to persuade Iowa voters they aren't beholden to their party or its leadership. Hinson has said she will stand with Trump on issues such as border security but stand up to him when she believes his policies are wrong for Iowa.

Turek, campaigning in a state that hasn't sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in 16 years, has described himself as "proudly a moderate" and said he and Trump could agree on many issues.

Key issues: Farmers are a major voting bloc in Iowa and rely on diesel to fuel their equipment. For months, Trump brushed aside concerns about soaring fuel prices, driven largely by the war with Iran. Less than two weeks before election day, he announced $8 billion US in one-time payments to farmers to offset diesel costs.

Other notable Senate races

North Carolina appears poised to be the mostly likely state for Democrats to flip.

Incumbent Republican Sen. Thom Tillis is retiring, Trump only carried the state by three percentage points in 2024, and Democratic candidate Roy Cooper served 16 years as North Carolina's attorney general and two terms as governor.

His opponent Michael Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee, is a political backroomer who has never held elected office.

Alaska has sent only one Democrat to the U.S. Senate in the past 50 years. But there are clear signs the Republicans are worried this time.

At Trump's behest, the Department of Justice launched a lawsuit seeking to bar the state from certifying the election if Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan loses. The ostensible reason: there is also an independent candidate on the ballot named Daniel J. Sullivan.

The Democratic candidate is Mary Peltola. She and Minnesota Democratic candidate Peggy Flanagan could become the first Indigenous women elected to the U.S. Senate.

In Kansas, no Democrat has won a U.S. Senate election since 1932.

Yet polls suggest that could change in 2026. Similar dynamics are at play in Kansas as in Iowa: farmers are upset by soaring diesel prices triggered by the Iran war and rising input costs resulting from tariffs.

Republican incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall is up against Democrat Adam Hamilton, founding pastor of a megachurch.

WATCH | How last winter's ICE crackdown in Minnesota could affect this fall's midterms: How the Minneapolis ICE crackdown could sway the midterm vote | Duration closed caption 8:50 For nearly two months this winter, Minneapolis was the explosive epicenter of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, leaving lasting fear and tension in the community. For The National, CBC’s Katie Nicholson goes there to find out how the scars of Operation Metro Surge could play out in the upcoming midterm elections.

House races to watch

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are up for election.

However, various websites that analyze U.S. politics — including the Cook Political Report, the University of Virginia's Center for Politics, Decision Desk HQ and 270toWin — currently rate no more than 50 of them as truly competitive.

Here are a few of the key Republican-held districts Democrats are targeting in their effort to take control of the House.

Virginia 1st district: (R) Rob Wittman (incumbent) vs (D) Shannon Taylor

Polls close in Virginia at 7 p.m. ET, so this race could provide one of the earliest indications of what kind of a night it will be for Republicans and Democrats. The district, which stretches from the suburbs of the state capital, Richmond, to the historic city of Williamsburg, was flagged by the Washington Post as one of the "bellwether races to watch" in the midterms.

Pennsylvania 7th district: (R) Ryan Mackenzie (incumbent) vs (D) Bob Brooks

This district, centred on the working-class city of Allentown, has swung between Democrats and Republicans four times since 2006. Latinos make up nearly one-quarter of eligible voters. Mackenzie won the seat in 2024 by a one-point margin. Brooks is a former firefighter who has never held elected office.

New York 17th district: (R) Mike Lawler (incumbent) vs (D) Cait Conley

Lawler's pitch to voters in this Hudson Valley district includes what he has called his "strong working relationship" with Trump as a way to get things done in Washington. Conley is a West Point graduate who served in Iraq and Afghanistan and is making her first run for office. She has put her military background front and centre in her campaign advertising.

Democrat Bobby Pulido, a famous singer among the Latino community, is trying to unseat Republican Monica De La Cruz in the race for the 15th Congressional district of Texas. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Texas 15th district: (R) Monica De La Cruz (incumbent) vs (D) Bobby Pulido

Democrats recruited a star candidate for this South Texas race: Pulido is a two-time Latin Grammy Award winner. De La Cruz tried to dismiss him as unserious by saying the election " isn't about who you want performing at your niece's quinceañera." Pulido seized on the remark by taking his campaign to quinceañeras, the traditional celebration of a girl's 15th birthday.

Ohio 7th district: (R) Max Miller (incumbent) vs (D) Brian Poindexter

This district in Cleveland's western suburbs wasn't originally a prime target for Democrats. That changed after Miller's ex-wife — the daughter of Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno — accused him of physical abuse, including throwing boiling water at her and holding a gun to her head. Miller has denied the allegations.

Poindexter is an ironworker and city councillor in the working-class community of Brook Park.

Michigan 10th district: (R) Michael Bouchard vs (D) Christina Hines

This race in Detroit's northern suburbs is open because incumbent Republican John James is running for governor. Bouchard is an Army veteran whose ads have focused on being tough on crime and securing the southern border.

Hines is a former prosecutor who boasts of having put " hundreds of predators, murderers, and pedophiles in jail ."

World.title: Big wins, shocking losses, and goodbye to a 46-year mayor: what to know about Ontario's 400+ elections
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There were more than 400 municipal elections in Ontario Monday, so naturally the results were all over the map.

From an anti-incumbent wave that hit many politicians, including one of Canada's longest-serving mayors, to several big cities that brought back almost every incumbent, here are some of the key headlines and takeaways from last night.

Chow wins easily in Toronto

After polling had suggested a "statistical dead heat," Toronto's incumbent Mayor Olivia Chow defeated challenger Brad Bradford with relative ease.

Political strategist Blue Knox, who served as former mayor John Tory's director of communications, said the Chow campaign struck a nerve with Torontonians by going after Bradford's pledge to create a public utility company to handle the city's water and wastewater. Chow said it would mean the city losing control of an asset and opening the door to privatization.

"Canadians like for their public institutions to stay public," Knox said.

Chow will oversee a progressive, new-look council with several of her key allies elected, putting her in a strong position to pursue her agenda.

Mississauga's first male mayor since 1978

Polling at only 12 per cent as recently as August, Alvin Tedjo climbed from those depths to the Mississauga mayor's chair, defeating incumbent Carolyn Parrish and former mayor Bonnie Crombie.



Tedjo is just the fourth person to hold the job in nearly half a century, marking a significant generational shift in a city long led by political veterans. He's also the first man to hold the job since 1978.

WATCH | Tedjo wins: Alvin Tedjo wins Mississauga mayoral race | Duration 1:01 Breaking news: Alvin Tedjo has won the 2026 Mississauga mayoral election. Tedjo was elected as Ward 2 councillor in 2022, and gained attention after being the only mayoral candidate endorsed by the Peel police union. He secured the election following concessions from his rivals.

Horwath out in Hamilton

Since amalgamation in 2000, Hamilton's incumbent mayors have lost their seats more often than they keep them, and that held true on Monday. Andrea Horwath, the former Ontario New Democratic Party leader and former Hamilton Centre MPP, was unable to secure a second term.

The new mayor is Keanin Loomis, former president and CEO of the Canadian Institute of Steel Construction and former head of Hamilton's Chamber of Commerce, who will be joined by eight new councillors in a strong vote for change in the city.

Milton's 46-year mayor ousted

At least two dozen incumbent mayors lost their seats Monday, including nine who had served their cities for more than a decade.

Gordon Krantz, Canada's longest-serving mayor of a major municipality, had been in charge of Milton council since 1980. He lost handily to councillor George Minakakis.

And in Sarnia, the area's Chamber of Commerce CEO Carrie McEachran defeated mayor Mike Bradley, who had held the chair since 1988.

Other long-time mayors who lost include Oakville's Rob Burton (20 years) and Niagara Falls' Jim Diodati (16 years).

Some larger cities stay the course

The winds of change did not sweep away everyone in Ontario.

Ottawa, Brampton, London and Kitchener were among the communities that kept their mayors and most of their councils.

Zack Taylor, an associate professor of political science at Western University in London, said limited information about candidates can make it harder for challengers to gain traction. Taylor described the London campaign as relatively quiet compared with some previous election cycles.

“It could just be that [London Mayor] Josh Morgan benefited from incumbency and also not really having any kind of scandals occur,” Taylor said.

Mark Sutcliffe gives a victory speech after being re-elected as mayor of Ottawa on Monday. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)

A good night for women

Niagara Falls, Port Colborne and North Bay each elected their first female mayors, Ottawa's council has more women than men for the first time since the 2001 amalgamation, and the community of Merrickville-Wolford elected an all-female council.

At her victory party, Niagara Falls mayor-elect Lori Lococo downplayed the accomplishment.

"I always hope that people vote for people based on their experience and skills, not because of their gender," she said.

Women made up 32 per cent of the candidates province-wide.

WATCH | North Bay's new mayor: North Bay mayor-elect Maggie Horsfield speaks with reporters | Duration closed caption 2:14 Maggie Horsfield has won the election in North Bay, Ont., making her the first woman mayor in the city's history. She spoke with reporters at her election night event.

Taxes, homelessness were key issues

Taxes were a running theme across many municipalities.

Tedjo in Mississauga promised a two-year tax freeze; Loomis in Hamilton promised to get taxes "under control"; and Windsor's new mayor Fred Francis promised to hold the line on taxes.

Other popular discussion points during the campaign were homelessness, encampments and community safety. These were key issues in places like Windsor, Thunder Bay and Oshawa.

Thunder Bay councillor-elect Julie-Ann Colquhoun said she wants to "help build a community where people feel safe … and people experiencing homelessness are supported with an understanding of the complexities they face."

World.title: N.S. woman refused to comply with phone scammer, so would-be fraudster swatted her house
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Lynn Colpitts from Truro, Nova Scotia says she was the victim of a swatting incident after refusing to follow instructions from an alleged scammer posing as a representative of her bank.

A Truro-area woman says she is shaken and terrified after a would-be fraudster sent heavily armed police from two different departments to her home over the weekend.

The original call seemed like a routine phone scam. A woman claiming to be from the CIBC fraud department called Lynn Clark Colpitts and said someone had applied for a credit card in her name. In order to block it, she advised Clark Colpitts to download an app called CIBC Guard.

Colpitts said she didn’t feel comfortable doing that or sharing any information over the phone. While she was on the call she conferenced her IT expert from work into the call who told her to do nothing until she contacted her branch.

"I told her politely, I said I'm sorry I have to go by what my IT guy told me to do. And then she used some profanity toward me,” Clark Colpitts said.

“She called me a f-----g b---h, twice, and then hung up on me.”

Clark Colpitts figured she’d dodged a scam but 20 minutes later things escalated.

'She was threatening me the whole time'

“She calls me back and says, ‘I've got a surprise for you. Go to your front door. There's a surprise waiting for you there.’ And I'm like, ‘What are you talking about?’"

Sure enough, as she stepped onto her porch she saw heavily armed officers from Colchester District RCMP and Truro Police in her yard and on the street.

“They holler at me and ask me who I am,” Clark Colpitts said. “And I tell them who I am and they tell me to get down to the end of the driveway.”

Several officers entered her home while Clark Colpitts tried to explain there was no such threat. While police checked on the property the fraudster kept up the phone calls to Clark Colpitts. She held it up so police could hear it.

“She was threatening me the whole time saying that she wasn't done with me and that this was gonna keep going on.”

RCMP explained to Clark Colpitts that they’d gotten a call about a hostage-taking — and shooting — at her address.

Calls, emails and death threats

“It appears to be a level of retribution by the fraudsters in this case,” said Staff Sgt. Marc Rose, commander of Colchester District RCMP.

“[It appears] they did this to cause her harm and pain and distress by having the police respond to her residence all because she didn’t follow the original instructions on the phone."

The calls from the female fraudster continued on Friday and into Saturday.

Staff Sgt. Marc Rose is the commander of Colchester District RCMP. (Galen McRae/CBC)

“She just kept going on and on and on. It was relentless," Clark Colpitts said.

And there were emails too. Death threats.

Clark Colpitts is a realtor. She got a phone call from a co-worker who said someone had hacked into their agency’s website, took down Clark Colpitts's photograph and replaced it with what Clark Colpitts says was a “deformed animal.” All of it has left her scared to be in her own home.

Swatting attack

David Shipley, CEO and co-founder of Beauceron Security, which is based in Fredericton, says Canadians have lost tens of millions of dollars to phone scams, but this is the first time he’s aware of it escalating into a “swatting” attack. That’s when a person calls police to someone’s property to report a crime or emergency that is entirely fictional.

“This seems like a criminal who was definitely not having a good day and decided to dramatically escalate the dangerousness and seriousness of this situation,” Shipley said.

“I would argue that this is a form of terrorism,” he said. “Canadians aren't used to having the SWAT team from the police department show up with assault rifles and body armour and riot shields to their front door. That's incredibly, incredibly traumatic.”

Rose said police have to take these calls at face value and deliver the appropriate response.

“We've offered victim support services to [Clark Colpitts] and we are working with our law enforcement partners in other countries — and in Canada — to determine if this connects to other offences and try to determine who's responsible for this.”

CIBC told CBC News in a statement that there is no app called "CIBC Guard" and that it would never contact customers requesting personal or financial information, or request that they download an app. It urged people to be extremely cautious when dealing with unsolicited emails, texts or phone calls, and not to rely on caller ID.

The bank said it's actively working to educate clients about impersonation and other scams, and it urges people to contact 911 if there is an urgent threat to their safety or the safety of others.

Meanwhile, Clark Colpitts says she's traumatized.

“There's so many things that could have gone badly wrong.”

World.title: Parks Canada ends search and rescue dog program
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Parks Canada has quietly axed a search and rescue dog program that dates back to the early 1970s.

“It’s a really big service to visitor safety and law enforcement,” said Scott Ward, a retired Parks Canada dog handler, who worked as a warden for 35 years and a handler from 1983 to 2000.

“It’s getting busier every year. The calls are going up. The visitor safety people are way busier now than they were in my era.”

Mike Henderson, a dog handler in Banff National Park from 2001-19, said he understands the need to save money, but cutting the canine program could reduce safety.

“You’re cutting a piece that’s not obsolete. It’s got 55 years of success, and we keep on proving ourselves. … It’s not like we sat on our laurels or were hyper expensive at any time,” said Henderson, who had three dogs — Attila, Atar and Cazz — and was involved in more than 1,000 calls.

The last search and rescue dog, Leroy, was retired last summer after a seven-year career. Leroy was involved in finding more than 50 people in the wilderness, located avalanche victims, recovered mountain fatalities, helped stop poaching and was a prominent public relations figure.

Henderson and Ward said a new dog went through about two and a half months of training to be brought into federal service only to have it cut.

The 2025 federal budget included $145 million in cuts to Parks Canada over three years.

A Parks Canada spokesperson said they would get back to CBC News on questions about why the dog program was cut, but didn’t provide an answer before publishing.

Cazz, a Parks Canada search and rescue dog, stands outside an illegal campsite on the edges of the Town of Banff. (Submitted by Mike Henderson)

'Why'd we get rid of it now?'

The search and rescue program was approved in 1970 and started in Jasper National Park.

It was highly used in the mountain national parks for backcountry rescues, to search for missing people, support local police, locate people who died in avalanches and find illegal campsites.

The program grew to six dogs, but was slowly whittled down. The Jasper field unit stopped using dogs more than a decade ago, leaving only Banff.

Sid Marty was a warden in Banff, Jasper and Yoho national parks from 1966-78. He said they worked closely with the search and rescue dog and its handler.

He said the dog could quickly find people caught in avalanches, helping to avoid Parks Canada staff getting caught in subsequent avalanches during a lengthy search.

Search and rescue dog Atar scopes out the scene of a collision involving multiple semi-trucks on the Trans-Canada Highway. (Submitted by Mike Henderson)

Ward said his dogs — Data, Smokey and Gypsy — were critical in finding missing people, such as kids who wandered away from campsites.

He said they were trained to search for human scent “as small as a paperclip in the grass to as large as a human body.”

Henderson emphasized the dogs went beyond search and rescue.

He said their day-to-day could have them handling illegal camping, responding to mental health calls, dealing with illegal campfires, monitoring area closures, removing food to avoid wildlife becoming habituated to it, and monitoring for poaching.

“You can put the rowdy campers to bed,” he said. “You roll in, ask nicely and light the dog up, and everyone says, ‘OK, we’re going to bed.’”

Henderson said consultation should’ve taken place to get a better understanding of what would be lost by cutting the program.

“Why'd we get rid of it now? It definitely needs to be spoken to,” Henderson said.

Former Parks Canada warden Mike Henderson and his search and rescue dog in Grasslands National Park in Saskatchewan during an anti-poaching operation. (Submitted by Mike Henderson)

Not only dogs getting the boot

Parks Canada is undergoing a “workforce adjustment” and recently notified 2,917 employees — more than half of its staff — they could be fired or moved to different positions. Andrew Campbell, acting CEO of Parks Canada, said in an all-staff email the federal agency has to cut about 500 full-time jobs.

The full rollout of the new plan is anticipated in 2027, and Campbell said they’re allowing people to voluntarily leave or retire to reduce the number of people who are cut.

“Parks Canada has used, and will continue to use, every tool at its disposal to minimize involuntary departures,” he said in a call to staff.

World.title: Ottawa tables new MAID legislation, excluding people suffering solely from mental illness
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The federal government has tabled new legislation that indefinitely excludes people suffering solely from mental illness from qualifying for medically assisted death.

During a news conference on Tuesday, Justice Minister Sean Fraser said the decision came after a period of "rigorous study" by Canadian lawmakers, including via a special parliamentary committee, and review by his own department.

"This wasn't a conclusion that we reached out of thin air," he said.

The legislation, Bill C-41, would amend the Criminal Code to "clarify that a person cannot receive medical assistance in dying on the basis of a mental illness."

It also would allow people to make what's known as an "advance request" for medically assisted death before losing the capacity to consent due to their health condition.

But the legislation outlines specific criteria that must be met, including being in "an advanced state of irreversible decline in capability" and "experiencing enduring and intolerable physical or psychological suffering that cannot be relieved through reasonable means."

It also states that MAID based on advance requests may only be provided in provinces that have established a "provincial legislated regime" outlining the rules and safeguards around such requests.

Asked whether that would create gaps in access across Canada, Fraser said the federal government decided to allow the provinces "to determine the extent to which they wish to embrace the next frontier on medical assistance in dying."

"From my point of view, this is going to be the start of a national conversation that will largely play out at the provincial level around the extent to access," he said.

WATCH | Canada shuts door on MAID for mental illness: Canada shuts door on medical assistance in dying for mental illness | Duration closed caption 2:04 Justice Minister Sean Fraser announced the government will not move forward with allowing medical assistance in dying (MAID) for those suffering solely from mental illness, angering some MAID advocates, but pleasing many in the medical community.

Maddison McKee, a spokesperson for the Alberta government, said the province would "carefully review the proposed [federal] changes and consider what further consultation may be needed in Alberta."

"Our priority will continue to be protecting vulnerable Albertans and ensuring appropriate safeguards are in place around consent and patient safety," McKee said.

Ottawa's plan drew mixed reaction

When Fraser announced Ottawa's plans earlier this month, Dying with Dignity Canada — a group that advocates for access to MAID — said it was a "profoundly disappointing day."

"Preventing a group of people from having the same access to a legal medical procedure as the rest of the population simply because of their diagnosis violates Charter rights. It is stigmatizing and unconstitutional," CEO Helen Long said in a written statement.

Inclusion Canada, an organization that supports people with intellectual disabilities, had welcomed the mental illness exclusion, however, saying the government recognized that "people with mental illness need treatment and support."

WATCH | Some advocates disappointed by mental illness exclusion: Advocates disappointed after Ottawa extends MAID exclusion for mental illness | Duration closed caption 5:29 Helen Long, CEO of Dying with Dignity Canada, which advocates for assisted-dying rules, shares her reaction to the federal government extending the MAID exclusion to those suffering solely from mental illness. She says given the number of delays already with the legislation, it is not a total surprise.

The group also raised concerns about advance requests for MAID. "Consent at the time is the most basic protection a person has. Parliament should not take it away," Inclusion Canada CEO Krista Carr said on Oct. 7.

Canada passed MAID legislation in 2016, but the Superior Court of Quebec struck the law down in 2019 because it was limited to those whose deaths were "reasonably foreseeable."

Parliament passed Bill C-7 in 2021 to align with the court's ruling. A planned expansion of medically assisted death to people suffering only from mental illness was pushed back several times to allow for further study.

In June, a special parliamentary committee recommended that people suffering solely from mental illness be excluded.
