World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: De la Espriella sacks interior minister after Congress bungles Colombia’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara hours after Congress found a procedural flaw in the passed 2027 budget, which makes the law invalid.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella briefly thanked Lara and announced he would be replaced by the ambassador to the Organization of American States, Alejandro Ordoñez.

The news surprised the interior minister, who suddenly left a congressional debate on a law to facilitate the demobilization of illegal armed groups after receiving a message on his phone.

Lara was apparently held responsible for the blunder of Congress, whose two houses approved the 2027 budget but with conflicting versions of an article on financial risk-coverage mechanisms for the Ministry of Finance.

By the time the error was detected, the budget debate had passed its October 20 deadline, forcing De la Espriella to issue a decree that would convert an older version of the budget bill into law.

The interior minister was the administration’s primary political liaison responsible for managing legislative procedure and whip operations in Congress.

Lara’s job was already under pressure after he failed to convince Congress to cede its presidency to the president’s candidate.

While Ordoñez returns from Washington, Justice Minister Ivan Cancino will assume the role of interior minister.

The incoming interior minister is an ultra conservative Catholic with ties to the Society of St. Pius X, which considers the modernizing reforms of the Catholic Church heresies and errors, and was declared in a schism with the church in June.

In Colombian politics and particularly among the opposition, Ordoñez is mainly remembered as the inspector general who illegally removed former President Gustavo Petro from his post as mayor of Bogota in 2013.

Petro was ultimately reinstated and would become president of the country in 2022.

World.title: Colombia’s Congress approves De la Espriella’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress agreed to increase the government’s 2027 budget despite promises by President Abelardo de la Espriella to reduce public spending.

Next year’s budget will be COP634.9 trillion, almost $204 billion, which is 16% more than last year’s budget and 10% higher than the proposal made by former President Gustavo Petro.

According to Finance Minister Miguel Gomez, the budget seeks to bring the State’s finances in line with reality.

The budget was approved in both the Senate and the House of Representatives with the support of De la Espriella’s government coalition.

The Historic Pact, the only leftist opposition party, rejected the budget and boycotted the vote.

On behalf of the national government, I would like to thank you all for your work over the past few months in passing the budget. I would also like to thank the opposition for the strength with which they defended their views. The message that Congress has sent today regarding the government’s economic policy is very important. It is the first step toward putting the country’s economy back on track toward growth, fiscal responsibility, and addressing the nation’s needs. Finance Minister Miguel Gomez

The budget seeks to reimpose the neoliberal model that had been abandoned by Petro and reduce public debt.

According to Green Party representative Jaime Raul Salamanca, who opposed the budget, funding for free higher education was cut in half from COP800 billion ($254 million) to COP400 billion (127 million).

“This cut raises concerns about its potential impact on the continuity and scope of this policy, which has enabled thousands of young people to enroll in public institutions of higher education,” said Salamanca.

The budget also cut the budget for the war crimes tribunal JEP, which could endanger the future of the peace process with the FARC and is opposed by the government.

World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: Colombia’s first lady promises transparency over earthquake donations
World.content:
Colombia’s first lady, Ana Lucia Pineda, vowed to reveal how much money she collected and spent in response to the August 10 earthquake that affected hundreds of thousands of people.

Amid mounting public pressure about where the money had gone, Pineda went on the morning program of public television channel Nuestro Caribe to promise that her foundation, Luz y Sonrisas, will take its finances public on Friday.

Carrying a white folder, the wife of President Abelardo de la Espriella stressed that “in the foundation’s accounts rest all, absolutely all of the monies from the donations we received during the ‘Colombia One Single Heart’ campaign” that was announced on August 12.

“A lie is not going to tear down the truth of who I am or what I represent, or how my children recognize me,” said Pineda.

Luz y Sonrisas was one of three NGO’s that were promoted by the De la Espriella government to collect contributions for victims of the earthquake.

Pineda’s foundation was the only one that could receive contributions from abroad.

Earlier in the week, news program Noticias Uno revealed that her foundation that was founded on July 7 lacked the tax exemption that would allow it to accept donations, a process that usually takes months.

In a press statement, tax office DIAN subsequently said that it had granted the tax exemption to the first lady and that she could legally accept financial contributions.

Pineda did not say how much money she had received, but said that she stopped supporting the initial relief efforts “because the humanitarian aid was sufficient, it was huge.”

The first lady vowed she had saved the donations for the reconstruction phase “because I have also taken the initiative to build and return to the victims a house that is durable for the families who lost everything.”

World.title: Colombia’s opposition takes to the street to protest De la Espriella
World.content:
Despite intimidation attempts by the national government and the police, tens of thousands of people took to the streets throughout Colombia to protest the far-right government of President Abelardo De la Espriella.

The protest had been organized by social organizations, labor unions and the country’s largest opposition party, the Historic Pact.

Opposition leader Ivan Cepeda, who joined the protests in Bogota, told a reporter that the government is “exercising a mafia-style rule in the service of the worst elements of Colombian politics—the drug trade.”

Contrary to what De la Espriella is saying, this is not a government that opposes drug trafficking; it is a government that supports the drug trafficking cartels, the paramilitaries, and the ultra-conservative forces that want to destroy people’s rights, the democratic advances made by President Gustavo Petro, and the progress achieved by the popular movement over the past four years. Senator Ivan Cepeda

“That’s why we’re here; we won’t allow people’s rights to be violated or trampled upon,” said the senator.

Hours ahead of the protest, the president signed off on a decree that changed the police response to protests and accused the organizers of being “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

Human rights organizations denounced that the security forces put snipers on the roofs of buildings in Bogota and in Cali, a helicopter flew over the heads of the protesters.

The protests sought to test the waters for an even larger “national strike” that is set for November and shut down parts of the country in 2021.

“We are only warming up,” warned Cepeda, who has yet to recognize De la Espriella as Colombia’s legitimate president after losing the elections in July.

World.title: Colombia’s national strike organizers “are instigators of evil,” claims De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called labor unions and social organizations who organized anti-government protests for Wednesday “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that the security forces were instructed to allow peaceful protests, but warned the protesters that “if they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is lawfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians.”

Wednesday’s protests are a preparation for a national strike that is set to take place in November and is supported by the country’s political opposition to the far-right government.

According to the president, “those who are promoting the strike and seeking to use it to once again cause chaos and destabilize the government are the very same people who left the country bankrupt, on the brink of a blackout, with the healthcare system in intensive care, energy sovereignty compromised, and public resources plundered and looted.”

“They are instigators of evil, not fighter for freedom,” said De la Espriella.

If they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is rightfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president stressed that he would be signing a decree that regulates public protests in an attempt to avoid the chaos that erupted during massive strikes in 2019 and 2021 an killed 80 people.

De la Espriella additionally is expected to present an “anti-terrorism stature” to Congress, which could see the prosecution of protest organizers on terrorism charges, according to opposition leaders and security experts.

World.title: Brazil investigates whether Flávio Bolsonaro left the country via Argentina after his defeat
World.content:
Brazil investigates whether Flávio Bolsonaro left the country via Argentina after his defeat

27th Tuesday, October 2026 - 16:32 UTC Full article

Judge Alexandre de Moraes ordered Bolsonaro, who is under investigation by the court, to surrender his ordinary and diplomatic passports within 24 hours and barred him from leaving the country

Brazil’s Federal Police are checking with Argentine authorities whether Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, defeated by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday’s presidential runoff, left the country across the Argentine border, after he failed to hand over his passports within the deadline set by the Supreme Federal Court. His campaign and the Argentine government deny that he has left Brazil.

Supreme Court Judge Alexandre de Moraes on Monday ordered Bolsonaro, who is under investigation by the court, to surrender his ordinary and diplomatic passports within 24 hours and barred him from leaving the country. In a video posted on social media, the senator said Federal Police officers served him notice “in the middle of the street” as he left the Brasília home of his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, and he agreed with his lawyers to hand over the documents on Tuesday morning. The deadline passed without police confirming the handover, and the passports were cancelled, according to the Brazilian press.

Argentine newspaper Infobae reported early on Tuesday that Bolsonaro had entered Argentina at Puerto Iguazú, in the Triple Frontier area, at around 2 a.m. using his national identity card, valid for travel between Mercosur countries, in order to continue to the United States on a private plane. According to the newspaper, it was a Gulfstream G400 owned by Argentine company Baires Fly, which requested immigration clearance for four passengers and three crew. Records on the Flightradar24 platform show the aircraft flew from Buenos Aires to Puerto Iguazú on Monday night.

Federal Police sources quoted by the newspaper Metrópoles said Bolsonaro had not passed through any official Brazilian border checkpoint, though they acknowledged it is possible to cross the border without being checked. His campaign’s general coordinator, Rogério Marinho, denied he had left the country, and the Argentine government also rejected the report. Since Tuesday morning, his allies had been unable to reach him, according to a columnist for the UOL news portal.

His brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, who has lived in the United States since 2025 after being convicted by the Supreme Court of coercion in the case over their father’s coup attempt, said on Friday that Flávio should leave the country if he lost. The senator refused to recognise Lula’s victory and later said he would “organise the opposition”. US President Donald Trump said on Monday, without offering evidence, that the election looked “rigged”.

World.title: A judge appointed by Jair Bolsonaro rejects his son’s case for annulling the election
World.content:
A judge appointed by Jair Bolsonaro rejects his son’s case for annulling the election

26th Monday, October 2026 - 13:39 UTC Full article

“Even before all these circumstances, we took all the necessary measures and were entirely successful. I repeat: there was no change resulting from the court ruling,” Nunes Marques said

The president of Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, Kassio Nunes Marques, who was appointed to the Supreme Federal Court by former president Jair Bolsonaro in 2020, said on Monday that the extension of voting hours did not change the result of the runoff won by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the former president’s son, had cited the extension in refusing to recognise his defeat and calling for the election to be annulled.

“Even before all these circumstances, we took all the necessary measures and were entirely successful. I repeat: there was no change resulting from the court ruling,” Nunes Marques told a press conference.

On Sunday night, Bolsonaro called it “unacceptable” that Supreme Court Judge Cristiano Zanin, whom he called “Lula’s lawyer” for having defended him in the Lava Jato cases, ordered at 5.01 p.m., when polls were due to close, an extension of voting until 7 p.m. “There is a lot to clarify before Brazil recognises this outrage that has just happened,” he said. “I will never know how many votes I could have had.”

Zanin ordered the extension at the request of Lula’s coalition, which reported a lack of buses to carry voters in cities such as Salvador and São Paulo. Bolsonaro’s campaign, for its part, had asked the electoral courts to extend voting in municipalities affected by rain, flooding and power cuts in states such as Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul. The measure applied only to polling stations still open; those that had closed at 5 p.m. did not reopen and followed the usual counting procedure.

Lula won with 51.78% of valid votes against Bolsonaro’s 48.22%, a margin of about 4.4 million votes. There is no record yet of the senator’s campaign having filed a formal challenge.

World.title: Debt, inflation and a hostile Congress: the economic challenges of Lula’s fourth term
World.content:
Debt, inflation and a hostile Congress: the economic challenges of Lula’s fourth term

26th Monday, October 2026 - 13:29 UTC Full article

Public debt has risen by more than ten points during the current term and exceeds 82% of GDP, driven by growing mandatory spending

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will begin his fourth term as Brazil’s president on January 1 with an economy that has grown more than expected and record-low unemployment, but with fiscal imbalances that markets punished heavily on Monday, the first trading day after his re-election. The dollar rose more than 12% at one point to 5.60 reais, the Ibovespa index triggered an automatic trading halt at the open and long-term interest rates jumped almost two points.

The reaction reflects investors’ bets on a victory by Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who promised sharp spending cuts. On Friday, the dollar had closed at 4.99 reais and the Ibovespa at 205,082 points, close to the record it reached after the first round. Analysts agree that the president’s first test will be the make-up of his economic team and his fiscal framework. These are the five main challenges he faces.

Debt

Public debt has risen by more than ten points during the current term and exceeds 82% of GDP, driven by growing mandatory spending, which leaves less than 8% of the federal budget for adjustable items. Lula has at times played down concerns over debt, arguing that stronger growth will solve the problem. His team has pledged to keep the current fiscal rules, which cap spending growth and set primary surplus targets, but meeting them will be harder given the commitment to raise the minimum wage above inflation, which also increases pension costs, and the new benefits announced during the campaign.

Inflation and interest rates

The Central Bank has cut the Selic rate five times in a row to 13.75%, but annual inflation exceeded the 4.5% tolerance ceiling in September, against a 3% target. The Monetary Policy Committee meets on November 4, and the real’s depreciation complicates further cuts. Lula proposes lowering rates through greater fiscal discipline without touching social programmes, while most economists argue a faster decline would require spending cuts.

Household debt

According to credit agency Serasa, nearly 84 million Brazilians and 9.3 million companies are behind on payments, a record attributed to high interest rates. The government is preparing new relief measures, such as buying distressed mortgages from banks at a discount and forgiving tax debts for small business owners, which analysts see as temporary relief.

A hostile Congress

Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party will hold the largest bloc in both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate, in the most conservative Congress since the return to democracy. That will hamper the government’s plans to cut tax exemptions and the approval of appointments to the Central Bank, regulators and the Supreme Court, which were already difficult during the current term. Bolsonaro, moreover, does not recognise the result and has said he will seek to annul the election.

Tax reform

The new value-added tax, approved in 2023, takes effect in January, but the government has yet to set its effective rate, which independent analysts put at around 28%. The government also postponed during the campaign a bill for a selective tax on products harmful to health or the environment, such as tobacco and alcohol.

World.title: Trump insults Norway and rejects its immigrants for not giving him the Nobel Peace Prize
World.content:
Trump insults Norway and rejects its immigrants for not giving him the Nobel Peace Prize

26th Monday, October 2026 - 13:24 UTC Full article

Trump has made no secret of his wish to win the prize

US President Donald Trump lashed out at Norway at a rally in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday, saying Norwegian immigrants are not welcome in the United States because the Nobel Committee did not award him the Peace Prize. Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide replied that the committee is independent.

“Frankly, Norway stinks. Norway has become a shithole country, in fact,” Trump said at a campaign event a week before the November 3 midterm elections. The president said he would welcome immigrants from certain countries but not from Norway, “because I didn’t get the Nobel Prize. So I don’t want anybody from Norway.”

“He knows very well that the Nobel Committee is independent. We have reminded him of that, in case anyone had any doubts, and that remains the case,” Barth Eide told Norwegian public radio NRK on Monday.

Trump has made no secret of his wish to win the prize. This year the Nobel Committee awarded it to South African jurist Navi Pillay, a former International Criminal Court judge and former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, a decision Trump called “shameful and embarrassing”. Last year, when the prize went to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, he also expressed anger at not being recognised. In 2018, during his first term, he was heavily criticised for using similar language about Haiti and several African countries.

World.title: Trump questions Lula’s victory as most of the region, including the right, congratulates him
World.content:
Trump questions Lula’s victory as most of the region, including the right, congratulates him

26th Monday, October 2026 - 13:16 UTC Full article

“They just applied the Biden playbook in Brazil. Bolsonaro had a big lead in the first round and was the clear favourite. But communists don’t give up power once they get it,” Trump said

US President Donald Trump cast doubt on Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election in Brazil and compared it with the 2020 US election, while most Latin American governments, including several right-wing allies of Washington, congratulated the Brazilian president. In Argentina, President Javier Milei remained silent.

“They just applied the Joe Biden playbook in Brazil. Bolsonaro had a big lead in the first round and was the clear favourite to win the second. But communists don’t give up power once they get it,” Trump said, according to the EFE news agency, without offering evidence of irregularities. Trump has never acknowledged his defeat by Biden in 2020. The White House has not formally commented on the result, which Senator Flávio Bolsonaro also refuses to recognise and has said he will seek to annul.

One of the first to congratulate Lula was Uruguayan President Yamandú Orsi: “I have just spoken with Brazil’s president-elect, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a friend. I congratulated him on his victory and on the democratic celebration that an electoral process represents.” Governments of the opposite ideological stripe also did so. Chile’s José Antonio Kast, an ally of the Bolsonaros, said the two countries “have a lot of future in common”; Paraguay’s Santiago Peña hailed “this great democratic day”; and Bolivia’s Rodrigo Paz noted that Bolivia and Brazil are “neighbouring and brotherly countries”. Ecuador’s Daniel Noboa called for working together against “common enemies”, and Panama’s José Raúl Mulino pledged to keep “working together”. Mexico’s Claudia Sheinbaum said: “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won.”

In Argentina, Milei, who backed Bolsonaro during the campaign and even accused Lula of seeking to “steal” the election, had issued no congratulations. The Peronist opposition, by contrast, celebrated. Former president Cristina Kirchner spoke of “a genuine electoral 17 October”, referring to Peronism’s founding date; Buenos Aires governor Axel Kicillof of “a historic night”; and former presidential candidate Sergio Massa wrote: “Today, as yesterday, on Lula’s side of life.”

Former Chilean president Gabriel Boric, who followed the vote in Brazil, thanked Lula “for never giving up the fight”. Congratulations from right-wing leaders such as Kast, Peña and Paz reflect the weight of Brazil, the region’s largest economy and the main trading partner of several of its neighbours. Lula will begin his fourth term on January 1.

World.title: Milei stays silent on Lula’s victory as Kast and Peña congratulate him
World.content:
Milei stays silent on Lula’s victory as Kast and Peña congratulate him

26th Monday, October 2026 - 13:05 UTC Full article

Neither the president nor Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno had issued a statement on the result, according to the Argentine press

Argentine President Javier Milei had not congratulated Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on his re-election in Brazil by Monday, unlike other right-wing South American leaders such as Chile’s José Antonio Kast, Paraguay’s Santiago Peña and Bolivia’s Rodrigo Paz. Milei, who publicly backed Senator Flávio Bolsonaro during the campaign, met his cabinet at the Casa Rosada first thing in the morning.

Neither the president nor Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno had issued a statement on the result, according to the Argentine press. “We have to wait,” official sources said. During election night, Milei shared social media posts questioning the extension of voting hours in Brazil, and on Monday he shared a message against the “average leftie”. Bolsonaro does not recognise Lula’s victory and has said he will seek to annul the election.

Kast, for his part, said he had spoken with Lula: “I have just spoken with the President of Brazil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and congratulated him on the election result.” The presidents of Mexico, Panama and Uruguay also congratulated the Brazilian leader, according to the newspaper La Nación.

Within the Argentine government, Bolsonaro’s defeat came as a surprise. “The rejection of Bolsonaro was very strong,” an official told the Noticias Argentinas news agency. At the Casa Rosada, the result is attributed to Lula’s latest economic measures, the shorter working week and the rejection the candidate generated among women and young people. A political figure who regularly visits government headquarters told Infobae the defeat weakens the idea of an international right-wing alliance that Milei had promoted. The Peronist opposition, by contrast, celebrated the re-election: Cristina Kirchner, Axel Kicillof and Sergio Massa linked it to Argentina’s 2027 elections.

Relations between the two presidents are strained. Milei repeatedly called Lula a “thief” and last week said he hoped he would not “steal” the election. In July, Brazil recalled its ambassador in Buenos Aires for consultations after earlier insults from the Argentine president. Brazil is Argentina’s main trading partner, and the two countries are Mercosur’s largest economies.

World.title: Brazil’s real plunges more than 8% and São Paulo stocks slump after Lula’s victory
World.content:
Brazil’s real plunges more than 8% and São Paulo stocks slump after Lula’s victory

26th Monday, October 2026 - 13:03 UTC Full article

The fall in Ibovespa futures hit the permitted limit shortly after the open and forced a temporary halt in trading, prompting the São Paulo stock exchange

Brazil’s real lost more than 8% against the dollar and futures on the Ibovespa index plunged 15% on Monday, in the first session after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s victory in the election runoff, a result markets had not expected. The dollar opened up 8.64% at 5.42 reais.

The fall in Ibovespa futures hit the permitted limit shortly after the open and forced a temporary halt in trading, prompting the São Paulo stock exchange, B3, to widen the daily fluctuation band to 20%. Brazil’s Treasury also cancelled the debt auctions scheduled for October 27 to 29. Brazilian assets trading abroad had anticipated the move: the exchange-traded fund of Brazilian stocks in Tokyo fell as much as 15%, according to Bloomberg. According to El País, it is the real’s steepest decline since 1999.

The sell-off reflects investors’ bets on a victory by Senator Flávio Bolsonaro after his first-round win, which on October 5 drove a 7.7% rise in the Ibovespa on expectations of greater fiscal discipline. “Markets were broadly positioned for a Bolsonaro victory,” said Eirini Tsekeridou, an analyst at Julius Baer. A Citibank survey of 73 fund managers showed 80% expected a fall of more than 5% if Lula won.

Analysts say attention will now turn to the stance of Bolsonaro, who does not recognise the result and has said he will seek to annul the election, Lula’s ability to build majorities in an opposition-dominated Congress and, above all, the make-up of his economic team. “Investors need a revised fiscal framework that generates primary surpluses sufficient to stabilise debt,” said Viktor Szabó of Aberdeen Investments. Brazil’s public debt exceeds 80% of GDP, and the ten-year bond yields around 6.5%, second in the region only to the 12% demanded on Argentine debt, according to the same analyst.

World.title: Lula wins Brazil’s presidency for a fourth time with 51.8% of the vote
World.content:
Lula wins Brazil’s presidency for a fourth time with 51.8% of the vote

26th Monday, October 2026 - 09:01 UTC Full article

Lula is the first candidate to win the presidency after coming second in the first round since Brazil returned to direct presidential elections in 1989

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won Sunday’s presidential runoff with 51.78% of valid votes against 48.22% for Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, according to the Superior Electoral Court, with 99.97% of the vote counted. Lula, 80, will govern the country for a fourth time, from 2027 to 2030, after overturning his first-round deficit.

The Workers’ Party candidate won 64.2 million votes, some 4.4 million more than the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who received 59.8 million. The court declared Lula mathematically elected shortly after 9 p.m. Brasília time, following a count in which the president overtook his rival when about half the votes had been tallied and never lost the lead. In Brasília, Bolsonaro supporters gathered on the Esplanade of Ministries left in silence as the result became known.

Lula is the first candidate to win the presidency after coming second in the first round since Brazil returned to direct presidential elections in 1989, and the first Brazilian elected to the office four times. He governed from 2003 to 2010 and returned to power in 2023 after defeating Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election with 50.90% of the vote, a narrower margin than Sunday’s. He will be 85 at the end of this term and will not be able to run again.

The result defied the polls, which until the last day showed a statistical tie with a slight edge for the senator. The latest Datafolha poll gave each candidate 50% of valid votes. Bolsonaro, of the Liberal Party, had won the first round on October 4 with 47.03% of the vote, some 56.1 million, against Lula’s 45.16%, a result that also surprised pollsters.

After that setback, Lula’s campaign threw itself into mobilising the roughly 33 million voters who stayed away in the first round, with particular attention to those over 70 and 16- and 17-year-olds, for whom voting is optional. In the final stretch, the government raised the Bolsa Família social programme, received by 20 million families, by 15%, and Congress approved the 40-hour working week with two days off, one of the president’s flagship pledges. Lula also announced subsidies, fuel tax cuts and debt relief programmes which, according to calculations by the newspaper Folha de S.Paulo, add up to almost 300 billion reais through 2027.

Bolsonaro, who received the backing of almost all right-wing and centre-right parties after the first round, focused his campaign on security, the cost of living and a promise to cut public spending while maintaining social programmes. He had pledged to pardon his father, sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup after the 2022 election, and during the campaign committed to respecting the result.

Voting day was marked by the extension of polling hours in some areas, ordered by a judge at the request of Lula’s campaign over public transport problems, according to El País, a decision criticised by opposition figures. The campaign was also shaped by the legal dispute with Meta, which both candidates accused of unequal treatment on its platforms, and by the agreement both signed at the electoral court to mutually lift the secrecy of their bank, tax and phone records.

Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, will take office on January 1 alongside Vice President Geraldo Alckmin and will have to govern with a Congress in which the Liberal Party will hold the largest bloc in both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate, foreshadowing strong parliamentary opposition.

Regionally, the Brazilian president will govern alongside neighbours that have mostly aligned themselves with Donald Trump’s administration, such as Argentina, Chile, Paraguay and Bolivia. Argentine President Javier Milei backed Bolsonaro during the campaign, repeatedly insulted Lula and even accused him of seeking to “steal” the election, while Lula used Milei as an argument against his rival in both debates. Relations with Washington, marked by the tariffs Trump imposed on Brazilian goods, which Lula blamed on the Bolsonaro family, will be another major challenge of his new term. Former Colombian president Gustavo Petro was among the first to congratulate him.

World.title: Government invests US $60M to restore polluted, drought-impacted Lake Pátzcuaro
World.content:
As part of the Plan Michoacán for Peace and Justice, the National Water Commission is investing 1.1 billion pesos (US $60 million) in the Lake Pátzcuaro Sanitation Plan, in order to restore the environmental health of one of the most emblematic bodies of water in Mexico.

Lake Pátzcuaro — a popular vacation region and an international landmark — is home to a rich biodiversity, including endemic species of birds, fish and other aquatic organisms.

Visitamos la obra de rehabilitación de la Planta de Tratamiento de Aguas Residuales en Quiroga, Michoacán. https://t.co/0yz5XQzAzJ — Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo (@Claudiashein) October 25, 2026

It is a central part of a region in western Mexico comprising archaeological, historical, recreational and cultural sites linked to the heritage of the Indigenous Purépecha peoples, lending identity, sustenance and life to the communities that surround it.

However, agricultural, industrial and domestic activities — especially the excessive use of fertilizers and pesticides and the discharge of untreated wastewater — have seriously degraded the water quality in the lake.

Six wastewater treatment plants are being renovated — in Las Garzas, Janitzio, San Pedrito, Quiroga, Tzintzuntzan and San Andrés Ziróndaro — and four new plants are being built — in San Juan Tumbio, Ihuatzio, Tzurumutaro and Quiroga.

More than 116 kilometers of sanitary sewer lines are being reconditioned and 10 area wetlands will be rehabilitated. Conagua will also oversee dredging and hydrological restoration to help reduce pollution in Lake Pátzcuaro.

These actions will be complemented by the removal of water hyacinth and a reforestation project, as well as the construction of terraces in the surrounding hills to contribute to the environmental recovery of the basin.

President Claudia Sheinbaum, who spearheaded the clean-up plan, toured the Quiroga Wastewater Treatment Plant on Saturday, thanking the workers involved in the rehabilitation projects. She also praised the Michoacán government for its effort to recover the springs that supply water to the ecosystem.

“The conservation of this ecosystem is fundamental for the communities of the region,” she said, adding that her administration will continue to support projects aimed at recovering Michoacán’s natural resources.

Luis Roberto Arias Reyes, the director of Conagua’s Michoacán office, said the Sanitation Plan will directly benefit more than 142,000 residents of the municipalities of Pátzcuaro, Tzintzuntzan, Quiroga and Erongarícuaro by providing more efficient hydraulic and sanitary infrastructure for wastewater management.

In a press release, the Michoacán government said the Lake Pátzcuaro clean-up project will generate economic growth for the Indigenous communities of the islands of Janitzio, Tecuena, La Pacanda and Yunuén, as well as for lakeshore towns such as Urandén and Huecorio, which depend on fishing and tourism as pillars of their economy.

With reports from ContraRéplica, El Sol de Morelia, La Jornada and Cambio de Michoacán

World.title: 8% salary increase among ’12 actions in 120 days’ promised by IMSS director: Tuesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🏥 Robledo presents 12-action plan for IMSS: IMSS director Zoé Robledo presented a plan of “12 actions” to be completed in 120 days in response to protests by IMSS workers. It includes an 8% salary increase, the transition of almost 11,000 temporary workers into permanent positions, the hiring of 2,500 specialist doctors and the provision of more than 18,000 additional beds and gurneys. The plan also promises “guaranteed” medicines and medical supplies, a program to clear the surgical backlog and the “strengthening” of emergency departments.

IMSS director Zoé Robledo presented a plan of “12 actions” to be completed in 120 days in response to protests by IMSS workers. It includes an 8% salary increase, the transition of almost 11,000 temporary workers into permanent positions, the hiring of 2,500 specialist doctors and the provision of more than 18,000 additional beds and gurneys. The plan also promises “guaranteed” medicines and medical supplies, a program to clear the surgical backlog and the “strengthening” of emergency departments. 🇧🇷 Sheinbaum recounts “very emotional” call with Lula: The president said her Monday phone call with Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was brief and that the reelected Brazilian president was “very happy, very excited” about the response from Brazilians at the ballot box. Sheinbaum said she invited Lula to visit Mexico and he invited her to go to Brazil. The two agreed to talk again to set a date and agenda for the visits.

The president said her Monday phone call with Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was brief and that the reelected Brazilian president was “very happy, very excited” about the response from Brazilians at the ballot box. Sheinbaum said she invited Lula to visit Mexico and he invited her to go to Brazil. The two agreed to talk again to set a date and agenda for the visits. 🗳️ Sheinbaum rejects claims Morena is to blame for INE problems: A day after endorsing Guadalupe Taddei’s resignation as National Electoral Institute (INE) president, Sheinbaum reiterated her call for a comprehensive audit of the electoral authority. She pushed back on journalist Carlos Loret de Mola’s claim that “Taddei is Morena,” saying: “Don’t come and tell us… that Morena is the problem.” Sheinbaum noted that Taddei was elected INE president in 2023 by the Chamber of Deputies.

Why today’s mañanera matters

Improving Mexico’s public healthcare system is one of the various challenges faced by the Sheinbaum administration, which has now been in office for almost 25 months. Deficiencies in the system have been brought into sharp focus this month by protesting workers from the Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS), Mexico’s largest public healthcare provider.

At President Sheinbaum’s Tuesday morning press conference, IMSS general director Zoé Robledo presented a plan aimed at improving conditions in IMSS hospitals and for IMSS workers, whose demands have included higher pay, the hiring of additional healthcare personnel in order to ease excessive workloads and an end to shortages of medicines and medical supplies.

The plan is the federal government’s most comprehensive response to IMSS workers’ complaints and demands. Its presentation came four days after the government unveiled a new initiative aimed at resolving long-running problems related to the supply and distribution of medications.

Whether the government’s latest initiatives significantly improve conditions in IMSS healthcare facilities and satisfy workers remains to be seen. Medicine shortages have persisted despite government efforts to address the problem through initiatives such as the establishment of a “mega-pharmacy” in 2023 and the creation of a distribution scheme called “Rutas de la Salud” (Health Routes) last year.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were Sheinbaum’s remarks about her telephone conversation on Monday with Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who was reelected on Sunday.

The president indicated that she will travel to Brazil at some point in the not-too-distant future.

A key focus of face-to-face talks between Sheinbaum and Lula would likely be the fledgling partnership between Mexico’s Pemex and Brazil’s Petrobras that is aimed at boosting oil production in the Gulf of Mexico.

Robledo presents 12-action plan for IMSS

Early in the press conference, Robledo presented a plan for IMSS healthcare facilities consisting of “12 actions” to be completed in a period of 120 days starting today.

He said that the actions in the plan “stem from what the [IMSS] workers themselves told us” and are needed.

The 12 “actions” of the plan Robledo presented are as follows:

An 8% salary increase for IMSS workers.

The transition of almost 11,000 temporary workers into permanent positions.

The hiring of 2,500 specialist doctors.

The provision of 100 pieces of high-tech medical equipment to IMSS hospitals.

The provision of 2,917 other pieces of medical equipment to IMSS hospitals.

The provision of more than 18,000 additional beds and gurneys to IMSS hospitals.

The commencement of a “permanent maintenance” program.

The “guaranteed” provision of medicines and medical supplies.

The “complete” provision of medications in IMSS pharmacies.

The commencement of a program aimed at clearing the surgical backlog in IMSS hospitals.

The provision of specialist medical appointments in December. (Robledo explained that appointments scheduled for December have commonly been rescheduled to January or even February.)

The “strengthening” of emergency departments, including via the hiring of additional personnel.

Sheinbaum recounts ‘very emotional’ call with Lula

Sheinbaum told reporters that her telephone conversation with Lula on Monday was “very emotional.”

“As you can imagine, he is very happy, very excited about the response from the people of Brazil” in Sunday’s election, she said.

🇲🇽🇧🇷Claudia Sheinbaum y Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva preparan un encuentro entre México y Brasil. La presidenta reveló que sostuvo una llamada telefónica “muy emotiva” con el presidente electo brasileño, en la que ambos intercambiaron invitaciones para visitar sus respectivos países. “Fue una llamada breve, lo invité a que viniera a México… me invitó a que fuera a Brasil”, contó Sheinbaum. Acordaron una segunda conversación para definir la fecha del encuentro. 🗞️Israel Aldave | @Radio_Formula — Azucena Uresti (@azucenau) October 27, 2026

“It was a brief call and I invited him to come to Mexico and he invited me to go to Brazil,” Sheinbaum said.

“We agreed to talk at another time to confirm and to set a date and agenda for these visits,” she said.

Sheinbaum rejects claims that Morena is to blame for problems at the INE

A day after endorsing Guadalupe Taddei’s decision to resign as president of the National Electoral Institute (INE), Sheinbaum reiterated her call for a comprehensive audit of the electoral authority to be carried out.

Taddei resigned amid allegations that lucrative INE contracts were improperly awarded to companies controlled by a businessman with whom she has a close personal relationship.

After advocating “constant audits” of the INE, Sheinbaum rejected claims that the ruling Morena party is responsible for improper conduct at the INE.

“Don’t come and tell us, like [journalist Carlos] Loret de Mola did yesterday, that Morena is the problem,” she said.

Sheinbaum highlighted that Taddei was elected INE president in 2023 by the Chamber of Deputies.

Taddei’s election occurred via sortition — also known as selection by lottery — as none of the candidates for president of the INE had the support of the required two-thirds of lawmakers in the lower house of Congress. At the time of her election, questions were raised about her family links to both the government and Morena.

In an El Universal column published on Monday under the headline “Taddei is Morena,” Loret de Mola described Taddei as a “morenista” and effectively accused the INE of favoring the ruling party under her leadership.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Mexico’s Charlyn Corral is named Best Striker of the Year at soccer’s biggest award ceremony
World.content:
Mexican soccer player Charlyn Corral, 35, received the Gerd Müller trophy for Best Striker of the Year during the 2026 Ballon d’Or ceremony on Monday, making history as the first Mexican woman soccer player to earn the coveted distinction.

“It fills me with pride and great satisfaction. After a career spanning more than 20 years, I realize today that the hard work, discipline and effort have been worth it,” Corral said during her acceptance speech at the London Palladium Theatre in London.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Liga Femenil BBVA (@ligafemenilbbva)

This is only the second time the award has been presented in the women’s category; the only other player to have received this recognition is Ewa Pajor, who won it in 2025 with 48 goals.

Corral, 35, who scored 49 goals across 49 matches for Club Pachuca Femenil and the women’s national team, shared the honor with English forward Harry Kane of Bayern Munich. Kane received the same award in the men’s category and was also the night’s biggest winner, taking home the Golden Ball.

“I think that when you do things with great faith — but, above all, with your heart — everything is worth it,” Corral added, dedicating her award to Club Pachuca’s management and coaching staff.

She also thanked her parents and her brother, “who have been, are and will be the foundation and support of my career,” she said.

Corral highlighted Mexico’s support for women’s soccer, noting that she knows things in the country “are being done well,” and asked the audience to recognize her compatriot Scarlett Camberos, forward for Club América Femenil, for being ranked among the 30 best players in the world in the nomination for the main Ballon d’Or.

The Gerd Müller trophy adds to Corral’s previous accolades.

Earlier this year, the forward was recognized by the International Federation of Football History & Statistics (IFFHS) as the world’s top goalscorer in 2025 for the second consecutive year with 57 goals, including 50 for Pachuca and seven for the national team.

While playing with Pachuca, Corral has won the 2025 Clausura tournament of the Liga Femenil and the 2024–2025 Campeón de Campeones.

With reports from La Jornada and ESPN

World.title: ‘Soy Frankelda’: The perfect family plan for a very Mexican Halloween
World.content:
If you’re looking for a movie to watch with your family this Halloween and want to avoid overly violent content or the same old repetitive classics, there’s a new option you should check out. It’s “Soy Frankelda” (“I Am Frankelda”), the first Mexican feature film animated entirely in stop-motion.

Directed by brothers Arturo and Roy Ambriz and produced under the creative mentorship of Guillermo del Toro, this film stands out for its dazzling technical craftsmanship, its balance between the spine-chilling and the endearing, and its focus on profound themes such as the power of imagination, artistic resilience in the face of rejection and the struggle for creative autonomy.

It’s currently available worldwide on Netflix and on Max in Latin America.

This ambitious film debut expands the animated universe that Cartoon Network Latin America introduced with the hit series “Los Sustos Ocultos de Frankelda” (“Frankelda’s Book of Spooks”), an anthology of horror stories narrated by the titular character. Over the course of its 113-minute runtime, the new film details the origins of the mysterious Topus Terrentus — also known as The Land of Spooks — and reveals how the dreamer Francisca Imelda evolves into the powerful ghostwriter Frankelda.

I Am Frankelda | Official Trailer | Netflix

Watch this video on YouTube

Praised by Screen Anarchy as “a universal and timeless tale destined to inspire” and described by IndieWire as “a lovingly handcrafted feast for the eyes,” “Soy Frankelda” envelops viewers in an atmosphere of lighthearted horror, perfect for a family Halloween screening.

Below, we outline four essential reasons to watch it this season.

Resilience and overcoming adversity: A story everyone can relate to

This gothic fantasy is set in Real del Monte in 1866, where we follow the journey of the imaginative horror writer Francisca Imelda (voiced by Mireya Mendoza), who is constantly marginalized by her community’s gender prejudices. Her life changes dramatically when she is approached by Herneval (Arturo Mercado Jr.), the prince from the Topus Terrentus, an enigmatic alternate dimension that serves as a reflection of her own mind.

Transformed into a sort of specter, Francisca ventures into this psychological landscape inhabited by the creatures born from her pen. There, she discovers that her characters have taken on a symbolic identity of their own and that the balance between fiction and reality is on the verge of collapsing. Together with Herneval, our fearless protagonist must confront Procustes (Luis Leonardo Suárez), the Royal Nightmare Maker, who has disrupted the flow of terror in the real world and is plotting to take over everything that exists. Saving the Topus Terrentus thus becomes an act of literary resistance: to prevent its destruction, Francisca must defend her calling against the forces seeking to silence her and claim control over her creations.

Beyond its elements of dark fantasy, the film also serves as a brilliant coming-of-age story. At the beginning of the film, the protagonist must face the real challenges of her environment: discrimination, rejection, frustration and the fear of failure. However, by exploring her own subconscious, this young woman manages to claim her identity and define her place in the face of those who try to suppress her.

The journey of self-discovery in “Soy Frankelda” offers a lesson that any viewer can relate to and that is worth remembering: Resilience is the ultimate weapon for protecting one’s calling, healing inner wounds and defending one’s talent against any form of oppression.

The charm of stop-motion: Puppets that exude mystery and natural strangeness

Produced in Mexico with indomitable resilience, “Soy Frankelda” stands as a beacon and a monumental milestone in Latin American animation.

Bringing the country’s first stop-motion feature film to life took more than three years and was a true odyssey for the Cinema Fantasma studio. The project involved moving forward without industry backing, stretching a modest budget and navigating constant logistical setbacks — all while keeping some 20 animation units working in parallel. However, this complex and sometimes chaotic process ultimately shaped one of the most visually ambitious films the genre has ever seen.

In a market oversaturated with virtual graphics and automation, this film stands out for its “handmade” style and vibrant originality. The technical crew integrated 2D textures, oil paintings for the backgrounds, cardboard cutouts and more than 190 puppets crafted with meticulous care. Overall, the design of Topus Terrentus shines with its imperfect and irregular charm. Every scene and each of its extravagant inhabitants — ranging from winged creatures and spider-like beings to an imposing two-headed griffin — demonstrate the team’s tremendous commitment to a daring visual vision.

It is precisely this magnetic imperfection that makes the film an ideal Halloween experience. In this sense, the irregular rhythm of the stop-motion animation conveys a “natural strangeness” and a three-dimensional presence that digital animation cannot replicate. This creates an atmosphere that is both unsettling and beautiful, evoking the classic spirit of dark fairy tales.

It’s worth noting that, although its content is suitable for all ages and takes care to avoid being visually jarring, the ideal age to explore this universe is 7 and up.

A spectacular gothic musical

Although directors Arturo and Roy Ambriz admit that they did not originally conceive this production as a musical, the soundscape — created by Mexican composer Kevin Smithers — took on such power that it ultimately shaped the spirit of the feature film.

“Soy Frankelda” is elevated by a dazzling soundtrack that features theatrical melodies and dramatic orchestral arrangements. It is not merely background music, but a narrative driving force that propels the story forward with complete fluidity.

Inspired by 19th-century Gothic Romanticism, the score uses piano and string arrangements to reflect Francisca’s initial isolation, her subsequent awakening and the somber grandeur of Topus Terrentus. This soundscape — winner of the prestigious Public Choice Award at the World Soundtrack Awards in Belgium — is complemented by an innovative approach: the incorporation of choirs singing in Enkárik, an original language created by a team of specialists to imbue Topus Terrentus with a mystical, ancient and supernatural atmosphere.

Operatic pieces such as “Eres Verdad, Eres Ficción” (“You Are Truth, You Are Fiction”) and “El Príncipe de los Sustos” (“The Prince of Spooks”) stand out in this solid repertoire. Not only do they serve important narrative purposes, but they also get under your skin, making it impossible to turn off the screen without finding yourself humming their melodies.

Rich Mexican mythology

“Soy Frankelda” is a proudly Mexican film, and that is evident in every aspect of it. It’s fair to say that the directors succeeded in honoring their country’s roots without resorting to clichés or common stereotypes. Or, as Roy Ambriz explained to El País: “All of our characters … are not the stereotypes that Mexican characters sometimes fall into. What’s important is to create a new Mexican aesthetic.”

Ultimately, the Topus Terrentus is a fusion of two powerful currents: the iconic illustrations of Gustave Doré and the mysticism of Mexican folklore. While the European style shapes the architectural framework of the spaces, caves and ruins of The Land of Spooks, local culture permeates the heart and evolution of the feature film. From the very beginning — and especially when crossing the veil into this extravagant dimension — the screen is filled with ingenious nods to the country, such as the Maya aluxes, the tradition of alebrijes and even a portrayal of general and dictator Porfirio Díaz.

This rich identity, which pays a heartfelt tribute to the land and its people, is another reason why this film deserves to be celebrated and enjoyed.

The perfect family plan for Halloween

“Soy Frankelda” has all the ingredients to become the ultimate family movie of the season.

A visual style brimming with fascinating creatures? Yes. An unforgettable gothic musical atmosphere? Yes. A dazzling mythology inspired by Mexican folklore? Yes. And a deeply human journey of self-discovery? Definitely yes!

Best of all, the film captivates fans and new viewers alike, with no prior knowledge of the series required.

If you need one more reason to dive into this universe, the endorsement from Guillermo del Toro himself — shared with Espinof — will dispel any doubts: “It’s a milestone for Mexican stop-motion animation. A true triumph of vision, tenacity and love for this craft.”

So turn off the lights and get ready for a very Mexican Halloween.

Carolina Alvarado is a Venezuelan journalist who has devoted much of her career to creative writing, university teaching and social work. She has been published in Lady Science, Latina Media, Global Comment, Psiquide, Cinetopic, Get Me Giddy and Reader’s Digest, among others.

World.title: PAN names 6 state coordinators ahead of 2027 gubernatorial elections
World.content:
The National Action Party (PAN) has now announced its presumptive gubernatorial candidates in six states after unveiling its pick in Querétaro on Sunday.

Gubernatorial elections will be held in 17 of Mexico’s 31 states on June 6, 2027. Voters will also elect 500 federal deputies and thousands of other officials at the state and municipal level on the same day.

As is the case with Morena, Mexico’s ruling party, the PAN is calling its presumptive gubernatorial candidates “state coordinators.”

In the PAN’s case, the presumptive candidates’ full title is “state coordinators for the defense of the homeland, the family and freedom.” They are almost certain to be officially designated as the party’s candidates at a later date.

The six presumptive gubernatorial candidates selected so far by the PAN are listed below in alphabetical order by the states they are seeking to govern. The PAN — currently Mexico’s main opposition party — governs four of Mexico’s 32 federal entities, including three states that will hold gubernatorial elections next year (Aguascalientes, Chihuahua and Querétaro).

The PAN’s presumptive gubernatorial candidates

BAJA CALIFORNIA SUR (BCS) : Francisco Pelayo Covarrubias, a federal deputy (currently on leave) and a former BCS state lawmaker and ex-mayor of Comondú, one of the five municipalities in BCS. The state is currently governed by Morena under the leadership of Governor Víctor Manuel Castro Cosío. It includes the municipality of Los Cabos, one of Mexico’s premier coastal tourist destinations.

: Francisco Pelayo Covarrubias, a federal deputy (currently on leave) and a former BCS state lawmaker and ex-mayor of Comondú, one of the five municipalities in BCS. The state is currently governed by Morena under the leadership of Governor Víctor Manuel Castro Cosío. It includes the municipality of Los Cabos, one of Mexico’s premier coastal tourist destinations. CHIHUAHUA : Marco Antonio Bonilla Mendoza, former mayor of Chihuahua city. Chihuahua is currently governed by the PAN under the leadership of Governor Maru Campos. The PAN’s governance of the northern border state has been in the spotlight this year after it emerged that CIA agents allegedly participated in a drug lab raid there without the authorization or knowledge of the federal government.

: Marco Antonio Bonilla Mendoza, former mayor of Chihuahua city. Chihuahua is currently governed by the PAN under the leadership of Governor Maru Campos. The PAN’s governance of the northern border state has been in the spotlight this year after it emerged that CIA agents allegedly participated in a drug lab raid there without the authorization or knowledge of the federal government. MICHOACÁN: Alfonso Martínez Alcázar, mayor of Morelia, the state capital, and a former state and federal deputy. Michoacán is currently governed by Morena under the leadership of Alfredo Ramírez Bedolla. The state made international headlines almost a year ago when the mayor of Uruapán, Carlos Manzo, was assassinated. The federal government responded to the murder and general insecurity in the state with “Plan Michoacán for Peace and Justice,” a 57-billion-peso initiative.

TLAXCALA: Miriam Martínez Sánchez, a deputy in the Tlaxcala Congress and wife of the PAN’s leader in the state, Ángelo Gutiérrez Hernández. Tlaxcala, Mexico’s smallest state by area, is currently governed by Morena under the leadership of Governor Lorena Cuéllar Cisneros.

Miriam Martínez Sánchez, a deputy in the Tlaxcala Congress and wife of the PAN’s leader in the state, Ángelo Gutiérrez Hernández. Tlaxcala, Mexico’s smallest state by area, is currently governed by Morena under the leadership of Governor Lorena Cuéllar Cisneros. QUERÉTARO: Felipe Fernando Macías Olvera, mayor of Querétaro city and a former federal deputy. Querétaro is currently governed by the PAN under the leadership of Governor Mauricio Kuri. The Bajío region is Mexico’s main data center hub, attracting billions in investment in recent years.

Felipe Fernando Macías Olvera, mayor of Querétaro city and a former federal deputy. Querétaro is currently governed by the PAN under the leadership of Governor Mauricio Kuri. The Bajío region is Mexico’s main data center hub, attracting billions in investment in recent years. ZACATECAS: Miguel Ángel Varela Pinedo, mayor of Zacatecas city and a former federal deputy. Zacatecas is currently governed by Morena under the leadership of Governor David Monreal.

The PAN has not yet named its presumptive gubernatorial candidates in Aguascalientes, Baja California, Campeche, Colima, Guerrero, Nayarit, Nuevo León, Quintana Roo, San Luis Potosí, Sinaloa or Sonora. It is possible that the PAN and the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) will nominate common gubernatorial candidates in some states. The PRI has not yet named any presumptive gubernatorial candidates.

Morena completed the selection of its 17 “state coordinators for the transformation and national sovereignty” last month. The party founded by former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador is currently in office in 23 of Mexico’s 32 federal entities.

With reports from El Financiero, SDP Noticias, Expansión, Político MX and El Economista

World.title: Government turning to AI to solve the acknowledged problem of medication shortages
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum has introduced an Advisory Council for the Digital Transformation of the Health Sector, aimed at improving control, storage and distribution of medications.

The move was in response to supply shortages publicized during recent mobilizations by Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) workers. The president has acknowledged the legitimacy of the complaints.

According to an announcement made during Sheinbaum’s morning press conference on Friday, the council will be divided into two groups of experts.

The first group will be the Advisory Board composed of four researchers specializing in logistics, engineering, information systems, and resource distribution, while the second group — dubbed the Youth AI Team — will be made up of five individuals specialized in artificial intelligence.

The project will use digital tools and AI to detect medication shortages, track warehouse inventory and expedite delivery to public hospitals and health centers.

“What we want is to modernize the system to ensure that the entire process — from procurement, warehousing and arrival at the hospital pharmacy, to distribution across various hospital departments and delivery to patients — is automated, so that we know the exact traceability of every medication,” Sheinbaum said on Friday.

Members of the council are expected to present their initial projects in November. The federal government plans to begin implementing the new system in January 2027.

Deputy Health Minister Eduardo Clark said the program aims to identify medication needs in real time, improve inventory management, and optimize distribution routes to reduce both time and costs. If a medication is unavailable at one pharmacy, healthcare staff would be able to determine whether it is in stock at another health facility or warehouse and arrange for its delivery.

The scale of the program’s challenge, however, is considerable.

According to figures presented by Clark, the health sector uses approximately 3 billion units of medicines and medical supplies each year. The products must be distributed among more than 1,000 hospitals and nearly 15,000 health centers and primary care units.

Sheinbaum explained that the lack of medication does not always stem from non-procurement. She noted that there are instances when medications have been purchased but fail to reach medical facilities on time, due to difficulties in the processes of storage, distribution and delivery.

Also, Sheinbaum’s administration recently said it has identified practices in which medications from the public sector end up being sold privately and, in some cases, outside of hospitals.

With reports from Latinus, Eje Central, La Silla Rota and Infobae

World.title: Mining giant Grupo México plans to expand its US copper operations to the tune of US $4-6B
World.content:
The mining and transportation conglomerate Grupo México announced on Thursday plans to double down on its investments in its U.S. copper mining unit, Asarco.

Grupo México plans to spend between US $4 billion and $6 billion over the next three years on Asarco projects, to expand the Ray and Silver Bell mines in Arizona and restart the Hayden smelter and refinery, the head of the mining division, Leonardo Contreras, told analysts on a call.

The investment is far higher than recent spending on the unit, which totaled just $101 million in 2024, and marks a significant expansion in the U.S. market.

It follows news of a 2% fall in copper output during the third quarter due to lower production in the U.S. and Peru. Even so, the firm’s profits grew by 56% during this period to a net profit of US $2 billion, owing to robust base metal prices. Overall revenue increased by 38% to $6.33 billion, surpassing consensus estimates from analysts polled by LSEG.

Corporate leadership has revised the company’s copper production target downward to 1.026 million metric tonnes in 2026, from the previously targeted 1.034 million tonnes.

Contreras emphasized that work is continuing on expanding the Ray facility as feasibility studies are conducted. In addition, the company is “increasingly optimistic” about the restarting of Hayden, which has an annual processing capacity of 1.4 million metric tonnes of copper concentrate.

“That would represent almost 350,000 metric ⁠tonnes of contained copper,” Contreras said. “If that feeds into our refinery, we could be looking at 500,000 metric tonnes of copper.”

The Silver Bell project is also in the feasibility stage, according to Contreras.

Grupo México plans to assess the potential to integrate Mexican concentrates and U.S. copper scrap into U.S. operations, according to Itaú analysts.

Grupo México’s focus on Peru

Grupo México will also continue expanding operations in Peru.

Its long-term growth focuses closely on its Peru operations through its Southern Copper subsidiary, with the delayed flagship Tia Maria project expected to finally come online in the first half of 2028.

Southern Copper is developing two other projects in Peru — Los Chancas and Michiquillay, both of which are expected to commence operations in 2032 and are expected to produce 130,000 and 225,000 metric tonnes of copper a year, respectively.

With reports from Reuters, Mexico Business News and Mexico Now

World.title: Morelia festival wraps 24th edition; ‘Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building’ takes top honors
World.content:
A childhood memory reshaped into fiction won big at the recently concluded Morelia International Film Festival, with “6 meses en el edificio rosa con azul” (“Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building”) taking both the judges’ top prize and the audience award.

The double win — the Ojo for best Mexican feature and the audience award in the same category — marked a meeting of jury and moviegoer tastes that the newspaper El Universal described as rare on the festival circuit.

Trailer de Seis meses en el edificio rosa con azul (HD)

Watch this video on YouTube

The 104-minute Spanish-language drama is the first fiction feature by Bruno Santamaría Razo, a documentary filmmaker born in Mexico City in 1986.

Planned for a 2027 theatrical release in Mexico — with no streaming dates yet announced — the film follows an 11-year-old boy discovering his feelings for his best friend as his family confronts his father’s HIV diagnosis in 1990s Mexico City.

Reconstructing family memories through imagination rather than strictly retelling events, the film premiered at Cannes Critics’ Week, becoming the first Mexican feature to compete in the section in 20 years.

The 24th edition of the Morelia International Film Festival (FICM) was held in the Michoacán capital from Oct. 16 through Sunday.

For its 25th anniversary next year, FICM officials are promising a landmark edition with major guests, bold retrospectives and a stellar lineup — and it will move the dates to the week immediately before the Day of the Dead.

This year’s festival included 96 Mexican films in competition, alongside international screenings, retrospectives and tributes.

The guest list was strong, as usual, with appearances by directors Guillermo del Toro (“Pan’s Labyrinth”) and Alfonso Cuarón (“Roma”), along with “Y Tu Mamá También” stars Diego Luna and Gael García Bernal — underscoring Morelia’s standing as a gathering place for Mexican cinema.

International guests included U.S. director James Gray, who presented “Paper Tiger,” which competed for the Palme d’Or at Cannes this year. The winner at Cannes, “Fjord,” also played in the FICM.

Festival president and Cinépolis CEO Alejandro Ramírez described this year’s event as a particularly Mexican celebration.

Mexican Nicolás Pereda won best director for “Lo demás es ruido” (“Everything Else Is Noise”), an absurdist comedy about a musician preparing for her first television interview. Its star, Teresa Sánchez, also a Mexican, won best actress.

Sam Louwyck of Belgium took best actor for playing a gay hairdresser in Mexican Nathalia Acevedo’s “Salón de belleza” (“Beauty Salon”).

Mexican Joaquín del Paso’s “El jardín que soñamos” (“The Garden We Dreamed”), about a Haitian family traveling north, earned a special mention and the cinematography award.

Mexican Fernanda Tovar received the first-time director award for “Chicas tristes” (stylized as “Sad Girlz” in translation), about two teenage girls supporting each other after one is sexually abused. Pablo Vaca’s “Forensita” won best Mexican documentary feature.

With reports from El Universal, Variety, Animal MX and Proceso

World.title: EU Chief Congratulates Serbia’s Students
World.content:
File photo: António Costa, president of the European Council, speaking in Helsinki in September 2025. (Photo: Finnish Government, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Published Tuesday, 27 October, 2:20 p.m. ET · Source: António Costa’s post on X, election-monitor projections, prediction markets

Key Facts Call: António Costa, president of the European Council (EU leaders’ body), phoned protest-born Student List leader Ilija Srdanović on Tuesday.

Message: Costa wants parliament convened and a government formed quickly, with a peaceful handover that respects the vote.

Result: Ipsos, a polling firm, and CeSID, an election monitor, project 141 of 250 seats for the students; 126 wins a majority.

Next: Parliament must meet and a prime minister must be chosen; who that will be is still open.

Prediction markets: Polymarket, a prediction market, gives economist Dejan Šoškić 37.0% and Srdanović 15.5% to be prime minister (2:11 p.m. ET, 27 October).

The European Union’s top summit chair has called the winner of Serbia’s election, and the winner is not Aleksandar Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which has run the country for 14 years. António Costa, president of the European Council, the body of EU national leaders, phoned Ilija Srdanović on Tuesday and congratulated him.

Srdanović is the cardiologist who leads the Student List, a movement that grew out of street protests. Read how the night unfolded in our Belgrade celebration report and what comes next in our guide to who holds power.

What Did Costa Say?

Costa wrote on X that he had a good call with Srdanović and congratulated him on the Student List’s victory. He said the priority now is to convene parliament and form a new government without delay.

That handover, he added, should be peaceful and fully respect the election results. Serbia’s place is in the European Union, Costa said, and Brussels is ready to support its European path.

He named three reforms that he said Serbian voters had asked for. They are the rule of law, the fight against corruption and media freedom.
