Email address Get the PDF Free. We send a confirmation link first, and the same address then receives The Rio Times Brief, our daily briefing. Unsubscribe with one click at any time; see our privacy policy. Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

What Happened in Kimbiri

The Kimbiri river rose suddenly on the afternoon of Monday, 26 October, after intense rain. The district lies in the Vraem, the valley of the Apurímac, Ene and Mantaro rivers, in Cusco.

Police, soldiers and civil defence brigades rescued eight people that night, including at least two minors. Six men were stranded on an islet near a bridge, and two others were trapped in a house.

Antonio Rivera, a government-appointed sub-prefect who coordinates the Vraem, said about 30 rustic homes were damaged in Santa Virginia. About 60 residents there evacuated.

Cusco governor Werner Salcedo said 65 families were affected, 45 in Santa Virginia and 20 in Pomorani. Roads and farmland were also damaged, and heavy machinery was sent to clear routes.

Kimbiri mayor Héctor Dipas Torres asked the army, firefighters and civil defence for help. Damage assessments were still under way on Tuesday.

Rivera said late on Monday that no deaths or missing people had been reported. Officials describe a sudden river rise, though Peruvians also use huaico for mud-and-rock flash floods.

Why It Matters

Peru is entering El Niño Costero 2026-27, a warming of the sea off its coast that brings heavy rain to the north. Senamhi said on 22 October that rain should become more intense and frequent from November.

Indeci, Peru’s civil defence institute, told local governments to clear evacuation routes and warned of landslides and huaicos. It also urged families to reinforce their roofs.

The Piura flood of 20 October and the US$5.2 billion El Niño stimulus show how Peru is preparing. The ministers’ visits to flood zones began earlier this month.

What It Means for You

US visitors to Tumbes, Piura or the northern beaches should expect flooded streets and possible delays through Thursday, 29 October. Check with airlines, bus lines and hotels before travelling.

The red notice also covers the whole Cusco region, so ask tour operators about road and rail conditions. Kimbiri is a river-valley district, not a usual tourist stop.

The US State Department, Washington’s foreign ministry, publishes a Peru travel advisory, which could not be opened for this report. Senamhi sends warnings through its Senamhi Perú Móvil app, and the Peru hub tracks the wider picture.

What Is Not Known

Whether anyone is missing in Kimbiri is unconfirmed, because one local report cites community authorities for two missing people. An official said late on Monday none were missing, and a report of swept-away fishermen is also unverified.

The Senamhi notice could not be opened, so its 11 regions come from coverage; one report lists only nine. Reports also differ on Kimbiri, with about 30 homes destroyed in one account and damaged in others.

One report gives a reading of 53.4 millimetres at Puerto Pizarro, which no second source repeats. Santa Virginia counts also differ, with about 60 residents in one account and 45 families in another.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a red alert in Peru?

It is the red level of Senamhi’s weather notices, here for rain of strong to extreme intensity. Notice No. 440 runs from Tuesday, 27 October, to 23:59 on Thursday, 29 October.

What happened in Kimbiri?

A river surge on Monday, 26 October, damaged homes in Kimbiri, in Peru’s Cusco region, and trapped eight people, who were rescued. Officials said late on Monday that no one was missing.

Why is northern Peru getting so much rain?

Peru is in El Niño Costero 2026-27, a warming of the sea off its coast. Senamhi links the storms to warm sea-surface temperatures and expects heavier rain from November.

Is it safe for US travellers to visit northern Peru now?

Expect flooded streets and delays in Tumbes and Piura through Thursday, 29 October. Check the State Department advisory, your airline and your hotel before you travel.

Sources: Senamhi, weather notices page (notice No. 440); Senamhi, communique No. 003, 22 October; Senamhi, press note on temperatures, 24 October; Ministry of Defence, sandbags in Tumbes, 23 October; Indeci, civil defence alerts (all accessed 27 October 2026).

World.title: Guatemalan military reportedly intimidates BDF escorting U.S. Embassy team at Cadenas outpost
World.content:
Guatemalan military reportedly intimidates BDF escorting U.S. Embassy team at Cadenas outpost

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize Defence Force (BDF) patrol reportedly faced intimidation tactics from the Guatemalan military while escorting members of the United States Embassy to Cadenas Outpost along the Sarstoon River today.

The trip was part of an ongoing communications project involving the remote military installation near Belize’s southwestern border.

Chief Executive Officer in the Ministry of National Defence Francis Usher noted that the Guatemalan military used intimidation tactics during the encounter.

Despite the reported incident, the BDF patrol remained professional and ensured the safety and security of everyone aboard the vessel while maintaining Belize’s presence in its territorial waters.

The incident has been reported to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which is expected to determine the appropriate course of action.

World.title: From commitments to action: Taiwan and the world creating climate solutions together
World.content:
From commitments to action: Taiwan and the world creating climate solutions together

By Peng Chi-ming – Taiwan Minister of Environment:

Mobilizing action globally to accelerate implementation of climate commitments

In 2026, extreme heat continued to sweep across the globe, with historically high temperatures occurring in many regions. Western Europe experienced its hottest June on record. These temperatures intensified drought and wildfires and put pressure on water resources. This disrupted public health, energy supplies, and economic activity. Taiwan has likewise faced climate risks including extreme heat, heavy rainfall, and typhoons. Climate change has become a shared challenge with profound implications for social stability, industrial development, and national resilience.

Against this backdrop, global climate governance is moving beyond the formulation of targets and commitments toward concrete implementation. At this year’s COP31 meeting, participants will emphasize the principles of dialogue, consensus, and action while working to turn commitments into concrete, trackable results. Even though Taiwan is not a party to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, it continues to work on climate governance in the spirit of the Paris Agreement. Having submitted its 2035 nationally determined contributions in 2025, Taiwan is now translating its emissions-reduction targets into action by many government agencies to reach a green industrial transition, resource circulation, climate adaptation, and a just transition. It is also collaborating with international partners to develop practical solutions.

Aligning with international norms while achieving concrete emissions reductions through transparent governance

Article 4 of the Paris Agreement calls on parties to progressively strengthen mitigation plans and reach nationally determined contributions. The enhanced transparency framework laid out in Article 13 calls for consistent, trackable information to assess progress on climate actions. Aligning with these international norms, Taiwan this year formally approved its third-phase greenhouse gas reduction action programs for six sectors, covering the years 2026-2030. These programs address energy, manufacturing, residential and commercial buildings, transportation, agriculture, and the environment, incorporating 20 flagship mitigation action plans, annual emissions targets, and 63 performance indicators. They further embed national mitigation goals into sectoral policies and allow for annual monitoring and evaluations. Taiwan’s latest national greenhouse gas inventory also shows that net greenhouse gas emissions in 2024 were 6.59 percent below 2005 levels and demonstrated a decline for the third consecutive year. Over the same period, real GDP continued to grow, even as carbon dioxide emission density fell 48.59 percent. This indicates a gradual decoupling of economic growth from carbon emissions.

As concerns transparency, Taiwan follows recommended frameworks set by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement. It regularly publishes related documents, including nationally determined contributions, biennial transparency reports, and national inventory reports, matching international practice. Through clear mitigation pathways, sectoral action, and transparent information, Taiwan will continue to assess its progress and turn climate commitments into measurable, trackable outcomes.

Pursuing net-zero and zero waste to enhance industrial competitiveness during the green transition

To accelerate the green industrial transition, Taiwan began collecting carbon fees this year, part of its effort to make carbon pricing a key policy instrument for the decarbonization of industry. The collection system is linked to voluntary reduction plans and preferential rates that encourage companies to incorporate emissions reductions into their investment and operational decisions. In the first year of collection, the carbon fee has thus far generated NT$4.97 billion in revenue, which goes to the Greenhouse Gas Management Fund, a dedicated fund for greenhouse gas reduction and climate change adaptation efforts. The fund offers loan credit guarantees and interest subsidies so as to optimize operations. Meanwhile, the Regulations Governing Subsidies for Greenhouse Gas Reduction Technologies and Climate Change Adaptation were promulgated to support reduction technologies and adaptation measures. Through such diverse instruments as subsidies, financing, and risk sharing, Taiwan’s framework will introduce more private capital in support of the net-zero transition.

During the next stage, a cap-and-trade system will be progressively developed. This will be called the Taiwan Emissions Trading System (TW-ETS) and will move toward a diversified carbon pricing framework in which the carbon fee and the ETS operate in parallel. The United Kingdom recently listed Taiwan’s carbon fee as a qualifying carbon pricing scheme under its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism. This will permit eligible Taiwanese products to claim carbon-price deductions in accordance with applicable rules, marking an important step in building links between Taiwan’s carbon pricing framework and international systems.

The industrial net-zero transition must extend beyond energy and carbon management to address the way resources are used. This year, Taiwan completed amendments to the Resource Circulation Promotion Act and the Waste Disposal Act, shifting management efforts from end-of-pipe treatment toward governance across the entire product life cycle. The government has identified eight major aspects of the circular economy: food, plastics, textiles, health, construction, electronics, inorganic resources, and circular industries. At present, there are 69 publicly listed companies in the circular economy sector, which generatesf over NT$1 trillion in total annual revenue. This shows that the circular economy is progressively taking shape as a green industry of scale. Taiwan continues to promote digital product passports, source plastic reduction, and reuse. Through legislation, industrial collaboration, and digital innovation, Taiwan aims to accelerate resource circulation and zero waste, and reduce its reliance on virgin resources, and lower its carbon burdens. This will enhance resource security, supply chain resilience, and green competitiveness.

Strengthening climate resilience and integrating adaptation into national planning and everyday life

Article 7 of the Paris Agreement sets out a global goal to enhance adaptive capacity, strengthen resilience, and reduce vulnerability to climate change. At COP30, participants adopted the Belém Adaptation Indicators to further advance the Global Goal on Adaptation toward measurable and trackable action. Taiwan continues to align with international adaptation efforts by integrating climate risk assessments into national and local governance and bolstering resilience to climate events like extreme heat and torrential rainfall.

In response to a growing heat risk, Taiwan this year used a 40°C extreme-heat scenario to advance cross-ministerial adaptation strategies, strengthening preparedness and coordination for public health, energy, transportation, occupational safety, and support for vulnerable groups. Furthermore, on the instructions of President Lai Ching-te, Taiwan established the national-level Urban Forest Promotion Committee to advance the National Green Canopy Program. This initiative makes urban forestry an element of national resilience infrastructure and integrates LiDAR remote sensing, 3D digital twin technology, and microclimate data to accurately identify heat hotspots and shading gaps, thereby creating a resilient terrestrial green network that balances climate adaptation with public health. Taiwan will draft an urban forests act that will promote professional certification for protecting trees while advancing the high-value circularity of wood. By guiding corporate ESG resources and encouraging community adoption, Taiwan will launch local demonstration zones, bringing to bear private sector expertise and emerging technologies to enhance urban resilience against extreme climate events and natural disasters.

Realizing a just transition and mobilizing society for net-zero

The preamble to the Paris Agreement emphasizes the need to take into account the imperatives of a just transition of the workforce and the creation of decent work and quality jobs. In recent years, the UNFCCC has furthered discussions on energy, industry, labor, and the social dimensions of the transition. At COP30, participants advanced mechanisms related to a just transition, strengthening international cooperation, technical assistance, capacity building, and knowledge sharing so that the needs and development opportunities of different groups could be addressed during the net-zero transition.

Taiwan has made leaving no one behind a core principle of its net-zero transition, and established a basis for governance that addresses a just transition via the Climate Change Response Act. To realize a just transition while implementing carbon reduction policies, Taiwan this year is conducting stakeholder consultations across six major sectors—energy, manufacturing, residential and commercial buildings, transportation, agriculture, and environment. By gathering a wide scope of public opinion and having each sector review and respond to this feedback, cross-ministerial collaboration is being improved. Subsequently, Taiwan will synthesize sectoral policies to draft a nationwide just transition action plan, crafting a national-level policy framework for a just transition and ensuring that social participation remains a vital component of net-zero policy planning and execution. This year, Taiwan used the Greenhouse Gas Management Fund to integrate cross-sectoral capacities and support workers, industries, regions, and groups affected by the transition. This will help advance green-collar talent development, the low-carbon transition of small and medium-sized enterprises, vulnerable groups, local participation, and transition governance.

Enhancing global partnerships to jointly craft climate solutions

Article 6 of the Paris Agreement encourages voluntary cooperation to enable higher ambition for climate action while promoting sustainable development on the basis of environmental integrity, transparency, and the avoidance of double counting. As relevant arrangements move into the stage of implementation, international climate cooperation is expanding from policy dialogue to mitigation projects, technology cooperation, capacity building, and investment, which are important pathways for accelerating implementation of the Paris Agreement.

Taiwan is moving forward with climate diplomacy through pragmatic action. Last year, Taiwan signed a memorandum of understanding on Paris Agreement cooperation with its diplomatic ally Paraguay. Today, the two countries are advancing 12 action plans for environmental governance, thereby implementing global climate action and substantive environmental cooperation through sharing technology and engaging in youth dialogue and exchanges on the circular economy.

Türkiye has labeled COP31 as the COP of the Future, emphasizing that commitment is a declaration of intent, while execution represents trust. As global climate governance enters a critical phase focused on practice and outcomes, Taiwan will continue to deepen global partnerships through pragmatic engagement, making concrete contributions, and sharing its experience with the net-zero transition. Taiwan seeks international support for its meaningful participation in the UNFCCC and global climate governance efforts. It firmly believes that achieving the goals of the Paris Agreement requires the participation of every partner with the capacity and willingness to act. Taiwan is ready to collaborate with other nations to transform climate commitments into action and together build a more resilient, sustainable net-zero future.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: Galen University completes training program for BDF and Coast Guard personnel
World.content:
Galen University completes training program for BDF and Coast Guard personnel

By Zoila Palma: Galen University successfully concluded its Training of Trainers Program on Friday, October 23, 2026, following a collaborative initiative with the Belize Defence Force (BDF) and the Belize Coast Guard (BCG).

The program brought together 36 participants to strengthen their instructional skills and professional capabilities.

Participants received training in adult learning principles, competency-based teaching and learning, online teaching methods, and practical microteaching exercises.

The program was designed to equip them with the knowledge and techniques needed to deliver effective training within their respective organizations.

Through guided activities, hands-on practice, and peer feedback, participants had opportunities to develop and refine their teaching skills, with an emphasis on competency-based instruction.

Galen University said the initiative reflects its commitment to professional development, stronger partnerships with Belize’s national security agencies, and innovative teaching approaches.

Galen congratulated all participants on completing the program and commended the BDF and BCG for their continued efforts in capacity building.

World.title: University of Belize explores partnerships with TaiwanICDF and Taiwanese Universities
World.content:
University of Belize explores partnerships with TaiwanICDF and Taiwanese Universities

By Zoila Palma: Today, the University of Belize (UB) welcomed representatives from TaiwanICDF and four Taiwanese universities to explore potential collaborations under the Taiwan–Caribbean Prosperity Academy initiative.

Discussions focused on opportunities for student and faculty exchanges, joint research, practical training, and professional development in areas including health sciences, agriculture, technology, and hospitality.

UB said the proposed partnerships could expand educational opportunities, promote knowledge-sharing, and strengthen connections between Belize and Taiwan.

World.title: Bulridge Limited recognized at Climate Awards 2026 for environmental efforts
World.content:
Bulridge Limited recognized at Climate Awards 2026 for environmental efforts

By Zoila Palma: Bulridge Limited has been recognized as an honoree at the Climate Awards 2026, hosted recently by the Climate Change Department in recognition of its commitment to sustainable forest management, forest restoration, and building a more climate-resilient Belize.

As part of its restoration efforts, Bulridge Limited has continued its 2026 Restoration Project, moving from seed planting to transplanting seedlings.

The company recently completed its first transplanting activity of the year, with volunteers successfully transplanting more than 175 seedlings into their permanent locations in the Mountain Pine Ridge Forest Reserve.

The company expressed gratitude to its volunteers for contributing their time and energy to the initiative, highlighting the importance of collective efforts in protecting Belize’s forests and natural heritage.

Bulridge Limited also thanked the Climate Change Department for the recognition and congratulated the other award recipients, reaffirming its commitment to forest restoration and a greener, more sustainable Belize for future generations.

World.title: International News: Canada seeks closer ties with EU advancing plans to reduce reliance on U.S.
World.content:
International News: Canada seeks closer ties with EU advancing plans to reduce reliance on U.S.

By Zoila Palma: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is seeking closer relations with the European Union as Canada works to reduce its economic dependence on the United States.

Carney is expected to host EU leaders this week, with discussions potentially including an unprecedented “associate member” status for Canada as both sides explore stronger cooperation, AFP reports.

Carney’s efforts come amid growing tensions with US President Donald Trump, whose tariffs have affected Canada’s economy and whose threats to annex the country have sparked widespread concern.

In August, Carney ended trade negotiations with the Trump administration, declaring that Canada’s future would not be decided in Washington. He has also questioned whether the United States can be trusted to honour its commitments.

Since taking office last year, Carney has moved to strengthen relationships with countries beyond the United States, including China, India, Saudi Arabia and Turkey.

His government is pursuing greater access to international markets, aiming to secure tariff-free access for Canadian businesses to three billion consumers worldwide.

World.title: International News: Trump questions Brazil election results as Bolsonaro’s party recognizes Lula’s victory
World.content:
International News: Trump questions Brazil election results as Bolsonaro’s party recognizes Lula’s victory

By Zoila Palma: U.S. President Donald Trump has questioned the legitimacy of Brazil’s presidential election, claiming that the vote appeared to be “rigged,” despite President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s victory over right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.

Trump made the remarks on Monday while speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, describing the election as a “bad look” for the world.

However, he indicated that he had not decided on any response and said his responsibility was to govern the United States, Politico reports.

Trump’s comments echoed allegations made by Bolsonaro, who has refused to concede defeat and called for the results to be annulled.

The losing candidate questioned a decision by a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice to extend voting by two hours in some circumstances to accommodate transportation delays.

The election has become a point of tension between Washington and Brasília, with Trump previously imposing high tariffs on Brazilian goods in an effort to pressure Brazil’s government over the prosecution of former President Jair Bolsonaro.

Those measures reportedly strengthened Lula’s political standing before relations between the two countries gradually improved. Following Lula’s victory, some allies of Trump have called for tougher action against Brazil, including cutting diplomatic ties, while questions remain over Washington’s formal response to the election outcome.

World.title: International News: Europe’s last fully integrated Penicillin plant faces threat from Chinese competition
World.content:
International News: Europe’s last fully integrated Penicillin plant faces threat from Chinese competition

By Zoila Palma: Europe’s only fully integrated penicillin manufacturing plant, located in Kundl, Austria, is facing an uncertain future as cheaper Chinese production intensifies competition in the pharmaceutical industry.

The facility, operated by Sandoz, produces penicillin from start to finish, including the active ingredients used in antibiotics that treat serious bacterial infections, Reuters report.

Sandoz says the plant is struggling to remain commercially viable as European governments prioritize lower medicine prices.

The company has asked the European Commission to investigate whether Chinese manufacturers are selling antibiotic ingredients below production cost, potentially with the support of government subsidies. The investigation could lead to trade measures against China. Sandoz has warned that the closure of the Kundl facility would leave Europe heavily dependent on foreign suppliers for essential antibiotics.

The dispute has raised wider concerns about Europe’s ability to secure essential medicines during future pandemics, conflicts or trade disputes.

Pharmaceutical experts warn that dependence on a small number of foreign suppliers could leave the region vulnerable to supply disruptions.

World.title: WATCH: Jamaicans divided over proposed 20-year minimum sentence for gun crimes
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaicans have expressed mixed reactions to a proposal by the National Security Council (NSC) to increase the mandatory minimum sentence for gun crimes from 15 to 20 years, with some welcoming the move as a crime-fighting measure while others believe the penalty is too harsh.

Observer Online took to the streets to gauge public opinion on the proposal, which was announced Sunday by the NSC, chaired by Prime Minister Andrew Holness.

The proposal has already drawn criticism from the Opposition People’s National Party (PNP), with Opposition Spokesperson on Justice, Zuleika Jess, arguing that it was put forward “without adequately addressing the legislation’s flaws”.

The existing 15-year mandatory minimum sentence under the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022, has also faced scrutiny from members of the legal fraternity, who have raised concerns about its broad application and staged demonstrations calling for legislative reform.

Speaking with Observer Online, some individuals supported the proposed increase, arguing that tougher penalties could deter individuals from possessing illegal firearms and help curb gun violence.

“Twenty year minimum, 20 years. It’s a bit harsh, but I feel like the Government is working a way to try to reduce crime because there’s a lot of fatality with gunman and all of them things…” one respondent said.

Another agreed, suggesting that the prospect of spending two decades behind bars could discourage illegal firearm possession.

“I think it’s appropriate because if you know you’re going to get sentenced to 20 years for having illegal firearms, [would] you put yourself in that position? No, I agree with it,” she said.

Another Jamaican encouraged those interested in owning firearms to pursue legal avenues rather than risk facing criminal penalties.

“Gun is a thing weh protect you and thing. Some man use it fi do wrong thing, some use it fi do the right but sometimes you can get right out of wrong same way. You have to just get your thing license, go to the proper place and look bout your thing. If you love gun so much, prefer you have a gun license or if you wah really be a gunholder, go inna the force or go join the JDF or police,” he said.

However, not everyone was convinced that a longer mandatory sentence was justified.

One respondent described the proposal as excessive, raising concerns about the consequences for young people who may become involved in firearm-related offences without having committed a violent act.

“I believe that it is excessive. I’m thinking that 20 years of someone’s life is like a half of their lifetime. What time would you get for one mistake? Especially if it’s a situation where you did not commit a crime, as in murder anyone or shoot up anyone or even use a firearm. Suppose it’s a situation where your teenager or young adult was caught up in bad company. It’s a harsh penalty. Your entire future is lost in 20 years,” she said.

(Video by: Llewellyn Wynter)

World.title: Mother, son killed in St Mary crash on her birthday
World.content:
An undated photo of 38-year-old Abigayle Whitehorn of Hamilton Mountain, St Mary,

ST MARY, Jamaica — What should have been a week of birthday celebrations ended in tragedy on Monday after a St Mary woman and her teenage son were killed in a motor vehicle crash along the Wilderness main road in Galina.

The deceased have been identified as 38-year-old Abigayle Whitehorn of Hamilton Mountain, St Mary, and her 18-year-old son, Tyreke Cameron.

Whitehorn was reportedly celebrating her birthday on the day of the fatal collision, having enjoyed an early celebration with friends at the Port Maria Bus Park on Sunday night.

According to police reports, the crash occurred about 2:00 pm when a white Toyota Hiace bus travelling towards Port Maria reportedly went out of control, veered into the opposite lane and collided head-on with a grey Toyota Fielder motor car.

Whitehorn, her son and another passenger were travelling in the Fielder towards Oracabessa when the collision occurred.

Several occupants of both vehicles sustained injuries and were rushed to the Port Maria Hospital, where Whitehorn and Cameron were pronounced dead.

The other injured individuals remain under medical care for serious injuries.

In the wake of the fatal crash, the St Mary police are appealing to motorists to exercise extreme caution while travelling on the nation’s roadways.

Investigations into the circumstances surrounding the crash are ongoing.

World.title: Criminalise gun couriers
World.content:
CHAMPAGNIE... it was also my expectation and hope that the National Security Council would have looked at specific criminalisation of couriers or shippers who are used to import illegal firearms into this country

Senior attorney Peter Champagnie, KC — who has been strident about the shortcomings of the 2022 Firearms Act since inception — on Monday welcomed amendments proposed by the National Security Council but is urging criminalisation of couriers or shippers who import illegal firearms into the country by virtue of lax inspection protocols.

His call comes in the wake of Sunday’s announcement by the Office of the Cabinet that the National Security Council (NSC) has recommended that individuals convicted of illegal possession of a firearm should now face a new minimum mandatory sentence of 20 years imprisonment instead of the current 15-year minimum.

The NSC also proposed that adults who groom children to use, store, transport, or acquire illegal guns will face a new criminal offence under the pending amendments to the Act “to address the gap whereby gangs seek to recruit and enlist minors in the commission of gun crimes”.

Additionally, the NSC agreed that further consideration should be given to how cases involving children found with illegal firearms are handled and assured that concerns raised regarding imitation firearms will be “clearly addressed to distinguish between toy guns and guns designed to realistically imitate a weapon”.

The council also said the review would include concerns surrounding firearms with expired licences. In the meantime, however, it said before the new provisions take effect, the Government will provide a gun amnesty and cash buy-back programme, giving anyone holding an illegal gun the opportunity to surrender it. The Ministry of National Security and Peace has been directed to have the draft legislation ready by the end of November 2026 for wider consultations.

On Monday, Champagnie, in an interview with the Jamaica Observer, applauded the pending changes but said, “It was also my expectation and hope that the National Security Council would have looked at specific criminalisation of couriers or shippers who, because of the lack of diligence that is applied to scrutinise and inspect shipments, are used to import illegal firearms into this country.”

“As I understand it presently, as it relates to Customs and what obtains, the worst that can be expected if a shipment is contaminated by illegal weapons or anything illegal is that there is perhaps a penalty or a hearing, or there is a suspension of that person’s licence or revocation. But I do believe that it needs to go further in the way of criminalisation, because what the National Security Council needs to also focus on is not just the tail end of the problem; that is to say, persons who are in possession of illegal firearms, but also the source of these firearms, because we do not manufacture firearms here; they have to come from somewhere other than Jamaica. And I think there needs to be stiffer penalties, or indeed penalties, in relation to that. Not just mere trafficking; it has to also reach the shippers and couriers, that is my view,” the prominent defence attorney said.

“They could easily create a mandate where shippers or couriers are required to containerise their shipment in a sterile era where it is video-recorded and presented, and where they would have to show that they took all reasonable steps to ensure that their cargo or the shipment is not contaminated,” Champagnie suggested.

Making it clear that he was speaking in a personal capacity and not on behalf of other legal bodies, Champagnie said he had no quarrel with the proposal to increase the statutory mandatory minimum from 15 to 20 years.

“That is the supremacy of Parliament. I can’t say that they have no authority for so doing and indeed, I have been on record over the years to say that this idea of giving someone who is caught with an illegal weapon three years or 18 months or even a fine is unacceptable. So I support the statutory mandatory minimum, and if they want to increase it, then that’s their right. However, I do believe that there needs to be a holistic approach with the Firearms Act to facilitate guilty pleas,” Champagnie maintained.

“There must be some incentive for persons wanting to plead guilty, and there must be some exceptional circumstances where a person found in possession of a firearm must be allowed to have a kind of discretion for that person to receive a sentence below the statutory mandatory minimum, and in those circumstances, there is authority for it in other jurisdictions where exceptions are specifically laid out. But certainly, in relation to the hardcore criminals and those that use imitation firearms to commit offences, they must expect severe penalties,” he argued.

Champagnie, in the meantime, said legislation which addresses the appeal process in circumstances where a sentence is excessive should also be revisited.

“We must also bear in mind that the prosecution now has the right to appeal if a sentence is given that is considered to be woefully inadequate for the circumstances, and there have been cases that have settled that. So, I would want that to be also considered, and I look forward to the actual details of the report and the recommendations beyond what has been issued by way of a press release, because one is not able to fully appreciate all of the nuances and the extent of the recommendations until we actually are able or in a position to examine the actual paper that is in the way of recommendations,” he told the Observer.

He said the planned silent protest on September 23 and a sit out by some attorneys as part of the push for a review of the Act had not been in vain.

“When the attorneys sought to bring some kind of pressure for the Government to re-examine the Firearms Act, the first comment that was made was that the legislation was up for review next year, and therefore we should await that period. I note, however, that there is a shift now, where there seems to be an intention to have recommended changes effected within this year. That is good, but what it demonstrates is that we are able to pivot and we are able to move with alacrity if the need arises,” he said in urging the authorities to ensure that practitioners from both the private and public bar are at the discussion table.

“I don’t think ever before in our legal history, we have had a situation where a legislation, in the way of the administration of the criminal justice system, has received universal comments in the way of shortcomings by not just the private bar but also the public bar, the prosecution, and in some instances the judges, as it relates to it facilitating guilty plea, and that is a major, major point to be made,” he argued.

“Anyone who is involved in the practice of law day to day will tell you that there are real issues. There are real issues also with licensed firearm holders who run the risk of getting 20 years just by being in possession of a licensed firearm and being caught for instance in a physical confrontation with another person even when they are not using it, so these are fundamental issues that I think need to be examined,” he said.

Section 14(3) of the Act dictates that a person commits a felony if they are in possession of a firearm or an imitation firearm at the time of committing, or when being apprehended for, any specific serious offence listed in the First Schedule of the provision.

World.title: Waiting in pain for 5 months
World.content:
Garfield Granston, who broke his spine in May, is seen at Black River Hospital.

THE wait continues for 57-year-old Garfield Granston — who broke his spine in May — to receive a procedure which remains stalled by an out-of-service machine at Kingston Public Hospital (KPH).

His stepdaughter, Elexso Smith, told the Jamaica Observer on Monday that the family has endured five long months awaiting a surgery date, but KPH has not delivered a clear timeline, leaving Granston at Black River Hospital (BRH) where he was initially admitted.

Granston’s ordeal began on May 15, 2026 when he fell from a tree and was rushed to BRH in his home parish of St Elizabeth. There, doctors determined that he had sustained fractures in two places along his spine and would require surgery.

The family was subsequently told that the hospital lacked the facilities to perform the procedure, and her stepfather was referred to KPH — Jamaica’s largest public multidisciplinary Type-A facility — with the hope of receiving the treatment he needed.

The procedure required 10 pedicle screws, 10 set screws, and two rods, at a total cost of $854,000. Faced with that bill, Smith said the family sought assistance from the Ministry of Health and Wellness, which provided a $554,000 subsidy, while they covered the remaining $300,000.

Smith shared that after the bill was cleared, she was certain that her stepfather would soon receive surgery. But when they took the receipt to Granston’s surgeon, another obstacle outside of her family’s control presented itself.

“Before we pay the money at KPH, and before we got help from the health ministry, the doctor was very harsh, because he was arguing saying that we have to pay the money before we can do surgery. When we get the receipt, and gave it to the doctor he said: ‘One more problem. The machine broke down’,” Smith told the Observer.

“Every time he is to go up there [KPH] they’re always putting him off or if he’s sent up there they send him back down [to BRH]. From the last time he went up there on the 30th [of June] he has not been back there. And then when they [BRH] call up there they say he mustn’t come, or there is no bed space,” she claimed.

The most recent update was delivered by doctors at Black River Hospital, notifying Smith and family that the surgery would not be possible until a bedsore that Granston had developed during his five-month stay completely healed.

She argued that the “cut”, slightly positioned above his lower back, was small, and should not, in her estimation, cause further delay.

Smith added that her stepfather’s care regimen has been stressful on the family, who argue that caring for him in his current state is significantly more difficult than if he were recovering from surgery.

“Sometimes we say that it would have been better if he was at home, you know, so you can spend a little time with him and do what you have to do. It’s really hard for us; you have to buy pampers and every little thing. If he did the surgery and can sit upright, we could push him in a wheelchair and help him to use the bathroom. So right now it’s just really hard,” said Smith.

Meanwhile, Granston remains at BRH where he receives treatment for pain but continues to bear the discomfort of his injuries.

“They’ve just been giving him pills. Right now, he’s been complaining about pain in his belly. About two weeks ago he had to do a test and we’re still waiting on those results. So it has just been hard on him, and hard on everyone,” Smith said.

Tired of waiting while her stepfather languishes in pain, Smith has called on KPH to provide a clear timeline for when his distress will end.

“I just want to find out what’s really happening with this surgery situation. It’s been months and nothing. We’re not hearing nothing at all. So we just want KPH to state what their position is with this surgery as soon as possible,” said Smith.

World.title: Bad Sekki jets to NY
World.content:
Bad Sekki.

For Jamaican comedian and social media personality Karlando “Bad Sekki” Bailey, the bright lights of New York City’s Times Square have long represented more than just a popular tourist attraction. They have been the setting for a video he has imagined creating for years, and come November, that dream could finally become a reality.

The popular content creator is now preparing for his first trip to the country, with plans to visit four cities, reconnect with family, and explore opportunities to further develop his craft.

But amid the excitement of travelling overseas for the first time, there is one particular moment Bailey is eagerly anticipating — standing in the heart of Times Square, surrounded by its towering digital billboards, and delivering a line he has long rehearsed in his mind.

“A just one video idea me have weh me really wah do from when, where I am in Time Square saying ‘New York’. That’s the main thing I am looking forward to,” Bailey shared.

The moment, although seemingly simple, carries considerable significance for the comedian, whose journey from working as a security guard to establishing himself as a popular Jamaican content creator has been marked by persistence, humour, and an ability to connect with audiences through everyday experiences.

His upcoming adventure, dubbed Bad Sekki Goes to America, will run from November 16 to December 2, 2026, documenting his experiences across four US cities while offering his followers a glimpse into a new chapter of his life.

For Bailey, the opportunity comes after a disappointing experience in March 2025, when his initial application for a US visa was denied. He subsequently shared the setback with his followers, generating encouragement from supporters who were eager to see him eventually realise his ambition.

Determined not to allow the rejection to derail his plans, Bailey reapplied in 2026 and was granted a visa in October.

“I felt happy and really thankful that I got it. I tried last year and didn’t get it,” he said, reflecting on the moment he received the good news.

According to Jason McNeish, who is spearheading the organisation of the trip, travelling to the United States has been one of Bailey’s long-standing aspirations.

“It has been a dream of his to travel and go to the US. He applied for his visa in 2025, which was denied. He reapplied in 2026 which was approved,” McNeish explained.

And while Bailey was ready to board a plane almost immediately after receiving his passport, McNeish said the team wanted to ensure that his first international experience would be memorable and beneficial to his career.

“He wanted to go the next day after he got the passport but we wanted to make it a whole trip. He will be visiting four cities so it took a longer time to plan,” he said.

The itinerary is being developed to combine entertainment, cultural exploration, family connections, and professional development, allowing Bailey to experience the United States both as a visitor and as a creative professional.

A major component of the trip will be content creation, with Bailey expected to document his experiences and share them with the audience that has supported his rise in Jamaica’s digital entertainment space.

New York, in particular, is expected to provide a backdrop for his signature brand of comedy, as he explores unfamiliar surroundings and captures the reactions and experiences that have become central to his appeal.

However, the trip will not be limited to sightseeing and social media videos.

McNeish revealed that plans are also being explored for Bailey to visit professional studios and gain exposure to international production environments, with the possibility of connecting with representatives associated with streaming giant Netflix.

“We are making it a full experience, he’s going to of course connect with family and more importantly for me he is going to get some professional development as well, so we are looking at visiting a few studios…” McNeish said.

He was careful to point out, however, that the proposed Netflix engagement has not been finalised. Discussions are ongoing with an agent affiliated with the company in the hope of arranging an opportunity during the visit.

The emphasis on professional development reflects an ambition to use the trip as a stepping stone towards expanding Bailey’s creative possibilities beyond the Jamaican market.

For the comedian, however, some of the most meaningful moments may come away from the cameras.

Among those eagerly anticipating his arrival is a cousin with whom he grew up, and who was one of the few people aware that he had decided to make another attempt at securing a visa.

“She was the first one I called. She was so happy for me because she was the only one I told that I was going to look about it,” Bailey recalled.

The planned reunion adds a personal dimension to an adventure that is already shaping up to be a significant milestone in his life.

The Bad Sekki Goes to America project will seek to capture those moments alongside the humour, excitement, and inevitable surprises of experiencing a new country for the first time.

World.title: Kane, Putellas taste Ballon d’Or glory
World.content:
Spain and Barcelona midfielder Alexia Putellas (right) and England and Bayern Munich forward Harry Kane pose with their trophies on stage after receiving their Ballon d’Or awards for the best female and male footballer during the 2026 Ballon d’Or France Football award ceremony at the Palladium Theatre in London, England, on Monday. (Photo: AFP)

LONDON, England (AFP) — Harry Kane became England’s first Ballon d’Or winner in 25 years in his native city of London on Monday, beating out stiff competition from Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe.

Alexia Putellas claimed the women’s prize for a third time to extend Spain’s domination of the award, thanks to her role in leading Barcelona to last season’s UEFA Champions League before moving to London City Lionesses.

The first-ever Ballon d’Or ceremony on English soil got off to an inauspicious start as the London traffic caused a delay of nearly an hour, with many of the star names arriving late.

But there was a happy ending for the hometown hero as Kane collected the crowning glory of his career to date.

The 33-year-old Bayern Munich forward struck a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for club and country last season, propelling the German giants to a league and cup double. He also scored six times as England finished third at the World Cup.

“Without you guys [his Bayern Munich teammates] and the rest of the team it wouldn’t be possible, the way you guys push me, the way we compete.

So thank you very much,” Kane said after collecting the award. Kane’s medal collection is limited to German domestic triumphs since he arrived at Bayern in 2023.

He was on the losing side for Tottenham in the 2019 Champions League final against Liverpool, and twice tasted bitter defeat in the final of the European Championship with England.

But his remarkable goalscoring consistency has earned him the highest individual award in football.

“Making the move to Bayern Munich was a big step in my career,” Kane told AFP earlier.

“Some people saw it as a risk but for me, it was always about improving and seeing if I could get better around the teammates, the team, the club — and it has pushed me onto another level.

“Being a number nine for Bayern and England, you are expected to score goals — and to do that the number of times I did last year is something I’m really proud of,” he added.

Winner in 2021 and 2022, Putellas’s third Ballon d’Or caps her return back to the top of the women’s game after an anterior cruciate ligament injury derailed her rise four years ago.

Putellas succeeds Spain teammate Aitana Bonmati, the winner the past three years who was sidelined by a leg break for most of last season.

“Ever since I suffered the injury I’ve been trying to enjoy every moment as if it were my last, because you never know if it’ll happen again,” Putellas told AFP in an interview last month.

“I never felt that the [Ballon d’Or] trophy was ‘mine’… Having already experienced it once, I’m able to enjoy it even more now,” she said.

Yamal made the boldest fashion statement of the contenders with a pink flower on the front of his black suit.

The Barcelona winger scooped up the first award of the night for young talent of the year for the third-consecutive time.

But the 19-year-old fell short of becoming the youngest-ever Ballon d’Or winner after he failed to produce his best form during Spain’s World Cup success.

Mbappe got the better of Yamal with two goals as Real Madrid edged Barcelona 2-1 in El Clasico on Sunday. But his wait to win the Ballon d’Or goes on despite his prolific year for France and Real Madrid.

Luis de la Fuente beat out Paris SaintGermain’s Luis Enrique and Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta to be named men’s coach of the year, after leading Spain to World Cup glory.

“I’m really privileged to work with a team of such high quality on a professional and human level,” de la Fuente said.

Barcelona’s Pere Romeu scooped the prize for women’s coach of the year. Arsenal’s Bukayo Saka won the Socrates award for his humanitarian work.

Paris Saint-Germain missed out on securing any of the main individual awards despite winning a second-consecutive Champions League, but did have the consolation of winning men’s club of the year.

Spanish duo Unai Simon and Cata Coll were named best men’s and women’s goalkeeper, respectively.

World.title: BAD BUNNY!
World.content:
Jamaica and Manchester City Women striker Khadija Shaw at the Ballon d’Or award ceremony in London, England, on Monday.

REGGAE Girlz superstar Khadija “Bunny” Shaw has spent her career defying expectations, and she reached another incredible milestone by being recognised as the third-best player in women’s football globally.

On Monday, Shaw finished in the top three of the Women’s Ballon d’Or Rankings, as announced at the awards ceremony in London, England. The Jamaican, who was tipped as one of the favourites, ended behind winner Alexia Putellas of Spain who was recognised for her quadruple-winning season with FC Barcelona last season.

Shaw is the only Jamaican to have ever been nominated for the Ballon d’Or, male or female, and she created further history by becoming just the fourth player from outside Europe to finish in the top three. She is also only the third North American player to achieve the feat, joining USA’s Megan Rapinoe, who won the award in 2019, and Alex Morgan, who finished third that same year.

Shaw had a remarkable season in England, guiding Manchester City to the Women’s Super League (WSL) and the FA Cup, ending their four-year title drought.

She finished with 21 goals to win the WSL Golden Boot for a third-straight season and was named WSL Player of the Season, Professional Footballers Association (PFA) Player of the Year, and Football Writers Association (FWA) Footballer of the Year.

Shaw improved on her ranking after finishing 24th in the 2023 race and 15th in 2024.

Despite not winning the overall award, the Reggae Girlz captain says she’s overwhelmed by the achievement.

“To be named as the third-best player by those who voted is a huge honour for me, and I’m extremely grateful for the recognition,” Shaw said. “[Manchester] City are a special club, and for them to trust me with leading our front-line week in, week out, is something I take immense pride in.

“I would like to thank my teammates and the staff for supporting me, on and off the pitch, so I can perform at my best. Recording a historic double last season was a campaign that will always hold a special place in my heart. This recognition would not be possible without them.”

Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts told the Jamaica Observer that Shaw deserves to be recognised as one of the world’s best.

“Bunny has been on the world stage for a number of years and we’re just super excited and happy that she would have achieved so much during her footballing career,” he said. “Bunny is one of our local players who would have ascended to the position of being a superstar, and she would have come up through a local parish programme and, of course, our national programme.

“It gives us more reason to be delighted and proud of the achievements of a local superstar. It has reached the level now that nothing that Bunny achieves is surprising because she seems to be head and shoulders above [other players], especially in Concacaf and certainly matching up with those worldwide. So, we are again basking in another historic achievement and I really want to personally, and certainly on behalf of the entire JFF, to extend again for the umpteenth time another congratulatory remark to the great Khadija “Bunny” Shaw. We are just super excited and we’re here to give her as much support as we can.”

Reggae Girlz Head Coach Hubert Busby says Shaw has further cemented her status as a legend in Jamaican culture.

“I think it’s well documented of what an impact, not just her but the women’s team, senior women’s team, has had on young girls in Jamaica and in the Diaspora. And to see one of our own highlighted when you’re watching these awards with the best of the best players and the distinguished guests who are there, it is remarkable just to know how far she’s come in this time,” he told the Observer.

“I just think she’s going to go from strength to strength. I still think she’s got a few more years left in her so we just continue to be revelled in her accomplishments. And, let’s not forget, she definitely is a national treasure, for sure.”

Shaw joined Erling Haaland and Kevin De Bruyne as the only Man City players in history to finish in the top three of the Ballon d’Or.

World.title: EU eyes global tax deal revenue to boost next budget
World.content:
Costa, who is brokering budget talks, is pressuring leaders to reach a budget deal among themselves by the end of the year — before elections in Poland, France and Italy threaten to derail the negotiations.

Yet after more than a year of haggling, EU governments are still at odds over five proposed new taxes that the Commission estimates would generate €65 billion per year.

Among the options on the table, a corporate tax known as CORE — which charges a lump sum on companies’ revenues exceeding €100 million — has emerged as the most unpopular option and is particularly toxic in Germany.

To break the deadlock, French President Emmanuel Macron supported funneling part of the tax on multinationals to the EU budget during a leaders’ summit in October, said two of the diplomats. They were granted anonymity, like others, to discuss the sensitive plans.

Supporters argue that this idea could garner more political support than CORE as it targets companies’ profits as opposed to their revenue.

“The corporate income tax is about taxing companies based on their profitability. CORE is not about that, CORE is about taking a toll blindly,” said Pascal Saint-Amans, a former OECD official and one of the architects of the global tax arrangement.

World.title: EU prepares for a grim future with new climate-proofing law
World.content:
“There is no alternative to continue to cut emissions more forcefully and to move full-frontal into clean energy,” Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra told reporters. “But at the same time, we do have to acknowledge that the problems we're facing have morphed into something that is so large that just doing that alone unfortunately no longer is good enough.”

The Commission’s proposed Climate Resilience Law asks governments to draft plans to prepare for a world that’s 2 degrees Celsius hotter in 2050 and 3C hotter by the end of the century, aligning with the United Nations’ latest projections that current global climate policies can only limit warming to 2.8C.

The same U.N. report also warned that the world can no longer limit warming to 1.5C, the lower bound of the Paris Agreement’s dual goals, and that steep emissions cuts are needed to achieve the best-case scenario of halting the rise in global temperatures at 1.8C.

The Commission insisted that Tuesday’s package did not amount to Brussels resigning itself to catastrophic levels of warming.

“Let me just be crystal-clear on the 1.5C, that remains our goal,” said Hoekstra. “At the same time, it would be unwise not to prepare for… the current trajectory the world is on.”

Regulation for the deregulation era

Under the proposed law, governments are “encouraged” to take the 3C scenario into account when designing policies, budgets and investments.

World.title: Frontex soll soziale Medien auf Hinweise zu illegaler Migration überwachen
World.content:
BRÜSSEL – Die Europäische Kommission stellte am Dienstag Pläne für eine umfassende Reform von Frontex vor. Damit sollen die Befugnisse und Kapazitäten der Agentur im Kampf gegen irreguläre Migration ausgeweitet werden. Künftig soll Frontex eine größere Rolle bei der Rückführung von Menschen ohne Aufenthaltsrecht übernehmen und Rückführungsmaßnahmen auch außerhalb der EU durchführen können. Zudem soll die Behörde neue Kompetenzen bei der Überwachung sozialer Medien erhalten.

Welche Rolle soziale Netzwerke bei der Verbreitung von Informationen spielen, die irreguläre Migration begünstigen können, zeigte sich im Juli in der spanischen Exklave Ceuta. Dort hatten innerhalb weniger Stunden Tausende Migranten unerlaubt die Grenze überquert.

Nach den neuen Plänen soll Frontex ein Zentrum zur Überwachung und Reaktion auf Online-Inhalte einrichten. Dieses soll öffentlich zugängliche Beiträge in sozialen Medien auswerten, um Entwicklungen zu erkennen, die für den Schutz der EU-Außengrenzen relevant sind. Darüber hinaus soll die Stelle Maßnahmen gegen illegale Online-Inhalte unterstützen, die mit Sicherheitsrisiken an den Grenzen zusammenhängen, erklärte die zuständige EU-Kommissionsvizepräsidentin Henna Virkkunen am Dienstag vor Journalisten.

World.title: EIB to sign framework deal with Canada on critical raw materials
World.content:
A Canadian flag flies by the waterfront of Lake Ontario in Toronto, Canada on Aug. 27, 2026. | Cole Burston/AFP via Getty Images

The European Investment Bank is due to sign a framework agreement with Canada this week that will pave the way for investments into critical raw materials and other areas, a Bank official told POLITICO.

The deal with the long-term lending arm of the European Union is expected to be signed on the sidelines of an EU-Canada summit on Thursday in Montreal, said the official who was granted anonymity to discuss internal preparations.

Such a deal would mark a concrete step toward closer ties amid broader discussions about cooperation on arctic security and the EU’s potential offer of “associate member” status to Canada. The summit will aim to highlight deepening ties between like-minded partners.

World.title: EU divisions persist on ‘associate member’ label for Canada
World.content:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, left, speaks with European Parliament President Roberta Metsola in the hemicycle of the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France on Sept. 17, 2026. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images

BRUSSELS — The EU was split Tuesday over whether to offer “associate membership” status to Canada, with several countries refusing to sign off on a statement containing that phrase just 48 hours before a summit between the two sides in Montreal.

After EU capitals could not agree on the language in the statement in talks between ambassadors Monday, they used the so-called silence procedure on Tuesday. That meant a new text would be adopted automatically without a formal meeting or vote, if no countries objected by midday.

But Germany, which is leading the push to have the term “associate member” fully removed from the text, was among at least four countries that broke the silence procedure before that deadline, said two EU diplomats, granted anonymity to speak freely. That means the topic will be discussed Wednesday at another meeting of EU ambassadors, just one day before the EU-Canada summit kicks off.

World.title: Frontex gets power to track migration talk on social media
World.content:
This article is also available in: German

The role of social media platforms in spreading information that contributes to illegal migration was central to the crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. | Tomohiro Ohsumi/Getty Images

The EU's border agency, Frontex, will be able to monitor social media for information about migration flows.

The European Commission on Tuesday unveiled a revamp of Frontex, strengthening its capabilities and capacity to tackle illegal migration. It will play a more prominent role in deporting people with no legal right to remain in the EU, including new powers to carry out return operations beyond the bloc’s territory and new oversight on social media.

The role of social media platforms in spreading information that contributes to illegal migration was central to the crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, where thousands of migrants illegally crossed the border within a few hours in July.

World.title: French government mulled blocking social networks and mobile internet amid protests
World.content:
Contacted by POLITICO, officials from Lecornu's office, the technology ministry and the interior ministry did not deny the move nor the letter's existence.

The government feared that the scenes of violence seen on Oct. 17 could repeat or escalate on the following weekend — a concern that did not materialize, as far fewer incidents were recorded on Oct. 24.

“What they wanted, above all, was to block the communication channels that allow gangs to meet up and organize,” said the employee of a telecommunications provider, who was granted anonymity to speak freely.

The move, however, would have also prevented peaceful protesters from communicating as well. Blocking access to social networks in a targeted area, such as a specific neighborhood, is not technically possible, while cutting access to mobile internet would cause major disruptions to other key services such as mobile payments, security-surveillance devices and emergency communications.

The government also considered a less radical solution that would disable geolocation display features “to prevent gatherings of people who don’t know each other, for example,” according to the official from the prime minister’s office.

Other limitations on social media access are being discussed in parliament as part of the debate on the so-called “who breaks pays” bill, which would hold people who "knowingly took part" in a riot financially responsible — whether or not they committed property damage themselves.

The same bill would require platforms to remove within 24 hours content that incites physical or sexual assault, theft, destruction, or property damage, “when such content is likely to cause a serious disturbance to public order” and within one hour content that encourages insurrection.

Other lawmakers are proposing measures ranging from tracking troublemakers via algorithmic video surveillance to penalizing online marketplaces that fail to prevent the sale of stolen goods.

World.title: French MPs will vote on Sánchez-style amnesty plan for undocumented workers
World.content:
Earlier this year, Spain moved to grant legal status to half a million unauthorized immigrants who could prove they had been living in Spain for at least five months, could provide proof of employment or a familial link to the country and did not have a criminal record.

Christophle wants to grant legal status to an estimated 300,000 to 400,000 people who have been employed in France for over six months but without proper documentation.

The bill is likely to unite left-leaning MPs in the French National Assembly, but opposition from center-right and far-right groups means it will probably fail.

However, Glucksmann’s campaign hopes the proposal will highlight a rift between lawmakers backing French President Emmanuel Macron and voters who elected him in 2022 — some of whom are more progressive on issues like immigration.

The debate on immigration will be an effective way to differentiate Glucksmann from his center-right rival Édouard Philippe, who believes that amnesty plans should be contingent on a European agreement, said an official who is backing the center-left MEP. It might also help poach Macron voters “who are completely opposed to a closed society,” he added.

Among those who voted for Macron in 2022, 29% plan to vote for Raphaël Glucksmann next year, according to a Cluster17 poll commissioned by POLITICO, against 49% for Édouard Philippe.

Glucksmann is currently projected to receive 13% of the overall vote, according to the poll, against 16% for Philippe. They both trail far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen (33%) and Mélenchon (18.5%). The top two candidates will advance to a runoff if no one wins a majority in the first round.

The bill is scheduled to be voted on Nov. 19.

World.title: Iraq sentences seven French nationals to prison for belonging to Islamic State
World.content:
An Iraqi court sentenced seven French nationals to prison on Tuesday for belonging to the Islamic State group.

 

Iraq's Supreme Judicial Council sentenced Lakhdar Sebouai, Adel Bou Aoun, Anas Abdul Rahman, Ziad Ahmad, Mehdi Sida and Benjamin Van Han to life imprisonment, which under Iraqi law is equivalent to 20 years.

The seventh defendant, Amza Benabed, 24, was given a 15-year prison term. They now have 30 days to lodge an appeal.

Under Iraqi law, decisions handed down by criminal courts are also subject to review by the Court of Cassation, whether or not the defendant has filed an appeal.

The seven men were deemed "particularly dangerous because of their role in threatening Iraq's national security, destabilising Iraq and Syria, and their involvement in inciting terrorist operations in other countries," a court statement said.

They were among 47 French citizens suspected of links to IS. Held in Syria until last year, they were transferred to Iraq so they could stand trial.

Defence lawyers and representatives of the French embassy were present at the hearing.

Islamic State

The Islamic State group swept across Iraq in 2014, seizing vast swathes of territory in the west of the country and in neighbouring Syria, where it established the seat of its self-proclaimed caliphate.

Although the organisation lost control of these areas several years ago, it still has active cells that periodically carry out attacks in both countries.

Iraq is currently holding thousands of people suspected of belonging to IS. They include more than 5,700 detainees transferred from north-eastern Syria after fighting broke out in January between Syrian government forces and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF).

The latter had long been guarding the detention centres where jihadist fighters and their families were held following the fall of the caliphate.

Some detainees linked to IS managed to escape during the January clashes, fuelling fears of larger-scale breakouts and leading to the transfer of the remaining prisoners to Iraq.

Iraq's national security adviser, Qasim al-Aboudi, said earlier this month that Syria had requested the transfer to Damascus of around 4,000 Syrians suspected of belonging to IS so that they could be tried there. Baghdad, however, rejected the request.

Al-Aboudi said that once their trials in Iraq were over, some detainees could be sent back to their country of origin to serve their sentences there. It is still not known whether the convicted French nationals could be repatriated.

In the past, Iraq has frequently executed people convicted of terrorism, prompting criticism from human rights organisations. However, the country does not apply the death penalty to foreign nationals whose home country does not provide for capital punishment.

World.title: Norway says 'successful' cyberattacks against the country have tripled in last six months
World.content:
Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) said on Tuesday that the number of "successful" cyberattacks targeting Norwegian organisations had trebled in the last six months as it warned of a continued threat to national security.

 

In a new report, the NSM - which is involved in efforts to counter espionage and hybrid threats - said the country's defence industry and space sector were particularly exposed to cyber risk.

"This also applies to critical infrastructure and service providers to organisations that are important to national security," it said.

"NSM has not previously made this type of assessment public," director Arne Christian Haugstøyl added. "We are doing so now because it is absolutely necessary to strengthen both the resilience and the ability to handle cyber operations in Norwegian organisations."

The report follows increasing warnings across Europe of suspected Russian hybrid attacks, including cyber operations.

In August, Norwegian media reported that a Russian hacker group had declared war on Norway while also claiming responsibility for a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack that had reportedly impacted multiple government digital services.

In its report published on Tuesday, the NSM did not point to a specific actor but said that certain businesses and organisations were being increasingly subjected to reconnaissance and ransomware and DDoS attacks.

The agency also warned of the threat posed by artificial intelligence technology, which it said posed a "serious risk" to Norwegian businesses and organisations.

“AI analyzes large amounts of data and identifies vulnerabilities faster than humans have been able to," Haugstøyl said. "These vulnerabilities open up new opportunities for cyberattacks at a faster pace and on a larger scale.

"This means that the risk is increasing, and the pace at which security measures are implemented must be accelerated."

World.title: Qatar urges Iran to 'show goodwill' by ending threats to the region and reopening the Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
Qatar urged Iran on Tuesday to “show goodwill” by stopping threats against countries in the region and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, as efforts to broker a deal with the United States continued.

 

"We have heard positive statements from the Iranian side on this issue, but they still need to show goodwill,” Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi, director of the foreign ministry’s Media and Communication Department, told a weekly briefing in Doha.

He said a Qatari delegation’s recent visit to Tehran was part of mediation efforts with Pakistan and other regional partners.

Asked whether the delegation had carried a new proposal, Al Hashmi said messages and ideas were still being exchanged with both sides. He gave no details of a proposal and did not announce a breakthrough.

Both Washington and Tehran had spoken about further escalation as well as the possibility of a diplomatic solution, he said.

“The mediator always holds on to this window of hope,” he said.

Regional security talks

On Monday, Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Iranian leaders in Tehran.

The three countries signed the Mecca mutual defence pact in August. Iranian state media said all four countries agreed to continue talks on peace and security.

Al Hashmi said Qatar and its Gulf neighbours were ready to take part in a regional security framework based on respect for sovereignty and a commitment not to attack one another.

He said Saudi Arabia’s efforts complemented the work of Qatar and Pakistan.

The talks come amid continuing attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis. Egypt’s parliament on Monday authorised military support to help defend the kingdom.

The US and Iran remain divided over the terms of a deal. Tehran wants the US blockade of its ports lifted and sanctions on Iranian oil exports removed. Washington is demanding that Iran reduce nuclear enrichment.

The war began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February. Iranian restrictions on shipping and the US blockade have severely disrupted traffic through Hormuz, a crucial route for Gulf oil and gas exports.

Brent crude rose above $117 (€105) a barrel last week, its highest level since April, following Iranian attacks on tankers near the strait. Crude flows through Hormuz were around 60% of normal, according to ANZ research.
