The United States has chosen Poland to host a new centre for servicing and maintaining missiles used in Patriot air defence systems, in a decision described as “historic” by both Washington and Warsaw. It was chosen ahead of bids from four other European countries, including Germany. The new centre will “dramatically shorten turnaround times and further secure critical supply lines”, said the US Department of War, announcing the decision on Tuesday. Undersecretary of War Michael P. Duffey added that the choice of a country on NATO’s eastern front “sends a clear message [that] the Alliance is united, serious about deterrence, and ready to back our words with action”. Poland Selected to Host Historic PAC-3 Missile Maintenance Facility, Strengthening Allied Burden-Sharing and Transatlantic Security – U.S. Department of War – Release | @DeptofWar https://t.co/2caqADRRx8 — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) October 27, 2026 The decision was welcomed by Polish leaders, with defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz saying that it shows “Poland is a trusted ally and holds an extremely important place on the map of global security”. His deputy minister, Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, said that Poland was chosen ahead of rival bids from Germany, the Netherlands and Norway to host the facility. However, US ambassador to Poland Thomas Rose indicated that Sweden, not Norway, was the fourth candidate. Kosiniak-Kamysz and Sobkowiak-Czarnecka both pointed to the role President Karol Nawrocki had played in securing the deal. On many issues, the government is in conflict with the opposition-aligned president, but the two sides worked together on the Patriot bid. Historyczna decyzja! Centrum serwisowania pocisków PAC-3 do systemów Patriot powstanie w Polsce! 🇵🇱 O europejską lokalizację tej inwestycji rywalizowały cztery państwa, obok Polski – Niemcy, Holandia i Norwegia. Już na etapie składania wniosków polska oferta została oceniona… pic.twitter.com/wUgFhzlzUk — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) October 27, 2026 Nawrocki, a conservative, is a close ally of his US counterpart, Donald Trump. The Polish president’s national security advisor, Bartosz Grodecki, claimed that it was “thanks to a conversation between” the two presidents that the new Patriot servicing centre was being established in Poland. The head of Nawrocki’s foreign policy office, Marcin Przydacz, meanwhile, thanked Washington for choosing Poland to host the new centre. “The Polish-American alliance and the good atmosphere in relations once again yield results,” he declared. “We can see what positive effects the President’s activity brings for Poland.” Poland is one of a number of European countries that operate Patriot air defence systems. Others include Germany, Greece, the Netherlands, Romania, Sweden and Ukraine. The new centre will service the PAC-3 missiles used in Patriot batteries. The competition to host the facility was announced in July, with the selection made by the US government in conjunction with American defence giant Lockheed Martin, the producer of missiles. In its press release, the Pentagon emphasised that, although Poland would host the new centre, its work would “be underpinned by robust, transatlantic industrial cooperation, with critical supply chain integration led by Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden”. Sweden will deploy Patriot air defence systems and around 100 accompanying military personnel to Poland later this year to protect the NATO logistics hub in the city of Rzeszów, which is the main conduit for aid to Ukraine https://t.co/cq9p7OVO7E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 6, 2026 Global demand for Patriot systems has risen significantly, with the United States expending at least 1,500 interceptors in its war with Iran, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Patriot systems have also been crucial in Ukraine’s defence against Russian ballistic missile attacks, although Ukraine’s supply of missiles is now almost entirely exhausted. After Trump recently suggested that he would authorise Ukraine to produce its own missiles, Poland offered to host any such factory, to ensure its security. However, today’s announcement concerns a site for maintaining and servicing, rather than producing, the missiles. Poland has proposed that, if the United States grants Ukraine permission to produce its own missiles for Patriot air-defence systems, the facility could be located on Polish territory to ensure its security https://t.co/jaQng5wtGg — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 28, 2026 The decision cements Poland’s position as one of Washington’s most important security partners in Europe. War secretary Pete Hegseth has praised Poland as a “model ally”, noting that it has for years met NATO’s defence spending targets, unlike many other member states. Poland has also been a significant customer for US defence firms. Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was NATO’s biggest arms importer, with 44% of the equipment it purchased coming from American suppliers. Last year, Poland signed a $2 billion deal for the US to provide logistical support and training for Patriot systems. This year, it was announced that Polish state defence group PGZ would become the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles. Poland will become the first country in Europe to produce cruise missiles developed by US defence firm Anduril Industries The agreement will "transform the continent's defence industry", claims Anduril https://t.co/LPJnwOLfp2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026 Warsaw is also currently lobbying for a new permanent US military base to be established in Poland, with the government and the president once again putting aside their differences to promote the idea. Last month, Nawrocki claimed that the proposed base, which he said would be called “Fort Trump”, was “confirmed”. However, Washington has not publicly announced any final decision. World.title: Germany’s economy minister hails Poland as “example of great success”
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Germany’s economy minister, Katherina Reiche, has praised Poland as an “example of great success”, saying that it offers a model for other countries. Speaking at the fourth Polish-German Economic Forum in Warsaw, which she opened on Monday alongside Polish finance minister Andrzej Domański, Reiche. Reiche highlighted the deepening trade ties between the two countries. She noted that bilateral trade last year exceeded €180 billion for the first time, up from €25 billion in 2000, reports Deutsche Welle. Germany has been Poland’s biggest trading partner for decades, although recent data suggest that China, for the first time in history, overtook Germany as Poland’s largest source of imports in July this year. Germany has also long been a major investor in Poland. But Reiche welcomed growing recent investments by Polish companies in Germany, which she said was helping to create jobs. Earlier this year, for example, Poland’s largest manufacturer of trains and trams, Pesa, announced the acquisition of German rival HeiterBlick as part of its efforts to expand its operations across Europe. Reiche noted that around 1,000 Polish companies have invested in Germany while about 1,600 German companies have invested in Poland, reports Reuters. Poland’s largest manufacturer of trains and trams, Pesa, has announced the acquisition of German rival HeiterBlick as it seeks to expand its operations across Europe https://t.co/N1wE1aYL5m — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 12, 2026 Among leading German firms with a presence in Poland are carmakers Mercedes-Benz, which recently invested around €1 billion to build its first electric-only van plant there, which produces its Crafer vans at a plant near the city of Poznań. Reiche also pointed to Poland’s stellar economic performance since joining the European Union in 2004, noting that its GDP has grown by an annual average of 3.8% over that period – twice the EU-wide average. Poland’s economy is on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to become part of the G20. Meanwhile, Domański used his remarks at the Polish-German Economic Forum to warn Europe against repeating past mistakes as it confronts a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape. He said the continent faced a “unique” historical moment. “The world is changing faster than ever, and we are facing new geopolitical, strategic, and technological challenges.” Europe would need a strong economy and new sources of growth to meet those challenges, he added, warning against what he called “economic naivety” and urging Europe – and Germany in particular – not to return to its previous approach to Russia. “I would like to state this very clearly: Europe must learn from the past. Under no circumstances can there be a return to the previous approach toward Russia. Poland will never agree to that,” Domański said, noting that this position applied in particular to renewed use of Russian energy imports. “We will only be resilient once we are truly independent of external, unstable suppliers of raw materials,” he added, emphasising that Poland and Germany must “work together to modernise the European energy market, focus on technological change and bear security in mind”. I nie chodzi tu tylko o… pic.twitter.com/NVPUjwx7jA — Ministerstwo Rozwoju i Technologii (@MRiTGOVPL) October 26, 2026 Following the forum, Domański and Reiche attended a meeting of the Friends of Industry, an informal initiative bringing together EU member states to coordinate positions on industrial policy, competitiveness and the operating conditions for European industry. The meeting was attended by representatives of 21 EU member states and European Commission Vice-President Stéphane Séjourné. Discussions focused on protecting and strengthening European industry’s competitiveness and economic security amid geopolitical challenges. “Today, we are facing the consequences of the fact that, in the past, competitiveness was often relegated to second, third or fourth place. Competitiveness took a back seat to other priorities, with the result that European industry now faces serious challenges,” said Domański. He proposed making competitiveness a core EU policy priority, cutting red tape, strengthening the single market, lowering energy costs, investing in strategic technologies such as AI, and tightening trade protections against unfair foreign competition. World.title: Witness testifies Polish president discussed “making money bringing girls” to hotel where they worked 20 years ago
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A former colleague of Polish President Karol Nawrocki from when he worked as a security guard in a hotel two decades ago testified in court that he told her it was possible to “make some extra money by bringing in girls”. She says she saw him escort a woman onto the premises. The testimony was given after the president himself sued the owner of a website that, just before last year’s presidential election, published claims that Nawrocki had been involved in procuring prostitutes while working at the luxury Grand Hotel in the town of Sopot. The court case began in September but, until now, hearings have been held behind closed doors. However, the judge decided that today’s session would be open to the public, with two former colleagues of Nawrocki giving evidence. The president himself is due to appear before the court in January. 🗣️ "Moją automatyczną oceną było, że to prostytutka i alfons." Nowe zeznania w procesie Karola Nawrockiego z wydawcą Onetu. Przed sądem stanęła była współpracowniczka prezydenta z sopockiego Grand Hotelu. pic.twitter.com/Cn6KyMSjcv — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 27, 2026 In May last year, less than a week before the second round of the election, in which Nawrocki was standing in a run-off against rival Rafał Trzaskowski, Onet, a leading news website, published an article titled “Karol Nawrocki and the secrets of the Grand Hotel”. It claimed, based on information provided by unnamed former colleagues of the future president, that he had “participated in bringing prostitutes for guests of the Grand Hotel in Sopot while working there as a security guard” almost 20 years earlier. Onet said that its interlocutors wished to remain anonymous for their own safety, but had expressed their willingness to testify in court if required. The revelations caused a major scandal, but were vigorously denied by Nawrocki, a conservative candidate aligned with the right-wing opposition, who called them a “pack of lies”. He then went on to narrowly defeat Trzaskowski in the election. Conservative presidential candidate @NawrockiKn says he will sue news website @onetpl for claims it published today that he procured prostitutes for clients at a luxury hotel when working there as a security guard. He called the report "a bunch of lies" https://t.co/WZ4rZWfFT1 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 26, 2025 Nawrocki then sued Ringier Axel Springer Polska (RASP), the Polish subsidiary of a German-Swiss media house that owns Onet, demanding an apology. RASP stood by Onet, saying that its reporting was “factual”. At today’s hearing, one of Onet’s sources, Natasza Geldon, who had worked at the hotel in 2006 and 2007, was questioned. She said that, one evening, she had noticed Nawrocki leading a man and a woman into the hotel, before then taking only the woman into an elevator and returning alone. This had struck her as unusual, because staff were not supposed to escort guests into the hotel, “let alone take them upstairs” in the lift, said Geldon, quoted by broadcaster TVP. “When Karol came back downstairs, I asked him what was going on,” continued the witness. “He said it was possible to make some extra money by bringing girls in, and asked if I wanted to join in.” Geldon refused the offer, telling the court that, “as a young girl, 19 years old, I had the impression that a pimp had been coming in with a prostitute”. However, when asked to confirm if she had seen prostitutes in the hotel, Geldon said: “I don’t know. It’s hard to say. It was just that one incident.” A second witness, Łukasz Franczak, described as a longtime friend of Nawrocki who worked alongside him in security at the Grand Hotel, also gave evidence on Tuesday after being called by Nawrocki’s legal team. He testified that there had been prostitutes in the hotel. However, he added that he had not heard of any organised operation to supply them to guests; nor had he witnessed Nawrocki procuring prostitutes or discussing payment for them, reported Onet from the hearing. Franczak’s testimony was welcomed by Nawrocki’s former national security advisor, Sławomir Cenckiewicz, who said that it showed those making claims against the president have no evidence of his involvement in any wrongdoing. Oni się wszyscy teraz nakręcają jak szaleni, nie czytając tego co sami piszą na własnej stronie… No i dowiedzieli się dzisiaj, że w hotelach bywają prostytutki 🙂 A ja to wszystko czytam na bieżąco, a tam słynny Łukasz z Gdańska, ulubiony świadek-historyk Antka Dudka, i… https://t.co/9sKGZT4PpD — Sławomir Cenckiewicz (@Cenckiewicz) October 27, 2026 RASP’s lawyers have called for Nawrocki himself to testify in the case. The president’s legal team wanted him to provide his testimony in writing, according to Onet. But on Tuesday, judge Aleksandra Orzechowska ordered Nawrocki to give testimony directly – either in person or remotely – at the next hearing, which is scheduled for 18 January 2027, reports broadcaster TVN. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with six alleged crimes, including inciting hatred against Jews and vandalising an LGBT+ exhibition. The other four allegations relate to an incident in which he confronted a doctor who performed a late-term abortion. The charges are the latest in a long line of legal cases against Braun, who is already on trial for attacking a Jewish ceremony in Poland’s parliament. However, his party continues to poll strongly, and may play a significant role in deciding what kind of government is formed after next year’s elections. Do sześciu razy sztuka. Grzegorz Braun dostał zarzuty, w tym za uwięzienie ginekolożki Gizeli Jagielskiej Wcześniej europoseł Grzegorz Braun pięć razy unikał przedstawienia zarzutów w Prokuraturze Okręgowej we Wrocławiu. Zainterweniował Prokurator Generalny Waldemar Żurek.… — Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 26, 2026 As a member of the European Parliament, Braun enjoys legal immunity from prosecution. However, in November 2025, the EP stripped him of immunity to face the six charges. Subsequently, prosecutors tried five times to present Braun with the charges. However, he evaded those attempts by filing motions to have prosecutors excluded from the case or simply by leaving the prosecutor’s office before the charges were read. In July, Poland’s justice minister and prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, filed a motion to the EP for permission to forcibly detain Braun and present him with the charges. That application has not yet been considered but, on Monday, Braun finally attended the prosecutor’s office and heard the charges. Afterwards, Braun told a small group of his followers and the media outside the office in Wrocław that he was the victim of a “state lynching” carried out by “the prosecutor’s office of the Hannukah cannibals, racists and genocide perpetrators”. Four of the charges against Braun relate to an incident in April 2025, when he entered a hospital and confronted a gynaecologist who had been involved in a late-term abortion that had drawn controversy and condemnation from right-wing groups. Braun claimed he was carrying out a citizen’s arrest, but is now charged with deprivation of liberty (for preventing the doctor from leaving her office), violating bodily integrity (by pushing her and holding her down), as well as insult and slander. The maximum sentence for those crimes is five years in prison. In separate proceedings, prosecutors later found that the doctor had not violated Poland’s strict abortion laws by terminating the pregnancy in the ninth month. The fifth charge Braun is now facing stems from an infamous incident in December 2023, when he attacked a Jewish Hanukkah celebration in parliament, putting out the candles with a fire extinguisher. Braun is already on trial over the incident itself. Now, however, prosecutors have charged him over a YouTube interview he gave shortly after the attack, in which they say he “described Hanukkah as a Satanic and racist celebration posing a threat to Polish Catholics, which should be counteracted”. For those remarks, he has been hit with a joint charge of inciting religious hatred and the obstruction of religious acts. The maximum penalty for those offences is a three-year jail term. Finally, Braun has been charged with destruction of property for an incident during his presidential campaign in March this year when he vandalised an exhibition about the local LGBT+ community in the city of Opole, spray-painting “stop the propaganda of perversion” on it. Police are investigating far-right presidential candidate and MEP Grzegorz Braun after he vandalised an LGBT+ exhibition. The city where it took place immediately cancelled a meeting he was due to hold there and is seeking compensation for the damage https://t.co/EbDpMzmpFw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 20, 2025 Braun has pleaded not guilty to all the charges against him, as he has done with a string of other charges for various offences relating to his antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT rhetoric and actions. In September, he was stripped of immunity by the EP for the sixth time in order to hear charges of Holocaust denial for his claims that the gas chambers in the Nazi-German death camp of Auschwitz are “fake”. Braun’s high-profile stunts have seen his popularity surge among a section of the electorate. He finished a surprise fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, with over 6% of the vote, and his Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party is now polling around 9%. If it manages to secure that level of support at next autumn’s parliamentary elections, KKP could become a key player in deciding what kind of government can be formed after what looks likely to be a very close contest between the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, and the right-wing and far-right opposition. Poland and Vietnam have upgraded their ties to a strategic partnership, pledging to deepen cooperation in trade and investment, security and defence, as well as education, science, technology and cultural exchanges. “Vietnam and Poland share a success story in terms of development,” declared Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a joint press conference with his Vietnamese counterpart Lê Minh Hưng in Hanoi on Monday. “The time has come to turn our successes into joint actions that will open up more opportunities.” The announcement comes amid a broader flurry of Polish diplomacy in Asia, with Tusk arriving in Hanoi following a visit to India and President Karol Nawrocki visiting the Philippines earlier this month. Poland also recently signed new strategic agreements with South Korea and Japan. 🇵🇱🤝🇻🇳 Polska i Wietnam wchodzą na poziom partnerstwa strategicznego! ✅ Podczas wizyty w Hanoi premier @donaldtusk oraz szef wietnamskiego rządu Lê Minh Hưng podjęli decyzję o podniesieniu wzajemnych relacji do rangi partnerstwa strategicznego, otwierając nowy rozdział we… pic.twitter.com/CCvHmc3eva — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 26, 2026 Tusk, who was making the first visit by a Polish prime minister to Vietnam in 16 years, pointed to the two countries’ rapid recent economic development. “Within a single generation, Vietnam achieved middle-income status”, while “Poland recently joined the ranks of the world’s 20 largest economies”. In fact, while Poland was forecast to join the world’s 20 largest economies last year, it eventually fell narrowly short. However, it is expected to soon overtake Switzerland, the current holder of 20th place. Tusk said that, during his visit, he had often heard people say that “Poland is the Vietnam of Europe and Vietnam is the Poland of Asia”. Last year, Hưng’s predecessor, Phạm Minh Chính, became the first Vietnamese prime minister in 15 years to visit Poland. The two countries first established diplomatic relations in 1950, and both leaders emphasised Poland’s large Vietnamese community, which dates back to students arriving around that time. Speaking on Monday, Hưng noted the two countries’ strong traditional ties, adding that Vietnam always remembers and is grateful for Polish support and assistance during his country’s struggle for independence and national reunification, reports the Vietnamese News Agency (VNA). The Vietnamese are Poland's largest non-European migrant group. Photographer Zula Rabikowska, through her images and interviews, offers an insight into their experiences, identities and the challenges they face https://t.co/tsRwHINapQ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 27, 2019 The new strategic partnership agreement signed by Tusk and Hưng pledges to “bring tangible benefits to both nations and contribute to peace, stability, cooperation and prosperity”. It contains commitments to “maintain regular high-level contacts”, reduce non-tariff barriers to trade, and strengthen cooperation on defence, including trade in military equipment. On Sunday, Poland’s deputy minister for state assets, Konrad Gołota, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that negotiations are already underway for Vietnam to buy Polish Krab howitzers and Rosomak armoured fighting vehicles, among other hardware. Polish arms firm Mesko has announced the best financial results in its 100-year history. Record revenues and profits were driven in large part by international demand for Mesko's flagship Piorun air-defence system, which has proved successful in Ukraine https://t.co/Dx1yY54qCP — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2026 Tusk, pointing to Poland’s current trade deficit with Vietnam, said that Warsaw’s “priority remains a better balance in trade”. “The sectors in which the Vietnamese side is most interested, and in which we really have something to offer, are the arms industry, satellite and space cooperation, pharmaceuticals and food, especially dairy products,” he added. Tusk also announced that the number of annual Polish-Vietnamese student exchanges would rise by 250% and noted that Poland’s national carrier, LOT, would resume direct Warsaw-Hanoi flights in the first quarter of 2027. Poland is taking steps to attract more foreign students as universities face lower enrollment due to demographic decline. Turkey, South Korea, Vietnam and Uzbekistan are among the countries with which the government is cultivating stronger academic ties https://t.co/r878KqS5OV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 25, 2026 The Polish prime minister acknowledged differences between Poland and Vietnam’s approach to Russia’s war in Ukraine. Vietnam, which has long maintained close ties with Moscow, has avoided condemning the Russian invasion. But he emphasised his belief that, “because of their history, wartime experience and international relations, both Vietnam and Poland can contribute a great deal to the peace process”. Tusk’s trip to Vietnam follows a three-day visit to India, where he and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a goal of doubling bilateral trade by 2030. Poland and India's PMs have, after meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies Polish-Indian relations are "gaining speed", said @narendramodi https://t.co/iIVIkCXnvr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 22, 2026 In April, Tusk visited South Korea, upgrading Poland’s relations with the country he described as Poland’s “most important ally after the United States”, and deepened Poland’s strategic partnership with Japan on the same tour. Earlier this month, Tusk also announced plans to visit China before the end of the year. Meanwhile, President Nawrocki visited the Philippines this month as part of a bid to secure backing from Asian nations for Poland’s hoped-for membership in the G20. World.title: Two thirds of Poles support liberalising abortion law, finds new poll
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Just over two thirds of Poles support liberalising the country’s abortion law, which is among the strictest in Europe, according to a new poll. However, most do not favour introducing abortion on demand, as protesters called for during demonstrations last week. The findings come shortly after parliament approved legislation intended to ease access to abortion. But the measures face a potential veto from right-wing, opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki. 🔴 Sondaż dla @rzeczpospolita: Niemal 7 na 10 Polaków chce liberalizacji przepisów ws. aborcjihttps://t.co/f7mxwygIxz — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 25, 2026 In 2020, Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means pregnancies can now only be legally terminated in two cases: where they result from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if they threaten the mother’s life or health. In a new poll by SW Research for Rzeczpospolita, a leading newspaper, a total of 67.2% of respondents said that they want to liberalise that law. However, only 37.7% favoured introducing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. Meanwhile, 29.5% preferred the softer option of returning to the situation from before the 2020 TK ruling – often referred to the “abortion compromise” in Poland – in which terminations were only available in three cases. A further 16.2% supported maintaining the current abortion law; 6.0% wanted to make the rules even tougher (which would involve removing one or both justifications for abortion that currently exist); and 10.6% said they had no opinion. The poll found that support for liberalisation of abortion was stronger among women (73.8%) than men (60.3%). The latest findings are consistent with previous polling, which tends to show that a significant majority supports liberalising the abortion law but that there is not a majority in favour of abortion on demand (although some individual polls have narrowly found such a majority). One member of Poland's likely new ruling coalition, The Left, says polls show a majority in favour of abortion on demand. In fact, they do not. And this issue is likely to be one of the hardest for the incoming government to resolve, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/4Nze9wwEC3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 20, 2023 The issue has caused significant political disputes in Poland, not only between the right-wing opposition and the more liberal ruling coalition, but also within the coalition itself. Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and one of its partners, The Left (Lewica), favour introducing abortion on demand. However, more conservative elements of the government, especially the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), prefer a return to the pre-2020 “compromise”. Much of the right-wing opposition, meanwhile, favours maintaining the status quo. However, some more moderate elements of the opposition have suggested it would be best to reverse the TK ruling and return to the “compromise”. Protests took place in towns and cities around Poland on Thursday evening, demanding that the government fulfil its promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws https://t.co/q7eK7mV9zr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 23, 2026 In 2024, due to disputes within his coalition, Tusk declared that it was unlikely there would be any abortion reform during the current parliamentary term due to differences within his coalition. However, last week the issue was revived, with the government’s majority in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, approving a bill that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling (but not introduce abortion on demand). It also passed another bill decriminalising providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions. After both bills go through the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but not block them, they will pass to President Nawrocki, who can sign them, veto them, or send them to the TK for assessment. Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has declared his opposition to abortion, and has vetoed a record number of government bills, it is widely expected that he will seek to block efforts to liberalise the abortion law. World.title: Time is running out for Germany to pay Polish WWII victims the compensation they deserve [Opinion]
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Philipp Fritz, Warsaw correspondent for Die Welt (which first published this article in German here) Negotiations on compensation for the still-living victims of the German occupation of Poland have been going on for years. There are some 30,000 to 50,000 such survivors, but their number dwindles every week. Berlin should act now. No “humanitarian gesture” has emerged. “The draft budget currently reflects the fact that no decision has been made,” said Josef Hinterseher, a German foreign office spokesman, at a press conference in late September. He thereby confirmed what many observers had suspected: survivors of concentration camps, ghettos and death marches, former forced workers and participants in the Warsaw Uprising who are still living in Poland will not receive any compensation, one-off payment or monthly pension from the German government. The German chancellor has announced that his country will offer support to surviving Polish victims of WW2 and will help strengthen Poland’s eastern border. However, in both cases he did not provide details of what these measures will involve in practice https://t.co/gKX6142Alo — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2024 Just a few sentences later, Hinterseher moved onto the next subject – the fact that two Russian oligarchs were to be removed from the EU’s sanctions list. Or at least, that Berlin had not been successful in opposing this decision. The fact that these two issues were dealt with publicly one after the other shows that the German government is quicker to reach a decision that makes Putin’s supporters’ lives easier than it is with victims of the Nazi terror. It is a declaration of moral bankruptcy. Warsaw and Berlin have been negotiating compensation for the last remaining victims of the German occupation of Poland for years. There are between 30,000 and 50,000 of them – aged over 90, often living alone and in poor health. Their numbers are dwindling every week. The fact that talks are taking place in Berlin ministries but without any decision being taken is met with sadness and fury in Poland. Increasingly, Poles are getting the impression that, even if the Germans manage to put up memorials, they cannot offer survivors tangible help when it is asked for. It is a common view that in Berlin the descendants of the perpetrators are simply waiting for the victims to die so that this pesky issue will sort itself out. Should that happen, those left behind will not forget, and the Germans will hardly be able to forgive themselves. Warsaw is no longer demanding war reparations from Berlin. In December 2023, Donald Tusk’s government switched to talking about “making amends”. Polish foreign minister @sikorskiradek has called on Germany to “think creatively” about compensating Poland for WWII. On a visit to Berlin, he also said that the new government would "end the cold war" waged by the former ruling PiS party against Germany https://t.co/kZ62nUuqqO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 31, 2024 This is not just splitting hairs. In so doing, Tusk put the ball in the German government’s court, giving it the chance to take action and, through a gesture recognising suffering and providing a relatively small sum of money, to offer people tangible help and do a service to the German-Polish relationship. Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz is reported to have offered Tusk a one-off payment in 2024, but Poland’s prime minister turned the sum down as insufficient. Instead, Polish diplomats are demanding monthly pensions. In any case, we are talking about a few hundred million euro: a relatively small amount compared to the equivalent of €1.3 trillion that Poland’s former ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party once demanded from Germany, and also in comparison to many other budget items – and yet still there is nothing about compensation in the budget planning. Poland is seeking $1.3 trillion in war reparations from Germany, but Berlin says the issue was legally settled long ago. Legal scholar @MPiatkowski1 examines the arguments of both sides, explains the legal context, and looks at what could come next https://t.co/xsKAY2TukS — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 9, 2022 Rumour has it that, in return for compensation, German foreign ministry officials are asking for a kind of Polish guarantee that in future there will be no more demands for reparations, or at least that at least the German gesture will receive good press in Poland. If that is true, it would be thoroughly indecent, bringing to mind an image of a perpetrator trying to buy his victim’s silence. This reflects a belief in objectification, an ugly bureaucratic mentality stemming from a system in which “work” in a ghetto counts towards statutory pension contributions, but no one can bring themselves to pay compensation. This issue can be resolved at the very top. Chancellor Friedrich Merz would have to work with the relevant ministries – the foreign office and finance ministry – to provide for compensation for the victims in the budget. This would be a belated but major and morally right gesture. If politics is too slow – time really is of the essence – then civil society should take it upon itself to show where it stands. Donations for the still living victims of the German tyranny or a fund from which survivors would receive monthly payments can be created from within society. Business can also get involved. German corporations which were guilty of, for instance, exploiting forced labourers in occupied Poland, or those that emerged from them, such as BASF, Siemens, Volkswagen, BMW and Deutsche Bank, could contribute. Poland covers almost all the costs of maintaining former Nazi-German camps on its territory. It has spent more on this than Germany has paid in compensation to Polish war victims It's time for Germany to fund preservation of the sites, argues @W_Kononczuk https://t.co/08nf4c2jMz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 25, 2026 Right now, since its state elections in September, Germany gives the impression of a country whose compass for right and wrong is broken. As of 6 October, the state parliament of Sachsen-Anhalt has as its vice-president Hans-Thomas Tillschneider of the AfD, a man who wrote on X that “the Poles have been getting on my nerves for a long time now”. In Berlin, not only did the left-wing Die Linke celebrate their electoral success with Israel haters and antisemites, they even tolerate them in their ranks. It is shameful. But now Germany, and particularly its government, has the opportunity to show that the rhetoric of responsibility for the victims is not merely empty words. That, contrary to a mood that does not support it, they are doing what is morally right. Time is running out, Germany – it’s your last chance. World.title: Leader of junior coalition partner quits Polish government
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, the leader of a junior party in Poland’s ruling coalition, has announced her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party, the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), in protest over a parliamentary vote on Thursday. Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) is set to remain in the government, thereby maintaining Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s parliamentary majority. However, the dispute has highlighted tensions within the ruling coalition just a year ahead of parliamentary elections at which it will seek another term. Dwukadencyjność samorządów została utrzymana. Tak zdecydował dziś Sejm. Wygraliśmy! Zmiana, której chce 75% Polaków dojdzie do skutku! Stało się to jednak pomimo głosów K15X. Koalicja, w tym niestety znaczna część posłów Polski 2050, stanęła przeciw ludziom, a za politykierskimi… — Katarzyna Pełczyńska (@Kpelczynska) October 22, 2026 Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, who serves as minister for funds and regional policy, made her decision in the wake of an unusual voting result in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, on Thursday. Another junior partner in the ruling coalition, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), had proposed a bill abolishing two-term limits for mayors. Those limits had been introduced in 2018 with the aim of reducing corruption and cronyism by preventing local officials from becoming entrenched in power. However, PSL, which has a strong presence in local politics, argues that the limits prevent effective, popular mayors from being re-elected, thereby denying voters the right to decide who they want to represent them. Although the government has a majority in the Sejm, the bill was narrowly defeated, with 213 votes in favour and 215 against, after 15 MPs from the ruling coalition joined with the right-wing opposition in voting against it. Pełczyńska-Nałęcz herself is not a member of parliament, so did not vote. Her party was split, with six MPs voting for the bill, three against, three abstaining, and three not voting at all. Aftewards, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz made clear that she opposed the bill and celebrated the fact that it was blocked. She also announced her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party. “The coalition, unfortunately including a significant portion of MPs from Poland 2050, stood against the people and in favour of backroom political deals,” she wrote. “I am leaving Donald Tusk’s government because values are more important to me than positions.” “I am leaving the party in the hands of its founder, who stepped away but then returned,” she added, referring to Poland 2050’s founder, Szymon Hołownia. “I hope that he remembers what values he came to power in the name of.” Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s decision follows a year of turmoil for Poland 2050. In September 2025, Hołownia, who had led the party since founding it in 2021, announced that he was stepping down. However, a first attempt to choose a new leader was invalidated in January after technical problems with voting. Hołownia then hinted that he may reverse course and seek to continue leading the party, though in the end that did not happen. In February, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz was chosen as the new leader. That prompted her rival candidate, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, to quit the party, taking half of its MPs with her. They formed a new group called Centrum (Centre). Both Poland 2050 and Centrum remain in the ruling coalition. However, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz has had an uneasy relationship with Tusk. Around half the MPs from Poland 2050, a junior member of Poland’s ruling coalition, have split from the party and formed a new parliamentary caucus. They expressed dissatisfaction with the actions of the party's recently elected new leader, @Kpelczynska https://t.co/IqU4vE1EEe — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 18, 2026 On Friday, Tusk, who is on a state visit to India, sarcastically responded to Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s resignation by saying, “I thought she’d at least call before she left”. He admitted that “cooperation [with her] has not been the easiest for a long time”. The prime minister, however, added that he “does not think [her resignation] will have any impact on the future work of the coalition…My intuition tells me that this is her individual decision”. Hołownia, who currently serves as head of Poland 2050’s parliamentary caucus, confirmed at a press conference on Friday alongside fellow MPs that the party intends to remain in Tusk’s coalition. But he also warned that, without Poland 2050, the government would not have a parliamentary majority. W @PL_2050 dowiedzieliśmy się o decyzji @Kpelczynska z mediów. Zaskakująca rezygnacja przewodniczącej z zaufania wyborców i odpowiedzialności powierzonej jej w bardzo trudnym momencie przez ludzi (w tym mnie) zaledwie po niespełna 1/3 kadencji – dla każdej organizacji byłaby… — Szymon Hołownia (@szymon_holownia) October 22, 2026 The episode highlights the tensions within the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right and contains parties that disagree on a number of issues. It also points to the pressure smaller coalition partners are feeling ahead of next autumn’s parliamentary elections. Only parties that win at least 5% of the vote nationally can enter parliament. But Poland 2050 has been polling at around 1% and PSL is on 3%. In the 2023 election, Poland 2050 and PSL in fact stood together as an alliance called the Third Way (Trzecia Droga), helping ensure that the two parties won enough votes to enter parliament. However, in 2025, they split from one another and confirmed that they would not stand together again. PSL and Poland 2050, the two parties that make up the Third Way alliance, have confirmed that they are splitting and will stand separately at the next elections. They will, however, remain part of @donaldtusk's ruling coalition https://t.co/NduEJY25eE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2025 The fact that the bill to end two-term limits for mayors was defeated has also caused tension between PSL and its coalition partners. In the wake of yesterday’s vote, PSL immediately announced that it would push for the introduction of two-term limits for members of parliament, arguing that the same rules should apply to national and local elected representatives. The right-wing opposition has long hoped that it could tempt PSL, the most conservative element of Tusk’s coalition, to quit the government. A recent report even claimed that US President Donald Trump had, at the behest of Poland’s opposition, suggested to PSL’s leader that he leave Tusk. World.title: Where to Celebrate Halloween in Prague: 6 Events for Children and Adults
World.content:
Prague will mark Halloween 2026 with events for children and adults, ranging from pumpkin carving and lantern parades to costume competitions and late-night club parties.

Here are some of the events planned across Prague, including admission prices where available.

Blackout Halloween Rave at SaSaZu

Blackout Events will hold its first Halloween rave on Tuesday, October 27, at SaSaZu, bringing hard techno, Halloween costumes and stage productions to the Prague club.

The lineup includes WYNTER at 9 p.m., HOOOR at 10:30 p.m., A.N.I. at midnight, NOTMYTYPE at 1:30 a.m. and KLAR at 3 a.m. The event is scheduled to finish at 4 a.m.

An afterparty will follow at Club Mecca in Holešovice from 3 a.m. The event is restricted to visitors aged 18 and over. Organizers say further program details will be published on Blackout Events’ Instagram account.

Halloween at Hybernia Theatre

Hybernia Theatre, near Náměstí Republiky, is also listed as a venue for a Halloween electronic music event. The program is set to combine electronic music, Halloween decorations and the historic theatre’s interior.

Italian DJ SPADA is announced as a special guest. Admission is listed at CZK 499, although the event date should be confirmed with the organizer before publication.

Spooks at Žluté lázně

Žluté lázně in Podolí will host a Halloween afternoon on Saturday, October 31, from 1 p.m. to 7 p.m.

Children can follow a spooky trail featuring a spiderweb tunnel, a mysterious castle and a series of challenges. The program will also include pumpkin carving, face painting and dancing.

The organizers will announce the winner of the best-costume competition at 6:10 p.m. Admission costs CZK 150, while children wearing costumes can enter for free. Pumpkins for carving will be available for CZK 100.

Halloween Among Dinosaurs at DinoPark Harfa

DinoPark on the rooftop of Galerie Harfa will offer Halloween activities on Saturday, October 31, including a trail where children can complete tasks among the dinosaurs.

The afternoon program will feature Stegoušek Kvído, a walking dinosaur character who will lead two lantern parades, at 4 p.m. and 5 p.m. Visitors should bring their own lanterns.

DinoPark will be open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Children in Halloween costumes can enter for CZK 50.

Pumpkin Carving at the Public Transport Museum

The Public Transport Museum in Střešovice will combine Halloween activities with a look at Prague’s historic trams and buses on Saturday, October 31.

Visitors can carve pumpkins and explore the museum’s collection of historic vehicles. Those arriving in costume will receive a gift.

At 4:45 p.m., the carved pumpkins will be lit in the museum courtyard. The museum will be open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Bloody Sexy Halloween Returns to SaSaZu

Bloody Sexy Halloween will return to SaSaZu on Friday, October 30, and Saturday, October 31, for two nights of music, performances and themed productions.

Founded in 2009, the event has become one of the region’s established Halloween parties, attracting more than 4,000 visitors in previous editions, according to the organizers.

One of the weekend’s main attractions is the Bloody Sexy Costume Contest. Participants can register at SaSaZu between 9 p.m. and midnight. Costumes are judged on creativity, originality and presentation, with the winner selected by audience applause at midnight and awarded CZK 40,000.

World.title: Thirty Seconds to Mars to Play Prague in 2027 With Special Album Tour
World.content:
Thirty Seconds to Mars will return to Prague on May 18, 2027, for a concert at the O2 arena.

The Jared and Shannon Leto-led band will revisit two of its best-known albums, A Beautiful Lie and This Is War, as part of a special world tour.

The American rock band will perform without an opening act, with the show expected to last approximately two hours. Tickets start at CZK 1,500, excluding ticketing fees, and VIP packages will also be available.



The concert is part of the band’s A Beautiful Lie vs This Is War tour, which focuses on two records that helped establish Thirty Seconds to Mars as a major name in alternative rock.

Tickets will be available through Ticketmaster and Ticketportal from October 30, 2026, at 10 a.m. Fan club members will have access to a presale beginning October 27 at 10 a.m. Live Nation, Spotify and O2 presales will follow on October 29 at 10 a.m.

Two albums that defined the band’s sound

Released in 2005, A Beautiful Lie marked a turning point in the band’s career, bringing its music to a much wider international audience. The album features some of Thirty Seconds to Mars’ best-known songs, including The Kill, From Yesterday and the title track.

The follow-up, This Is War, arrived in 2009 and expanded that sound. Tracks such as Kings and Queens, This Is War and Closer to the Edge became signature songs, helping the band reach a broader audience.

From alternative rock to global tours

Led by brothers Jared Leto, the band’s vocalist, and Shannon Leto, its drummer, the group continued to develop its sound on Love, Lust, Faith and Dreams in 2013 and America in 2018. The latter included the singles Walk on Water and Rescue Me.

In 2023, the band released its sixth studio album, It’s the End of the World but It’s a Beautiful Day, exploring a different musical direction while maintaining its focus on melody and emotional themes.

The band has also received several MTV awards and a Billboard Music Award. Its touring history includes a Guinness World Records recognition for the longest concert tour.

The 2027 tour will take Thirty Seconds to Mars across Europe, the United Kingdom, South Africa and other destinations. Its Prague stop will bring the band’s anniversary celebrations and catalogue of established hits to the Czech capital for a show centred on two of its most influential albums.

World.title: Prague Tram Disruptions Will Affect Six Lines During Autumn School Break
World.content:
Prague tram passengers will face several service changes during the autumn school break, including a five-day suspension between I. P. Pavlova and Otakarova.

The changes come as Prague Public Transit Company adjusts services for the school holidays and carries out track repairs. Passengers travelling through Nusle, Vršovice and Žižkov should check their routes before setting off.

Six Tram Lines Affected by Track Repairs

Tram services between I. P. Pavlova and Otakarova will be suspended in both directions from approximately 4:30 a.m. on Wednesday, October 28, until midnight on Sunday, November 1.



Tram line 13 will be suspended entirely during this period. Lines 2 and 21 will be combined into one route, with trams running from Petřiny to Karlovo náměstí before continuing as line 21 to Slivenec. The same arrangement will apply in the opposite direction.

Other services will follow diverted routes. Tram line 6, travelling from Nádraží Holešovice, will run from Karlovo náměstí via Albertov, Ostrčilovo náměstí and Divadlo Na Fidlovačce to Otakarova, where it will rejoin its regular route.

Line 11 will be diverted from I. P. Pavlova via Náměstí Míru, Čechovo náměstí, Nádraží Vršovice and Otakarova. It will return to its usual route at Náměstí Bratří Synků and continue towards Spořilov.

Night tram line 96, which connects Petřiny with Spořilov, will also be diverted. It will run via Náměstí Míru, Čechovo náměstí, Nádraží Vršovice, Otakarova and Náměstí Bratří Synků.

A replacement bus service, X11, will operate during the day between Nádraží Vršovice and Sarajevská. It will also stop at Fričova, Divadlo Na Fidlovačce and Otakarova.

Žižkov Tram Restrictions to Last Until December 18

Separate restrictions in Žižkov have been in effect since October 11, with tram services suspended in both directions between Nákladové nádraží Žižkov and Ohrada. The disruption is scheduled to continue until December 18.

Tram lines 9 and 10 currently terminate at Nákladové nádraží Žižkov and are linked to each other. Lines 16 and 34 have been cancelled, while lines 5, 7, 11, 95 and 98 are operating on modified routes.

Three additional tram services have been introduced to help passengers travel through the affected area. Line 30 connects Sídliště Ďáblice with Spojovací via Palmovka and Ohrada. Line 37 runs from Lehovec to Spojovací, also serving Palmovka and Ohrada. Night line 90 connects Vozovna Kobylisy with Spojovací via the same two stops.

Replacement buses are running along the suspended section. Daytime services X9 and X95 connect Nákladové nádraží Žižkov, Biskupcova, Ohrada and Vozovna Žižkov. Night bus X98 serves Olšanské hřbitovy, Želivského, Nákladové nádraží Žižkov, Biskupcova, Ohrada and Vozovna Žižkov.

World.title: The Piano Bar Prague Combines Dining and Live Music at Savarin Palace
World.content:
Located inside Savarin Palace on Na Příkopě, The Piano Bar Prague brings together a restaurant, cocktail bar and live music venue under one roof.

The concept offers an alternative to an evening spent moving between different venues in the city centre.



The venue combines dinner, drinks and live performances, with separate spaces for dining, socialising and dancing.

Dining and Cocktails in One Venue

The restaurant is led by Executive Chef Ari Munandar, whose previous experience includes working at Mandarin Oriental, Hilton and SaSaZu. The menu focuses on contemporary cuisine, with an emphasis on ingredients, flavour and presentation.

Cocktails are also a central part of the offering, with the bar serving guests throughout the evening. The layout allows visitors to move from the dining room to the bar or lounge without leaving the venue.

Live Music and Dancing

Live music is another key element of The Piano Bar Prague. The program ranges from piano performances to live bands, depending on the evening.

While some guests may visit for dinner or drinks, the venue also caters to those looking for a later night out. The main bar and dance floor provide space for music and dancing, while the lounge offers a quieter setting for conversation.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Piano Bar Prague (@thepianobar_prague)

The different areas are designed to accommodate a range of occasions, from dinners for two and gatherings with friends to private celebrations and corporate events.

A Historic Setting in Prague 1

The Piano Bar Prague is located in Savarin Palace, a historic complex on Na Příkopě, one of Prague’s main shopping streets. Its central location makes it accessible to both residents and visitors staying in the city centre.

World.title: Smartwings Launches Direct Flights Between Prague and Lisbon
World.content:
Smartwings has launched a new direct route between Prague and Lisbon, with flights operating three times a week.

The first service departed on Friday, October 23, with every seat occupied, according to airline spokeswoman Vladimíra Dufková.

The new connection links Prague with the Portuguese capital on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays.



The route adds Lisbon to Smartwings’ existing scheduled services to Portugal, which already include Porto, Funchal on the island of Madeira, and Ponta Delgada in the Azores.

Flights are operated by Boeing 737 aircraft with a capacity of 189 passengers. The journey from Prague to Lisbon takes approximately three hours and 40 minutes, while the return flight takes three hours and 25 minutes.

One-way tickets start at CZK 2,940. The fare includes one piece of cabin baggage measuring up to 55 × 40 × 23 centimetres and weighing no more than eight kilograms.

Smartwings to Resume Prague–Bucharest Flights

Smartwings will also resume scheduled flights between Prague and Bucharest on November 26. The service will operate four times a week, on Tuesdays, Thursdays, Fridays and Sundays.

One-way fares for the Romanian capital start at CZK 2,470, including cabin baggage, Dufková said.

The two routes form part of Smartwings’ winter 2026–2027 flight schedule, which includes direct services from Czech airports to 39 destinations. The Smartwings Group will also operate flights from Poland, Slovakia and Hungary during the winter season.

World.title: Grand Jour de Champagne Returns to Prague With 30 French Producers
World.content:
Prague will host the 19th edition of Grand Jour de Champagne from November 5, bringing together French champagne producers, exclusive tastings and a gala dinner prepared by a two-Michelin-starred chef.

The festival’s main event, the Champagne Exhibition, will take place at Kaiserštejn Palace in Malá Strana, featuring around 50 cuvées from more than 18 champagne houses.

Visitors can sample different styles, meet producers and discover brands including Louis Roederer, Piper-Heidsieck, Philipponnat, Telmont and G. H. Mumm. Selected bottles will also be available to purchase at special festival prices.



The exhibition will run in two sessions, from 14:00 to 17:00 and 17:00 to 20:00. Tickets cost CZK 2,180.

Two-Michelin-Star Chef to Prepare Gala Dinner

Another highlight will be the Champagne Gala Banquet at Prague’s Municipal House, where French chef Valentin Loison will prepare a five-course tasting menu paired with champagnes from selected producers.

Loison, 32, earned two Michelin stars at his restaurant Bulle d’Osier in Langres, France, within approximately 18 months. The evening will also feature a musical performance by Czech violist Jitka Hosprová.

The gala begins at 20:00, with individual tickets priced at CZK 9,400.

Exclusive Tastings and Masterclasses

The festival programme also includes specialist tastings and masterclasses for champagne enthusiasts.

One session will focus on Louis Roederer’s Cristal, featuring vintages including 2006 and 2016, at the Zlatá Praha restaurant. Other events will explore the Meunier grape variety and pair foie gras with a rare 1996 de Venoge Blanc de Blancs Magnum.

Some masterclasses are limited to just 12 participants.

Tickets

Tickets and the full programme are available here. For additional information, contact [email protected].

Readers registering through Prague Morning can enter the code PM2026 in the designated field after their surname to help organisers identify their registration. Priority consideration is subject to ticket availability.

World.title: Beyond Tacos: Meet the Founders of La Casa Azteca in Prague
World.content:
La Casa Azteca brings traditional Mexican food and cultural celebrations to Prague.

Run by Miguel, originally from Mexico, and Modar, who comes from Syria, the restaurant draws on their experience in the city’s Mexican food scene while introducing customers to dishes and traditions from beyond the familiar.

Two routes to Prague

Modar arrived for work as a structural engineer. While learning Czech, he found himself working in a Mexican restaurant, where he became interested in the food and the business.

“I fell in love with the Mexican concept and the Mexican food, so I had to stay,” he says.



Miguel, meanwhile, had already spent years living abroad, including five years in Montreal and time in the United States. He had always wanted to experience different countries, and Prague was another step in that direction.

Still, the city felt unlike anywhere he had been before. He remembers seeing a tram when he first arrived and feeling as though he had landed in a fairy-tale country.

The two eventually met through Prague’s Mexican restaurant scene, around nine years ago. What started as a shared connection to Mexican food eventually grew into a business partnership.

Keeping Mexican food authentic — and introducing it to Prague

At La Casa Azteca, Miguel and Modar want to keep the food close to what customers would find in Mexico, combining street food with dishes more commonly associated with traditional restaurants. The menu includes mole, chiles, flautas and tacos, with each dish bringing its own flavours and character.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Azteca Cocina & Bar (@azteca_prague)

Keeping those flavours in Prague, however, sometimes means working with ingredients that are harder to find locally. Herbs commonly used in Mexico can be difficult to source, while ingredients such as tortillas and chillies can also be more expensive. Some elements therefore have to be substituted without losing the character of the dish.

They have also had to navigate some of the expectations Czech customers bring with them. Part of that process has been showing customers that Mexican cuisine goes well beyond the familiar image of tacos, enchiladas and very spicy dishes.

“People think that in Mexico we are always eating spicy food,” Miguel says. “It’s true, but not all our food is tacos and enchiladas. We eat normal food too — pasta, a piece of meat with rice.”

The same approach extends to drinks. Mezcal is still relatively unfamiliar to many Czech customers, so the team uses the restaurant as a place to explain where it comes from, how it is produced and how different varieties can taste.

“It’s something that people can explore,” Miguel says. “They appreciate the taste. They appreciate the liquor. It’s not just a party drink.”

Building a business abroad

Although Miguel and Modar have around nine years of experience in Prague’s Mexican restaurant scene, La Casa Azteca is a newer chapter. The current project, which combines a restaurant with a neighbouring service window, has been running for around six months.

Starting their own business required learning how to navigate the Czech system from scratch. “We had to learn so much about running a business in the Czech Republic,” Modar says. “Everything is very well organized and very well thought out, so you really need to be prepared. You have to pay attention to every detail and every small thing.”

There was also the risk that came with building something abroad, without the same safety net they might have had at home. “I think it’s harder to take risks when you’re living abroad because, if you fall, there’s no one to pick you up. The stress is greater. But at the same time, you know there’s no way back, so you have to make it work,” Modar says.

Celebrating Mexican culture in Prague

Beyond the menu, Miguel and Modar celebrate Mexican traditions through events at the restaurant. After marking Mexican Independence Day in September, they are now preparing for the Day of the Dead, with Mexican dancers, live mariachi music, decorations and special dishes planned for the end of October.

World.title: Turn a Sleepover Into a Special Memory With atelier stories
World.content:
A sleepover with friends can be one of those childhood moments that children remember for years.

But for parents, organising one often means buying decorations, preparing bedding, rearranging furniture and dealing with the cleanup afterwards.

Prague-based atelier stories takes care of everything, bringing a fully styled teepee sleepover directly to the family home. Parents choose the theme, date and number of children, while the company handles the delivery, setup, styling and collection.

Founded by Jana Hrochová, who has a background in event production, organisation and guest services, atelier stories was created around a simple idea: making special moments for children without turning them into another project for parents.



The concept works for birthdays, but it doesn’t have to be a special occasion. A weekend with friends, a school holiday or simply an evening when children want to do something different can become a small adventure at home.

Families can choose from three themes: Mermaid World, Wizard Academy and SPA Night. Each setup features coordinated colours, soft textiles, fairy lights and themed accessories. The result is a playful sleeping space designed to appeal to children while remaining stylish enough to fit comfortably into the family home.

Every booking includes the equipment and styling, with teepees assembled and individual sleeping spaces prepared with mattresses, bedding, pillows, blankets, decorative cushions and other details suited to the chosen theme. Optional extras include creative kits, themed activities, photography and Instax memories.

The service is designed to make the experience as easy as possible for parents. There is no need to buy decorations, assemble teepees, wash bedding or find storage space for the equipment afterwards. Once the sleepover is over, atelier stories returns to dismantle the setup, pack everything away and collect it.

Quality, comfort and hygiene are central to the service. The equipment and textiles are cleaned and prepared between bookings, and each sleeping space is carefully arranged to ensure children have a comfortable place to settle in for the night.

Families can book a sleepover for one night or an entire weekend. Prices start at CZK 3,490 for two children for one night, or CZK 4,900 for two children for a full weekend, from Friday to Monday. Both options include the equipment, styling, setup and collection, with delivery within Prague included free of charge.

The service can also make a thoughtful gift from grandparents. Instead of another toy or physical present, a gift voucher gives grandchildren an experience to look forward to.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by atelier stories | tématické přespávačky pro děti (@atelierstories.cz)

Vouchers can cover a complete sleepover or contribute towards one, allowing the family to choose the theme and date later. They are valid for one year and delivered by email within 24 hours of payment.

While at-home sleepovers remain the main focus, atelier stories also creates children’s lounges and play areas for weddings and other events, giving younger guests a dedicated space to play and relax while adults enjoy the occasion.

World.title: Hungary’s new expressway opens – Drivers can use it for free for now!
World.content:
The first 28-kilometre section of Hungary’s M49 expressway, connecting the M3 motorway with Ököritófülpös, has been completed and opened to traffic. The four-lane road became available to motorists at 2 PM on Tuesday, the Minister for Transport and Investment announced at a press conference at the site.

Dávid Vitézy said the HUF 138 billion (EUR 376 million) project, financed from the Hungarian state budget, would take traffic away from Main Road 49, which leads towards the Hungarian-Romanian border. The new expressway is expected to reduce through traffic in Mátészalka and surrounding settlements by 70%.

Photo: MTI

When will the M49 become a toll road?

Construction is already under way on the next section of the M49, which will extend to Csenger, near the Hungarian-Romanian border. Under the contract, the HUF 141 billion project is scheduled for completion in 2029. It is then expected to connect with the Romanian expressway section running from the border to Satu Mare, which is also due to be completed that year.

Motorists can use the newly opened Hungarian section of the M49 free of charge for the rest of 2026. The road will be added to the country’s toll road network in 2027, Vitézy announced in a Facebook video.

Photo: MTI

A long-awaited transport project

The minister recalled that the development had been planned for many years. The first plans for the road connection appeared in 2007, while the former National Infrastructure Development Company (NIF) commissioned route assessments and environmental impact studies in 2010.

Detailed planning for the construction permit and the selection of the final route took place in 2018 and 2019. NIF signed the construction contract with Duna Aszfalt in 2022.

The completed section features 22 new structures, including bridges. Four junctions have been built, including the connection to the M3 motorway, alongside new roundabouts and connecting roads. A separate 3.3-kilometre bypass has also been constructed near Győrtelek, Vitézy said.

Photo: MTI

If you missed it: New motorway connecting Hungary to southern neighbour is only one approval away

Next section faces funding changes

Vitézy noted that the previous government had redirected funding allocated to the continuation of the M49 to other projects before the election. Although the construction contract remains valid and work is continuing, the necessary funding had not been secured in the central budget.

In recent weeks, the ministry reviewed the project and revised its funding plans. Under the new financing arrangements, implementation will be rescheduled through to 2029, the minister explained.

The ministry has also asked the contractor to cut costs. As a result, a planned ten-lane border crossing facility on the Hungarian-Romanian border will not be built. Vitézy said the aim was to reduce the construction contract’s value by at least HUF 3 billion, a proposal already put to Duna Aszfalt.

On the Romanian side, the construction contract for the expressway was signed in October 2025. Work on the section connecting Satu Mare with the Hungarian border could begin in spring 2027, with the Romanian continuation of the M49 expected to be completed in the second quarter of 2029.

Photo: MTI

More funding for road maintenance and railways

The minister also outlined wider transport plans. The government intends to increase funding for the maintenance of the national road network fivefold and strengthen the capabilities of state-owned road operator Magyar Közút by increasing its budget.

The government is also working to end motorway concession arrangements. From 1 April 2027, Magyar Közút is scheduled to take over the operation of Hungary’s motorway network.

Turning to regional public transport, Vitézy said a detailed feasibility study was being prepared for a comprehensive reconstruction of the Debrecen–Mátészalka railway line. Meanwhile, the construction tender for the modernisation of the Debrecen–Nyíregyháza railway line is expected to be published at the end of this year or early next year.

World.title: Hungary’s energy giant MOL emerges as leading contender for one of Saudi Aramco’s European assets
World.content:
Hungarian energy group MOL could be the leading candidate to acquire some of Saudi oil giant Saudi Aramco’s assets in Poland, including its 30 per cent stake in the Gdańsk oil refinery, according to Polish media reports. A deal would strengthen MOL’s position in one of Central Europe’s key fuel markets, although no sale has been confirmed.

MOL could link Polish retail and refining operations

Polish newspaper Rzeczpospolita reports that Saudi Aramco has appointed investment bank JPMorgan Chase to assess potential options for its Polish interests. Three prospective buyers have reportedly been identified, with MOL considered a strong contender alongside international energy companies BP and Shell.

A potential acquisition would build on MOL’s existing presence in Poland. In 2022, the Hungarian company bought 417 filling stations in the country for more than USD 600 million (approximately EUR 538.4 million) as part of the asset disposals associated with the merger of Polish energy groups Orlen and Lotos.

Buying a stake in the Gdańsk refinery could allow MOL to source fuel more directly for its Polish service stations, potentially strengthening its supply chain and expanding its role beyond retail distribution into refining.

Analysts cited by Rzeczpospolita see the refinery interest as commercially attractive, although fluctuating refining margins could make its value difficult to assess. The newspaper reports that a complete Saudi Aramco withdrawal from Poland is considered less likely than a sale of selected assets, which could include the fuel wholesaler Aramco Fuels Poland and the refinery stake.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Orlen faces restrictions on buying back its stake

Poland’s state-controlled Orlen owns the remaining 70 per cent of the Gdańsk refinery. However, it may not be able simply to buy back the Saudi stake.

The European Commission required the disposal of certain Lotos assets as a condition of approving the Orlen-Lotos merger, with the aim of preserving competition and preventing excessive market concentration. That history complicates the ownership question, although Polish authorities could have a significant say in assessing a potential new investor, given the refinery’s importance to national energy security.

Any transaction would therefore involve more than a straightforward commercial decision, with competition rules and the interests of the Polish state likely to be important considerations.

If you have missed it: MOL signs deal to buy Russian stake in Serbia’s NIS oil company – UPDATE: MOL reaction

Regional expansion brings opportunities and risks

The reported sale discussions come as MOL is also pursuing a possible acquisition of the Russian-owned stake in Serbia’s NIS oil company. If both transactions were completed, they could significantly strengthen the Hungarian group’s refining and fuel-market position across Central Europe.

However, expanding on two fronts would also bring substantial financing requirements and potential regulatory hurdles. Competition authorities would need to assess the implications of any deal, while the commercial case would depend on the price of the assets and future refining profitability.

For now, Saudi Aramco is reportedly examining its options rather than committing to a sale. MOL’s status as a potential frontrunner remains based on Polish media reporting and analyst assessments, and the eventual buyer, scope and timing of any transaction are still uncertain.

World.title: Breaking: Hungary issues international arrest warrant for former central bank governor’s son
World.content:
Hungarian authorities have issued European and international arrest warrants for Ádám Matolcsy, the son of former National Bank of Hungary governor György Matolcsy, and businessman György Stofa in connection with an investigation into suspected economic fraud and other alleged offences.

Suspects believed to have left Hungary

The Budapest-Capital Regional Court confirmed on Tuesday that the warrants had been issued by the Buda Central District Court. The proceedings concern suspected fraud causing particularly substantial financial damage and the alleged use of forged private documents. According to the court, investigators considered it necessary to question both men as suspects.

However, authorities have been unable to establish their whereabouts or carry out the interviews, and measures to locate them have so far proved unsuccessful. Neither man is at his registered address in Hungary. Investigators have received information suggesting that both may have left the country and could be outside Europe. Nevertheless, the court considered it justified to seek them within the European Union as well as internationally.

The warrants will become visible in the relevant databases once the necessary administrative procedures have been completed. Hungarian authorities are seeking the men’s extradition or surrender so that criminal proceedings can be conducted. The court said it had considered whether issuing the warrants was proportionate, concluding that the nature of the alleged offences and the potential penalties justified the measure.

Screenshot from police.hu

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Alleged roles in suspected financial fraud

Based on the evidence currently available, prosecutors believe that Ádám Matolcsy may have instigated alleged economic fraud causing particularly substantial financial damage, as well as the use of forged private documents. Stofa is suspected of having participated in the alleged fraud as a co-perpetrator and of directly committing the document-related offence.

These are allegations at the current stage of the investigation and have not been established by a court verdict. Stofa was previously associated with Optima Zrt., the company involved in managing funds linked to foundations established by the National Bank of Hungary, according to Hungarian watchdog K-Monitor.

Stay up-to-date: The UN was no friend of Orbán – So why is he now linked to its top job?

Wider investigation into central bank-linked funds

The warrants form part of a broader investigation into suspected financial misconduct connected with the central bank’s affairs. On 21 October, prosecutors detained former central bank governor György Matolcsy, who was questioned by the Central Investigative Prosecutor’s Office and named as a suspect in alleged economic fraud and the use of forged private documents.

Two other individuals were also detained: a representative involved in a loan agreement with the Central European III Private Equity Fund and a lawyer who participated in a securities transaction. Hungarian news outlet Válasz Online reported that those detained included Mihály Valkó, chief executive of Quartz Investment Fund Management, and Tamás Sándor, a lawyer who regularly represented the Matolcsy family.

The investigation continues, with the international warrants marking a further step in efforts to locate and question two people whom authorities say they have so far been unable to reach.
