World.title: Hungary launches Wekerle housing scheme with cheaper mortgages and EUR 1.7 billion for renovations
World.content:
Hungary has unveiled an extensive new housing programme offering discounted mortgages for younger buyers, state subsidies for energy-efficient home renovations and the return of government-backed housing savings. The Wekerle programme, announced by Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s government, is designed to make homes more affordable while encouraging construction and modernisation across the country.

The measures will be introduced in stages from October 2026, with the wider programme expected to run until 2030. The government also plans to expand affordable rental housing and student accommodation, using both domestic and European Union funding.

Cheaper mortgages for buyers aged 18–45

The new Wekerle+ Purchase and Construction Loan becomes available from 28 October, although individual banks may need a few extra days to prepare their systems.

Applicants aged 18–45 can apply for a fixed-rate mortgage to purchase or build a home. The annual interest rate will be 3% for new properties and 5% for existing homes, with interest-rate support available for up to 25 years.

The scheme is not conditional on marriage or having children. However, the property must serve as the buyer’s home rather than an investment, and borrowers will be required to live there for five years.

The government has introduced price limits to prevent public money from supporting luxury property purchases. The maximum eligible price is HUF 100 million for an apartment and HUF 150 million for a family house, while the price per square metre cannot exceed HUF 1.5 million.

Parents or siblings may also join an application as co-borrowers if the applicant’s income is insufficient, although they will not acquire ownership of the property through this arrangement.

Existing Otthon Start (Home Start) mortgage contracts will remain valid. Some buyers who have already signed purchase agreements may also have a 15-day transition period to switch to the new scheme, subject to the applicable conditions.

Finance Minister András Kármán, Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Economy and Energy Minister István Kapitány. Photo: MTI

If you missed it: Government measures could give Hungary’s housing market the boost it needs

HUF 633 billion for home renovations

One of the programme’s largest elements is a HUF 633 billion (EUR 1.7 billion) funding package for energy-efficiency improvements, covering everything from panel blocks and brick-built apartment buildings to detached houses.

The renovation support will help households pay for insulation, window and door replacement, shading systems, more efficient split air conditioners and, in some cases, solar panels. The government also plans to support heating-system upgrades.

The Wekerle+ Renovation Support and Loan scheme will offer fixed-rate loans at 3% interest, with the maximum loan amount rising from HUF 6 million to HUF 15 million. Depending on the property’s energy performance, applicants may also qualify for a non-repayable grant covering 30–50% of eligible costs, up to HUF 7.5 million.

To qualify, renovations must deliver energy savings of at least 30%. Unlike the purchase mortgage, the renovation scheme is not restricted by age, marital status or parenthood, and will be available across Hungary.

The programme is expected to launch in stages in 2027, with support for family houses scheduled to begin in February and applications for apartment-building renovations opening in March.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

State-backed housing savings return in 2027

Hungary will also reintroduce state-supported housing savings from January 2027, reviving a system whose previous government subsidy was abolished in 2018.

Under the Wekerle+ Housing Savings scheme, the state will supplement eligible deposits for up to ten years. During the first five years, the subsidy will cover 10% of contributions, up to HUF 120,000 annually. From the sixth to the tenth year, the rate will rise to 20%, with an annual cap of HUF 240,000.

The maximum subsidy will therefore be available to savers who deposit HUF 100,000 per month. Over ten years, the government contribution could reach HUF 1.8 million, excluding interest and subject to the scheme’s conditions.

Participating banks must offer at least 3% interest on savings. The money can be used to purchase a property, finance renovations or cover a mortgage deposit. The scheme will be open regardless of age, location or family status.

Affordable rentals and student accommodation planned

The Wekerle Sándor Housing and Dormitory Construction Programme will address another persistent problem: the shortage of affordable rental homes and student accommodation.

The government plans to allocate HUF 30 billion in EU funding in the first year, followed by a further EUR 550 million over the next three years. New housing is expected to be concentrated in areas with good public transport connections.

Together, these measures are intended to increase the supply of homes while improving access to both home ownership and affordable renting.

Government expects no major construction price surge

Prime Minister Péter Magyar said the government does not expect the programme to drive up construction and renovation prices significantly. Rather than introducing price caps, the government intends to spread support across different groups and types of housing.

The administration also expects smaller businesses to benefit indirectly, as local construction companies and contractors carry out much of the building and renovation work.

The funding for energy-efficiency improvements will partly come from EU Cohesion Fund money previously frozen and subsequently brought back to Hungary, according to the government’s announcement.

The Wekerle programme is intended to create a more sustainable housing market, combining support for buyers with investment in existing homes, new construction and affordable rentals.

Where to find the details: The government has published information about the schemes on the official Wekerle programme website. As the measures launch in stages, applicants should check the relevant eligibility rules and bank requirements before applying.

World.title: Nursery workers in Hungary charged for verbally abusing and taping mouth of 3-year-old
World.content:
Two nursery workers in southern Hungary have been charged with endangering a minor after allegedly verbally abusing a three-year-old boy, repeatedly pulling him around and, in one incident, taping his mouth shut. Prosecutors are seeking suspended prison sentences and a permanent ban on both women working in professions involving children.

Child allegedly insulted and physically mistreated

The charges were announced by the Kaposvár District Prosecutor’s Office, which said the alleged incidents took place at a nursery in a village near Kaposvár, in Somogy County. According to the indictment, the two women, employed as a nursery educator and a childcare assistant, repeatedly mistreated the boy from November 2024 onwards.

They allegedly called him derogatory names, including terms equivalent to “disgusting”, “hateful” and even the f-slur, and repeatedly pulled him around as a means of disciplining him.

The most serious incident reportedly occurred during lunch, when the child crawled under a table. The childcare assistant allegedly became angry, led him to a bed and covered his mouth with a wide strip of adhesive tape. A few seconds later, she tore the tape off while the boy was crying.

Prosecutors said the child did not suffer physical injuries. However, they argued that both employees had seriously breached their professional duties and endangered the boy’s physical and emotional development.

Workers dismissed after incident came to light

The case reportedly took place at a nursery in Zselicszentpál, which opened in 2023. The incident came to light after a parent entering the building and another childcare worker allegedly witnessed the child’s mouth being taped.

The municipality subsequently filed a complaint, prompting a police investigation on suspicion of endangering a minor. The employer immediately terminated both women’s public-sector employment once the allegations emerged.

At the time, the village’s mayor, Katalin Szabó, told local news outlet Sonline that the employees had been hired with strong recommendations and that she had never imagined the nursery would face such a situation.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Prosecutors seek permanent ban from working with children

The Kaposvár District Prosecutor’s Office has submitted the indictment to the Kaposvár District Court. It is seeking suspended prison sentences for both defendants and asking the court to permanently prohibit them from any profession involving the education, supervision, care or medical treatment of anyone under 18.

The charges have not yet resulted in a court verdict. The proposed professional ban would prevent the women from returning to a broad range of roles involving children if imposed by the court.

World.title: Hungary’s refusal to join Ukraine loan could cost valuable EU funds
World.content:
Hungary could face a fresh dispute with major European Union member states over its decision to stay out of a proposed EUR 45 billion loan for Ukraine, as disagreements over Kyiv’s financing threaten to spill into negotiations on the bloc’s next long-term budget.

EUR 45 billion loan puts Hungary at odds with Kyiv’s supporters

The EU is considering raising the money on financial markets, backed by its common budget, to help cover Ukraine’s funding needs in 2027. Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic are expected to remain outside the proposed arrangement, continuing their opposition to participating in joint EU borrowing for Ukraine.

According to Politico, diplomats say some of Kyiv’s strongest supporters could take a tougher line towards countries declining to contribute when negotiations begin over the EU’s 2028–2034 budget. The talks will determine the scale and distribution of future cohesion and agricultural funding, making the dispute potentially significant for Budapest.

German diplomat questions increased EU support

A German diplomat quoted by Politico questioned why German taxpayers should finance increased cohesion payments for countries that do not participate in common efforts to support Ukraine’s security. The remarks suggest that Hungary’s stance could become a point of contention in broader budget negotiations, although Berlin has not formally announced that participation in the loan would be a condition for receiving additional EU funding.

The issue could complicate Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s stated ambition to secure an additional EUR 2 billion in EU funding in the next budget period, partly to compensate for support Hungary has previously lost. Cohesion funding helps finance infrastructure, regional development, business support and energy projects.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

PM Magyar’s position remains unclear

Hungary’s position may also extend beyond the previous government of Viktor Orbán. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has said he discussed the issue with Magyar and that they agreed their countries would not participate in joint borrowing for Ukraine. Magyar has not publicly confirmed that account or outlined his position in detail.

Stay up-to-date: The UN was no friend of Orbán – So why is he now linked to its top job?

Loan and budget arrangements remain undecided

The proposed EUR 45 billion package is itself still under discussion. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has previously indicated that Ukraine could need around EUR 70 billion in additional support, while Brussels is also seeking greater contributions from partners including the United Kingdom and Canada. The possible use of frozen Russian assets remains controversial, with Belgium among the countries expressing serious reservations.

EU leaders are expected to revisit Ukraine’s financing at a special summit scheduled for 26–27 November. By then, the debate may clarify both the structure of the loan and whether opposition to it will influence negotiations over future EU spending.

For now, neither the final loan arrangements nor the next EU budget has been agreed. Any direct link between Hungary’s refusal to participate and reductions in, or restrictions on, its future funding remains a possibility rather than an established policy.

World.title: Serbia’s shock election result echoes Hungary’s political earthquake – But there is one big difference
World.content:
Serbia’s student-led opposition has scored a decisive victory in the country’s snap parliamentary election, drawing striking comparisons with Hungary’s political transformation in April 2026. Both countries have seen voters rally behind new political forces promising change after years of dominance by established leaders. However, the movements behind the two victories differ significantly in their leadership, political outlook and challenges ahead.

According to preliminary results announced by Serbia’s Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) on 26 October, the Student List secured 52.71% of the vote, translating into 140 seats in the 250-member National Assembly. The electoral list led by President Aleksandar Vučić received 39.17%, equivalent to 104 seats.

The results, based on votes processed from 8,187 polling stations, give the student-backed movement an absolute parliamentary majority. Vučić conceded defeat on election night.

Hungary and Serbia: voters demand change

The similarities with Hungary are hard to ignore. On 12 April 2026, Péter Magyar’s Tisza Party won Hungary’s parliamentary election with 141 of the 199 seats, ending Viktor Orbán’s 16 years as prime minister. Tisza secured more than 70% of parliamentary seats, while the Fidesz–KDNP alliance was reduced to 52.

In both countries, political newcomers capitalised on widespread dissatisfaction with the established political order. Anti-corruption promises, demands for accountability and calls to improve public institutions became central themes in their campaigns.

The two elections also took place against a backdrop of criticism over unequal campaign conditions, including concerns about media coverage and the use of state resources. These issues were particularly prominent in Serbia, where election observers have documented concerns about the fairness of the electoral environment.

Both countries also have complicated relationships with Russia. Orbán maintained close ties with Moscow during his time in office, while Vučić has pursued relations with Russia alongside Serbia’s stated ambition to join the European Union. Political change in either country therefore carries implications beyond its borders.

A student movement versus a single political leader

Perhaps the biggest difference lies in how the two challengers organised themselves. Hungary’s political transformation centred on Magyar, a former Fidesz insider who built Tisza into a major electoral force in a relatively short period. The party offered a recognisable political programme, combining a pro-European orientation with promises to tackle corruption and restore public trust.

Serbia’s Student List, by contrast, emerged from a grassroots protest movement and has no single, established leader. Its candidates include academics, professionals and public figures, while its supporters come from diverse political backgrounds. The movement’s decentralised structure helped it unite people around demands for accountability, but governing as a cohesive administration could prove considerably more difficult.

The Serbian protests began after a concrete canopy collapsed at Novi Sad railway station on 1 November 2024, killing 16 people. The disaster triggered demonstrations over alleged corruption, government accountability and the handling of major infrastructure projects.

The movement’s success at the ballot box now presents a new challenge: translating its broad anti-corruption message into a detailed programme and selecting leaders capable of implementing it.

Why Serbia’s future matters to the EU

The two countries also occupy very different positions in Europe. Hungary is an EU member, meaning its government directly influences decisions within the bloc. Magyar’s victory created expectations of a change in Budapest’s relationship with Brussels, particularly over the rule of law and European funding.

Serbia, meanwhile, remains an EU candidate country, with accession negotiations facing significant obstacles. The Student List has emphasised domestic reforms, but its foreign policy direction remains less clearly defined than Tisza’s. Its candidates have also expressed support for maintaining ties with Russia, while the question of EU membership remains politically sensitive.

International observers have already highlighted the scale of the challenge facing Serbia’s incoming political leadership. In their preliminary assessment of the 25 October vote, the OSCE’s election observation mission reported serious inequalities in campaign opportunities, including the misuse of state resources, pressure on voters and pronounced bias in media coverage favouring the incumbent camp.

The Student List must now demonstrate that it can improve the institutions it campaigned against.

Two victories, one message

Hungary and Serbia have not followed identical political paths. One elected a leader-centred, pro-European party in a regularly scheduled parliamentary election; the other backed a decentralised student-led movement in a snap poll following prolonged street protests.

Yet both results demonstrate how dissatisfaction with long-established political power can create opportunities for relatively new challengers.

For Hungary, the decisive question is how Magyar’s government delivers on its promises. For Serbia, it is whether a movement built around protest can transform its electoral mandate into stable, accountable government. The victories may look similar from a distance, but what happens next will determine whether they lead to equally lasting political change.

World.title: Erasmus+ is finally back at all Hungarian universities – When can students go abroad again?
World.content:
Hungarian university students can once again access the full Erasmus+ exchange programme after all the necessary funding agreements were signed, ending years of restrictions on institutions run by public-interest asset management foundations.

The Erasmus+ student exchange programme has fully returned to all Hungarian universities, European Commission Executive Vice-President Roxana Mînzatu announced on Monday. The Tempus Public Foundation, which coordinates the programme in Hungary, confirmed that all the necessary funding agreements have now been signed following the removal of the legal obstacles.

🇭🇺🇪🇺 @EUErasmusPlus is back for students at every Hungarian university! For almost four years, students at some Hungarian universities missed out on opportunities that their peers across Europe could enjoy. Today, that changes. And I am happy to welcome them back to the Erasmus+ family! Students from all Hungarian universities can now access these opportunities again, with applications possible as early as this autumn. This means more opportunities for young people. More connections across Europe. And more doors open for every Hungarian student. #erasmusasaright — Roxana Mînzatu (@RoxanaMinzatu) October 26, 2026

When will students be able to study abroad again?

Despite the agreements being signed, students should not expect regular exchanges to resume immediately. According to the Tempus Public Foundation, regular student mobility is expected to restart in the second semester of the 2026/2027 academic year.

Some other forms of mobility may begin earlier, including short-term exchanges, blended mobility combining online and physical activities, and opportunities for university staff.

The access will allow students to study at partner universities abroad and gain professional experience through international placements. University lecturers and other staff will also be able to participate in exchanges, international research cooperation and professional development.

The affected institutions can additionally rejoin Erasmus+ partnership projects and apply for centrally managed funding opportunities.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Why were Hungarian universities excluded?

The restrictions date back to December 2022, when the Council of the European Union introduced measures under its rule-of-law conditionality mechanism. The measures prohibited new EU funding commitments with public-interest asset management foundations, known by their Hungarian abbreviation, KEKVA, and the institutions they maintained.

The EU raised concerns about transparency, conflicts of interest and the involvement of political decision-makers in these foundations. As a result, 21 Hungarian universities operating under the foundation model were unable to renew their Erasmus+ funding agreements when the previous agreements expired.

Although these institutions were not formally expelled from Erasmus+, their students could no longer participate in the programme through the affected universities in the usual way. The previous government launched a separate Pannónia mobility programme to mitigate the consequences.

If you missed it: FM Anita Orbán: Hungarian students to regain access to Erasmus+

What changed in October 2026?

The breakthrough came after Hungary’s new government agreed on reforms with the European Commission. On 13 October, EU member states unanimously ended the conditionality procedure, clearing the way for the affected universities to sign new Erasmus+ agreements.

The Tempus Public Foundation said it had begun notifying institutions about the signing process immediately after the decision.

World.title: EU Commission Unveils Reforms to Beef Up Border Agency
World.content:
The European Commission unveiled on Tuesday a series of measures designed to give the EU’s border control agency, the Warsaw-based Frontex, more powers to combat the entry and enhance the return of illegal immigrants.

“The new reality requires a new mandate for Frontex,” European Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy Henna Virkkunen told a press conference. “With these important proposals we are significantly strengthening our external borders and the support we can offer our member states.”

Key measures the European Commission are proposing, which will still need to be agreed by the member state governments in the Council of the EU, include more resources and operational capacity, a Quick Reaction Force to intervene in crisis situations, and a new Online Monitoring Centre to scan social media and identify bad actors in order to early detect potential threats at the borders. It will also develop a dedicated Return Coordination Centre and will now be able to help carry out returns of migrants from third countries by facilitating deportations from return hubs.

While the irregular entry of migrants to the bloc are well down from their peak during the migration crisis of 2015-2016, when almost 1.5 million first-time asylum applications were made by new arrivals, the latest EU-wide Eurobarometer survey still found 65 per cent of EU citizens were concerned about uncontrolled immigration. This has led to big electoral gains by far-right parties in the member states and the European Parliament, prompting the European Commission to take a more robust approach to irregular migration.

More recently, July’s Ceuta migrant crisis, when an estimated 70,000 to 80,000 Moroccan migrants mass-crossed the border into the Spanish North African enclave, partly fuelled by disinformation online, has added to the sense that more must be done to strengthen border insecurity.

“Our borders face new challenges: orchestrated crossings by smuggling networks, changing routes, hybrid threats, instrumentalization of migration – no member state can meet these challenges alone,” said European Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner. “Our response has to be faster, stronger and better coordinated.”

Brunner noted that the return rate of migrants who have no right of stay in the EU was still too low at 32-33 per cent, and the proposed new powers for Frontex will make the agency “the central EU actor on returns”.

Following the entry into force of the new Return Regulation on October 16, the European Commission is proposing a new regulation to digitalise the return, readmission and reintegration procedures across the EU, with the aim of modernising the handling of return cases by simplifying and speeding up administrative procedures through digitalisation, reduced administrative burdens, and improving data collection and sharing.

This will require more manpower and the European Commission is proposing to gradually increase Frontex’s standing corps to 30,000 officers by doubling the amount of Frontex’s own standing corps officers and creating a new “European border and return reserve” of 17 000 officers ready to be deployed when needed. According to Politico, the agency had around 7,800 personnel in its standing corps in early 2026 and is working towards a target of 10,000 by 2027.

World.title: Bulgarian Govt Criticised for Using State Resources to Promote Presidential Candidate
World.content:
Allegations that the Bulgarian government used official channels to promote presidential candidate Iliana Iotova have sparked a slew of accusations between opposition leaders and media associations on one side and Prime Minister Rumen Radev and his government on the other.

On Tuesday, the Association of European Journalists – Bulgaria accused Prime Minister Radev, who backed Iotova for the presidency at the first round of elections last weekend, of trying to force the media to be his mouthpiece.

The row erupted on Monday, after Radev said that voters in the upcoming second-round runoff will have to choose between “peace and war”. The suggestion was that Iotova can maintain balance in relations with Russia while opposition candidate Andrey Gyurov’s pro-EU and pro-Ukraine positions equate to warmongering.

The same message was published in a post on the government’s official Facebook page and in a press release sent out on Monday by the government’s press office, which included the message, “Let’s vote for Iliana Iotova so Bulgaria can be in safe hands.”

Gyurov and other opposition politicians claimed that Radev’s government was breaching the electoral code, which prohibits government information services from being used for partisan promotional purposes. The Central Election Committee has been notified of the allegations.

Later on Monday, the government’s official Facebook page published a statement saying there was no violation since the campaigning for the November 1 runoff has not yet started and the prime minister’s statements should “be covered in their entirety” by the media.

The statement also criticised “the negative example” of “some media outlets” who “silence, twist, manipulate, cut down and insinuate political narratives in the words of the prime minister”.

The Association of European Journalists – Bulgaria retorted with a statement saying that the government’s “attempt to lecture the media on professional journalistic standards” was “dangerous”.

“The expectation that all media outlets should republish the prime minister’s statements ‘in their entirety’ demonstrates a profound lack of understanding of journalistic work,” the statement said.

“Under the Bulgarian Media Code of Ethics, journalists are committed to ensuring the accuracy of information. This provision is important, but it is a distortion to interpret it as prohibiting journalists and media outlets from critically analysing the Prime Minister’s positions,” it added.

The first round of the presidential election was held on Sunday with no candidate receiving an outright majority. A runoff between acting President Iotova and opposition candidate and former interim prime minister Gyurov is scheduled for November 1.

Sunday’s results were unexpected as Gyurov had been far behind in opinion polls before the vote. The elections were also notable for their low voter turnout, with one polling agency estimating that only 22.5 per cent of eligible voters cast ballots.

World.title: What Does Aleksandar Vucic’s Defeat Mean for Balkan Autocrats?
World.content:
When the student protests in Serbia gathered momentum in 2025, Aleksandar Vucic, the president at the time, promised that he would defeat them and write a book on how to prevail against “colour revolutions” – an unmistakable allusion to Ukraine’s Maidan uprising, which unseated a corrupt administration.

Instead, he may now have to write another book on how power is lost through arrogance, institutional capture and the mistaken belief that fear can substitute for legitimacy. His defeat in the snap parliamentary elections of October 25 is not merely a change of government; it represents a profound rejection of the model of autocratic governance he built over more than a decade.

Yet this defeat did not occur in a vacuum. It followed nearly two years of student-led mobilisation that gradually expanded beyond universities and became one of the broadest civic movements in Serbia’s post-communist history.

World.title: Bosnian Court Verdicts for Wartime Sexual Violence Show Leniency and Disparities
World.content:
At the entity level, cases involving wartime sexual violence are notable for the inconsistency of judgments.

In the Federation, sentences ranged from one year to 13 years and six months, for offences including the rape of women, girls and men, multiple rapes, sexual abuse in camps and a combination of sexual and physical violence.

The average sentence was just over six years, while in some cases the perpetrators, including those whose victims were minors, were sentenced to just a year in prison having struck plea agreements. Such agreements can allow the convicted perpetrator to avoid prison altogether in exchange for paying an 18,000-euro fine.

Sentences in Republika Srpska ranged from two to 15 years in prison. In the case of the shortest sentences, the courts cited mitigating circumstances. In one, for example, the District Court in Banja Luka cited the fact the accused was an older juvenile at the time the offence was committed. In some cases, the courts cited no aggravating circumstances at all, despite the crimes involving sexual violence.

In the Federation, some cantonal courts cited as mitigating circumstances the accused’s marital status, the fact he had children and no prior convictions, and his conduct during the trial. In one case, the court cited the fact that the accused had not committed any other criminal offences since the crime in question. The passage of time was also taken as a mitigating circumstance, as was the accused’s advanced age.

In the autonomous Brcko District, sentences ranged from four to 15 years, and most commonly between four and six years even in cases of multiple rapes.

The cases in Brcko include that of Monika Karan, one of the few women convicted of war crimes in Bosnia. Karan was found guilty in 2013 of the psychological and sexual humiliation of detainees in the ‘Luka’ camp. The court found Karan had forced a detainee to strip naked, touched his genitals and forced him to touch her under threat of death.

Though finding that Karan’s acts caused her victim great psychological suffering, the court sentenced her to just four years in prison – below the statutory minimum.

As mitigating circumstances, the court cited her age at the time the offence was committed – 26 – as well as her family circumstances and the absence of prior convictions.

“Unfortunately, sexual violence leaves lasting consequences on victims, and such lenient sentences do not reflect the seriousness of that crime,” said Midheta Kaloper, head of the Association of Victims of War – Foca 92-95.

Experts say that overly lenient sentences undermine public trust in the judicial system and discourage victims from reporting violence.

“That is why it is high time that the sentencing policy was seriously reviewed,” Kaloper told BIRN.

“Institutions and society need to send a clear message that such acts must not be tolerated. Victims’ associations have advocated and appealed for these cases to be tried exclusively before the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina.”

World.title: Journalist-Turned-PM Faces Daunting Challenges in Romania
World.content:
What do journalism and diplomacy have in common? For Luca Niculescu, both offer the opportunity of direct engagement with people, demand effective communication, and require an ability to build relationships and ask the right questions.

Diplomacy, however, operates by different rules, particularly when it comes to freedom of public expression. This limitation is offset, according to Romania’s new prime minister, by the satisfaction that comes from serving the public interest and making a tangible difference to people’s lives.

Niculescu, 55, began his career as a radio journalist in 1992 and went on to become editor-in-chief of Radio France Internationale, RFI, while also contributing regularly to several French media outlets.

In 2016, he made the transition to diplomacy as Romania’s ambassador to France. He returned to Bucharest in 2022 to coordinate the country’s bid to join the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, OECD, and last week became prime minister.

World.title: Serbian Students’ Mass Support ‘Forced Vucic to Concede’ Election
World.content:
In a park next to the presidency building in central Belgrade, the campsite known as Caciland had become a symbol of the impunity enjoyed by the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS. Fenced off with metal barriers for more than a year and guarded by police, it occupied public land but served as a gathering place for SNS supporters.

Just after polls closed in Sunday’s elections, that changed, as Serbian citizens began celebrating in the streets across the country. Dancing and singing, supporters of the opposition Student List symbolically brought an end to the SNS’s 14-year rule by entering the tent camp and taking back the park for the public.

The results of the elections have electrified the country and brought a sigh of relief from political observers who feared the polls might have been severely rigged to put the SNS back into power, backed up by the muscle of the security forces. Jelena Loncar, an associate professor at Belgrade University’s Faculty of Political Sciences, told BIRN that the election results show that “Serbia is not moving towards a closed authoritarian regime.”

World.title: Czech Govt Faces Backlash Over Rushed Public Media Funding Reform
World.content:
Despite the cold and rainy weather that descended over the Czech capital, thousands of protesters filled Prague’s Old Town Square on Sunday afternoon, heeding the call of the Million Moments for Democracy movement with banners reading “Resign!”, “Hands off public media!”, “Shame!”, “We’ve had enough!”, and more colourful and explicit drawings and captions.

Other smaller demonstrations took place throughout the weekend across Czechia, including Brno, Liberec and Ceske Budejovice, hastily organised protests that testified to a sudden mood shift in society as fears of a government media grab intensify.

One of the governing coalition’s top campaign promises, the long-debated yet long-delayed reform to abolish license fees and fund both Czech TV (CT) and Czech Radio (CRo) directly from the state budget, appeared to have stalled in recent months.

But on Friday, the ruling three-party coalition of ANO, the ultraconservative Motorists for Themselves and the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD) party abruptly pushed through a priority reading of the bill.

This led to a swift and immediate response from citizens. Hundreds of protesters gathered on Malostranske Square in central Prague, and dozens were even blocked by the police from entering the lower house of parliament later that evening.

After a fast-track procedure that limited speaking time and set a fixed voting deadline, government MPs eventually approved the draft at around 04:30 in the early hours of Saturday morning, sending the bill to a second reading following hours of heated debate that saw personal attacks and vulgarities fly from both sides of the aisle.

According to the proposal, CT should receive an annual 5.7 billion crowns (234 million euros) from the state budget in 2027 (a billion crowns less than its 2026 license fee revenues), while CRo should also see its funding cut by 400 million crowns to a little over 2 billion crowns.

No ‘nationalisation’, Babis vows

Repeating the mantra pushed for the past year, government officials dismissed any concerns about the independence or the future of the public service broadcasters. “I reject the idea that changing the financing of public media is an attack on democracy or the end of the independence of public media,” insisted Culture Minister Oto Klempir, arguing that many other European countries fund their public broadcasters in a similar way.

A long-time critic of the public service media’s coverage and management, Prime Minister Andrej Babis accused the opposition of “lying, inciting hatred and dividing society”, while drawing a feeble comparison with protesters’ attempt to enter the Chamber of Deputies in Prague last Friday with the Capitol riots in Washington DC in January 2021.

He did, however, try to strike a reassuring tone as well. “Their funding will be guaranteed by law as a mandatory expenditure and linked to inflation,” he vowed. “No government will be able to arbitrarily cut [funding] based on whether it likes or dislikes a broadcast.”

This, however, did little to assuage widespread concerns that the government’s reform could put the two public service broadcasters under greater political control.

Warning that the reform threatens their editorial independence, undermines the stability of their funding and could lead to the nationalisation of both entities, staffers at CT and CRo have declared a day-long strike for November 3. “We ask everyone who is not indifferent to the fate of CT and CRo to make their position known publicly and loudly,” stated the Verejnopravne initiative, which is backed by about 3,200 of the 4,200 employees at the two broadcasters.

Addressing both the content of the bill and the fast-track legislative push, criticism has come from all corners, including the Czech Journalists’ Syndicate, the European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders, over a dozen other domestic and international media freedom groups, as well as President Petr Pavel – whose signature would be needed for the bill to come into force.

“I repeat that the media must have clear guarantees of independence in every respect, both in terms of content and funding,” Pavel said, additionally calling on politicians from both sides of the aisle to take it down a notch and work to deescalate tensions.

Experts also weighed in on the issue. “The way the rules of procedure [in the lower house of parliament] were handled in this case bears the features of a power grab, in which we can see inspiration from the rhetoric and tactics of leaders like Donald Trump and Viktor Orban,” argued political scientist Eva Klusova from the Czech Academy of Sciences.

Hypothesising that the reform could be a way for the government to cover up their earlier setback at this month’s recent municipal and senatorial elections, media expert Martina Urbanikova highlighted that the funding for public service media isn’t included in the 2027 state budget, and that the legislative agenda made it uncertain the reform could take effect from January.

But in the wake of Sunday’s street protests, Prime Minister Babis vowed not to back down, adding on Monday that specific provisions were still under consideration, including the option to allow for voluntary license fee payments.

Meanwhile, Million Moments for Democracy called for another mass demonstration, set to take place on Prague’s Letna plain on November 15, two days before commemorations marking the start of the 1989 Velvet Revolution.

World.title: Kosovo Woman Murdered Hours After Reporting Domestic Violence to Police
World.content:
The Basic Prosecution in Peja/Pec. Photo: Peja Basic Prosecution.

Arlinda Zekaj was murdered on Sunday evening in the village of Vitomirica, near Peja/Pec, shortly after returning from the police station where she reported domestic violence. Three days beforehand, she had asked the local prosecution to intervene to save her life.

“I hope the day never comes when you and the responsible institutions are forced to account for your actions only after my life has been taken,” Zekaj had written on October 22 in a letter to Lumturije Vucetaj, chief prosecutor of the Peja Basic Prosecution office. The letter called for urgent action against officials she accused of failing to protect her from domestic violence.

Three days later she was murdered with an axe, allegedly by her brother-in-law, who remains at large.

Zekaj is the seventh woman to be murdered by a family member in 2026 in Kosovo.

Kosovo police announced that they received a domestic violence report at around 7 p.m. on Sunday after which the police interviewed Zekaj and arrested her ex-husband for domestic violence. He was “placed in 48-hour detention. The victim was then taken to her home in the village of Vitomirica voluntarily,” the police statement reads.

“At around 9:10 pm, we were notified that she had been found dead”, the statement continues.

On Monday morning, Zekaj’s lawyer Adelina Shala contradicted the police statement, writing on Facebook that “it wasn’t the victim’s will” to return home. On Sunday evening, Shala accused Kosovo authorities of failing to protect her client, writing that “the state killed Arlinda”.

The prosecutor’s office in Peja/Pec stated in a late night press release that Vucetaj had ordered Zekaj’s letter to be registered for examination by the competent prosecutor, including “an assessment of potential criminal liability for abuse of official position or authority”.

Kosovo’s Chief State Prosecutor requested a detailed report and review on Monday to determine “whether there were institutional or individual failures” and how the victim’s letter was handled.

Kosovo President Justina Shiroka Pula called for “an urgent, comprehensive and impartial investigation. It must be clarified whether all necessary measures were taken to assess the risk and protect her.”

The Collective for Feminist Thought and Action, an activist group, called for a nationwide protest on Wednesday, “as an act of revolt and a final call to protect women’s lives”.

The Kosovo Women’s Network (KWN) said that “the case is particularly concerning given the challenges [Zekaj] had faced regarding custody and contact with her child, as well as the concerns raised about the institutional handling of her case”.

There have been a number of recent murders of women in Kosovo by family members.

On October 9, Nafije Bogujevci and her brother Egzon Bogujevci were shot dead. Nafije’s husband later turned himself in to the police. In late August, two women were allegedly killed by their husbands within days. The first victim was 25 years old and pregnant, the second aged 80. The first was shot, the second beaten to death.

On the last Friday in August, dozens of people marched through Pristina to demand justice for the victims of femicide and to call on authorities to treat gender-based violence in Kosovo as a national emergency.

World.title: Ryanair Directly Connects Zagreb and Warsaw Over Winter
World.content:
October the 27th, 2026 – Ryanair has directly connected Zagreb with the Polish capital of Warsaw during the winter schedule, with flights for as little as 17 euros.

The wildly popular Irish low-cost carrier Ryanair has introduced yet another brand new air route connecting Zagreb and Warsaw, specifically Warsaw-Modlin Airport. Poslovni reports that the first flight was operated as part of the winter timetable for the 2026/2027 season on October the 26th, giving passengers from Croatia another option for travelling to Poland. The new route will operate on Mondays and Saturdays, with two flights a week from Zagreb and two from Warsaw.

There are some ultra-cheap tickets being offered on this new route, with the differences in prices show that having a certain degree of flexibility when choosing your desired travel dates can really pay off. Since prices change depending on demand and seat availability, it is always recommended to check the current offers on Ryanair’s website or on the company’s mobile app before booking.

On the occasion of launching this new route from Zagreb Airport, Ryanair’s Director of Communications Jade Kirwan highlighted the importance of expanding the offer for passengers from Croatia. “We’re very pleased that we saw off the first flight operating on the new Zagreb–Warsaw (Modlin) route, on which the first set of very many passengers who will travel with us this winter departed,” Kirwan said.

She added that the new route will give passengers a greater choice of destinations at affordable prices. “The route will operate four times a week, offering passengers from Croatia even more travel options at the most affordable prices in Europe. The entire winter timetable for 2026 is available for booking via our app and website,” she stated.

World.title: Croatian Campsites are the Most Expensive in Europe
World.content:
October the 27th, 2026 – Croatian campsites might be considered the most expensive in Europe, but the Germans still deem them the best. Here’s how much an average day costs.

For the ever-keen German campers, Germany itself is the most popular camping destination, while Croatia is the third most popular foreign destination, behind Italy and France, with the Netherlands in fifth place. Poslovni reports that Croatian campsites can expect continued strong demand from the German market throughout 2027, given that German campers give them the highest quality ratings in all of Europe, even though according to new research they are simultaneously the most expensive. This was highlighted by Uwe Frers, CEO of PiNCAMP, part of the German automobile club ADAC system.

German tourists, along with Slovenian and Austrian visitors, are the most numerous guests filling up Croatian campsites, and the German market is of particular importance for this segment, as well as for overall Croatian tourism. In a recent interview with Hina, Frers explained that ADAC’s digital tourism platform PiNCAMP also cooperates with the Dutch automobile club ANWB and the Swiss TCS.

“These auto clubs are among the largest in all of Europe, with a total of around 30 million members, many of whom are campers,” says Frers. At the recent Croatian Camping Congress, Frers presented one of their newer surveys on campers’ attitudes towards the quality and prices of campsites in 2026 and for 2027, conducted on the German and Dutch markets. For this purpose, they surveyed more than six thousand campers in two studies during the first three quarters of 2026.

around 25% of germans now go camping

The research showed that campers have positive attitudes and that demand from these two countries for Croatian campsites is growing. Demand from German campers is growing particularly strongly, for which Frers sees reasons in the rising number of camping vehicles in that country, from last year’s 1.7 million to this year’s 2 million, which is also a new record and, as he adds, “a great figure for the camping sector.” They also established that around 25 percent of Germans now go camping, which is a 19 percent increase compared to data from 2023. Frers also noted that a quarter of all camping vehicles in Europe are registered in Germany, followed by France with 19 percent, the United Kingdom with 13 percent, and the Netherlands with a 9 percent share.

interesting results for croatia and croatian camping

For Croatia specifically, he cites two interesting research results. The first is quality, which is the most important novelty, because campers gave it the best ratings. The second result is that Croatia is at the same time the most expensive camping destination. “In the past, we discussed how someone can be the most expensive and yet not the best. Now we can end such discussions, because Croatia has shown that it is the best in camping in terms of quality, so it is therefore justified that it also leads in price levels,” Frers believes.

He finds it interesting that Croatia has pursued a fairly aggressive pricing policy in recent years, but that this has now changed, because the average price increase in camping in Europe is around 8 percent, while Croatia with 7 percent is below that average. “So, being a leader in quality, while at the same time keeping price growth below the average, is the right tactic for surviving in this market,” Frers recommends. When asked about the average prices, he said that in Croatia it is €77 per day in a campsite, which is also the highest price among all countries, while the European average is around €50.

“In Europe, there are regions that are extremely cheap, as well as some very expensive ones. Croatia is clearly positioned in the luxury segment, and that position is further strengthened by its ‘leadership’ in quality, which is additionally confirmed in the research by campers stating that Croatian campsites offer good value for money,” says Frers.

However, he adds, in the research 56 percent of respondents said they had no opinion on this, which means they do not have a negative attitude either, while the remaining 44 percent are divided – half of them consider the Croatian camping offer acceptable and good, and the other half poor. “The fact that more than half of the respondents have no opinion at all I consider a good starting point for attracting new guests to Croatian campsites that should be utilised,” Frers stated.

croatia is the third most popular camping destination

For German campers, Germany itself is the most popular camping destination, while Croatia is the third most popular foreign destination, behind Italy and France, with the Netherlands in fifth place. Croatia is rated the best by the largest number of respondents (22 percent) in terms of price-quality ratio for camping, followed by Germany, Italy, Switzerland and Austria. In terms of quality, Croatia also occupies the leading position with the best average campsite rating of 3.9 stars, while the Netherlands, Luxembourg and France have 3.7 stars, Spain 3.6, and Italy 3.5. In terms of camping prices per day for 2027, Croatia leads with an average of €77, Switzerland is second with €65, followed by Italy with €64, Austria with €61 and the United Kingdom with €55.

World.title: Omiš Fire Claimed 6 Lives, Yet There’s No investigation Result Yet
World.content:
October the 27th, 2026 – The horrific Omiš fire has now tragically claimed six lives. Despite the severity of the disaster, there has still been no investigation result even after two months.

73 days have now passed since the major fire that broke out on the 13th of August in Lokva Rogoznica and spread down towards Omiš. Katarina Ergovic Arnaut reports for Index that the public still has no answer to the crucial question: how exactly this enormous fire started and who, if anyone, is responsible for it. In the meantime, the number of victims has risen to a horrendous six. Just two days ago, a 66-year-old woman who had been being treated in hospital since August for serious injuries sustained in the fire, died in hospital.

Despite the sheer scale of the tragedy, the police and the County State Attorney’s Office in Split have so far not publicly released the results of the investigation, nor have they announced whether the cause of the fire has been determined. It has also not been announced that anyone has been suspected or arrested in connection with its outbreak.

camera footage was examined and experts have been on the terrain taking samples

The investigation was launched immediately after the fire. The State Attorney’s Office (DORH) announced 71 days ago, on 15 August, that a crime scene investigation had been carried out at the place where the fire started in Lokva Rogoznica, involving the police, a fire and explosion protection inspector, and chemical-physical experts from the “Ivan Vučetić” Centre. Material samples were taken at the site where the fire broke out. Orders were also issued for the seizure of surveillance camera footage from the entire burned area, surveying of the terrain, and photographing of destroyed houses, other buildings and vehicles.

DORH stated at the time that the necessary expert examinations and other actions would be carried out in order to establish all the circumstances of the event. Over two months later, the results of these procedures have still not been presented to the public.

the fire directly affected around 1,000 hectares

According to the findings of the on-site investigation at the time, the fire broke out on the 13th of August around 20:00 in a heavily forested area next to the road in the wider Lokva Rogoznica area. Carried by strong winds, it spread quickly towards Omiš along a strip approximately 23 kilometres long and up to one and a half kilometres wide. Around 1,000 hectares of thick pine forest, grass and Dalmatian shrubs were burned. Numerous houses, business premises, plantations and vehicles were also claimed by the flames, and material damage in the multi millions was caused. Several dozen people were also injured to some extent or another in the fire.

The first victim, a seasonal worker from neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina, Dragana Antešević (34), tragically died during the fire itself. Later, retired firefighter Drago Lelas (79), Katica Nikolić (58), Ivana Kovačić (41), a 70-year-old man who was being treated at KBC Split, and the 66-year-old woman who died two days ago also succumbed to their injuries.

the question of responsibility

With each new victim, the importance of answering the question of how the fire started and whether anyone bears responsibility for the tragedy grows further. The question of the warning system’s response also remains open, because the SRUUK system was not activated during the fire. The system was introduced precisely so that citizens in crisis situations, such as major fires, floods, earthquakes or other immediate dangers, would receive timely warnings and instructions on how to protect themselves. The heartbroken families of the deceased and the public are therefore still waiting for the results of the investigation, as well as an answer to the question of whether all available mechanisms for warning the population were used on the night of the fire.

World.title: Ryanair Increases the Number of Flights From Zagreb This Winter
World.content:
October the 27th, 2026 – The ever popular Ryanair is increasing the number of flights from Zagreb Airport this winter, and here are the most popular routes.

Irish low-cost airline Ryanair is increasing the number of flights from Zagreb this winter. Poslovni reports that according to data from the aviation portal Zamaaero, the number of weekly flights is rising from 73 to 78, and passengers will have 18 routes available. While some destinations will have fewer departures, the number of flights to others is increasing. Malta stands out in particular, with ten flights per week announced – three more than last winter. The number of departures will nevertheless change during the winter timetable.

malta gets an increase

Although it is most often associated with summer, Malta is a Mediterranean archipelago that offers plenty of content during the colder part of the year as well. The mild Mediterranean climate is one of the main reasons to visit in winter. Average maximum daily temperatures in December are around 17 degrees, while in January and February they range between 15 and 16 degrees. The capital Valletta, whose historic core is under UNESCO protection, is an unmissable location. It is known for its Baroque architecture, narrow streets and distinctive wooden balconies. The Co-Cathedral of St John houses works by the painter Caravaggio, and the Upper Barrakka Gardens offer a view of the Grand Harbour.

ryanair’s expansive list of zagreb winter flights

According to data from the Zamaaero portal, the following routes from Zagreb have been announced for this winter: Alicante twice a week, Basel six times (one flight more), Beauvais twice, Bergamo six times (two flights more), Charleroi five times (one flight less), Dublin five times, Eindhoven twice and Gothenburg twice a week (one flight less).

Routes to Paphos, Lanzarote and Memmingen remain at two flights per week. The number of flights to London Stansted increases to 13 per week (three more), to Malaga to five (one more), and to Rome to four (one more). Weeze will have five flights per week (one more), and Karlsruhe/Baden-Baden three (one less).

A novelty in this year’s winter timetable from Zagreb is the route to Warsaw Modlin, which will operate twice a week. At the same time, routes to Hahn, Pisa and Thessaloniki are being discontinued. The stated numbers refer to the announced weekly frequencies, which may change during the winter. According to Zamaaero, Ryanair will have 98 flights from Zagreb in the first week of the winter timetable, 86 in the second, and 75 flights per week at the beginning of December.

World.title: Marble Torso of Roman Emperor From Salona Sold in New York for Over $34 Million
World.content:
October the 26th, 2026 – A stunning marble torso of a Roman Emperor that originated from Salona in Croatia was sold in New York for over $34 million. The head is likely still buried somewhere in Croatian soil.

Croatian cultural heritage is breaking records. Ana Vela reports for Dnevnik that a remarkable marble torso of a Roman emperor originating from Salona was sold across the pond in New York for over $34 million. With that, it set the record for the highest price a Roman antiquity has ever achieved at any auction. At the same time, a painting by Croatian artist Vlaho Bukovac also set a record with its sale in Vienna. This is the story of artworks whose value has skyrocketed.

After 15 minutes of bidding, the fall of the hammer marked a sale at a price almost three times higher than the starting estimate for the Salona torso. “When I heard how much it was sold for and that it was more than $34 million, I was shocked because in 2010, it was sold for seven million, and at that time, it was estimated at one to one and a half million dollars. Perhaps then there was a realistic chance of participating in the auction. However, this amount is, in my opinion, beyond all reason,” said Dražen Maršić from the Department of Archaeology at the University of Zadar.

croatia could unfortunately do nothing but watch the sale…

“We even considered whether it would be possible to find some funds, but an amount of $34 million is truly enormous and exceeds the budget for the construction and equipping of an entire new museum,” said Nina Obuljen Koržinek, Minister of Culture and Media.

The torso is otherwise part of a collection put up for sale by an anonymous collector. “It’s the most significant item at the auction. It is a Roman torso from the first half of the first century,” said Calvine Harvey, the auction specialist. Croatian experts had long been convinced that it was lost forever. New information arrived in 2010 when it first appeared at auction. “Around 1857, an ancestor of the then owners, Aloys Maximilian Neumann, bought the torso from a collector in Split,” said Maršić. There were no legal obstacles and therefore no basis for a restitution claim. “It’s a legally sold work of art that left the territory of Croatia a long time ago,” the Croatian minister explained.

The new owner is unknown. “If we find out who now owns it, whether a collector or a museum, then we will try to have it come to an exhibition in Croatia,” the minister added. Hope remains that the head of the Roman emperor is still somewhere in Salona. “There is a realistic possibility that the head is still buried somewhere, either in an archaeological context or buried as was done with similar objects of Roman art during the early years of Christianity,” said Maršić.

vlaho bukovac also wows in vienna

From Vienna comes another record auction news. Vlaho Bukovac’s “Pink Dream” was sold for almost half a million euros, becoming the most expensive Croatian painting ever sold at an official auction. “The moment when we can reach for restitution is when we can establish that the artwork was illegally taken out,” concluded Obuljen Koržinek.

World.title: Drivers in Croatia Could Have to Pay 3X Higher Fines
World.content:
October the 26th, 2026 – Drivers in Croatia could need to pay 3X higher fines for driving offences as stricter traffic rules loom.

Last year, out of a total of 320,046 recorded speeding offences, cameras detected 200,137 of them, or 62 percent. Poslovni reports that a new Rulebook (Pravilnik) proposes a reduction of the so-called safety margin, which means that speed exceedances recorded by cameras will be tolerated significantly less than until now. Under the current rules, 3 km/h is deducted from the measured speed up to 50 km/h. For speeds from 51 to 100 km/h the tolerance is 10 km/h, and above 100 km/h 10 percent of the measured speed is deducted, rounded up to the higher value.

With the new rulebook, for example, a driver travelling at 86 km/h in a built-up area with a 50 km/h limit would be granted a tolerance of only five instead of the current 10 km/h. The relevant speed would be 81 km/h, which is 31 km/h above the limit, and the fine would amount to €390 instead of €130.

cameras record the vast majority of driving offences

If current trends continue, such a change would also significantly increase revenues from fines. Data from the Ministry of the Interior show that fixed speed monitoring devices recorded the majority of such offences. Last year, out of a total of 320,046 established speeding offences, cameras recorded 200,137 of them, or 62 percent. In the first eight months of this year, out of a total of 226,302 speeding offences, fixed devices recorded 145,129 of them, which is 64 percent. Data for last year also show that the most numerous were those exceeding 10 to 20 kilometres per hour above the permitted speed in built-up areas, with a total of 124,611 such cases.

more locations than cameras

Croatia currently has 206 fixed cameras that are distributed across a total of 807 locations. The Ministry of the Interior explains that the cameras are relocated at different time intervals, depending on the assessment of the competent police administration. The highest number of locations for installing cameras is in the area of the Split-Dalmatia Police Administration and the Zagreb Police Administration, with 86 in each, followed by the Međimurje Police Administration with 62 locations. The fewest are in the area of the Karlovac Police Administration, with 12, and the Požega-Slavonia Police Administration, where there are 13.

Although fixed cameras primarily serve to determine speeding, they can also record other traffic offences. “If, for example, the offence of using a mobile phone while driving, not wearing a seat belt or some other unlawful behaviour is visible on the recording, the driver or passenger can also be fined for such offences,” the Ministry of the Interior explains.

revenue from fines is increasing

The Ministry of the Interior states that it does not keep separate statistics on the amounts collected by type of offence, but collectively for all monetary fines under the Road Traffic Safety Act. Nevertheless, the Annual Report on the Execution of the State Budget shows that last year, 2025, €80.77 million was collected from fines for traffic and other offences under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Interior. That is €11.6 million more than in 2024.

World.title: Croatia is the Leading Charter Power, But Earns Less Than Greece – Why?
World.content:
October the 26th, 2026 – Croatia is the world’s leading charter power, yet it earns less than Greece does from the same sector. The big questions is why?

Croatia is the number one charter power in the world with nearly five thousand vessels in its fleet. In the first eight months of this year, more than 431 thousand charter guest arrivals and more than 2.7 million overnight stays were recorded. However, market saturation has led to charter prices, especially for sailing yachts, falling by 50 percent or more during the peak season. As Alenka Juricic Bukarica reports for Glas Istre, this is not only the case this year. At the same time, competition in other Mediterranean countries is growing, especially in Greece, which last year had just over 3,000 vessels in charter. That is still fewer than Croatia, but with a clear upward trend.

Rising operating costs in recent years have also significantly changed conditions on the Croatian charter market, particularly for smaller vessels, and have negatively affected the return on investment and, consequently, the interest of new investors. Croatia is no longer perceived as a cheap destination, and there has also been a change in the structure of guests: instead of professionals, charter is increasingly chosen by people who are not normally involved in sailing, which increases demand for skippers and hostesses. Ultimately, people from the industry say that in some cases better prices can be achieved on the market in September than in the peak season…

in typical croatian style, there’s a paradox…

The current situation on the Croatian charter market was recently analysed by Ani Trstenjak, head of the Yacht Rent charter agency, and Daniela Gračan from the Faculty of Tourism and Hospitality Management (FMTU) in Opatija. Nautical charter has become, they emphasise, an important part of the tourism economy. It has attracted domestic and foreign capital and created a business ecosystem that includes vessel owners, charter companies, marinas, service providers, intermediaries and numerous providers of supporting services.

However, the success that for decades was measured by fleet growth, number of bookings and total revenue is opening an increasingly uncomfortable question – can Croatian charter continue to grow in the same way without endangering its own profitability.

“Market analysis by the vessel rental platform Yacht-Rent.com for 2026 points to an interesting paradox. Namely, Croatian sailing yachts and catamarans are among the cheapest compared to competing markets, while at the same time achieving high occupancy. Croatian charter does not primarily suffer from a lack of demand, but from a structural problem where demand is increasingly difficult to convert into revenue and profit. At the same time, it is clear that revenue is necessary to cover operating costs, financing, maintenance, depreciation and fleet renewal,” Trstenjak explained.

She clarified that Yacht-Rent’s market analysis for this year compares prices and bookings of vessels across six Mediterranean markets. It covers the operating season from 1 April to 2 November 2026, and expresses prices per person (berth) per week so that different vessel sizes can be compared on a comparable basis. According to that analysis, Croatia has the lowest average weekly price per berth among the compared markets for both sailing yachts and catamarans.

an exceptionally demanding market

Specifically speaking, sailing yachts in Croatia achieve an average weekly price per berth of €355, compared to €454 in Greece and €494 in Turkey. The price in Croatia is 22 percent lower than for a sailing yacht in Greece and 28 percent lower than in Turkey. At the same time, Croatian sailing yachts have an average of 19.4 booked weeks, slightly more than 19 weeks in Greece and significantly more than 17 weeks in Turkey. The estimated gross seasonal revenue per berth in Croatia amounts to €6,887, compared to €8,626 in Greece and €8,398 in Turkey.

The situation with catamarans is similar to that of sailing yachts. The average price of €706 per berth per week in Croatia is 16 percent lower than in Greece and 14 percent lower than in Turkey. Catamarans in Croatia are on average booked for 18.8 weeks during the season, which is close to 19.2 weeks in Greece, but significantly more than 15.4 weeks in Turkey. Despite this, the estimated gross seasonal revenue per berth in Croatia amounts to €13,273, while in Greece it reaches €16,147. Turkey achieves €12,659 in seasonal revenue per vessel.

“These data shows that Greece in the observed sample manages to combine high utilisation with a higher price. Croatia, on the other hand, achieves high capacity utilisation with a significantly lower price,” pointed out the head of the Yacht Rent agency. Adding that Croatian charter today operates on a highly competitive Mediterranean market, she also recalled that a guest can today easily compare prices, year of construction, equipment and capacity of vessels, rental conditions, additional costs and available destinations. And when vessels are very similar to each other, price becomes one of the most important decision criteria. However, she stresses, price is not the cause of the crisis, but its symptom.

higher and higher costs

Although not all segments of charter are equally price-sensitive, Trstenjak explains that luxury crewed vessels, differentiated service, special routes and a top customer experience can have greater pricing power. A standard sailing yacht comparable to dozens of other vessels at the same destination has significantly less room to raise its price independently. Charter companies today face high costs for berths, servicing, spare parts, insurance, labour, cleaning, administration, sales and distribution. Financing, depreciation and the need for fleet renewal, berth prices and insurance also play a significant role. All of this leads charter firms to accept a lower price in order to still rent out the vessel. In the short term such a decision can be rational, our interlocutor says, if the booking covers the additional costs of the rental and contributes to covering fixed costs. However, in the medium or long term, such a decision can be disastrous.

“When discounts become a permanent way of doing business, a serious problem arises that Croatian charter has been facing since 2023. Revenue may cover part of the costs, but it very likely no longer leaves enough funds for equipment renewal, major services, vessel replacement and return on capital. A company can therefore have high turnover, positive operating profit and at the same time an insufficient return on the capital invested in charter management. Every charter company wants to have enough vessels to attract guests, expand its offer and increase turnover.

But when a large number of investors make similar decisions, total supply can grow faster than demand. The number of available vessels increases, but the number of guests and attractive periods does not necessarily grow at the same speed. Therefore, an individual discount may be rational, but collective reliance on discounts can reduce the profitability of the entire market because supply does not adjust quickly enough,” Trstenjak says.

capital investment

She also addressed the problem of charter management, i.e. the fact that many Croatian citizens or companies, as well as foreigners, have in recent years seen the purchase of a sailing yacht or catamaran as a profitable form of capital investment. For the vessel buyer, the charter company handles the rental business, while the owner can use it for part of the year and collects income from the rental. Maintenance costs of the boat are borne by the owner. In such a model, the vessel owner expects a return on capital, the charter company wants to achieve the highest possible margin, while the guest wants the best price-quality ratio.

“If the vessel was purchased with excessively high expectations regarding rental price and number of booked weeks, a change in market conditions can seriously endanger the profitability of the investment. The owner expects a return, while the charter company has to choose between a lower price and the risk of unfilled periods,” our interlocutor warned. She concludes that the Croatian charter market has matured and that it is actually very important to make better use of the season and develop the offer outside the main summer months. At the same time, marinas, anchorages and the preservation of the sea must not be neglected, because it is precisely the quality of the destination that attracts guests. “The future of the charter sector does not depend only on further growth, but on how sustainable and profitable that growth will be,” concluded Ani Trstenjak.

a charter loss of €35 million…

The HUP Nautical Sector Association presented the Blue Book of Croatian Nautics and an initiative for the establishment of a National Nautical Council that should define a common development vision until 2040 at the Biograd Boat Show.

According to HUP’s analysis, entrepreneurs in nautics last year achieved €2.8 billion in business revenue and €1 billion in export revenue, employing 18,323 people. Business revenues rose 9.4 percent and exports 14.8 percent compared to the previous year. The analysis is based on HUP’s register of more than 3,200 mapped economic entities in activities related to nautics. In the period from 2021 to 2025, exports grew 70.8 percent, from €597.1 million to more than €1 billion. The share of gross investments in fixed assets in business revenues simultaneously increased from 11.7 to 18 percent. In the Blue Book, however, a warning was issued about pressure on the profitability of charter, which last year recorded a net loss of €34.7 million. “For the further growth of Croatian nautics, safer investment conditions, faster procedures and the availability of qualified workers are needed.

The Blue Book shows that revenue per employee in the sector from 2021 to 2025 rose by 43 percent, from €108.5 thousand to €155.1 thousand, which confirms the potential for creating greater added value. We want more design, production and servicing to take place in Croatia and for a larger part of the value created to remain in the domestic economy, while preserving the sea and the coast,” said Irena Weber, Director General of HUP. Luciano Beg, president of the HUP Nautical Sector Association, also pointed out that in addition to counting berths and overnight stays, the success of nautics should be measured by the production of vessels and equipment, overhauls, innovations, exports and quality jobs, and that this requires a long-term vision and better coordination between the economy, state institutions and the scientific community.
