World.title: Sulu gets over 3,000 new teaching positions amid shift to DepEd control
World.content:
The Department of Education says it is ‘fast-tracking the deployment and appointment protocols to guarantee that salaries, benefits, and operational support continue without interruption’

MANILA, Philippines – The government approved the creation of over 3,000 teaching positions in Sulu as the province’s education office transitions to the jurisdiction of the Department of Education (DepEd).

The DepEd announced on Tuesday, October 27, that the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) approved the creation of the following positions:

3,618 positions for Teacher I to Master Teacher II for kindergarten, elementary, and junior high school

Nine teaching-related positions, including Head Teacher I and School Principal I and II

In an explanation sent to Rappler, the DepEd said the figure came from the deployment plan it submitted to the DBM. The plan “directly facilitates the structured transition and absorption” of existing personnel of the Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (MBHTE-BARMM) into the national government framework.

Voters in Sulu had rejected the Bangsamoro Organic Law in a 2019 plebiscite, but the province was still initially included in BARMM because the then-ARMM provinces were deemed to have voted as a single bloc. Sulu’s exclusion from the new region was only finalized after a Supreme Court ruling in 2024.

By 2025, the province had reverted to the Zamboanga Peninsula, following an executive order issued by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

“DepEd, in coordination with the DBM, Regional Office IX, and local government partners, is fast-tracking the deployment and appointment protocols to guarantee that salaries, benefits, and operational support continue without interruption,” the agency said in a news release.

Ronelo Al Firmo, the DepEd Zamboanga Peninsula director, said he will also discuss possible promotions for teachers.

“Just imagine, may mga magre-retire na pero Teacher I pa rin. Kaya very important talaga na mai-discuss sa kanila ‘yong ECP, ‘yong Expanded Career Progression, para at least before sila mag-retire, at least makatikim man lang sila ng isang promotion,” Firmo told Radyo Pilipinas Jolo.

(Just imagine, there will be teachers who will retire as Teacher I. That’s why it’s very important to discuss with them the ECP, the Expanded Career Progression, so that they’ll be able to experience at least one promotion before they retire.)

The DepEd announced the formal transition of Sulu’s education office to its jurisdiction on October 20. Along with that was the DBM’s approval of the creation of 84 non-teaching plantilla positions.

Of the 84 positions, 40 are held by current MBHTE-BARMM personnel deployed to Sulu, and are already prioritized for absorption under Civil Service Commission rules.

Marcos also visited Sulu on October 20 to lead the rollout of the state health insurer’s Yaman ng Kalusugan Program or YAKAP health caravan at Kawmpang Elementary School in Patikul town. The provincial capitol and offices are located in this town.

During the budget deliberations at the House of Representatives’ plenary in September, the DepEd committed to absorb Islamic Studies and Arabic Language teachers from the MBHTE-BARMM into the DepEd by January 2027. – Rappler.com

World.title: With El Niño, 2026-2027 northeast monsoon may not be as cold
World.content:
The intensifying El Niño is expected to lead to less pronounced cold surges during the period of the northeast monsoon

MANILA, Philippines – The northeast monsoon or amihan is here, the weather bureau announced on Tuesday, October 27.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) explained in a statement that it has observed “a surge of northeasterly winds and lower air temperatures over extreme Northern Luzon” in the past few days.

The period of the northeast monsoon, also known as the country’s cool and dry season, lasts from October until February or March. It typically brings surges of cold temperatures, especially in January and February.

But PAGASA has said that this amihan may be warmer than usual due to the ongoing El Niño, which is predicted to become very strong before the end of 2026 and persist until the first quarter of 2027.

El Niño is a natural phenomenon characterized by “unusually warm ocean surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific,” according to the World Meteorological Organization.

In the Philippines, the phenomenon causes below-normal rainfall and higher temperatures. Forecasts show nearly the entire country will be experiencing drought by the end of February 2027.

The onset of the northeast monsoon also comes around three weeks after PAGASA announced the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat. – Rappler.com

World.title: [OPINION] Twilight time for the CPP-NPA’s forever war
World.content:
The communist party could take the cue from the its counterparts in Nepal, who signed a peace agreement with the Nepalese government in 2006 and became the ruling party through democratic elections in 2008–2009 and has been in the ruling coalition several times since then

After the split in the Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP) in 1993, many doubted that the communist insurgency waged by the CPP and its New People’s Army (NPA) would ever recover. But it did, even surpassing the peak armed strength achieved in the 1980s, first in 2005 then again in 2017.

Since then, however, the CPP-NPA, reeling from the government’s intense counter-insurgency operations, has fallen into a slump, in fact, into the most serious crisis in its entire 58-year history.

Is it twilight time for the CPP-NPA insurgency?

From very modest beginnings, the CPP-NPA grew into a powerful nationwide rebel force during the era of President Ferdinand Marcos, Sr. When the NPA launched its Maoist-style “protracted people’s war” in 1969, it started out as a ragtag band of about 60 fighters, nine automatic rifles and 26 single-shot rifles and pistols in Central Luzon. During the period of martial law, the NPA established guerrilla fronts in all of the country’s strategic mountainous areas outside of the Moro areas. NPA guerrillas engaged the Philippine military in tactical offensives, and built up its armed strength.

In the early 1980s, some CPP cadres advocated adjustments to the party’s revolutionary strategy, arguing that its Maoist strategy, which involved “encircling the cities from the countryside” was much too weighted in favor of military over political struggle and rural over urban struggles. They put forward such alternative strategies as the Vietnamese version of “protracted people’s war” which regarded both military and political struggles as fundamental and decisive, and the “insurrectional strategy” of the Sandinistas in Nicaragua, which had asserted the primacy of the “insurrectional mass movement” over the military struggle.

Because of the CPP’s boycott of the 1986 presidential election, the CPP and the open “national democratic” (ND) movement were left out of the “people power” uprising. But apart from being a tactical mistake, the boycott fiasco also showed up the flaw in the CPP-NPA’s revolutionary strategy. While its forces were still struggling to develop its military struggle along the stipulated stages of Mao’s “protracted people’s war,” the Filipino masses had toppled the Marcos dictatorship through an unarmed insurrection.

Peace negotiations between the government of the late president Corazon Aquino and the CPP’s politico-diplomatic arm, the National Democratic Front (NDF) in 1986-87 quickly collapsed. The government had demanded that the CPP-NPA-NDF lay down its arms, while the NDF had insisted that the talks address the roots of the country’s problems. (The NDF conducted peace talks with each of the post-authoritarian administrations, but did not reach a comprehensive political settlement with any of them.)

Beginning of a decline

For a while after the boycott fiasco, the NPA continued to grow, reaching its highest level in 1987. The NPA was widely reported to have swelled to 25,000 fighters, although CPP founding chair Jose Ma. Sison later belied that the NPA ever reached that number in the 1980s. The CPP-NPA measures its armed strength mainly in terms of high-powered rifles (such as M16, M14, AK-47 and M1 Garand). According to Sison, the NPA’s armed strength “increased to 6,100 automatic rifles in 1986 and still further increased by some hundreds in 1987,” its highest level up to that time.

Then the decline started. The political fallout from the boycott fiasco started impacting on the CPP-NPA. This was compounded by the revelations about the killings of hundreds of suspected government spies in the CPP-NPA’s anti-infiltration purges in 1982-89. The fall of the socialist states in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union raised questions about the very rectitude of the revolutionary left’s socialist project.

Disagreements within the CPP leadership related to revolutionary strategy, analysis of the contemporary situation, alternative social order, intra-party democracy and other major questions reached a boiling point in the early 1990s. Sison wrote up “Reaffirm Our Basic Principles and Rectify the Errors,” in which he lashed out at those critical of the party’s Maoist tenets, accusing them of propagating a line of “military adventurism” and “insurrectionism.” The CPP split into “reaffirmists” and “rejectionists,” with the “reaffirmists” emerging as the legatee CPP. Through most of the 1990s, the CPP-NPA suffered an ebb.

At the turn of the millennium, however, the CPP-NPA started to recover. NPA guerrilla attacks picked up in many regions. The CPP-NPA intensified its collection of “revolutionary tax” from mining, agribusiness, telecommunications and construction firms, as well as of “permit-to-campaign” fees from politicians campaigning in or near NPA zones during election periods. In 2005, the NPA armed strength, it was claimed, surpassed the earlier 1987 peak by a few hundred high-powered rifles.

Various counterinsurgency measures undertaken during the administration of President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, however, soon took their toll on the CPP-NPA, which then suffered a decline. In 2002, following the 9-11 terrorist attacks in the U.S., the CPP and the NPA had been included in the list of “foreign terrorist organizations” (FTOs) of the US, the European Union and Australia. The next year, as government-NDF peace talks seemed to be going nowhere, President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo added the CPP-NPA to her government’s counter-terrorist Oplan Bantay Laya, which originally targeted the Abu Sayyaf only. The Oplan strategy combined combat, intelligence and civil-military operations, and emphasized the “neutralization” of communists. Scores of open ND leaders and activists were arrested, tortured, disappeared or summarily executed. In 2006, Arroyo declared an “all-out war” against the CPP-NPA and the extrajudicial killings of leftists worsened. NPA armed strength was said to have dropped by 21.6% over 2006-2009.

Starting in 2010, however, the CPP-NPA recovered again. NPA guerrilla operations intensified all over the country. In Mindanao, where the NPA was strongest, tactical offensives reportedly increased from 250 in 2010, 350 in 2011, 400 in 2012, more than 400 each in 2013 and 2014, and more than 500 in 2015. The NPA’s arena of operations, it was further claimed, expanded to 110 guerrilla fronts in 73 of the country’s 81 provinces. According to Sison, NPA armed strength “surpassed the previous 2005 peak by 3 per cent” – that is, to over 7,000 high-powered rifles.

Storm clouds

But storm clouds were brewing. In late 2018, President Rodrigo Duterte adopted a “whole-of-nation” approach in combating the CPP-NDF insurgency, a year after it had terminated peace talks with the NDF. The approach, which sought to mobilize and synchronize civilian government agencies, local government units, and military forces in counterinsurgency efforts, combined barangay development projects (roads, water systems, other infrastructure, schools, health stations and livelihood assistance) with localized peace engagements (including local integration of former rebels) in conflict-affected areas. To implement such a strategy, Duterte created a multi-agency National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC), headed by the president himself. President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. continued Duterte’s “whole-of-nation” approach.

From the government’s viewpoint, the “whole-of-nation” strategy has been a tremendous success. In 2024, Marcos claimed that no NPA guerrilla fronts remained active across the country. The NTF-ELCAC added that the NPA had been reduced to only 785 “remnants.” In the light of many reports of clashes between the military and the NPA over the last two years, the government’s exultant claims are not credible.

But the CPP-NPA has indeed suffered grave setbacks. Since the launching of the “whole-of-nation” approach, NPA numbers have dropped considerably, and guerrilla attacks have declined. The International Crisis Group (ICG) estimates that the NPA has shrunk to between 1,200 and 2,000 fighters. The CPP-NPA no longer provides figures of NPA tactical offensives, but the number of clashes between government forces and Red fighters are indicative of the CPP-NPA’s decline. According to the international NGO Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), only 106 clashes occurred between government forces and the NPA in 2025 versus 273 in 2020 – a 61% decline in five years. Mindanao, as a whole, is no longer the main NPA flash point. The main areas of armed encounters have shifted from Western Visayas and Northern Mindanao to Eastern Visayas and Caraga.

Over the past eight years, many top CPP-NPA leaders have been killed by the military – in combat or through summary execution. Among them are CPP chairman Benito Tiamzon and secretary-general Wilma Tiamzon, as well as Julius Giron, Antonio Cabanatan, Jorge Madlos, Menandro Villanueva, Maria Concepcion Araneta, Eugenia Magpantay, Randall Echanis and Mariano Adlao. Some other top leaders, such as Victor Ladlad and Rey Casambre. have been arrested and incarcerated.

The Philippines’ “all-of-nation” approach has been widely criticized for thousands of human rights violations – illegal arrests, detentions, torture, extrajudicial killings and disappearances. Many open, legal progressive activists have become easy targets of government harassment and repression. Obsessed with its counterinsurgency drive, the government has largely ignored the criticisms and denunciations of human rights groups.

According to the ICG, the CPP-NPA is at its lowest ebb in decades. Will it be able to recover as it has in the past?

Massive losses

One factor that will make recovery difficult is that the CPP-NPA has lost many of its most experienced leaders over the past eight years or so. Apart from top leaders killed or arrested and imprisoned by the military, some senior, long-serving leaders have passed away peacefully, among them Sison himself, Jose Luneta, Fidel Agcaoili and Luis Jalandoni. A few other veterans have been incapacitated by health problems. The loss of the likes of Sison, Jalandoni and Madlos has also left a big gap in the CPP-NPA’s public-facing spokespersons.

The CPP-NPA may partially recover for a while, but one thing is definite: it will never be able to achieve the total military victory that it has long aspired for. Its fundamental Maoist principles stipulate that before the revolutionary forces can triumph, the “protracted people’s war” has to progress from guerrilla warfare to regular mobile warfare and eventually to positional warfare; and from strategic defensive to strategic stalemate and eventually to strategic offensive. All through nearly six decades of fighting, the NPA has been stuck in guerrilla warfare and the strategic defensive.

Endeavoring to extricate the CPP-NPA from its guerrilla warfare rut, NPA chieftain Romulo Kintanar had pushed for the establishment of bigger NPA formations and for “regularization” in the 1980s. Sison accused him of “military adventurism” and had him expelled from the CPP-NPA, then assassinated. Kintanar had established extensive international linkages for the NPA, knowing that only external sources could provide a sizeable and steady supply of arms and ammunition needed for moving up to regular warfare. This international network withered away after the takeover of the NPA by the “reaffirmist” CPP leadership. (It must be noted here that the Moro National Liberation Front and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, during their wars for secession, did manage to secure arms from external sources, but still did not achieve military victory against the government.)

The CPP-NPA’s “protracted people’s war” has gone on much longer than any of America’s “forever wars.” As defined by Cambridge Dictionary, a forever war is “a war that never ends because it cannot be won.” It is a prolonged, open-ended armed conflict without a clear, achievable endpoint or decisive victory. The war without end between the government and the CPP-NPA has already claimed between 40,000 to 60,000 lives. Yet, each year, on the NPA’s anniversary on March 29, it celebrates the protraction of its “people’s war.”

It’s twilight time for the CPP-NPA’s forever war. Mao’s rural and peasant-based “protracted people’s war,” employed in “semicolonial, semifeudal” China a century ago, simply has been a bad fit for an urbanizing Philippine society with a middle income economy that has shifted away from agriculture and is increasingly dominated by wage labor and the service sector.

Communist insurgencies are on the wane worldwide. The CPP-NPA insurgency is one of a handful of major communist insurgencies still surviving in the contemporary world. Two of them, both Maoist, have not fared any better than the CPP-NPA. India’s Naxalites (Communist Party of India – Maoist), who have waged a 59-year-old “people’s war,” are dwindling, reduced to isolated pockets and struggling with recruitment and funding, with a leadership severely degraded. Peru’s Shining Path (Communist Party of Peru), whose founder, Abimael Guzman, was captured in 1992 and died in prison in 2021, has been all but dismantled, with a few splinter groups financing themselves mainly through cocaine trafficking.

If the CPP still hopes to come to power, it should work out a comprehensive political settlement with the government and strive to turn its still appreciable mass base into an electoral base. All of the government-NDF peace negotiations have come to naught. The CPP-NPA-NDF has only been interested in eking out tactical gains – propaganda, release of political prisoners, immunity for “NDF negotiators,” so-called “belligerency status” – while still obdurately aiming for total military victory. Protracted negotiations was merely a tactic in its “protracted people’s war.”

The CPP could take the cue from the its counterparts in Nepal, the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist, now Maoist Centre), which signed a peace agreement with the Nepalese government in 2006 and became the ruling party through democratic elections in 2008–2009 and has been in the ruling coalition several times since then.

Back in 1991, writing under the pseudonym Omar Tupaz, I commented on the CPP-NPA’s Maoist “protracted people’s war” strategy: “It will be difficult, if not impossible, to win a revolution in the 1990s by continuing to adhere to a basic strategic framework of a bygone era.” Unfortunately for the CPP-NPA, this seems to be coming to pass. – Rappler.com



Nathan Gilbert Quimpo authored Contested Democracy and the Left after Marcos and co-authored Subversive Lives: A Family Memoir of the Marcos Years. In the 1980s and 1990s, he penned critiques of the communist party’s revolutionary strategy under the pseudonym Marty Villalobos and Omar Tupaz.

World.title: Who is Retrina Fuentes, the judge behind arrest orders vs Duterte critics?
World.content:
Fuentes once served as executive judge of the Davao City Regional Trial Court

Veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. was arrested on Saturday, October 24, over a cyber libel case filed by an unidentified complainant at the time. It was Davao City Presiding Judge Retrina Espe Fuentes who issued the warrant of arrest.

On Monday, October 26, Lustre’s lawyer, Dino de Leon, told Rappler that it was lawyer Mans Carpio — husband of Vice President Sara Duterte — who was the complainant in Lustre’s case.

Based on the Supreme Court’s (SC) tracker, Fuentes is currently the presiding judge of Davao City Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 10. The court is located in Benigno Aquino Hall of Justice, in Matina, Davao City.

Fuentes was Davao City’s 1st vice executive judge in 2016, according to the Philippine Judicial Academy Bulletin. At the time, Presiding Judge Emmanuel Carpio was sitting as executive judge.

Presiding Judge Carpio is the uncle of Mans Carpio. In her 2024 Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth, Vice President Duterte listed Emmanuel Carpio as her uncle-in-law.

At the time of Fuentes’ appointment as 1st vice executive judge, Rodrigo Duterte was president, while his daughter Sara was Davao City mayor during that period.

Based on SC Office of the Court Administrator’s Administrative Order No. 231-2022, Fuentes became Davao City’s executive judge on November 1, 2022 under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

The Fraternal Order of Saint Thomas More in Davao City posted a congratulatory message after Fuentes’ appointment. She held the position from 2022 to 2024, according to SC spokesperson Camille Sue Mae Ting.

“Davao Regional Trial Court Executive Judge is now Judge Rowena M. Apao Adlawan,” said Ting.

According to the SC’s AM No. 03-8-02-SC, the Court may appoint executive judges and vice executive judges in stations where there are more than two RTC branches. Their appointment will be based on their administrative qualifications, experience, and seniority, among others.

“The Executive Judge shall take charge of the administrative work of the Supreme Court in all first and second level courts. The Executive Judge derives his/her powers and prerogatives through delegation by the Supreme Court,” said the order.

Lustre’s arrest

Lustre, the 72-year-old veteran journalist was attending the Saturday News Forum event in Quezon City when Quezon City police from the Quezon City Police District arrested him.

After nearly a day in detention, he was able to post a P48,000-bail at past midnight on Sunday, October 25.

Lustre is the author of the book, “Kill, Kill, Kill: Extrajudicial Killings in the Philippines.” It’s about former president Rodrigo Duterte’s war on drugs that killed nearly 30,000 people, according to several human rights groups. Duterte is now detained in The Hague, Netherlands over his crimes against humanity case that stemmed from the said campaign.

After his release from temporary detention, Lustre said he is scheduled to release a new book titled, “MISFIT SARA Life and Times of Vice President Sara Duterte-Carpio; The Impeachment Trial of a Filipino Vice President.” The Vice President is currently in the middle of her impeachment trial that could remove her from the position and bar her from running for president in 2028.

The information sheet against Lustre reads: “The above-named accused, with deliberate intent, willfully, unlawfully, and feloniously, through his Facebook account under the name ‘Philip Jr. Lustre,’ published and posted written statements, thereby making an imputation of a crime against Atty. Manases R. Carpio, a private individual and on the said date, was actually residing in Davao City, through the internet using the social networking platform called ‘Facebook.com,’ by saying: ‘Sumuka si Mans Carpio ng P300-M sa operasyon ng Marines: P150M kay Mike; P50M kay Levi; at P5M sa bawat isa sa 18 Marines?‘ which published statement, taken in its plain, natural, and ordinary meaning, directly imputes upon Atty. Manases R. Carpio, the commission of a crime, specifically bribery or corrupt.”

Bello’s case

Fuentes was also the judge who signed the warrant of arrest against another Duterte critic and former vice presidential candidate, Walden Bello.

In 2022, at the height of the campaign season, former Davao City public information officer Jefry Tupas filed a cyber libel complaint against Bello. Tupas was seeking P10 million in damages after being allegedly accused by Bello on social media of being a drug addict and dealer.

Duterte’s aide was embroiled in a controversy in 2021 after attending a beach party in Mabini, Davao de Oro that was later raided by anti-narcotics agents. The operation supposedly happened an hour after Tupas and companions had left the party.

On August 8, 2022, QCPD personnel arrested Bello over a warrant issued by Fuentes for two counts of cyber libel. He was later freed after posting a P48,000-bail for each of the counts.

Bello, at the time, labeled Tupas’ case as “clearly a politically-motivated move.”

The following year, Bello filed a petition with the SC seeking to decriminalize libel in the Philippines.

In February this year, the former vice presidential bet issued an apology to Tupas, saying his statements were “unfounded.”

Other cases handled

In 2019, Fuentes was the judge who ordered the arrest of Italian Lorenzo Marchesi, who was 57 years old at the time. He was ordered arrested over alleged possession of child sexual abuse and exploitation materials.

Marchesi was arrested after a search of his electronic devices allegedly revealed a collection of illegal materials.

Last September, Fuentes was the same judge who issued a warrant of arrest against a man wanted for rape. She issued the warrant on September 2, 2026.

“The accused, identified only by the alias ‘Abdul,’ was properly informed of the cause of his arrest and apprised of his constitutional rights, including his rights under Republic Act No. 9745, or the Anti-Torture Act of 2009, in a language or dialect known to and understood by him,” said the PNP.

“The arrested person was identified as a top 3 most wanted person, municipal level, under the PNP e-warrant system,” it added. – Rappler.com

World.title: Make LGU funds ‘results-based’ amid pork barrel concerns — World Bank
World.content:
“We believe that LGSF can support genuine regional development so long as obviously it’s effectively utilized,” World Bank lead urban specialist Makiko Watanabe says

MANILA, Philippines – The World Bank said the proposed P58-billion Local Government Support Fund (LGSF) in the 2027 national budget could help power regional development, but recommended tying allocations to actual project results and encouraging local governments to invest together, amid concerns the fund could become a source of political patronage.

Makiko Watanabe, the World Bank’s lead urban specialist for East Asia and the Pacific, said the Philippine government could adopt performance-based or results-based financing to improve accountability and reward local government units (LGUs) that deliver.

“The short answer is, yes, we believe that LGSF can support genuine regional development so long as obviously it’s effectively utilized,” Watanabe said when asked by Rappler during the launch of the World Bank’s From Cities to Corridors report on Tuesday, October 27.

She suggested that allocations be made “performance-based or results-based” rather than set in advance, and that funding encourage “inter-LGU type of investments” rather than isolated projects.

These could include shared transportation and digital infrastructure, as well as disaster resilience projects that have spillover benefits beyond a single municipality or city.

World Bank Philippines division director Zafer Mustafaoğlu likewise emphasized the need for accountability, efficient spending, and timely project completion, while suggesting too that authorities should consider the economic potential of neighboring LGUs when allocating resources.

The proposed LGSF has drawn scrutiny over concerns that it could be used for discretionary spending and political patronage. Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito has questioned the criteria for distributing the more-than-P58-billion fund and called for safeguards to ensure that allocations address local development needs rather than reward political allies. Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian also said that the LGSF needed to be transparent to promote good governance.

Issues in local project funding

The World Bank’s latest report also identifies weaknesses in how local projects secure funding.

Only about 30% of investment proposals endorsed through regional development councils receive funding in a given budget cycle, which may create “uncertainties among LGUs about which of their endorsed priorities will receive the national government support,” the World Bank report said.

It also notes that projects outside local annual investment plans (AIP) can receive funding when they have political backing, while planned projects may go unfunded.

“While AIP is a standard vehicle for investment planning, [focus group discussion] shows that projects are also budgeted outside the AIP when there is political support, whereas AIP-listed items go unfunded when local priorities do not align,” the World Bank said in its report.

SITTING ON CASH? A World Bank analysis of 2023 year-end cash balance as a share of annual operating revenues by urban LGU size shows that LGUs are not utilizing large amounts of cash on hand. Chart from the World Bank’s report

Beyond the allocation process, many LGUs struggle to spend the funds they already have. Capital investments account for only about 15% of annual LGU expenditure, while poor project preparation and procurement add to delays.

This has left local governments sitting on cash reserves, with large urban LGUs holding an average of P9,263 per person in year-end cash on hand balances in 2023, funds that the World Bank said could have been better used to address infrastructure and service needs.

The report’s main recommendation is to shift away from individual LGU support to what it calls interconnected “corridor-based” development, with aligned national and local plans and better project implementation capacity. – Rappler.com

World.title: Myanmar Migrant Applications Plunge at Thai CI Centers Amid Boycott
World.content:
The number of Myanmar migrant workers applying for Certificates of Identity (CI) in Thailand has dropped sharply in the past few days following the launch of a social media campaign against the CI process, according to migrant groups and agents.

The Myanmar regime opened five Thai hubs on October 14, offering migrant workers CI required for residency and work. In exchange, workers must comply with a new Labor Ministry mandate to remit 25 percent of their wages through official channels and pay 2 percent annual tax.

The number of registered Myanmar workers in Thailand rose to nearly 3 million as of November 2025, but a significant population remains undocumented.

Many migrants say that as low-wage workers they can barely afford CI application fees, while the regime’s mandatory 6,000-baht remittance rule adds an extra layer of cost.

Labor activists say the boycott is also being driven by reluctance to legitimize the regime or help fund its ongoing military attacks on civilians.

Migrants launched the online campaign on Oct. 18, calling on the Thai government to grant them residency-work permits without CI documents.

Regime Labour Minister Maung Myint slammed the campaign on Oct. 20, insisting the new process was meant to ease CI registration for workers in Thailand. He claimed that around 1,500 workers had used the new centres in the first few days. However, migrant workers groups and agents said applications have plunged as the campaign gains momentum.

“Very few workers are applying for the CI,” Khaing Gyi of the Aid Alliance Committee, which assists migrants, told The Irrawaddy on Tuesday.

“Normally, the CI centre in Samut Sakhon alone receives over 1,000 CI applications daily,” he said, adding that the hub has gone quiet in the past few days.

He estimated that at least 500,000 workers are due to apply for their CI, but few are showing up at centers.

Labor activists said workers were also delaying CI renewal because of the cost.

“Migrants’ income levels vary,” Naing Aung Aung of the Arkan Worker Organization in Thailand told The Irrawaddy. “Some took loans to pay for passport and visa issuance. They don’t have extra savings.”

He said the regime’s remittance scheme is unviable given it can easily be bypassed by bribing corrupt officials. Applicants can secure a CI without evidence of remittance for a fee of 1,500 baht, according to labor activists and agents.

Experts note the new policy benefits the cash-strapped regime while piling financial burdens on low-paid workers and cutting remittance lifelines for their families at home. They argue that instead of restrictions and punishment, workers should be offered incentives to remit money through official channels.

Under the current scheme, Myanmar workers lose at least 5,000 kyats for every 100 baht they remit via regime-endorsed channels. While official channels offer 125 kyat per baht, informal markets offer upwards of 130.

The Labour Ministry continues to push the new scheme, projecting that 2026 inflows will match last year’s total of US$ 5.6 billion. Annual remittances have more than doubled since 2019, driven by the mass emigration of workers escaping the turmoil and economic collapse that followed the 2021 coup.

World.title: Hostage Diplomacy: How the Myanmar Junta Is Weaponizing Jailed Aung San Suu Kyi
World.content:
As the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)’s November summit approaches, the Myanmar junta—desperate for international recognition—has made a series of minor concessions regarding access to jailed civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

Highlighting the regime’s ongoing atrocities against civilians, observers and anti-regime groups have warned that the regime’s moves are merely a ploy to win resumption of full participation in ASEAN and ease international pressure.

Since the 2021 coup, the Myanmar regime has been barred from attending high-level ASEAN summits for failing to comply with the bloc’s peace plan, which calls for the immediate cessation of violence against civilians and the opening of a dialogue among all concerned groups, among other things.

Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to meet with ICRC representatives in Naypyitaw on August 3, and to receive books and a diplomatic letter from King Charles on October 19. The jailed Nobel Peace Prize laureate was also permitted to talk with her youngest son, Kim Aris, on October 22, for the first time in the five years since her arrest.

Domestic and regional observers warn that the regime has started using Aung San Suu Kyi as a political bargaining chip to gain access to the bloc’s upcoming summit.

“The regime led by the sham president Min Aung Hlaing has been trying to scam the world by using hostage diplomacy,” said Debbie Stothard, founder and coordinator of the Alternative Asean Network on Burma.

She cited another recent instance of hostage diplomacy, in which the junta jailed 78 Filipino trafficking victims who had escaped from scam centers. Instead of repatriating them, the regime used the victims as a bargaining chip in negotiations with Maria Teresa Lazaro, the Philippine foreign secretary, who was forced to request the release of her compatriots during a visit to Naypyitaw in January, then thank the internationally-isolated regime for freeing the jailed Philippine nationals.

An ASEAN humanitarian delegation led by the bloc’s special envoy Maria Teresa Lazaro is scheduled to visit Myanmar for two days starting Wednesday.

The tactic was used again with the detention of U.S. citizen Adam Castillo, which allowed the regime to secure engagement with the U.S, Stothard said. A delegation of U.S. officials visited Naypyitaw to secure Castillo’s release.

“The regime continues to use its hostage diplomacy by … dangling Aung San Suu Kyi to secure normalization of relations with ASEAN,” she said. “ASEAN and the international community shouldn’t be easily scammed this way. They shouldn’t be normalizing relations with a gangster who is the architect of genocide and war crimes.”

Thailand welcomed the U.S. engagement with the regime and expected discussions to be held at the upcoming ASEAN summit in Manila on how to proceed with the Myanmar issue, Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told media on Friday.

The minister, who is working to improve relations between ASEAN and the military regime, commented that the regime’s granting of permission for Aung San Suu Kyi and her son to speak represented a positive development.

Further evidence of the regime’s concerted effort to secure ASEAN’s recognition and support can be seen in Naypyitaw’s recent decision to form an ASEAN Affairs Committee to communicate and cooperate with the bloc.

Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe, who chairs the committee, said it was formed to foster additional channels of engagement with ASEAN. The regime is currently engaging regional neighbors on a country-by-country basis according to priority levels, he added.

Coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing has been engaging with the U.S., and in recent months has visited ASEAN members Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam and Malaysia.

David Gam Awng, deputy foreign affairs minister of the civilian National Unity Government (NUG), told The Irrawaddy he shares the view that the regime is using Aung San Suu Kyi as a political bargaining chip to secure Min Aung Hlaing’s attendance at the upcoming ASEAN summit.

“Civilian leader Daw Aung San Suu Kyi is entirely innocent and is merely a political hostage unjustly detained by the regime for political reasons. Allowing her to receive books and gifts sent by King Charles and permitting a 20-minute phone call with her son is purely a political transaction by the regime,” he said.

He said the regime’s recent moves are a political ploy, despite some ASEAN member countries’ characterization of them as a positive development, and warned that “ASEAN needs to see this reality.”

Mon Mon Myat, lecturer at the Department of Peace Studies at Thailand’s Payap University, remarked that the junta’s apparent relaxation regarding access to the jailed civilian leader “might include hopes of being allowed to attend the ASEAN summit. It appears they urgently need both international recognition and assistance. On the other hand, they might be pushing for this out of fear of becoming more isolated on the international stage if the ICJ ruling comes out later this year.” The International Court of Justice is considering a genocide case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar over the military’s persecution of the Rohingya minority in Rakhine State.

The regime’s charm offensive may be having some effect. Former Japanese Prime Minister Fumio Kishida said in an exclusive interview with Nikkei Asia on October 12 that Japan should assist in Myanmar’s reintegration into ASEAN. For the time being, however, ASEAN as a bloc is upholding its summit ban, citing the failure to honor its peace plan. Known as the Five-Point Consensus, the plan established over five years ago in Jakarta includes calls for an immediate end to violence and the holding of dialogues. Both coup president Min Aung Hlaing and his rubber-stamp parliament have formally rejected the plan. Meanwhile, the regime continues its five-year campaign of airstrikes, shelling and village burnings.

The NUG’s David Gam Awng said ASEAN must clearly and decisively call out the regime’s total failure to implement the peace plan. He warned that bilateral engagement with the junta by individual member states is emboldening the regime’s war crimes against civilians, rather than applying necessary pressure.

“While ASEAN member states may have different views on the country’s crisis, there must be definite consequences if the junta fails to comply with the agreements. Without clear repercussions for their defiance, the regime has absolutely no incentive to cooperate,” he added.

Citing the junta’s ongoing attacks on civilian targets, Stothard noted that hostage diplomacy is a smokescreen for the regime’s continued brutality against its own people.

“ASEAN and the international community should not be engaging or dancing with a regime that has turned Burma into a transnational crime hub, created the worst humanitarian crisis in the region, and will negatively impact ASEAN for years to come,” Stothard said.

World.title: The Fatal Flaw in China’s Myanmar Policy is Economic Collapse
World.content:
While Beijing’s military‑centric approach — backed by its “three bottom lines” — defines China’s Myanmar policy, the ground reality shows that civil war is not the only source of instability. Alongside the widening conflict, Myanmar’s foundations are being shaken by a deepening economic crisis with historical echoes. The collapse of General Ne Win’s Burma Socialist Programme Party regime four decades ago was not triggered by battlefield defeat, but by economic breakdown — a reminder that today’s regime faces the same danger.

Deepening economic crisis

When Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi visited in August 2024, the junta was facing not only military setbacks but also severe inflation marked by surging commodity prices. Thanks to Chinese financial assistance, inflation eased after his trip and the kyat stabilized at around 4,000 per US dollar. But it plunged again after military-staged elections early this year and now hovers near 4,600 per dollar.

Starved of hard currency, the junta restricted imports and choked off border trade. The cost of fuel and cooking oil surged, followed by staples such as rice, eggs, and onions, as well as household electronics and medicines. Vehicle prices soared, and black markets reemerged. Domestic manufacturing, agriculture, and livestock industries — reliant on imported technology, seeds, feed, fertilizers, and medicines — were hit hard, while foreign investment also dwindled.

As the kyat weakens, commodity prices are surging again and shortages are widespread. This is not merely a policy miscalculation: the junta channels all foreign currency into military spending, compounding the economic crisis. Without an end to war, the economic crisis cannot be fixed.

Corrupt state apparatus

Another major issue is systemic corruption in the bureaucracy. Graft grew steadily under military rule from 1988 to 2010 but was restrained somewhat by public oversight during the 2010–2020 reform period. But since the 2021 coup, the entire machinery of government — from Min Aung Hlaing and the top brass down to the lowest ranks — have exploited power for personal gain.

Legal restrictions and licensing requirements have become tollbooths for bribery. Payment is required for import permits, ID cards, passports and the right to travel at home or abroad. Importers routinely pay bribes, while ordinary people face extortion by soldiers and police on the streets. This endemic corruption has also facilitated the boom in narcotics production and online fraud gangs.

Narcotics and online scams

Myanmar is among the world’s largest producers of heroin, methamphetamine, and synthetic drugs, with output now rising annually as officials, soldiers and police turn a blind eye in exchange for bribes.

Online scam syndicates previously confined to borderlands are now spreading inland. Evidence from Karen State and northern Shan’s Kokang shows that gangs are relocating under the protection of military‑linked MPs, administrators, border guards, police, and senior officials. Even as criminal syndicates elsewhere in northern Shan are dismantled, Muse—the only border town Naypyitaw still controls thanks to China—remains an online scam hub, highlighting the regime’s complicity in cyber-fraud.

In other words, the economic crisis is not a standalone problem, but deeply intertwined with systemic corruption, narcotics production, and scams.

Poverty and social collapse

Illicit revenues from narcotics and scam syndicates have flooded Myanmar, fueling inflation and driving property values to unsustainable heights. Ordinary citizens are bearing the brunt as the country’s economic crisis deepens. Chinese loans cannot solve this problem.

The persistent civil war, combined with entrenched corruption and criminality, rampant inflation, and worsening shortages, has created a dire situation. While a handful of elites hoard wealth, most of the population struggles to afford basic food, leaving Myanmar society fractured and unstable.

A UNDP report released on October 8 revealed that one in three Myanmar citizens — over 17 million people — are already experiencing multidimensional poverty, with another 19 million at risk. In total, about 37 million people, or 68 percent of the population, are either poor or vulnerable to poverty.

Years of conflict, displacement, economic collapse, and climate shocks have devastated housing, healthcare, education, and livelihoods, worsening deprivation.

China’s other Myanmar headaches

Beyond these crises, China must also reckon with four other problems.

First is anti‑China sentiment — which is rising not only among resistance forces but also within the regime itself. Resistance anger is fueled by Beijing’s support for a failing military regime, not hostility toward Chinese people.

For the regime, however, anti‑China sentiment remains a core worldview. In times of political, economic, or military crisis, the Myanmar military often resorts to Burman nationalism, routinely stoking anti‑China and anti‑Muslim prejudice. In this way, it diverted public anger over rice shortages in 1967 by orchestrating anti‑Chinese riots. Today, the regime sponsors ultranationalist groups such as Ma Ba Tha to sustain this narrative.

Propping up the regime offers China no protection from Naypyitaw’s deep-seated disdain. This hostility is not incidental but fundamental; Beijing will be forced to confront it again and again no matter how much support it provides.

Second, the regime’s corrupt apparatus continues to protect online scam syndicates, undermining China’s efforts to suppress them.

Third, the regime has closed key border trade gates including Muse and Chinshwehaw once worth billions annually to China. At a time when Chinese goods are cheaper than Japanese or Western equivalents, the border-trade shutdown is a major loss. Meanwhile, talk of opening trade routes with India has alarm bells ringing in Beijing.

Fourth, the regime is seeking to reestablish relations with the United States. While China might accept restoration of normal diplomatic ties, anything deeper would be difficult for Beijing to tolerate given its red line over Western engagement with ethnic armed groups.

‘Three bottom lines’ collapse

China’s policy goal is stability in Myanmar. But by betting on the Myanmar military to deliver it, Beijing has tethered itself to failure. The regime’s reliance on force over negotiations, corruption over the rule of law, entanglement with narcotics and scams—coupled with economic breakdown—guarantee perpetual instability.

Despite Beijing’s support, Myanmar remains mired in conflict and crisis. The “three bottom lines” have not been upheld: civil strife is intensifying, ASEAN engagement is faltering, and international powers are finding new entry points.

China’s core objective — stability in Myanmar — remains unfulfilled.

World.title: Malaysia to Seek Clarification Over Reports of Detained Myanmar Returnees
World.content:
KUALA LUMPUR—Malaysia will seek clarification from Myanmar over reports that hundreds of migrants recently returned to the country are being held in military detention, Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan said on Monday.

Malaysia in late September sent back around 1,500 Myanmar nationals as it launched a scheme that rights groups say may endanger migrants by returning them to the war-torn country.

Kuala Lumpur said the group agreed to “voluntary” repatriation from detention centers amid an uptick in anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia.

Myanmar pledged “safe and dignified” returns for its citizens displaced abroad, after criticism from the United Nations and rights groups.

Mohamad told parliament on Monday that Malaysia’s charge d’affaires in Myanmar would investigate the allegations and learn the condition of those reportedly detained.

“If there is news that the 300 people are still being detained, we will ask the Myanmar government to explain to us,” he told parliament in response to a lawmaker’s question.

“We will ask the Myanmar government to ensure that the assurances it gave us are honored,” he added.

Myanmar news outlet the Democratic Voice of Burma reported on Thursday that more than 400 ethnic Rakhine residents who returned from Malaysia earlier this month “remain in military custody” after arriving in Yangon.

They were among a group of 1,476 returnees who arrived by ship outside Yangon, the first of 5,000 that Kuala Lumpur says Myanmar agreed to take back amid the anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia.

An additional 3,524 people are expected to be repatriated in a second phase.

The UN has warned conditions in Myanmar, which has been consumed by civil war since a 2021 military coup, mean safe homecomings cannot be guaranteed as required under international law.

Myanmar’s coup leader turned president Min Aung Hlaing has been a pariah in many capitals abroad since the putsch, but Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim invited him for talks about returning Myanmar migrants earlier this month.

During the visit, Min Aung Hlaing said migrants from his country held in Malaysian detention centers will be returned home “as soon as possible”.

“We will take those verified nationals back as soon as possible,” he told a joint news conference with Anwar.

The opaque repatriation scheme has been criticized by rights monitors, some fearing ethnic Rohingya may be sent back to a country where they have experienced persecution that rights experts say amounted to genocide.

World.title: Regime Disguises Military Jet Fuel as Diesel to Evade Sanctions: JFM
World.content:
The Myanmar regime and companies linked to it have engaged in international trade fraud, using proxy firms and misclassifying aviation fuel as diesel to conceal imports of fuel used in airstrikes targeting civilians, according to an investigation released Monday by rights group Justice For Myanmar (JFM).

The findings are based on leaked documents from the regime’s Ministry of Commerce, confidential records from its Foreign Exchange Supervisory Committee (FESC), and an analysis of supply networks and market prices.

JFM said the FESC plays a critical role in approving imports of jet fuel that are intentionally and falsely declared as diesel, and in concealing the true buyers.

The FESC was established in 2022 to centralize and strictly regulate foreign currency conversions, imports and overseas transfers. It consists of six high-level regime officers, including Vice-President Nyo Saw, who has served as its chairperson since 2024.

Known to be an important figure in the management of the personal business empire of regime leader Min Aung Hlaing’s family, Nyo Saw is himself sanctioned by the EU and Canada.

The evidence indicates that six aviation fuel shipments arrived using these “evasive measures” between December 2024 and November 2025, JFM said.

During the same period, the regime stepped up airstrikes nationwide as it prepared for its sham election held in December 2025 and January 2026. The imports covered 843,000 barrels worth US$109.6 million and originated in or transited through Singapore and South Africa, the group said.

According to its findings, two Myanmar companies, Dynamic Wave and PP Petroleum Co. Ltd, were listed as importers in the contracts in order to hide the identity of the real buyer, National Energy Prime Aviation Services Co. Ltd (NEPAS).

Contracts naming Thai company Tawan-Oil Trading as the seller showed that Dynamic Wave served as a proxy importer for NEPAS in three shipments valued at $68.49 million and comprising 527,624 barrels.

Separately, Reuters reported on Monday that jet fuel imported under contracts identifying South Africa as the source was actually shipped from Iran. It said Tehran was the Myanmar military’s primary supplier of jet fuel between October 2024 and December 2025.

PP Petroleum imported another three shipments of aviation fuel misclassified as diesel, worth $41.06 million, according to contracts listing Singapore as the loading port. These were also for NEPAS, according to JFM.

NEPAS is a joint venture between regime-controlled Myanmar Petrochemical Enterprise and partner Asia Sun Group.

Asia Sun Group, a network of companies monopolizing the jet fuel supply chain, has established many shell companies in response to sanctions and public scrutiny. PP Petroleum is part of Asia Sun Group.

Some Asia Sun Group companies are sanctioned by the U.S., UK, EU, Canada and Australia—with sanctions dating back to 2022 and 2025—but NEPAS and MPE remain unsanctioned, JFM noted.

Based on its examination of regime documents and an analysis of market prices, JFM found that the regime deliberately mislabeled jet fuel as high-speed diesel to avoid scrutiny, bypass international regulations and minimize sanctions exposure risk.

Highlighting Thai supplier Tawan-Oil Trading and Singapore’s role as a loading hub, JFM called on both countries to investigate the Myanmar regime’s customs fraud and bar their territory, ports and banks from enabling jet fuel shipments.

The rights group demanded that South Africa block all fuel exports to Myanmar and investigate regime documents falsely listing the country as the fuel’s origin. It called on governments to stop granting “false legitimacy” to the regime.

JFM spokesperson Yadanar Maung said the regime’s use of trade fraud to facilitate jet fuel imports suggested that sanctions and public pressure “are biting,” but “clearly not enough.”

She urged governments to coordinate sanctions against the aviation fuel supply networks feeding the regime, and to investigate trade fraud by the regime and its partners to halt the “slaughter of civilians.”

The UNHCR, the UN’s refugee agency, said Myanmar military airstrikes remained the main cause of civilian deaths in the country, and called for an end to the transfer of arms, ammunition, jet fuel and dual-use equipment to the regime.

More than 6,200 civilians have been killed in over 14,000 regime airstrikes since the 2021 coup, according to the now-dissolved Human Rights Ministry of the National Unity Government.

World.title: Myanmar Regime’s Minimum Rice Price ‘a License to Squeeze Farmers’
World.content:
Rice farmers across Myanmar have voiced concern that the minimum price set by the regime is far below market rates and would not even cover their skyrocketing production costs.

The regime’s Committee for the Protection and Promotion of the Rights and Interests of Farmers last week set the minimum floor price for 100 baskets or about 2.09 tons of rice at 1.35 million kyats (around US$300) for monsoon paddy or unmilled rice harvested this year and summer paddy to be harvested next year.

Farmers report that the current market price for 100 baskets ranges from 1.9 to over 2 million kyats, with some areas seeing around 3 million kyats. Premium Paw San rice is selling for 5 to 6 million kyats.

“Here in Naypyitaw, the market price is 1.9 to 2 million kyats,” one farmer told The Irrawaddy. “And even at that rate, after deducting labor and other expenses, almost nothing is left. Costs are too high. Setting the base price at 13.5 million kyats is unacceptable.”

In principle, the base rate is set only in case the market rate is for some reason lower and aims to ensure that farmers are paid fairly—in other words, farmers cannot be paid less than the base rate but can be paid more.

But farmers fear the yawning gap between the two rates is apt to push down market prices to the point where they no longer make any profit at all. That means the regime is tacitly encouraging brokers to weaponize the base price to negotiate lower rates, and farmers burdened with debt will be forced to sell anyway.

Instead, farmers say the calculation should take into account fertilizer, pesticide and labor costs plus loan interest. Farmers say they cannot buy supplies at the regime’s official prices either but must pay market rates for fertilizer, pesticides and harvest labor.

“Fertilizer is sold for 80,000 to 150,000 kyats a bag, and if we buy on credit, monthly interest is 3,000 to 5,000 kyats for each 100,000 kyats borrowed,” said a farmer from Ayeyarwady Region. “So a base price of 1.35 million kyats doesn’t even cover expenses.”

Farmers estimate production costs per acre are around 1.2 million kyats excluding interest, but this year’s monsoon harvest has fallen to only 68 to 75 baskets per acre. If paid the base price of 1.35 million kyats for 100 baskets, they would lose around 200,000 to 300,000 kyats per acre.

According to the Myanmar Rice Federation, Myanmar earned $338 million from rice exports in the first half of fiscal 2026, which began in April.

World.title: Myanmar War Crimes Survivors Look to Denmark for Justice
World.content:
Forty homes. That is how many a woman, now living in Denmark, watched burn in her village in Chin State, western Myanmar. Family members and friends were killed or left permanently disabled by landmines planted by the junta. Like tens of thousands of others from Chin State, she was driven across the border into India.

On Monday, she is asking the Danish authorities to investigate the men responsible.

She has filed a criminal complaint in Copenhagen against members of the Myanmar junta. For her safety she cannot be named. The crimes in the complaint include deliberate killing, mass arson and the forced displacement of tens of thousands of people.

This is possible because of a change in Danish law. Legislation that came into force last year specifically criminalizes war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide. It gives Danish prosecutors a route that did not exist before.

Her lawyer, Copenhagen-based Eddie Omar Rosenberg Khawaja, puts it plainly. “Under the new Danish legislation it no longer matters where the crimes took place, or the nationality of the perpetrators or the victims,” he says. “Victims living in Denmark can request that Danish authorities hold commanders under whose watch atrocities against them occurred responsible.”

That matters because there is nowhere else to go. Myanmar’s courts are controlled by the generals. The Security Council has failed to act. International courts in The Hague—the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice—have also been slow. For the people of Chin State, a Danish police station may be one of the few doors that open.

It also fits Denmark’s own history. Tracy Bawi Hlei, chairperson of Myanmar Action Group Denmark (MAGD), which supports the case, says: “Denmark has a history of aligning itself with the pro-democracy movement in Myanmar since before the 1990s, through development aid, support of activists, bypassing the military government and standing in solidarity with human rights movements.”

She sees this case as the next step. “Now, Myanmar people and Danish activists who are part of communities and movements in Denmark are taking a stand for accountability and the international rule of law.” Survivors and crucial evidence, she explains, were identified within Denmark through a collaboration of civil society groups, including MAGD and the Chin Community Denmark (CCDK), which also supports the case.

I run the Myanmar Accountability Project, which supports cases against the junta in Southeast Asia and Europe. I believe the basis for a Danish case is strong.

The Danish government has said so itself. In a statement to the UN on September 30, 2025, Denmark said, as a matter of public record, that Myanmar suffers from a lack of accountability and continued impunity. This complaint invites Denmark to act on that.

The timing is pointed. The Danish Foreign Ministry is closing its embassy in Myanmar. This case allows the Danish government to send a signal that it remains engaged with issues of justice and accountability, and that the rightful aspirations of the people of Myanmar to a just, peaceful and dignified life must be respected.

Meanwhile, the junta is seeking legitimacy. Min Aung Hlaing, the general who led the coup, is now president after sham elections that offered the people of Myanmar no real choice. Those who lived through his campaigns of burning and killing are expected to accept this as normal. They do not.

The country’s condition leaves no room for complacency. According to the latest UN report, more than 16 million people need aid, and the junta is blocking humanitarian access to vast areas where the need is greatest. Nearly 3.8 million people are estimated to have been displaced, many of them several times. A UN Development Programme report published last month found that two-thirds of the population are living in poverty or at immediate risk of falling into it.

The violence is on a scale that few outside the region grasp. More than 100,000 people have died in conflict-related violence since the coup. That makes Myanmar’s conflict the fourth deadliest in the world. This is not a frozen conflict. It is a war on civilians, and state-wide repression compounds the inhuman levels of killing, making justice and accountability even more important.

What the complainant seeks is limited. She is not asking Denmark to end a war. She is asking its police to open an investigation and its prosecutors to take her evidence seriously. She is asking that the commanders responsible be held accountable.

Denmark has said impunity in Myanmar must end. Its new law now gives it a way to act on that. She has come forward, at a risk to herself that most of us will never face. It is now for Danish authorities to decide whether the law means what it says.

Chris Gunness is founder and director of the Myanmar Accountability Project.

World.title: China Taps Myanmar’s Rare Earth Surge, Coffee Sell-Off, and More
World.content:
China’s rare earth imports swelled by Myanmar supply

China’s rare earth imports surged to 5,021 tons in September, up 23 percent from August, according to data from the Shanghai Metals Market.

Shipments of rare earth oxides from Myanmar accounted for 70 percent of the total, while arrivals from Laos fell to 1,369 tons. Together, Myanmar and Laos accounted for 97 percent of total imports. Cumulative imports for January–September reached 46,466 tons, up 14 percent year‑on‑year.

Rare earth mines along Myanmar’s northeastern border with China supply roughly half the world’s heavy rare earths, including strategically scarce dysprosium and terbium used in magnets crucial to China’s high-tech supply chain.

The surge comes as the US reengages with Myanmar’s regime, fueling speculation that global competition for rare earth resources is driving Washington’s policy recalibration. However, almost all of Myanmar’s rare earth mines are located in territory beyond regime control.

Myanmar specialty coffee faces Chinese fire sale

A Chinese fire sale beckons for Myanmar’s once-booming specialty coffee market. Once backed by USAID and American buyers, the coffee industry collapsed after the 2021 coup as Shan farmers responsible for some of the world’s finest beans were deprived of access to Western markets, transparent trade and certification. With the lucrative export path blocked, the regime and its Myanmar Coffee Association (MCA) are now aggressively pivoting to China.

MCA chairman Myo Aye told Xinhua that cooperation with Yunnan has deepened since the military takeover, with new MoUs locking in China as the top destination for Myanmar’s 3,000–4,000 tonnes of annual exports—tumbling from pre-coup levels of more than 5,000 tonnes. He said the association is looking to attract Chinese investment in value-added processing facilities, roasting plants and supply-chain logistics.

Myanmar’s coffee basket of Shan State has been ravaged by some of the fiercest fighting triggered by the 2021 coup.

Agriculture supplants industry at Myanmar-China forum

The Seventh Myanmar–China Think Tank Forum kicked off in Mangshi, Yunnan Province on Wednesday, with agricultural cooperation placed firmly at the center of discussions. Launched in 2017, the annual forum takes a different theme each year, but its underlying focus has consistently been the now stalled China–Myanmar Economic Corridor, a project designed to give Beijing direct access to the Indian Ocean.

This year’s session saw Myanmar regime officials highlight opportunities in rice and coffee. Yunnan is a major buyer of both. They urged deeper cooperation to expand exports, boost trade and investment, develop value‑added products, and facilitate technology exchange.

The forum comes as regime leader Min Aung Hlaing promotes agriculture as the key sector to revive an economy devastated by his coup and international sanctions. He has emphasized rice, cotton, oilseed crops, pulses, and rubber as priority industries to drive growth.

Earlier this month, Myanmar’s Pawsan variety won global recognition at the World Rice Conference 2026. At the 23rd China–ASEAN Expo in Nanning last month, three Myanmar rice exporters signed five MoUs with Chinese companies. According to the Myanmar Rice Federation, Myanmar earned US$ 338 million from rice exports in the first half of FY2026–27, which began in April.

Travel alert over Myanmar scams sparks Thai pushback

The Chinese Embassy in Bangkok issued a safety advisory on Oct. 16 warning its citizens of trafficking risks linked to scam compounds along the Thai–Myanmar border, prompting a scrambled response from Thailand’s foreign and tourism ministers.

The advisory cautioned Chinese nationals to be on alert for kidnapping and trafficking schemes disguised as high‑paying job offers, fraudulent investment projects, and bogus filming contracts targeting livestreamers and entertainers. It urged travelers to verify overseas employment opportunities, avoid suspicious transport arrangements, and steer clear of high‑risk areas on the Thai-Myanmar frontier where criminal networks remain active despite official crackdowns.

The warning followed recent cases that rattled public opinion in China, including the abduction of a shopping livestreamer who was lured by a bogus contract to Thailand before being trafficked to Myanmar last month. The high‑profile kidnapping of soap actor Wang Xing in Myawaddy in 2025 had already triggered a trilateral crackdown by China, Thailand, and Myanmar.

Following the latest advisory, a Chinese actress cancelled a fan meeting in Bangkok, underscoring the potential impact on Thailand’s tourism sector.

Thai Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow responded by urging the embassy to ensure its warnings are proportionate to the situation and avoid sparking unnecessary alarm. He stressed that Thailand takes visitor safety seriously and will investigate incidents, but cautioned that exaggerated advisories risk undermining confidence in Thailand as a safe destination. Chinese nationals are Thailand’s largest tourism market.

Naypyitaw eyes tourism lifeline in Kunming

Even as reports of trafficking and scam compounds along the Thai–Myanmar border dominate headlines in China, Myanmar’s regime is pressing ahead with plans to lure Chinese visitors back to Myanmar to revive a tourism industry shattered by the 2021 coup.

The regime’s Hotels and Tourism Ministry has announced it will open a tourism promotion office in Kunming, Yunnan Province. At the China–Myanmar cultural tourism exchange meeting held in Kunming from October 13–17, Tourism Ministry Secretary Maung Maung Kyaw described the proposed office as a potential “major corridor” for public‑private cooperation between the regime and Chinese tour companies. A business‑to‑business memorandum of understanding was also signed between Chinese and Myanmar tour operators.

Chinese travelers remain Myanmar’s largest foreign tourism market, but numbers have collapsed since the coup. Just over 250,000 Chinese arrivals were recorded last year—a fraction of the pre‑coup boom—despite having access to visas on arrival. In 2019, Myanmar saw 749,719 Chinese arrivals out of a total 4.4 million tourists.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: South Korean Burger Chain Mom’s Touch to Open 50 Outlets in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – South Korean burger chain Mom’s Touch plans to open at least 50 outlets in Kazakhstan over the next decade as it expands into Central Asia through a franchise agreement with local food group Shin-Line, The Korea Herald reported Oct. 26.

The first outlet is expected to open in the first half of 2027. The agreement also covers the Kyrgyz Republic, while the company plans to expand into major Kazakh cities, including Astana.

“We are preparing to open our first store in the first half of next year and develop Kazakhstan into a key base for our Central Asian operations,” a Mom’s Touch official said in a comment to The Korean Herald.

Mom’s Touch plans to introduce its signature chicken burgers made with whole chicken-thigh fillets, along with fried chicken and pizza.

Its local partner, Shin-Line Group, has a cold-chain logistics network serving about 10 countries and operates more than 70 outlets of a South Korean convenience store chain, mainly in Almaty.

The expansion follows Mom’s Touch’s entry into Uzbekistan in 2025.

Founded in South Korea in 2004, Mom’s Touch built its brand around chicken burgers made with whole chicken-thigh fillets rather than ground meat. Its signature Thigh Burger has helped establish the chain as a major domestic competitor to international fast-food brands.

World.title: Kazakhstan Targets Domestic Drone Industry Development by 2029
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan aims to develop its domestic drone industry by 2029, focusing on local manufacturing, digital flight management, workforce training and the use of unmanned systems across key economic sectors, the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development reported on Oct. 27.

Eighteen government bodies, including the ministries of transport, defense and internal affairs, will coordinate efforts to establish common regulations, develop infrastructure and expand the use of drones while addressing public safety concerns.

Domestic production and digital infrastructure

Kazakhstan plans to introduce a unified digital platform for unmanned aircraft systems and automated traffic management (UTM). The service will bring aircraft registration, applications and flight route approvals into one electronic system. To support local manufacturing, the government proposes incentives, public procurement preferences and long-term offtake contracts for companies registered with Astana Hub. Support will target production of critical hardware, communications systems and secure software, rather than basic assembly alone.

The country also aims to establish at least two research and development centers in partnership with universities and international technology companies and train at least 1,000 specialists, including engineers, drone operators, software developers and cybersecurity experts.

From classrooms to industry

Drone education is expected to expand from schools to technical colleges and universities. Planned measures include aeromodelling classrooms, specialized equipment for science and technology education, updated university curricula and annual student competitions in unmanned technologies.

The government also wants to expand drone use in agriculture, energy, mining, logistics, municipal services, emergency monitoring and environmental protection. Relevant agencies will identify practical applications and develop guidelines and incentives for businesses and public institutions.

Supporting infrastructure will include vertiports, drone ports, automated charging stations, radio frequencies and satellite communication channels. A pilot project to test autonomous freight transportation is scheduled for 2027-2028.

Safety and regulation

The government is considering transferring some oversight of drone operations to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, introducing mandatory liability insurance for drone owners, and setting cybersecurity requirements for communications. Operator certificates would be issued through specialized public service centers. The ministry has invited domestic entrepreneurs, developers and engineers to submit projects with export potential and proposals for implementing the initiative.

The broader objective is to build a domestic industry that can supply Kazakhstan’s economy and compete in international markets.

World.title: Kazakhstan Maps Water Risks Through 2040 as Regional Cooperation Takes Center Stage
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan is seeking to make water-sharing across Central Asia more transparent through real-time monitoring and shared data as it prepares for possible declines in water availability through 2040. The country does not currently face a nationwide water deficit, but its dependence on rivers flowing across national borders makes water security a regional issue, Water Resources and Irrigation Minister Nurzhan Nurzhigitov said in an interview with Tengrinews published on Oct. 27.

Kazakhstan’s average annual river runoff is about 100 billion cubic meters, with approximately 45% of its river water coming from abroad. The economy, agriculture, industry and housing and utilities sectors collectively use about 25 billion cubic meters annually, according to the minister.

Seven of Kazakhstan’s eight river basins are connected to transboundary waters. The country receives water from the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, China and Russia.

The dependence is particularly pronounced in the south, where much of the country’s irrigated agriculture is concentrated. About 90% of the water supplied by the Syr Darya River to the Turkistan and Kyzylorda regions is transboundary. Approximately 75% of the water available to the Zhambyl Region from the Chu River comes from Kyrgyzstan.

“Water availability has become a strategic issue and a matter of national security,” Nurzhigitov said.

Building trust through shared data

One of Kazakhstan’s priorities is to improve the transparency and accuracy of information exchanged by countries that share river basins. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have agreed to automate water accounting at 10 sites along the Syr Darya, with five in each country. The German Society for International Cooperation, or GIZ, helped prepare the project documentation. Kazakhstan has already built two hydrological monitoring stations using funds from the Turkistan regional administration. The minister said the two countries had jointly checked the stations and could now see the same data in real time.

In January 2026, Kazakhstan proposed developing a plan to digitize the entire Syr Darya basin. Tajikistan agreed to participate, and a working group was established involving Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Its first meeting was planned for early November, with Kyrgyzstan potentially joining the initiative later.

“If we digitize the entire basin, we will see how much water flows through it and how each country fulfills its obligations. This will increase trust. There will be no situation where one country says, ‘I sent this much water,’ while another claims it received nothing,” Nurzhigitov said.

The plan for automated water accounting across the Syr Darya basin has already been developed and sent to the countries concerned, according to a note accompanying the Tengrinews interview. However, the minister did not specify a timeline or cost for a fully integrated system. The current initiative is narrower than a shared digital platform covering all five Central Asian countries. Its initial working group involves three countries, with Kyrgyzstan expected to be invited later.

Kazakhstan is also developing its own water information infrastructure. The ministry is creating a national information system and plans to open public access to selected data in 2027. The ministry is also developing the TALSIM hydrological modeling system for flood forecasting, developed in cooperation with the United Nations Development Program (UNDP), and wants to add drought-prediction capabilities.

Cooperation or competition over water?

Nurzhigitov emphasized the importance of regional cooperation, saying that water brings Central Asian countries together rather than inevitably pushing them toward conflict.

“Water unites us,” he said.

In 1992, the five countries’ water ministers signed an agreement in Almaty to use water jointly and rationally. The International Fund for Saving the Aral Sea and its associated commissions provide additional mechanisms for regional dialogue.

According to Nurzhigitov, the commissions meet at least four times a year to discuss water forecasts, available volumes and allocation limits. He said there had been no violations of agreed limits over the past three years.

Kazakhstan has also proposed a framework convention on the rational use of Central Asia’s water resources. The ministry has approved the draft domestically and sent it to neighboring countries. Discussions are underway to combine the countries’ proposals into common rules that could help limit climate change’s impact.

Asked whether one country might decide to take more water than agreed, Nurzhigitov pointed to water diplomacy and the obligations shared by countries along transboundary rivers.

“That will not happen, because water diplomacy and accountability exist. These are transboundary rivers, and each country has obligations that must be fulfilled. That is why this will never happen,” he said.

Drought exposes the limits of regional agreements

Kazakhstan’s experience in 2021 demonstrated the economic and social consequences of severe drought. According to official figures published by the Prime Minister’s press service on Aug. 12, 2021, 1,161 head of livestock had died in the Mangystau Region by Aug. 10. Another 553 livestock deaths were reported in the Aral district of the Kyzylorda Region amid a lack of water at watering points and dry pastures.

Water shortages again threatened agricultural production in the Zhambyl Region in 2023, when low inflows affected the Chu and Talas river basins. Reporting by Kazinform on Aug. 11, 2023 detailed the scale of the shortfall. From April 1 to Aug. 11, inflow into the Kirovsk Reservoir in Kyrgyzstan, which supplies the Talas River, reached just 60 million cubic meters, compared with 300 million cubic meters during the same period a year earlier. Inflow into the Orto-Tokoy Reservoir, which releases water into the Chu River, reached 55 million cubic meters, against 256 million cubic meters in 2022.

The shortage put about 4,000 hectares of onions and sugar beets at risk, Kazinform said, citing a regional official from the agency responsible for maintaining hydraulic structures.
