Usupashvili is convinced that once power changes hands, the evidence gathered during these proceedings will be used to seek a ban on Georgian Dream itself.

“The case will be heard in the same courtroom, but by different judges — perhaps even by some of those currently in office. They have a habit of switching sides whenever power changes hands. And these are the very people who will have to ban a party that resorts to such actions,” Usupashvili said.

“Healthy opposition” and a one-party system

Usupashvili says the demand to ban five opposition parties has no legal basis and amounts to purely political persecution. He calls it “an attempt by Georgian Dream to pave the way for a constitutional coup”.

In his assessment, the ruling party aims to eliminate its opponents, secure a constitutional majority and reshape the Constitution to suit its own interests.

Usupashvili recalls Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s statement that Georgian Dream would hold a constitutional majority in parliament once the opposition parties were banned.

Responding to the government’s argument that a ban would pave the way for a “healthy opposition”, Usupashvili said: “They want to appoint the opposition themselves.”

He says that over the past 12–14 years, the government has failed to name a single opposition party it considers healthy, apart from its own offshoots.

Usupashvili compares the logic behind the petition to Article 6 of the Soviet Constitution, which established the Communist Party as the sole legitimate political force. He argues that if the court rules that only the ruling party represents the interests of the state, Georgia will return to a constitutionally enshrined one-party system, placing it among the enemies of the free world.

What lies ahead for the opposition parties, and what should they do now?

Usupashvili believes that a ban on political parties would pose a less serious threat to the parties themselves than to the country as a whole.

“A political party is a tool for conducting political activity. Elections took place in 1990 even though not a single political party had been registered. Nevertheless, a way forward was found — we managed to register directly for the elections. There are mechanisms available.”

He says the parties should already be discussing what they will do if a ban comes into force.

“We need to talk about this because the situation will change fundamentally. Under these circumstances, we must not fall into their trap or start playing by their rules. Their ‘game’ is to drive the active part of society — ordinary citizens — into a state of utter despair.”

Usupashvili says political leaders need to reassess and analyse current events and find a way forward.

“We must understand what is really happening — why is all this happening to us? The political front needs renewal. Fifteen to 20 years ago, I was a party chairman. We set up local branches and held meetings. Yes, we faced interference and persecution, but we still managed to achieve something. The situation is different now. However, examples from Hungary and Guatemala show that change is possible even under such circumstances.”

Usupashvili stresses that it is crucial for active citizens — those who believe in their country’s independence, freedom and progress — not to give in to despair.

World.title: Opinion: Why agreement between Abkhazia’s interior ministry and Russia conflicts with Abkhaz law
World.content:
The opposition in Abkhazia is demanding the immediate resignation of Interior Minister Robert Kiut. The call follows an agreement he signed with Russia’s Interior Ministry. The opposition argues that the deal violates Abkhazia’s constitution and undermines its national interests.

One provision has provoked particular outrage. It envisages sharing with the Russian side data on individuals who could “destabilise the situation in the border region”. Many suspect that the agreement would legitimise a growing trend in which Russian authorities punish Abkhaz public figures and politicians who oppose arrangements with Russia that they consider detrimental to Abkhazia.

Prominent Abkhaz public figure Akhra Bzhania has examined whether the agreement complies with Abkhaz law. He concludes that it does not.

Akhra Bzhania: “Most supporters of the agreement between Abkhazia’s Interior Ministry and Russia cite legal continuity with the provisions of the 2014 Treaty of Alliance between Russia and Abkhazia as their main argument. But can these references really be considered made in good faith?

Here is what Article 10 of the 2014 treaty says in its main provisions on cooperation between the two sides’ interior ministries:

1. Within one year of the treaty’s entry into force, the parties must establish a Joint Information and Coordination Centre for their interior affairs agencies.

2. The Joint Information and Coordination Centre for Interior Affairs Agencies is responsible for:

organising the exchange of operationally significant information between the law enforcement agencies of the Russian Federation and the Republic of Abkhazia, as well as maintaining the necessary operational and forensic records;

compiling and maintaining a specialised database on organised criminal groups whose illegal activities affect the interests of the contracting parties;

collecting, consolidating and analysing information on efforts to combat organised crime and other serious offences;

assisting with the international search for and extradition of people who have evaded criminal prosecution or the enforcement of a sentence;

facilitating the implementation of necessary coordinated measures to combat serious crimes that threaten the security of the contracting parties;

developing and submitting proposals to the contracting parties on improving the effectiveness of their cooperation.

None of these provisions, nor the treaty as a whole, states or implies that the Joint Information and Coordination Centre (JICC) may be used to “monitor and analyse the crime situation and operational environment in the Republic of Abkhazia, as well as the activities of Abkhazia’s interior affairs agencies”, as stated in Article 1 of the new agreement.

That last point is particularly absurd. Why have an entire ministry if it needs to rely on an external organisation to monitor its activities? Not to mention that Abkhazia’s Interior Ministry may have internal matters that the JICC should know nothing about.

The 2014 treaty also says nothing about the JICC, let alone specialised units of Russia’s Interior Ministry, tackling “economic crime and corruption” in Abkhazia.

Nor does it mention any Russian Interior Ministry units directly engaging in “countering the spread of criminal ideas on social media and messaging platforms”. Yet Article 4 of the new agreement between the two interior ministries explicitly includes this provision.

Incidentally, many have interpreted this clause as an attempt to monitor online spaces for dissenting views.

There is also the fact that the very definition of what constitutes “criminal” content online may differ significantly between our two countries. In Russia, for example, even this text, published on Facebook, a platform owned by Meta, is illegal.

And, of course, the 2014 treaty nowhere states that the Russian and Abkhaz interior ministries will “conduct joint operational and preventive measures in border areas” — activities that infringe on our sovereign jurisdiction. Yet Article 6 of the new agreement explicitly provides for them.

And so it goes with many other provisions…

International treaties are not folk songs from which you can create a new work by developing the main theme. They are complete legal documents, and their provisions cannot be freely reinterpreted.

For this reason, and because the two instruments differ substantially in their content, the new agreement cannot be said to “derive” from the 2014 treaty, as some “experts” are trying to argue. If anyone really wants to establish a new legal framework for the work of Abkhazia’s Interior Ministry, they should try doing so openly and through the lawful procedure. Then we can see how that works out.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Ramiz Mehdiyev to be stripped of state awards
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. Former head of the Presidential Administration of Azerbaijan Ramiz Mehdiyev will be stripped of his state awards.

According to the verdict issued by the Baku Court on Grave Crimes on October 22, 2026, a submission has been ordered to be forwarded for consideration of the question of stripping Ramiz Mehdiyev of his state awards.

Ramiz Mehdiyev was awarded the Istiglal Order in 2008, the Sharaf Order in 2013, and the Shohrat Order in 2018.

As previously reported, under the verdict issued by the Baku Court on Grave Crimes on October 22, 2026, Ramiz Mehdiyev was found guilty of committing crimes under Articles 193-1.3.2, 274, 278.1, and 311.3.3 of the Criminal Code of Azerbaijan and sentenced to 14 years in prison.

However, taking into account Ramiz Mehdiyev’s age and health condition, the court ruled that the sentence would be suspended.

World.title: Azerbaijan-Türkiye relations are strong and unbreakable – Bahçeli
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. The brotherly ties between Azerbaijan and Türkiye are so strong and historically significant that they transcend all political and diplomatic issues and cannot be constrained by temporary developments.

This is stated in a declaration by Devlet Bahçeli, leader of Türkiye’s Nationalist Movement Party, ahead of the upcoming Summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) in Ankara and the 35th anniversary of the independence of OTS member states.

According to him, the brotherhood between Türkiye and Azerbaijan is unbreakable, rooted in the will of both nations and the history of their shared struggle, and passed down from generation to generation. “The same can be said of all brotherly states of the Turkic world,” he noted, stressing that the escalation of misunderstandings must not be allowed.

“We must not allow seeds of discord to be sown among us. No disagreement should lead to long-term estrangement. Our bonds of brotherhood are built on mutual respect and faith in a shared future. It is the duty of every member of the Turkic world to contribute to our historical closeness, avoid disagreements, and refrain from actions that could weaken our future,” the politician stated.

The MHP leader called for leaving a “strong Turkic world” to future generations.

World.title: India’s Rossari Biotech eyes supplying Turkmen oil, gas sector (Exclusive)
World.content:
ASHGABAT, Turkmenistan, October 27. The Indian company Rossari Biotech Limited is exploring opportunities to enter the Turkmenistan market and supply specialized chemical products to the state-owned corporations "Turkmengaz" and "Turkmennebit," the representative of Rossari Biotech Limited, Ketan Gadhiya, told Trend on the sidelines of the 31st International Conference and Exhibition "Oil and Gas of Turkmenistan" (OGT 2026) in Ashgabat.

According to him, the company specializes in manufacturing products for the textile industry, the healthcare and food sectors, household chemicals, personal hygiene, as well as for agriculture and the oil and gas sector. Rossari Biotech is a publicly traded company whose shares are listed on the Indian stock market.

"For us, participating in OGT 2026 is a good opportunity to explore the prospects of operating in the Turkmenistan market and to support ‘Turkmengaz,’ ‘Turkmennebit,’ and other national oil and gas companies operating in the country," Gadhiya noted.

In the first phase, the company intends to study the technical requirements of Turkmen customers for chemical products, identify suitable products, and provide samples for testing.

"First and foremost, we want to review the specifications of chemical products, identify suitable products, and provide high-quality samples for testing. After that, we will explore opportunities for further cooperation with all national oil and gas companies," Rossari Biotech’s representative said.

He added that participating in OGT 2026 allows the company to assess potential demand and establish contacts with representatives of Turkmenistan’s oil and gas industry.

Rossari Biotech Limited is an Indian manufacturer of specialty chemical products, founded in 1997. The company provides chemical solutions for the oil and gas and textile industries, household chemical manufacturing, agriculture, and other sectors. According to the company, its product portfolio includes more than 4,300 products, and its operations span over 65 countries.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s Economy Ministry signs cooperation deal with Spain’s IE University
World.content:
Photo: Ministry of Economy of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. A framework agreement on cooperation was signed between the Ministry of Economy and the Spanish university IE.

This was reported by the Ministry of Economy.

The document on the establishment and development of the Economic Observatory provides for joint research and the expansion of dialogue on economic development issues.

A framework agreement on cooperation for the establishment and development of the Economic Observatory was signed in Baku between the Ministry of Economy and the Spanish university IE. The document was signed by Deputy Minister of Economy Samad Bashirli and Executive Director of the Spanish university IE, Santiago Íñiguez de Onzoño.

The agreement provides for joint research and economic analysis aimed at economic diversification, increasing productivity, and strengthening competitiveness, as well as promoting dialogue between the government, the business community, and academia.

As part of the Economic Observatory’s activities, plans include studying economic development trends and factors influencing future growth, as well as conducting economic monitoring and international comparisons. The research program will be determined jointly, taking into account Azerbaijan’s economic priorities and the academic expertise of IE University.

IE University is a higher education institution based in Spain. The university offers bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral programs, as well as executive education programs for executives. Its activities span the fields of education, research, innovation, and international cooperation.

World.title: Ramiz Mehdiyev sentenced to 14 years in prison
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. Former head of the Presidential Administration Ramiz Mehdiyev has been sentenced to 14 years in prison, Trend reports.

The trial of Mehdiyev, who was charged with committing particularly serious crimes against statehood, has concluded.

Under a ruling issued by the Baku Court of Grave Crimes on October 22, 2026, Ramiz Mehdiyev was found guilty of crimes under Articles 193-1.3.2, 274, 278.1 and 311.3.3 of the Criminal Code of Azerbaijan and sentenced to 14 years in prison.

Taking into account his health due to existing medical conditions and his age, the court ruled, pursuant to Article 70 of the Criminal Code, that the prison sentence should be suspended.

The ruling also provides for a submission to be made for consideration of the issue of stripping Ramiz Mehdiyev of his state awards.

In addition, the court ordered the confiscation of Mehdiyev’s assets in favor of the state.

World.title: Azerbaijan prosecutor general meets acting UN counterterrorism head in Baku (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. As part of the third high-level meeting of law enforcement officials from member states of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation on combating corruption, held in Baku on October 27, Kamran Aliyev, Prosecutor General of the Republic of Azerbaijan, met with Alexandre Zouev, the Acting Under-Secretary-General of the United Nations and Head of the UN Office of Counter-Terrorism (UNOCT).

This was reported by the press service of the Prosecutor General’s Office.

It was noted that, in welcoming the guest, the Prosecutor General highlighted the fruitful partnership that has developed between Azerbaijan and the UN and emphasized the importance of furthering cooperation between the Prosecutor General’s Office and the relevant UN agencies.

The meeting addressed the current state and prospects of cooperation between Azerbaijan and the UN Office of Counter-Terrorism, the coordination of international efforts in the fight against terrorism, the strengthening of the institutional capacity of law enforcement agencies, and the expansion of mutual exchange of expertise.

In the context of previous discussions, the importance of a high-level event on the role of law enforcement agencies in combating climate change, which took place in November 2024 as part of COP29 and was jointly organized by the Office of the Attorney General, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), and the Ministry of Interior of the United Arab Emirates.

Furthermore, referring to bilateral meetings held in previous years, the importance of further developing existing cooperation through concrete initiatives was noted.

The Prosecutor General expressed the readiness of the Prosecutor’s Office of the Republic of Azerbaijan to expand ties with relevant UN agencies, study international best practices, and implement joint practical initiatives.

Expressing his gratitude for the warm welcome, Alexandre Zouev emphasized the importance of developing cooperation between Azerbaijan and UN agencies, strengthening the capacity of law enforcement agencies, and exchanging international best practices.

At the conclusion of the meeting, the parties expressed their mutual interest in continuing cooperation to expand international collaboration in the fight against terrorism and to strengthen interaction with relevant UN agencies.

World.title: Australia's rising road toll reverses hard-won safety improvements
World.content:
After decades of a declining death toll, the number of people being killed on Australian roads is once again rising.

"Something is changing, and not for the better," said Australian Automobile Association managing director Michael Bradley.

"Cars have never been safer, we're spending a huge amount of money on roads, yet more people are dying.

"It's pretty confounding, and it's a trend we haven't seen for decades."

Michael Bradley wants more research into the attitudes and behaviours causing the recent increase in road deaths. (Supplied: australian AUtomomnile )

Road deaths peaked in the 1970s, before steadily declining for 40 years as seatbelt and drink-driving laws were introduced.

But that changed in 2020, when the trend unexpectedly reversed.

'You never get over it'

Australia is now on track for its sixth year in a row of increased fatalities, with the number of deaths to the end of September already the highest recorded in 15 years.

Roadside memorials are a common sight along Australian roads. (Andrew O'Connor)

While the number of deaths remains low compared with previous decades, the rise is disturbing for road safety researchers like University of Melbourne associate professor Milad Haghani.

"It appears some of the progress we've been making has been wiped away," he said.

"The biggest increase in fatalities is among vulnerable road users like pedestrians, cyclists and motorbike riders, so that's something we need to be addressing."

The trend is pushing Australia further from its national target of halving road deaths by 2030 and reaching zero by 2050.

'It is devastating'

It is a chilling trend for the thousands of Australian families living with the ripple impacts of a preventable death.

Yvonne Sampi mourns her late son, who died on his way to a funeral in 2017. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)

Bardi woman Yvonne Sampi knows first-hand the visceral grief behind the numbers.

Her son, Mervyn, was killed as he drove to a family funeral in 2017.

The 31-year-old, who loved fishing and camping, left behind a young son.

"I think all mothers, when they lose their children, they think 'why has this happened?'" Ms Sampi told the ABC.

" It is devastating, and you never get over it. "

Mervyn Davey, photographed with his son and his father before his death. (Supplied: Yvonne Sampi)

What is causing the increase?

Australia's population growth can partly explain the increase in deaths.

The rate of fatalities per 100,000 people has remained relatively stable in recent years.

However, road safety advocates say the rising death toll is alarming given vehicles have never been safer, and road fatalities are reducing internationally.

Six children were injured in this crash in regional Western Australia in 2022. (ABC News)

Australia has plummeted in international road safety rankings, according to Professor Teresa Senserrick, who heads the Centre for Road Safety Research at the University of Western Australia.

"Just over two decades ago we had reached the top 10 of the best-performing OECD countries, and it was a very exciting time, so it's quite sad to look at the stats now and see we've only just scraped into the top 20 nations."

Teresa Senserrick has been researching road safety for more than 20 years. (ABC News: Aran Hart)

Nations such as Spain have slashed fatality rates by reducing speed limits, criminalising some dangerous driving practices, increasing enforcement and investing in high-speed rail.

Spain joined several other EU member states by reducing speed limits in urban areas to 30 kilometres per hour.

Professor Senserrick said policy-makers need to be willing to push through changes that may be unpopular with a vocal minority of voters.

"The speed limits we have in Australia have not changed much since … the 1970s," she said.

"During that time our population's grown, as well as the number of vehicles and size of vehicles, so we just can't continue while allowing such high speeds, both in urban areas and remote and regional areas where crashes are more likely to be fatal."

Most fatal crashes occur in urban areas, although those in regional and remote areas are more often fatal. (ABC News: Sally Rafferty)

More drugs, less booze

Dr Haghani said there was evidence that drug use and bigger cars are factors contributing to the number of deaths.

"If you look back twenty years ago, the biggest risk factor in fatal crashes was drink-driving, but that's been replaced by drug-driving.

"Drugs are now detected in the systems of nearly 17 per cent of people involved in fatal crashes, and that's a big concern."

Testing has shown that higher, heavier cars are more likely to cause fatal injuries to pedestrians. (Supplied: ANCAP Safety)

Every year the average Australian car is bigger and heavier, which can be safer for drivers but increases the risk of pedestrian deaths.

Dr Haghani this year co-authored a study that found every extra 10cm of vehicle height increased the odds of a pedestrian death by 11 per cent.

"If we do not regulate and create incentives for people to buy more reasonable size cars then this will continue, and we'll end up with a road eco-system that's increasingly risky for pedestrians and cyclists."

Milad Haghani has published several papers on what's causing the recent uptick in deaths. (Supplied)

'Too much speculation'

Road crash data has never been so public or detailed, with online dashboards tracking deaths and infrastructure spend.

But the Australian Automobile Association said big gaps remained in knowledge of what was being done across states and territories.

General manager Michael Bradley pointed to the lag in serious crash data.

"We've got a national target to reduce serious injuries by 2030, but there's a three-year lag in the data available," he said.

"At the end of the days there's too much speculation and not enough evidence-based policy.

"Canberra is distributing billions of dollars, and we need to make sure money is being directed to what is actually working."

The Office of Road Safety did not respond to questions or a request for an interview.

Instead, the Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts said in a statement, "the Australian Government contributes to better road safety outcomes in a number of ways, including overseeing the entry of new, safer vehicles into the Australian market, making significant investments in infrastructure to build and maintain safer roads, and funding other non-infrastructure initiatives to improve road safety".

Where to from here?

The national target of eradicating traffic deaths by 2050 is linked to the roll-out of autonomous and connected vehicles, which can detect pedestrians and other hazards more precisely than humans.

First responders are often traumatised by the scenes they encounter on Australian roads. (ABC News)

According to Professor Senserrick, the technology is developing rapidly, and there are already applications to introduce the vehicles to Australia.

"However, it's going to take a long time to get enough turnover in the vehicle fleet to have lots of those vehicles in place, so it's important we continue with road safety policies if we're going to try to reach the national targets."

World.title: How Australian publishers tell if a book has been written by AI
World.content:
Is artificial intelligence an "existential threat" to traditional book publishing?

That's the impression we get from the headlines: online sellers flooded with AI "slop" books, publishing houses inundated with AI-generated submissions, book deals falling apart, and three literary prize winners so far this year being accused of using the technology.

Louise Doughty, a judge on the 2026 Commonwealth Short Story Prize whose winner was accused of AI use, thinks so.

"We're only at the beginning of understanding the depth of that threat, and how we can combat it," she said.

Readers can still discern whether a text is AI-generated through certain "tells". (Getty Images: imaginima)

Readers struggling to 'keep up' with evolution of AI text

How do we even tell whether a book is AI-generated?

ABC Radio National's Critics Corner spoke to Matthew Rubery, professor of Modern Literature at Queen Mary University, trying to answer this big question plaguing some readers.

He said individual readers could still broadly discern whether a text was AI-generated, through "tells" including:

"It's not X, it's Y" constructions

Always giving three examples

Laboured metaphors

But Dr Rubery said the signs of AI usage "change a lot" and it was "very tough to keep up with it".

Matthew Rubery spoke to Radio National's Critics Corner about AI disclosure. (Supplied)

One potential solution to the issue is a "human-authored" certification.

Many certification schemes are gaining traction around the world, using a range of methods including interviewing the author, asking for their edit history and using AI tools to analyse their work.

Trevor Woods, CEO of the human-authored certification company Proudly Human, said he expected the AI tools to get less and less effective over time.

In the meantime, however, the service has attracted a spike in interest which Mr Woods said could birth a "brand new industry".

Loading...

He predicts the certification industry could be worth "hundreds of millions or billions of dollars" at its height, adding that individual authors, publishers and writers' groups would be footing the bill.

When asked whether big tech companies or governments should be paying for the schemes, he said that was not a realistic aspiration.

"It's like asking the bad guys that have robbed you of everything to then give you a little bit of money back to try and make you feel better about it," he said.

Beyond the issue of writers bearing the cost of relieving readers' uncertainty around AI, Ms Doughty expressed concern about the emerging trend of using AI tools to detect AI-generated writing.

She said the tools were used to level accusations at this year's Commonwealth Short Story Prize winner, despite the prize's own investigations finding the winning work was human-authored.

"It's important for the industry to be aware of and guard against frivolous or malicious accusations of AI being used to derail a writer's career," she said.

Louise Doughty was a judge on the 2026 Commonwealth Short Story Prize. (Supplied)

She said the accusation "will always be easier to level at new authors" who did not have a body of work that AI tools could refer to, producing false positives and degrading reader trust.

"Absolutely, we must not end up with books written by AI, but we must also view AI diagnostic tools with the same level of scepticism," she said.

Ultimately, Dr Rubery says, "there will be too many challenges for this to be successful" in the long run.

But advocacy groups have tabled another solution at last week's Joint Select Committee hearings on artificial intelligence.

Groups like the Australian Publishers Association say the government should enact laws requiring the disclosure of AI use in texts, among other improvements.

However, there are fears that the government is going the other way, favouring the interests of tech companies over authors and publishers.

Copyright changes to 'displace' authors from the book market

A proposal leaked last month revealed the government was considering watering down copyright law to create an "opt-out" system where tech companies could train their AI models on authored work without permission until rights holders told them to stop.

At the Joint Select Committee hearings last week, writers and publishers urged the government not to pursue the changes.

"AI companies seeking an opt-out model are asking government to reverse a basic principle: if you want to use someone else's work, you should first seek permission," Hachette Australia and New Zealand head Louise Stark said while fronting up to the committee.

Louise Stark spoke at the committee this week. (Supplied: Hachette Australia and New Zealand)

" An opt-out model shifts the burden onto the very people whose rights should be protected. "

A submission by the Australian Society of Authors noted it was not a future issue.

Tech companies have already scraped vast amounts of authored work in what a Microsoft executive termed "the largest theft of labour in human history".

The ASA also cited a UK report which found 86 per cent of authors surveyed reported a drop in income due to generative AI.

Kylie Moore-Gilbert, author of The Uncaged Sky, attributes a drop in income to AI-generated summaries and knock-offs of her memoir posted online.

Kylie Moore-Gilbert says her memoir was scraped and reproduced with AI. (Supplied)

"If someone wanted to read a condensed version of my book in a couple of hours without paying for it, they could listen to this instead," she said.

"Each time a reader watches or listens to such a clip rather than reading or listening to my book is a sale I lose and royalties I don't receive."

Although more than 150 legal cases have been launched in the US over the use of generative AI, the courts have not yet provided definitive answers about enforcing such copyright infringements.

It means AI-generated books are free to "displace" writers from receiving compensation for their own work, says Australian Publishers Association head of policy Stuart Glover.

Tech companies train their large language models on books without permission. (Getty Images: imaginima)

Dr Glover, who also fronted the Joint Select Committee last week, said it was difficult to determine just how hard AI displacement had hit the publishing industry overall.

However, he attributes the softening of the non-fiction book market to AI.

He said instructional books such as travel guides and cookbooks were at "particular risk".

"Anything which has a hard reference edge to it I suspect is in a kind of terminal decline," he said.

"It's very much a mixed picture, and it requires responsible regulation by the government."

AI could train without paying creators, documents reveal Leaked government documents reveal AI companies would be allowed to train their models on online content without paying its creators as long as they struck deals with enough rights holders.

A crackdown on copyright would put more legal pressure on publishers to ensure their writers were not using AI.

"For copyright to subsist it must be created by a human author," Australian Copyright Council CEO Eileeen Camilleri said.

She said using an AI spell-checker or editor would not void an author's copyright, but "where you put in a prompt and get it to generate … copyright is unlikely to subsist".

Dr Glover said that was because "copyright is vested in the expression … the kind of words that you use to create a work".

"It's not vested in the underlying ideas," he said.

"If you generated an output through a machine, even if you had a really great underlying idea but you used the machine to write the idea, then you've got no way of protecting that work and anyone can copy it."

If an author has used AI and it is discovered after their book's release, the publisher may not be able to sell it exclusively.

As a result, publishers have become more vigilant about the work in their submissions inboxes — from updating author contracts and applying for human-authored certifications to getting cold feet about publishing new writers.

The Joint Select Committee on Artifical Intelligence's final report is due on November 30.

World.title: Twelve-year-old wins national slam poetry competition with 'Dear ChatGPT'
World.content:
Two months ago, Blake Mackenzie's year six teacher introduced his class to slam poetry.

While it was the first time 12-year-old Mackenzie had encountered the art form, his teacher was impressed with the poem he produced.

"[She] said, 'Hey, this is really, really good … I think you should enter this in a competition,'" he tells ABC Arts.

Mackenzie took her advice, advancing through his local heat in Newcastle and the NSW state final to make the Australian Poetry Slam national final, held at the Sydney Opera House.

There, he performed I Love My Country, a poem about racism and inequality in Australia, and Dear ChatGPT, reflecting on the impact of AI on everyday life.

Mackenzie's performance saw him named 2026 Youth Champion, an experience he likens to "a dream".

"I was so full of adrenaline, and my heart was beating so fast. It feels great even now, to be honest," he says.

"I still can't believe it."

Central Australian poet Bivor, an environmental consultant who emigrated to Australia from Bangladesh three years ago, was named 2026 Adult Champion.

Bivor was encouraged to pursue slam poetry by the executive director of Red Dirt Poetry, Laurie May. (Supplied: Nicola Bailey)

Bivor, who lives in Alice Springs, performed two poems: Ourselves, and Politics Is Doing You, a rousing plea for political literacy.

"I feel like people need to know about politics," he says.

The pair will share a $20,000 prize package, which includes publishing opportunities and invitations to perform at writers' festivals in Australia and overseas in their roles as 2026 Australian Poetry Slambassadors.

What is slam poetry?

Originating in Chicago in the 1980s, slam poetry can take any form, from a story to verse, as long as it's performed on stage in a competition.

"There's actually no such thing as slam poetry — there's no genre," Words Travel CEO Miles Merrill, a Chicagoan who brought slam poetry to Australia when he moved here in the 90s, explains.

"There's nothing that distinguishes it other than it's performed writing."

Loading Instagram content

Poetry slam contestants have two minutes to perform their work, with points docked for exceeding the time limit.

Judges, picked at random from the audience, hold up score cards rating each performance.

"We have a very scientific system where we throw five chocolates into the audience," Merrill says.

" Whoever catches a chocolate gets a PhD in poetry for the night. "

Every contestant competes in the first round, with the top five going through to the second.

Points are awarded for literary flair, the quality of the performance and its emotional heft.

Arantza García Ferrand, the 2025 Australian Poetry Slam champion, says the best slam poetry blends good writing with strong performance elements.

"The trap that sometimes people fall into is preferring one skill over the other," she says.

"This isn't just a theatre monologue, but it's also not just reciting poetry out loud. It needs to be a good mix of both to really engage your audience."

An art form for everyone

Slam poetry is defined by its accessibility, allowing poets to bypass traditional gatekeepers like editors and publishers to reach an audience.

"Anybody can get up on the mic," Merrill says.

"[As a result] there's a lot of people from diverse communities representing themselves."

Arantza García Ferrand has signed with Adelaide micro publisher Pink Shorts Press to write a memoir. (Supplied: Rory Biddell)

García Ferrand says poetry that is too highbrow can fail to land with the audience.

"When you're writing, you need to … make sure that the audience understands everything you're saying and you're not getting too complex with the word choices or the concepts."

García Ferrand, whose family emigrated to Australia from Peru when she was two, explores themes of family, immigration and culture in her work.

She also draws inspiration from everyday life.

"I love taking, like, a small intimate moment that I experience and then expanding on that and seeing how I can reflect it on bigger world issues," she says.

At the 2025 national finals, she performed Nine Suitcases and a Pram, a poem recounting her family's immigration story.

Loading Instagram content

"[It's about] everything they packed in the nine suitcases they brought to Australia — but, because it's a poem, getting a bit more metaphorical about what's in the suitcases," she says.

García Ferrand also speaks Spanish and has been experimenting with integrating the language into her poetry.

"When I first began, I was scared to use it because to me it was like, who's going to understand it in the audience?" she says.

"After having spoken to a few other Spanish poets that do use it in their work, it was such a beautiful reflection to be like, no, actually, the audience doesn't need to understand every word. And even if they don't understand the words, they understand why I'm using them."

The power of words

García Ferrand says there is a thrill in baring your soul on stage.

"Very few times in our lives do we get to have a space just for ourselves to be able to talk about something incredibly personal to us.

" To do it in a room full of people watching can be incredibly electric. "

The emotional responses poems can elicit from the crowd always surprise Merrill, who teaches a slam poetry course at NIDA.

"We're not using props or costumes or stage settings but still we're getting tears and standing ovations for people who are just standing there with a microphone," he says.

"It reinforces this idea that authentic, vulnerable, direct human-to-human communication is one of the most powerful things we can have, particularly in this age of screens."

Miles Merrill congratulating Blake Mackenzie at the Australian Poetry Slam final at Sydney Opera House. (Supplied: Nicola Bailey)

And what is Mackenzie's advice to prospective slam poets?

"Just be authentic; be you," he says.

"It's not about the competition, it's not about the points, it's just about you expressing yourself and being passionate about the message you're trying to share.

World.title: 'Critical habitat' decision could affect Macquarie Harbour salmon farms
World.content:
Tasmania's environment department is considering declaring Macquarie Harbour a "critical habitat" for the endangered Maugean skate, which could have significant ramifications for the salmon industry on the state's west coast.

If approved, it would be the first time a critical habitat has been designated since the Threatened Species Protection Act came into force three decades ago.

Plibersek did not act on advice to halt salmon farming Former environment minister Tanya Plibersek was advised by her department to revoke salmon farming approvals in Tasmania's Macquarie Harbour amid concerns about the industry's impact on the endangered Maugean skate, FOI documents show.

It would require a management plan to be developed for the purpose of protecting the prehistoric ray species, which is found only in Macquarie Harbour.

The same waterway is used by three major aquaculture companies to produce thousands of tonnes of farmed salmon each year.

Details of the critical habitat consideration were revealed in Right to Information (RTI) documents released by the Department of Natural Resources and Environment.

The Maugean skate is an endangered species found in Macquarie Harbour. (ABC News: Jordan Young)

The documents show the Scientific Advisory Committee (SAC) wrote to the department in April to say it had received advice from four independent experts who agreed:

Macquarie Harbour is "critical" to the Maugean skate's survival and recovery.

There are multiple interacting threats, "including declining dissolved oxygen, aquaculture impacts and climate influences that pose a high risk".

The threats "at least in part, [are] manageable through targeted human intervention at the scale of the harbour".

On that basis, the SAC concluded:

" Macquarie Harbour meets the criteria for designation as a critical habitat for the Maugean skate. "

Under the act, the decision on whether to declare the harbour as a critical habitat now rests with the department's secretary, Jason Jacobi.

Prime minister promises law change to protect salmon farms Anthony Albanese has written to the salmon industry to confirm laws will be introduced that will protect salmon farms on Tasmania's west coast.

In August, Mr Jacobi agreed to a $12,800 funding request for the SAC to get additional independent advice to develop the geographical boundaries for a potential declaration.

"I agree that further scientific advice on spatial delineation is the next important step … to assist SAC in evaluating a range of scientifically defensible boundary options for habitat(s), including consideration of the smallest ecologically meaningful area through to broader, practical boundary configurations where supported by evidence."

The decision on whether Macquarie Harbour will be declared critical habitat for the Maugean skate rests with environment department secretary Jason Jacobi. (ABC News: Sophie Zoellner)

Declaration would require management plan

If a critical habitat declaration is made, a management plan would then need to be developed in consultation with affected landowners and leaseholders within 90 days.

Jan McDonald, an environmental law expert at the University of Tasmania, said this could include "additional controls" on salmon farms.

"The land management plan could potentially require significant destocking and potentially the cessation of salmon aquaculture in Macquarie Harbour," Dr McDonald said.

"That really remains to be seen.

"We don't know yet what the scope of the spatial designation will be and what is ultimately indicated as necessary for the purposes of conservation and management."

Dr McDonald said a critical habitat declaration could also trigger a requirement for the government to pay compensation to affected parties.

A captive breeding program is adding to the numbers of endangered Maugean skate. (Supplied: David Moreno)

Environment group says entire harbour should be declared critical habitat

Environment Tasmania, which has been campaigning with the Environmental Defenders Office on the issue, said all of Macquarie Harbour, not just a section of it, should be declared a critical habitat.

"[The Maugean skate is] not going to respect delineation that is set by bureaucrats," Environment Tasmania's Jess Coughlan said.

"The entire harbour, including the area of the Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage Area and the areas occupied by salmon farms, are the only habitat on earth where this species exists.

"Therefore, this environment, the entirety of the harbour, is critical to its survival and the entire harbour should be listed as critical habitat."

Independent MP Peter George, who submitted the RTI request, said a designation would help protect the species.

"And if this means reducing or eliminating salmon farming, which is by far the biggest problem in that harbour, then so be it, because it is certainly of national and international importance that we look after the Maugean skate," Mr George said.

Peter George says salmon farming is "the biggest problem in that harbour". (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Tasmanian Greens deputy leader Vica Bayley said the declaration needed to be made urgently.

"We're getting into an El Niño summer where we know there's going to be marine heat wave situations and terrestrial heat wave situations," Mr Bayley said.

"And it's a significant problem, and we can't afford for the skate to suffer another long hot summer subject to the impacts of aquaculture."

Environment Tasmania says all of Macquarie Harbour should be declared critical habitat for the Maugean skate. (Supplied: Jane Ruckert)

Industry says it can coexist with Maugean skate

Salmon Tasmania did not respond directly to questions about whether it supported or opposed a potential critical habitat declaration.

But in a statement, a spokesperson said: "The salmon industry actively supports efforts to ensure the Maugean skate's long-term survival in Macquarie Harbour, contributing to both ongoing research and the oxygenation program to inform our management practices.

" The evidence shows that aquaculture coexists with the Maugean skate in the Harbour and production levels have significantly reduced as part of responsible adaptive management. "

A diesel-powered generator is used to draw up low-oxygen water, fill it with highly concentrated bubbles of oxygen and pump it back into Macquarie Harbour. (ABC News: Meg Powell)

In a statement, the department said it was committed to supporting science-based conservation of the Maugean skate.

"NRE Tas is not in a position to comment on the timing of any decision, the potential extent of any area that may be considered, or any implications for particular industries, activities, approvals or licences.

"Any consideration of a declaration would be subject to a consultation process that takes on board the views of all affected stakeholders."

It also said recent monitoring results had shown "encouraging signs" for the Maugean skate population and environmental conditions in Macquarie Harbour.

Maugean skate from a captive breeding program have been released into Macquarie Harbour. (Supplied: Mark Priest)

Maugean skate numbers fell by almost 50 per cent between 2014 and 2021 due to reduced oxygen levels, which coincided with a substantial increase in salmon farming.

The dramatic decline prompted environmental groups to seek a review of the federal government's 2012 approval of the expansion of salmon farming in Macquarie Harbour.

The oxygenation project started in response to concerns about low oxygen levels in the water at Macquarie Harbour. (ABC News: Meg Powell)

But before the federal election last year, parliament passed an amendment barring reconsideration of approvals for industries that have operated for more than five years.

Earlier this year, the federal environment minister decided not to "uplist" the Maugean skate from endangered to critically endangered, based on advice from the independent Threatened Species Scientific Committee.

Several skates were released into the harbour in June as part of a captive breeding program designed to protect the species.

World.title: Business Council names Victoria worst state for business, again
World.content:
The peak business body has again branded Victoria the worst Australian jurisdiction to operate in, because of its relatively high taxes and complicated licensing rules.

The Business Council's "regulation rumble", an annual ranking of state and territory policies, has placed the state last every year since the first edition in 2023. South Australia has topped the list every year, and did so again.

Bran Black, the lobby's chief executive, said Victoria "continues to face serious challenges" and that its "high taxes and unnecessary regulation" were factors in the state's sluggish economy and high unemployment.

Victorian Premier Ben Carroll has attempted to reposition the 12-year-old Labor government as pro-business after taking the leadership in the final months before the November election.

Tax down? Top ranking

The ranking represents the Business Council's subjective assessment of favourable business policies. States are rewarded for lower taxes on payrolls and on land, whether via land taxes or stamp duties.

They are also rewarded for approving planning applications faster, making licensing simpler, and making workers' compensation and insurance cheaper.

While the rankings have not changed much over four years, several jurisdictions have improved their standings by streamlining their planning systems as part of nationwide efforts to boost housing construction.

While Victoria is streamlining planning approvals through its 'Better Decisions Made Faster' laws, this was not factored into the rankings because the legislated reform does not take effect until 2027. The council noted the laws would likely see improvements.

Southern lights

South Australia's strength in the rankings comes chiefly from its payroll tax, which has the lowest average rates. It is also the only jurisdiction to adjust the thresholds for payroll tax for inflation. The Business Council says payroll taxes discourage job growth.

The state is also rewarded for its simplified licensing system, a particular concern for the Business Council. Whereas the most complex state, Tasmania, had 38 separate hoops for a cafe owner to set up shop, South Australia had far fewer.

The Northern Territory bolstered its standing because of its efforts to speed up approvals. New South Wales also sped up its planning system, but its system remains among the most complex and is still wracked with delays. The state ranks fifth overall.

South Australia came at the top of the table, as it has for each of the four years the rankings have been published. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

The ACT ranks highly because it does not levy land tax on commercial property and has relatively low stamp duties. The council does not differentiate between the two types of property taxes, although economists say stamp duties are less efficient.

Queensland and Western Australia are ranked sixth and seventh, Queensland penalised chiefly for its heavy restriction on retail trading hours, its disparate planning rules and its high land taxes, and Western Australia for levying payroll tax on smaller businesses.

Mr Black said businesses were "buried under mountains of red tape" across Australia, which was "wasting time and money", but saw some bright spots, especially from the wave of planning reforms.

"Everyone can lift their game by learning from what others are doing well … There's a lot to be optimistic about. Reform is starting to land," he said, adding that the federal government was also working across jurisdictions "to even out the rules".

Business wooed ahead of state election

Both major parties in Victoria have promised to lift the land tax-free threshold, rolling back changes made in 2024 by former premiers Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan, which captured an extra 250,000 Victorian workers.

Labor's proposed wind-back would be slower than that of the Coalition, which has also pledged to remove payroll tax for private schools and remove stamp duty for first homebuyers.

Victorian Opposition Leader Jess Wilson and Premier Ben Carroll have both offered forms of payroll tax relief. (ABC News)

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has promoted both lower taxes and lower debt as part of her election pitch, though several economists have raised doubts about her "contradictory" policies.

"We have to get business back at the centre of the economy, investing and creating jobs in this state," Ms Wilson told a business lunch on Tuesday for the Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

"I want to keep working with you to find competitive advantages and maximise growth and jobs," Mr Carroll told the same forum.

While the Coalition needs to overcome a 16-seat deficit to form a majority government, polling suggests Ms Wilson is most likely to be victorious next month.

World.title: Crossbench push to give Australians a free way to fight back against big tech
World.content:
Australians would have a free and simple way to raise complaints against tech giants under a crossbench amendment to Labor’s proposed digital safety laws.

Independents and the Greens are in favour of establishing a new industry-funded online ombudsman to resolve disputes, but the federal government has argued its draft digital duty of care bill already puts the onus on big tech to provide Australians with effective complaint pathways.

Mackellar MP Sophie Scamps will today put forward an amendment that would create an external avenue for appeal in cases like a small business owner being locked out of their social media account or individuals wanting harmful content addressed.

Labor has the numbers in parliament to pass the bill in the lower house without entertaining any changes but needs the support of the Greens, who are also in favour of an online ombudsman, to get the duty of care through the Senate next month.

Wells opens door to lawsuits against big tech Labor is considering a Greens push to let Australians sue online platforms for harm as the Coalition maintains its opposition to new digital safety laws.

The Coalition party room yesterday resolved to oppose the legislation after likening the digital duty of care to political censorship.

Labor's proposed duty would require online platforms like Facebook, TikTok and Instagram to take reasonable steps to prevent a range of harms for children, including bullying, misogyny and content promoting eating disorders.

Big tech would also have to limit adults' exposure to "serious" harms like threats of violence, stalking and the non-consensual sharing of intimate images.

The bill would also pave the way for Australians aged 16 and over to switch off algorithm-driven feeds and see content only from accounts they chose to follow.

Push for independent big tech watchdog

Ms Scamps said establishing an Online Services Ombudsman within the remit of the existing Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman would help people who currently felt "powerless" to resolve their problems.

"For many Australians, dealing with big tech platforms can feel like shouting into the void, with complaints met by automated responses, endless online forms or no meaningful response at all," she said.

" When platforms fail to act, there is nowhere independent to turn. "

Ms Scamps said Labor's bill provided for stronger internal complaints and dispute resolution processes, but that alone was "not enough".

Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman Cynthia Gebert said the crossbench amendment was the "missing piece" in the government's digital agenda.

"People want someone to turn to when they're locked out of their social media account without warning or realistic avenue to appeal against big tech companies," she said.

Ms Gebert said thousands of people and small businesses were already reaching out seeking help she was unable to provide despite wanting to.

"The TIO stands ready to expand our role to help people when things go wrong online," she said.

Greens want laws with 'teeth'

Greens communications spokeswoman Sarah Hanson-Young said her party would be fighting to ensure the digital duty of care had "real teeth," prioritising tougher fines and the right to privately sue big tech.

"We know that these companies only respond to one thing: penalties that hit them where it hurts," she said.

Senator Hanson-Young said Australians also needed an external complaints pathway that was free from the "whims" of big tech moderators.

"This would put the safety of user, accountability and basic decency ahead of corporate profits," she said.

Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young says her party wants to see an option to privately sue big tech. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

A spokeswoman for Communications Minister Anika Wells said the government understood how "frustrating" it was for Australians to report a complaint to a tech company and hear nothing back.

She said Labor's proposal empowered the eSafety commissioner to create "enforceable standards" to resolve disputes, which currently do not exist.

The Coalition will oppose Labor's bill, with Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson taking issue with what she described as "dangerously vague" definitions and concerns the government would be able to spread propaganda.

"This is information control because of the wide range of discretion, both of the minister and also the eSafety commissioner, to determine what is harm online," she told News24 earlier this week.

World.title: Israel election 2026 LIVE updates: Netanyahu, Eisenkot go head-to-head in nation’s first election since October 7 attacks
World.content:
Good morning and thanks for joining our live coverage of Israel’s election, which is widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s almost two decades in power.

Polls close at 10pm in Israel (7am AEDT) in the first national elections since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, a day that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil.

By 6pm and with hours remaining until polls closed, nearly 67 per cent of eligible voters had cast a ballot, according to Israel’s central election committee, the highest since 1973.

Netanyahu’s hold on power is at stake, with the prospect of a return to war with Iran dominating the final days of the campaign.

Centrist rivals are promising to usher in a new era, but the polls have shown a close result between the two blocs, and it may take time before clear results are known.

Voters line up to cast their ballots. AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg

Israeli media reports passed by the official military censor and published in the final days of the campaign have stated that Netanyahu pressured his military chief to provoke a confrontation with Iran ahead of the elections, suggesting high-level leaks from within the defence establishment. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz denied the reports.

US President Donald Trump told Fox News on the weekend he was deciding whether to “make a deal” with Iran or “finish it off”, adding: “It’s getting to be decision time.”

Netanyahu posted an alarming AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv and spoke about using cryptocurrency to avoid international sanctions in the final days of the campaign.

World.title: The worrying pattern confronting Steve Smith and Australia
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket The worrying pattern confronting Steve Smith and Australia Daniel Brettig October 28, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Cape Town: Australia’s coach Andrew McDonald presaged this match by speaking about how Steve Smith’s remarkable Test career would deserve prolonged celebration whenever he retired. But there was no sense of celebration among Pat Cummins’ team about how abruptly Smith withdrew himself from the team for its return to Newlands for the first time since the 2018 ball tampering scandal. The episode will hasten discussions about how much longer the 37-year-old has left in the baggy green cap. Steve Smith during the second Test. AP Mitchell Starc stuck pointedly to matter-of-fact words about Smith’s neck niggle after the game, while a selection of furrowed brows and raised eyebrows from others made it clear that the series of events this week and on match morning had not gone down particularly well. “Didn’t know anything about it until well, I sort of knew something was going on yesterday when I was trying to get my laundry at the hotel and I couldn’t get in the room,” Starc said. “But I didn’t know he wasn’t playing until I went out to warm up today.”





“You don’t play 100-odd Test matches without playing Test matches where you’re not 100 per cent fit, so hopefully that’s the case this week,” Cummins said. “Even though he’s probably not going to be 100 per cent, hopefully he can compartmentalise that, like he’s done many times before with other things, and can come out and ... contribute like he does every week.” On Tuesday morning, Smith arrived early to the ground with head coach McDonald, selection chair George Bailey and assistant Michael Di Venuto, alongside team doctor Leigh Golding. Australia’s Steve Smith receives medical attention during day four of the second Test. AP Photo He walked to the Newlands nets with a heat patch on the left side of his neck, the trouble area that has affection since the first innings of the Gqeberha Test, and faced a few deliveries from Di Venuto before walking out of the net, speaking with McDonald and Golding and ruling himself out of the game.





As one former Australian player once said of another cricketer of recent vintage, the player’s “biggest downfall” was that they had to get “pushed onto the ground to play”, and teammates and selectors “just got sick of it in the end”. Smith came to South Africa wanting to make an impact, but he was also clearly concerned about unwanted triggers from the past. His media engagement has been restricted to one interview with Howard in Gqeberha, while fellow vice-captain Travis Head has steadily taken on greater levels of responsibility. There is no suggestion that the current Australian setup want to push Smith out the door. Quite the contrary in fact. “It’ll be a big loss, no doubt, when he goes to fill the space of runs there, and it’s probably going to be more of a collective, isn’t it, to bridge the gap between, you know, a player that’s averaged 55 and whoever comes in and not putting the expectations on that player that replaces him at four to be able to do that?” McDonald had said. Steve Smith seen nursing his injured neck during the second Test of the series. Fox Cricket



“But I think it’s going to be an ongoing conversation. The longer he plays for us at this level, I think the better we will be. But if the day comes where he does, you know, decide to retire, then we’ll respect that, celebrate it. We’ll celebrate it, and hopefully it can be seen as a celebration rather than shifting to what’s next.” Yet for all that strong sentiment, even Smith’s biggest backers ended this day with questions about his overall health, happiness and the sustainability of an approach that, this week at least, looked like it required 100 per cent comfort in order to perform. World.title: The parents ditching IVF and embracing the ‘turkey baster’
World.content:
Sydney couple Emma Mansell and Sarah Hopkins conceived three of their four children with the “turkey baster method”. Facebook groups, Reddit threads and good old-fashioned set-ups from mutual friends are some of the ways parents are finding private sperm donors.

Bungles, cost-of-living pressures and sperm shortages are only some of the reasons Australians are fleeing the regulated system. But what awaits them in the “Wild West”?

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Emma Mansell always dreamed of a “cheaper by the dozen family”. After growing up an only child, the wholesome, busy chaos of a large family held great appeal. But with out-of-pocket costs typically $5000 to $10,000 per IVF cycle in Australia, the double-digit dream remained unreachable. “The reality was that if I wanted my big family, I had to find a different way,” Mansell said. Instead, Mansell had three children in Sydney’s northern beaches through what’s colloquially known as the “turkey baster method” after an online search for a sperm donor. Mansell and Hopkins with their children Aubrey-Rose, 8, Brooklyn-Louise, 9 and Kennedy, 6, who were conceived through informal sperm donation, and Hendrix, 3, conceived through IVF. Glenn Campbell Just as “test tube babies” (children born from IVF) are not actually created or grown in test tubes, a turkey baster – the giant bulb pipette-like kitchen tool, used for keeping roasting meat moist – is usually not the vehicle for semen during at-home artificial insemination.



Instruments vary. One Adelaide Hills mother told this masthead she used a menstrual disc. But the honour is mostly reserved for needle-free syringes, which is what Mansell used to start a family. “We stayed in really fancy hotels,” Mansell said. “The donor just looked like a businessman who was coming in [for] a meeting.” Mansell and wife Sarah Hopkins waited in the hall while the donor completed his end of the deal, before coming back into the room to finish the job. “It’s totally awkward,” Mansell said. “No one’s comfortable with the process.” “It never feels normal ... but it’s like brushing your teeth – you have to do it to have clean teeth. I had to do this to get pregnant.” The number of Australians bypassing licensed sperm banks and IVF clinics in favour of private donor agreements and at-home insemination is unknown.





Fifteen women learned this the hard way, inadvertently giving birth to 27 half-siblings from the same Melbourne donor between 2020 and 2024. Many met the man through the popular Facebook group Sperm Donation Australia. The group’s Perth-based founder Adam Hooper claimed the donor in question was banned from the group in 2021, which the donor disputes. Related Article Opinion

Fertility Our fertility industry is a mess. As a donor, I know what could fix it Gary Nunn Contributor In the regulated system, clinics are responsible for tracking how many families have had children from the same donor, to comply with local statutory limits. Victoria caps sperm donors at 10 families and New South Wales at five, partly to prevent accidental incest between half-siblings. Hooper said births among his Facebook group had recently dropped – with 606 reported in 2025, down from 903 in 2023 – which he attributed to heightened cost-of-living pressures. This masthead cannot independently verify the number of births, which were self-reported by parents on Hooper’s website. Sperm Donation Australia has about 23,000 members, but it’s not the only group of its kind. Private donors can also be found in smaller area- and year-specific Facebook groups, Reddit threads, international websites, Tinder-like apps and beyond.



Ellie Sedgwick loved the idea of raising a baby on her own. Earlier this year, she conceived through the turkey-baster method with a man who previously donated to a Victorian clinic. Her son is due in February. Audrey Richardson After six years researching every possible pathway to single motherhood, Ellie Sedgwick has seen them all. Born and raised on Sydney’s northern beaches, the 36-year-old photographer traverses the country in her Toyota Coaster. She didn’t want a partner putting a stop to that because they had welcomed a child together. Related Article Fertility Single at 30, Chloe decided to freeze her eggs. She wasn’t prepared for what came next She also didn’t want to be stuck co-parenting with a former partner she “absolutely hates”. “I honestly always liked the idea of doing it on my own,” Sedgwick told this masthead while on a women’s retreat in Lombok. “I’ve never doubted that I could do it.” Her grandmother suggested a sperm donor. Sedgwick was open to the idea – she is bisexual, and knew she would have to go down that avenue anyway if she ended up with a woman – but IVF was too expensive.

World.title: ASX set to edge up, tech stocks drive Wall Street higher
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to edge up, tech stocks drive Wall Street higher Stan Choe October 28, 2026 — 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are leading Wall Street mostly higher as their yo-yo moves swing back upward. The S&P 500 rose 0.6 per cent and pulled within 1.3 per cent of its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 39 points, or 0.1 per cent, in early afternoon trade, and the Nasdaq composite was 1.2 per cent higher. Wall Street was boosted by strength in technology stocks. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to edge higher, with futures pointing to a rise of 11 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.5 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US70.28¢ at 5.10am AEDT. The majority of stocks within the S&P 500 were falling, but the gains for influential AI stocks made up for that. AI stocks are on track for a second winning day after swerving for weeks on worries about whether their boom is under threat because of how expensive it’s become for companies to borrow money to build data centres and buy more AI chips.



Broadcom climbed 4 per cent after announcing a $US63 billion ($89.7 billion) financing deal where several Wall Street firms will help Anthropic get access to Broadcom’s XPU AI accelerators and networking solutions. Elsewhere in the industry, Nvidia rose 1 per cent and was the only force stronger than Broadcom pushing the S&P 500 higher. CoreWeave, a company that’s borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, jumped 7.3 per cent, though it’s been careening between big gains and losses within each of the past few days. Related Article Opinion

AI ‘Bold, but sane’? The future of AI is riding on Anthropic’s float Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist General Motors climbed 5.5 per cent after saying it’s moving its stock from a listing on the New York Stock Exchange to the Nasdaq. The automaker said the Nasdaq, which is home to several of the world’s biggest technology stocks, is a fit for its tech-driven strategy. The move could also allow GM to join the Nasdaq 100 index, which would force investment funds that mimic the index to buy it. GM began trading on the NYSE in 1911.



JetBlue Airways flew 18.8 per cent higher even though it reported a larger loss for the summer than analysts expected. CEO Joanna Geraghty said the company expects to return to making sustained operating profits next year and to deliver at least $US1 in earnings per share in 2028. Investors may have been bracing for something worse after the airline’s stock came into the day with a loss of nearly 48 per cent for the year so far. Another travel company, Royal Caribbean Group, also helped lead the market and rose 8.4 per cent. The cruise operator delivered a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, while raising its forecast for profit over the full year. Companies overall are under pressure to deliver big growth in profits. Expectations are high among financial analysts and investors, and that’s what allowed their stock prices to run to records recently despite high inflation, high interest rates and other concerns weighing on the market. Boeing fell 9.4 per cent after reporting a larger loss for the latest quarter than analysts expected.



Hilton Worldwide Holdings sank 3.4 per cent after reporting weaker revenue for the summer than analysts expected. It also gave a range as a forecast for profit in the final three months of the year whose midpoint fell below analysts’ expectations. The hotel company said it expects to see “increased impact from the Middle East” during the quarter. Sherwin-Williams fell 2.6 per cent after delivering a weaker profit than analysts expected. High mortgage rates have helped chill the housing industry, which in turn pressures demand for the paints and coatings Sherwin-Williams sells. Related Article Unfair dismissal Coles worker sacked after restraining suspected thief to receive $6500 “Customer sentiment and the leading indicators we track point to muted demand over the remainder of the year and into 2027,” CEO Heidi Petz said. At the same time, her company is dealing with inflation pushing up its costs for raw materials. Confidence among US shoppers has tumbled recently as pressure keeps building on them from high inflation. But a report on Tuesday said that US consumer confidence improved in October, when economists expected further weakening.



In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady a day before the Federal Reserve is scheduled to announce its latest decision on interest rates. The Fed last month hiked the fed funds rate for the first time in three years in hopes of slowing inflation, but the widespread expectation on Wall Street is that it will hold rates steady this time. The yield on the 10-year Treasury remained at 5.00 per cent, where it was late Monday. Helping to keep yields in check was a drop for oil prices. The price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 1.1 per cent to $US109.51. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. Stocks jumped 3.1 per cent in Seoul and fell 1.3 per cent in Shanghai for two of the bigger moves. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
