World.title: The type of borrower falling behind on their mortgage
World.content:
PropertyNewsHome loans The type of borrower falling behind on their mortgage Alice Uribe October 28, 2026 — 5:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

Borrowers who took out home loans requiring low documentation, including self-employed or small business owners, are falling into arrears at a greater level than the rest of the mortgage market. Mortgages classed as non-performing, or 90 or more days behind on repayments, have remained relatively steady over recent years, sitting at 1.0 per cent of loans for the June 2026 quarter, according to Australian Prudential Regulation Authority data analysed by Canstar. But arrears have edged higher for low-doc lending by banks recently, hitting 4.9 per cent of outstanding loans for the June quarter, up from 4.2 per cent at the same time in 2025. The main originators of low-doc loans are non-bank lenders, and these types of loans comprise a small percentage of all mortgages among banks, experts say. Low-doc home loans are designed for small business owners and sole traders who aren’t able to provide full paperwork, including tax returns, to pass a bank’s standard serviceability checks.



Loans requiring low documentation may attract higher rates than traditional mortgages with recent rate hikes putting a “squeeze” on those paying higher than average rates, Canstar’s data insights director Sally Tindall said. Related Article Interest rates How far house prices have risen since the last time rates were this high “When the RBA tightens the screws on mortgages, the pressure on low-doc borrowers tends to increase even further as they’re usually already paying a premium on their interest rate,” she said. “If cash flow then tightens on the back of a cut down in consumer spending, those low-doc borrowers who don’t have a decent buffer can quickly find themselves with zero breathing room.” According to research from Canstar, one non-bank lender offers an advertised interest rate for a low-doc home loan starting at about 7 per cent, but only if the borrower has 45 per cent equity in their loan. The rate then climbs to as high as about 12.29 per cent for those with smaller deposits.



APRA data shows low-doc loans comprise about 0.1 per cent of all mortgages among banks. “However this does not illustrate the volume of low-doc loans in the broader mortgage market,” said Tindall, noting a number of non-bank lenders still offer these types of loans. Loans requiring low documentation may attract higher rates than traditional mortgages. Sam Mooy Erin Kitson, an analyst at S&P Global Ratings said, while not presenting a systemic risk, low-doc loans were more vulnerable to arrears, as it was often self-employed borrowers who take them out. “The cashflows of these borrowers are more exposed to deteriorating economic conditions, including rising interest rates, given the more direct impact it has on their income,” she said.



“Borrowers with low-doc loans are more likely to experience arrears pressure before more traditional loan types, given the greater sensitivity of self-employed borrowers’ cashflows to changing economic conditions.” Chief executive of mortgage brokerage Shore Financial Theo Chambers said higher rates and economic conditions could be a contributing factor to arrears levels, rather than low-doc borrowers being “necessarily higher-risk customers.” Most home owners are up to date with their mortgages. Oscar Colman “In reality, many are successful self-employed individuals and business owners with strong assets, substantial equity and healthy cash flow, but whose income doesn’t always fit the traditional assessment model,” he said. “Low-doc loans are already priced at higher interest rates, and therefore they’ve had rate rises to an already higher rate, coupled with pressure on higher living costs have placed on households and small businesses.”



Anthony Landahl, managing director at mortgage broker Equilibria Finance said all the banks had “good, strong, attractive offers” for self-employed borrowers. “Low-doc loans are mainly provided by second-tier providers, as distinct from the main banks, but they absolutely still have a role in our lending space,” he said. There is a misconception that low-doc home loans are more risky, experts say. Louie Douvis “And there is a bit of a misconception around low-doc loans that they’re more risky. But we don’t find that they’re more risky by their nature. Many low-doc borrowers are successful self-employed Australians whose income doesn’t fit traditional PAYG [Pay As You Go] lending models.” Landahl said there were strong lending standards.



“It’s still got to meet all of the consumer lending criteria. Verification requirements are still strong, and borrowers ultimately need to demonstrate they can service the loan.” Related Article Residential property Housing with benefits: Why co-housing could be the new Australian dream Kitson said arrears spikes for low-doc loans could be more pronounced than other loan types because of the declining balance outstanding of these types of loans across the broader mortgage market. “Based on APRA stats, they now comprise around 0.12 per cent of total loans outstanding, down from 0.88 per cent back in 2019, so the declining denominator will cause a more pronounced increase in arrears in percentage terms,” she said. Mortgage arrears across the country remain low despite a recent pickup, according to the RBA, with support from the strong labour market and savings buffers.



But Kitson said recent interest rate rises are yet to surface in mortgage arrears performance as there is often a lag between a rate increase and the increase in a borrower’s actual mortgage repayment. “Rising cost-of-living pressures are not yet manifesting in material arrears increases. Mortgage arrears are one of the last places for financial pressure to manifest,” she said. Property alerts are now available in the SMH and Age apps. World.title: Thinking of delaying downsizing? It could cost you more than you think
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingProperty downsizing Opinion Thinking of delaying downsizing? It could cost you more than you think Rachel Lane Money contributor October 28, 2026 — 5:01am

October 28, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The most common downsizing regret I hear isn’t selling at the wrong price, it’s not making the move sooner. When property prices fall, it is tempting to put your downsizing plans on hold. Nobody wants to sell their home for less than they think it was worth six months or a year ago. But before you decide to wait, ask yourself three questions. What matters is not just what you sell your current home for but what it will cost to move and how much you will have left over. Dominic Lorrimer Have you really lost money or just missed the peak? If you have owned your home for decades, chances are you bought it for a fraction of what it is worth today. Even if the market has softened, you can still be selling for a considerable profit. Take a home that was worth $1.2 million at the start of the year but could achieve $1.1 million today. If you bought it for $250,000 three decades ago, you might feel you have lost $100,000. In reality you are selling for $850,000 more than you paid, before allowing for inflation, improvements and ownership costs.



The old investment mantra “time in the market, not timing the market” is worth heeding. You will never pick the top or the bottom of a market – no one can. You only know the top has passed when prices fall, and the bottom was reached when prices start recovering. Editor's pick Opinion

Aged care How a rule change could save aged care users thousands Rachel Lane Money contributor The property market moves in cycles; “riding it out” could mean waiting years. Exactly how long depends on how much further prices fall and how quickly they recover. There is no guarantee the price you are chasing can be achieved again and it’s a very real risk that you end up selling for less than you could have today. What could your home buy you today? Every home costs money to hold, and rates, insurance and maintenance continue regardless of market changes. There is also an opportunity cost. The money tied up in your home could be released to invest, spend or buy a more suitable property (or a combination thereof).



If you are selling one home and buying another, your next home may also change in value, and not necessarily in the same direction or at the same rate. Changes in the property market don’t affect every property in the same way at the same time. What matters is not just what you sell your current home for but what it will cost to move and how much you will have left over. How do you want to spend the next chapter? The cost of waiting is not just financial. It can affect your health, happiness and independence. If staying means struggling with stairs, battling maintenance or becoming socially isolated, what is the price of holding on? Your home might be worth more in the future but that does not guarantee you will be better off. Where you live affects how you live, so your lifestyle deserves a place in the decision.



When it comes to downsizing decisions, sometimes the biggest loss is not the money you think you have missed out on but the time spent waiting for the perfect moment to begin your next chapter. Rachel Lane is the author of Downsizing Made Simple, a book and website aimed at demystifying downsizing. Advice given in this article is general in nature and not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.content:

As the long-awaited M1 extension to Bankstown opens on Friday, we take a look at how it happened and what it means for the city. See all stories .

The number of passengers forecast to board driverless trains has been increased at four stations along the final stretch of Sydney’s $30 billion M1 metro line during the morning peak hour, as expectations grow about the popularity of services from the south-west into the central city. The patronage forecast for the 8am to 9am peak on weekdays has been raised the most for Dulwich Hill station – up by 300 passengers to 1000 – followed by stations at Hurlstone Park, Canterbury and Belmore, which each have been increased by 200 commuters. Locals check out the renovated Dulwich Hill station on the M1 metro line during a community open day in August. Sitthixay Ditthavong The projections for Bankstown and Campsie have dropped by 100 passengers each to 2100 and 1400, respectively, from forecasts last year. The drop for Bankstown has been attributed to reductions in on-street parking spaces. Residential development is the main driver of changes to forecasts by Sydney Metro for stations along the south-west section, as well as the fact that there had been two years of growth since the T3 heavy rail line was closed to be converted to carry driverless trains. The M1 line’s final stage between Bankstown and Sydenham will open early on Friday.



Sydney Metro customer and planning executive director Samantha Phillips said the changes to the station patronage modelling primarily reflect residential development in areas along the corridor, and expected demand for high-frequency train services. “[The modelling is] showing a higher number of people using the metro than previously on the T3 [heavy rail line], and also people’s propensity to choose it because of the higher frequency and higher reliability,” she said. Phillips said she was curious to watch, once the line opens, the extent to which people walked further than usual or caught other public transport such as light rail to “travel back to go forward” on metro trains. “Our models suggest that some people will do that because it’s a faster trip,” she said. “Safety, reliability and frequency – they’re the three things that really drive customer satisfaction and keep people turning up.”



The modelling forecasts 9500 passengers will use the south-west section from 8am to 9am on weekdays, a 34 per cent rise on patronage on the T3 heavy rail line before it was closed in September 2024. The latest forecasts represent a 10 per cent increase in passengers in the hour-long period compared to Sydney Metro’s estimates in September last year of 8600 commuters when the line opens. Bankstown metro station is at the southern end of the M1 line. Sitthixay Ditthavong Sydney Metro is forecasting a 13 per cent surge to 300,000 passenger trips on weekdays along the M1 line when the final 13-kilometre south-west section opens and extends it to 66 kilometres of track between Tallawong and Bankstown via the central city. Phillips expects people to use cycling and pedestrian paths along the corridor to access metro stations and catch trains. “There’s going to be a lot of people wanting to cycle up or walk up and access the service,” she said.



Inner West Council Mayor Darcy Byrne said the easier transport access provided by the metro line from other parts of the city would be a shot in the arm for the local economy, especially nightlife and hospitality. Related Article Sydney Metro Why some train doors will not open when final section of Sydney’s metro line starts Byrne said significant increases in homes planned near the metro stations would also make residential developments more feasible. “Over the next decade, with the metro open and our housing plans approved, you’ll see significant increase in housing along the south-west line,” he said. “The point of the metro is that you’re providing a really good long-term public transport option that can support the increased housing that will come over time.” The $57 million GreenWay, which weaves north to south through five inner-west suburbs, was completed last year, while a 13.8-kilometre pathway dubbed the MetroWay will be built parallel to the Southwest Metro line. The two will intersect at Dulwich Hill.



Planning consent requires the MetroWay to be completed within two years of the opening of the metro train line between Bankstown and Sydenham. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: I have a very personal health condition. How much do I need to share at work?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? I have a very personal health condition. How much do I need to share at work? Kirstin Ferguson October 28, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Each week Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: a personal health condition, a nosy direction and feeling taken for granted. You don’t need to apologise for wanting the details of your condition to remain private. Dionne Gain I have been diagnosed with a medical condition of a very personal nature. I will need several scattered days off and possibly two weeks for an operation. My colleagues are extremely nosy, while my manager tells his EA everything, and she then circulates it around the office. I am angry at the thought of everyone knowing my business and continually questioning me. Should I invent a less personal procedure as a cover story, or am I legally required to tell my employer exactly what treatment I am having? Related Article Got a Minute? Can my boss really tell me what I can or can’t do on my lunch break? Do not invent a cover story. You don’t need to and doing so means you are being dishonest and will need to remember details which will ultimately undermine your credibility, right as you want your employer to respect your boundaries.



That said, you also don’t need to tell your employer your full medical history. They need to know you have to take medical leave and how long it will be, and you will need some paperwork from your doctor to show you are unfit for work. On your return, your employer will have to know whether you have any restrictions they should be aware of. The ins and outs of what you are having done are your business. I would put in writing to your manager a note to the effect that you will require leave for a medical procedure, and you will provide the necessary medical certificate and paperwork. I would also note in writing that you prefer to keep your medical information confidential and ask them to do the same. If anyone asks what your medical condition is, simply say, “I am just having a simple procedure which I prefer to keep private. Thanks for understanding.” Do not feel you need to apologise, and be consistent in your response. I am new to an HR manager role and struggling to protect staff confidentiality. Whenever an employee leaves my office after a private discussion, one director immediately demands all the details. He then appears to share them with other managers, who have mentioned matters they should not know. I told him some conversations were highly personal and should remain confidential, but he insists that, as a director, he is entitled to know about every staff issue. I am sure this is wrong, but how should I respond?



You are right to be concerned about this. If people feel they can’t confide in you, no one will be coming back to tell you issues that the business needs you to know. Related Article Got a Minute? My colleagues exclude me from conversations. Why are people so rude? Your director needs to understand that being in their role does not automatically entitle them to information. I think you need to set a clear guideline or policy with the chief executive or board governing confidential employee information. It could be something like a commitment from you to escalate any matters to them where it requires organisational action or a material risk. This could include disclosures around health and safety concerns, serious misconduct, legal obligations or key decisions the organisation must make. The guidelines or policy should then agree that everything else has to remain confidential to you to preserve the credibility of the HR role and to uphold individual privacy concerns. You might also want to try and move your office, so it is not so obvious who is coming in to meet you, and you don’t have every nosy parker on your doorstop the moment they leave. I work in distribution alongside a cleaner, a driver and an assistant stock manager. I reliably complete my duties, but two colleagues regularly tell management they have done work that I actually performed. They have now been recognised and rewarded for my contribution, while I feel as though I have been pushed aside and treated like nobody. I want to ask my manager for support, but I am unsure whether it is appropriate or how to explain what has been happening. What should I do?

World.title: Israel election 2026 LIVE updates: Netanyahu, Eisenkot go head-to-head in nation’s first election since October 7 attacks
World.content:
Good morning and thanks for joining our live coverage of Israel’s election, which is widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s almost two decades in power.

Polls close at 10pm in Israel (7am AEDT) in the first national elections since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, a day that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil.

By 6pm and with hours remaining until polls closed, nearly 67 per cent of eligible voters had cast a ballot, according to Israel’s central election committee, the highest since 1973.

Netanyahu’s hold on power is at stake, with the prospect of a return to war with Iran dominating the final days of the campaign.

Centrist rivals are promising to usher in a new era, but the polls have shown a close result between the two blocs, and it may take time before clear results are known.

Voters line up to cast their ballots. AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg

Israeli media reports passed by the official military censor and published in the final days of the campaign have stated that Netanyahu pressured his military chief to provoke a confrontation with Iran ahead of the elections, suggesting high-level leaks from within the defence establishment. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz denied the reports.

US President Donald Trump told Fox News on the weekend he was deciding whether to “make a deal” with Iran or “finish it off”, adding: “It’s getting to be decision time.”

Netanyahu posted an alarming AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv and spoke about using cryptocurrency to avoid international sanctions in the final days of the campaign.

World.title: The worrying pattern confronting Steve Smith and Australia
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket The worrying pattern confronting Steve Smith and Australia Daniel Brettig October 28, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Cape Town: Australia’s coach Andrew McDonald presaged this match by speaking about how Steve Smith’s remarkable Test career would deserve prolonged celebration whenever he retired. But there was no sense of celebration among Pat Cummins’ team about how abruptly Smith withdrew himself from the team for its return to Newlands for the first time since the 2018 ball tampering scandal. The episode will hasten discussions about how much longer the 37-year-old has left in the baggy green cap. Steve Smith during the second Test. AP Mitchell Starc stuck pointedly to matter-of-fact words about Smith’s neck niggle after the game, while a selection of furrowed brows and raised eyebrows from others made it clear that the series of events this week and on match morning had not gone down particularly well. “Didn’t know anything about it until well, I sort of knew something was going on yesterday when I was trying to get my laundry at the hotel and I couldn’t get in the room,” Starc said. “But I didn’t know he wasn’t playing until I went out to warm up today.”





“You don’t play 100-odd Test matches without playing Test matches where you’re not 100 per cent fit, so hopefully that’s the case this week,” Cummins said. “Even though he’s probably not going to be 100 per cent, hopefully he can compartmentalise that, like he’s done many times before with other things, and can come out and ... contribute like he does every week.” On Tuesday morning, Smith arrived early to the ground with head coach McDonald, selection chair George Bailey and assistant Michael Di Venuto, alongside team doctor Leigh Golding. Australia’s Steve Smith receives medical attention during day four of the second Test. AP Photo He walked to the Newlands nets with a heat patch on the left side of his neck, the trouble area that has affection since the first innings of the Gqeberha Test, and faced a few deliveries from Di Venuto before walking out of the net, speaking with McDonald and Golding and ruling himself out of the game.





As one former Australian player once said of another cricketer of recent vintage, the player’s “biggest downfall” was that they had to get “pushed onto the ground to play”, and teammates and selectors “just got sick of it in the end”. Smith came to South Africa wanting to make an impact, but he was also clearly concerned about unwanted triggers from the past. His media engagement has been restricted to one interview with Howard in Gqeberha, while fellow vice-captain Travis Head has steadily taken on greater levels of responsibility. There is no suggestion that the current Australian setup want to push Smith out the door. Quite the contrary in fact. “It’ll be a big loss, no doubt, when he goes to fill the space of runs there, and it’s probably going to be more of a collective, isn’t it, to bridge the gap between, you know, a player that’s averaged 55 and whoever comes in and not putting the expectations on that player that replaces him at four to be able to do that?” McDonald had said. Steve Smith seen nursing his injured neck during the second Test of the series. Fox Cricket



“But I think it’s going to be an ongoing conversation. The longer he plays for us at this level, I think the better we will be. But if the day comes where he does, you know, decide to retire, then we’ll respect that, celebrate it. We’ll celebrate it, and hopefully it can be seen as a celebration rather than shifting to what’s next.” Yet for all that strong sentiment, even Smith’s biggest backers ended this day with questions about his overall health, happiness and the sustainability of an approach that, this week at least, looked like it required 100 per cent comfort in order to perform. World.title: The parents ditching IVF and embracing the ‘turkey baster’
World.content:
Sydney couple Emma Mansell and Sarah Hopkins conceived three of their four children with the “turkey baster method”. Facebook groups, Reddit threads and good old-fashioned set-ups from mutual friends are some of the ways parents are finding private sperm donors.

Bungles, cost-of-living pressures and sperm shortages are only some of the reasons Australians are fleeing the regulated system. But what awaits them in the “Wild West”?

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Emma Mansell always dreamed of a “cheaper by the dozen family”. After growing up an only child, the wholesome, busy chaos of a large family held great appeal. But with out-of-pocket costs typically $5000 to $10,000 per IVF cycle in Australia, the double-digit dream remained unreachable. “The reality was that if I wanted my big family, I had to find a different way,” Mansell said. Instead, Mansell had three children in Sydney’s northern beaches through what’s colloquially known as the “turkey baster method” after an online search for a sperm donor. Mansell and Hopkins with their children Aubrey-Rose, 8, Brooklyn-Louise, 9 and Kennedy, 6, who were conceived through informal sperm donation, and Hendrix, 3, conceived through IVF. Glenn Campbell Just as “test tube babies” (children born from IVF) are not actually created or grown in test tubes, a turkey baster – the giant bulb pipette-like kitchen tool, used for keeping roasting meat moist – is usually not the vehicle for semen during at-home artificial insemination.



Instruments vary. One Adelaide Hills mother told this masthead she used a menstrual disc. But the honour is mostly reserved for needle-free syringes, which is what Mansell used to start a family. “We stayed in really fancy hotels,” Mansell said. “The donor just looked like a businessman who was coming in [for] a meeting.” Mansell and wife Sarah Hopkins waited in the hall while the donor completed his end of the deal, before coming back into the room to finish the job. “It’s totally awkward,” Mansell said. “No one’s comfortable with the process.” “It never feels normal ... but it’s like brushing your teeth – you have to do it to have clean teeth. I had to do this to get pregnant.” The number of Australians bypassing licensed sperm banks and IVF clinics in favour of private donor agreements and at-home insemination is unknown.





Fifteen women learned this the hard way, inadvertently giving birth to 27 half-siblings from the same Melbourne donor between 2020 and 2024. Many met the man through the popular Facebook group Sperm Donation Australia. The group’s Perth-based founder Adam Hooper claimed the donor in question was banned from the group in 2021, which the donor disputes. Related Article Opinion

Fertility Our fertility industry is a mess. As a donor, I know what could fix it Gary Nunn Contributor In the regulated system, clinics are responsible for tracking how many families have had children from the same donor, to comply with local statutory limits. Victoria caps sperm donors at 10 families and New South Wales at five, partly to prevent accidental incest between half-siblings. Hooper said births among his Facebook group had recently dropped – with 606 reported in 2025, down from 903 in 2023 – which he attributed to heightened cost-of-living pressures. This masthead cannot independently verify the number of births, which were self-reported by parents on Hooper’s website. Sperm Donation Australia has about 23,000 members, but it’s not the only group of its kind. Private donors can also be found in smaller area- and year-specific Facebook groups, Reddit threads, international websites, Tinder-like apps and beyond.



Ellie Sedgwick loved the idea of raising a baby on her own. Earlier this year, she conceived through the turkey-baster method with a man who previously donated to a Victorian clinic. Her son is due in February. Audrey Richardson After six years researching every possible pathway to single motherhood, Ellie Sedgwick has seen them all. Born and raised on Sydney’s northern beaches, the 36-year-old photographer traverses the country in her Toyota Coaster. She didn’t want a partner putting a stop to that because they had welcomed a child together. Related Article Fertility Single at 30, Chloe decided to freeze her eggs. She wasn’t prepared for what came next She also didn’t want to be stuck co-parenting with a former partner she “absolutely hates”. “I honestly always liked the idea of doing it on my own,” Sedgwick told this masthead while on a women’s retreat in Lombok. “I’ve never doubted that I could do it.” Her grandmother suggested a sperm donor. Sedgwick was open to the idea – she is bisexual, and knew she would have to go down that avenue anyway if she ended up with a woman – but IVF was too expensive.

World.title: ASX set to edge up, tech stocks drive Wall Street higher
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to edge up, tech stocks drive Wall Street higher Stan Choe October 28, 2026 — 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are leading Wall Street mostly higher as their yo-yo moves swing back upward. The S&P 500 rose 0.6 per cent and pulled within 1.3 per cent of its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 39 points, or 0.1 per cent, in early afternoon trade, and the Nasdaq composite was 1.2 per cent higher. Wall Street was boosted by strength in technology stocks. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to edge higher, with futures pointing to a rise of 11 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.5 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US70.28¢ at 5.10am AEDT. The majority of stocks within the S&P 500 were falling, but the gains for influential AI stocks made up for that. AI stocks are on track for a second winning day after swerving for weeks on worries about whether their boom is under threat because of how expensive it’s become for companies to borrow money to build data centres and buy more AI chips.



Broadcom climbed 4 per cent after announcing a $US63 billion ($89.7 billion) financing deal where several Wall Street firms will help Anthropic get access to Broadcom’s XPU AI accelerators and networking solutions. Elsewhere in the industry, Nvidia rose 1 per cent and was the only force stronger than Broadcom pushing the S&P 500 higher. CoreWeave, a company that’s borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, jumped 7.3 per cent, though it’s been careening between big gains and losses within each of the past few days. Related Article Opinion

AI ‘Bold, but sane’? The future of AI is riding on Anthropic’s float Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist General Motors climbed 5.5 per cent after saying it’s moving its stock from a listing on the New York Stock Exchange to the Nasdaq. The automaker said the Nasdaq, which is home to several of the world’s biggest technology stocks, is a fit for its tech-driven strategy. The move could also allow GM to join the Nasdaq 100 index, which would force investment funds that mimic the index to buy it. GM began trading on the NYSE in 1911.



JetBlue Airways flew 18.8 per cent higher even though it reported a larger loss for the summer than analysts expected. CEO Joanna Geraghty said the company expects to return to making sustained operating profits next year and to deliver at least $US1 in earnings per share in 2028. Investors may have been bracing for something worse after the airline’s stock came into the day with a loss of nearly 48 per cent for the year so far. Another travel company, Royal Caribbean Group, also helped lead the market and rose 8.4 per cent. The cruise operator delivered a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, while raising its forecast for profit over the full year. Companies overall are under pressure to deliver big growth in profits. Expectations are high among financial analysts and investors, and that’s what allowed their stock prices to run to records recently despite high inflation, high interest rates and other concerns weighing on the market. Boeing fell 9.4 per cent after reporting a larger loss for the latest quarter than analysts expected.



Hilton Worldwide Holdings sank 3.4 per cent after reporting weaker revenue for the summer than analysts expected. It also gave a range as a forecast for profit in the final three months of the year whose midpoint fell below analysts’ expectations. The hotel company said it expects to see “increased impact from the Middle East” during the quarter. Sherwin-Williams fell 2.6 per cent after delivering a weaker profit than analysts expected. High mortgage rates have helped chill the housing industry, which in turn pressures demand for the paints and coatings Sherwin-Williams sells. Related Article Unfair dismissal Coles worker sacked after restraining suspected thief to receive $6500 “Customer sentiment and the leading indicators we track point to muted demand over the remainder of the year and into 2027,” CEO Heidi Petz said. At the same time, her company is dealing with inflation pushing up its costs for raw materials. Confidence among US shoppers has tumbled recently as pressure keeps building on them from high inflation. But a report on Tuesday said that US consumer confidence improved in October, when economists expected further weakening.



In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady a day before the Federal Reserve is scheduled to announce its latest decision on interest rates. The Fed last month hiked the fed funds rate for the first time in three years in hopes of slowing inflation, but the widespread expectation on Wall Street is that it will hold rates steady this time. The yield on the 10-year Treasury remained at 5.00 per cent, where it was late Monday. Helping to keep yields in check was a drop for oil prices. The price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 1.1 per cent to $US109.51. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. Stocks jumped 3.1 per cent in Seoul and fell 1.3 per cent in Shanghai for two of the bigger moves. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: The type of borrower falling behind on their mortgage
World.content:
PropertyNewsHome loans The type of borrower falling behind on their mortgage Alice Uribe October 28, 2026 — 5:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

Borrowers who took out home loans requiring low documentation, including self-employed or small business owners, are falling into arrears at a greater level than the rest of the mortgage market. Mortgages classed as non-performing, or 90 or more days behind on repayments, have remained relatively steady over recent years, sitting at 1.0 per cent of loans for the June 2026 quarter, according to Australian Prudential Regulation Authority data analysed by Canstar. But arrears have edged higher for low-doc lending by banks recently, hitting 4.9 per cent of outstanding loans for the June quarter, up from 4.2 per cent at the same time in 2025. The main originators of low-doc loans are non-bank lenders, and these types of loans comprise a small percentage of all mortgages among banks, experts say. Low-doc home loans are designed for small business owners and sole traders who aren’t able to provide full paperwork, including tax returns, to pass a bank’s standard serviceability checks.



Loans requiring low documentation may attract higher rates than traditional mortgages with recent rate hikes putting a “squeeze” on those paying higher than average rates, Canstar’s data insights director Sally Tindall said. Related Article Interest rates How far house prices have risen since the last time rates were this high “When the RBA tightens the screws on mortgages, the pressure on low-doc borrowers tends to increase even further as they’re usually already paying a premium on their interest rate,” she said. “If cash flow then tightens on the back of a cut down in consumer spending, those low-doc borrowers who don’t have a decent buffer can quickly find themselves with zero breathing room.” According to research from Canstar, one non-bank lender offers an advertised interest rate for a low-doc home loan starting at about 7 per cent, but only if the borrower has 45 per cent equity in their loan. The rate then climbs to as high as about 12.29 per cent for those with smaller deposits.



APRA data shows low-doc loans comprise about 0.1 per cent of all mortgages among banks. “However this does not illustrate the volume of low-doc loans in the broader mortgage market,” said Tindall, noting a number of non-bank lenders still offer these types of loans. Loans requiring low documentation may attract higher rates than traditional mortgages. Sam Mooy Erin Kitson, an analyst at S&P Global Ratings said, while not presenting a systemic risk, low-doc loans were more vulnerable to arrears, as it was often self-employed borrowers who take them out. “The cashflows of these borrowers are more exposed to deteriorating economic conditions, including rising interest rates, given the more direct impact it has on their income,” she said.



“Borrowers with low-doc loans are more likely to experience arrears pressure before more traditional loan types, given the greater sensitivity of self-employed borrowers’ cashflows to changing economic conditions.” Chief executive of mortgage brokerage Shore Financial Theo Chambers said higher rates and economic conditions could be a contributing factor to arrears levels, rather than low-doc borrowers being “necessarily higher-risk customers.” Most home owners are up to date with their mortgages. Oscar Colman “In reality, many are successful self-employed individuals and business owners with strong assets, substantial equity and healthy cash flow, but whose income doesn’t always fit the traditional assessment model,” he said. “Low-doc loans are already priced at higher interest rates, and therefore they’ve had rate rises to an already higher rate, coupled with pressure on higher living costs have placed on households and small businesses.”



Anthony Landahl, managing director at mortgage broker Equilibria Finance said all the banks had “good, strong, attractive offers” for self-employed borrowers. “Low-doc loans are mainly provided by second-tier providers, as distinct from the main banks, but they absolutely still have a role in our lending space,” he said. There is a misconception that low-doc home loans are more risky, experts say. Louie Douvis “And there is a bit of a misconception around low-doc loans that they’re more risky. But we don’t find that they’re more risky by their nature. Many low-doc borrowers are successful self-employed Australians whose income doesn’t fit traditional PAYG [Pay As You Go] lending models.” Landahl said there were strong lending standards.



“It’s still got to meet all of the consumer lending criteria. Verification requirements are still strong, and borrowers ultimately need to demonstrate they can service the loan.” Related Article Residential property Housing with benefits: Why co-housing could be the new Australian dream Kitson said arrears spikes for low-doc loans could be more pronounced than other loan types because of the declining balance outstanding of these types of loans across the broader mortgage market. “Based on APRA stats, they now comprise around 0.12 per cent of total loans outstanding, down from 0.88 per cent back in 2019, so the declining denominator will cause a more pronounced increase in arrears in percentage terms,” she said. Mortgage arrears across the country remain low despite a recent pickup, according to the RBA, with support from the strong labour market and savings buffers.



But Kitson said recent interest rate rises are yet to surface in mortgage arrears performance as there is often a lag between a rate increase and the increase in a borrower’s actual mortgage repayment. “Rising cost-of-living pressures are not yet manifesting in material arrears increases. Mortgage arrears are one of the last places for financial pressure to manifest,” she said. Property alerts are now available in the SMH and Age apps. World.title: Thinking of delaying downsizing? It could cost you more than you think
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingProperty downsizing Opinion Thinking of delaying downsizing? It could cost you more than you think Rachel Lane Money contributor October 28, 2026 — 5:01am

October 28, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The most common downsizing regret I hear isn’t selling at the wrong price, it’s not making the move sooner. When property prices fall, it is tempting to put your downsizing plans on hold. Nobody wants to sell their home for less than they think it was worth six months or a year ago. But before you decide to wait, ask yourself three questions. What matters is not just what you sell your current home for but what it will cost to move and how much you will have left over. Dominic Lorrimer Have you really lost money or just missed the peak? If you have owned your home for decades, chances are you bought it for a fraction of what it is worth today. Even if the market has softened, you can still be selling for a considerable profit. Take a home that was worth $1.2 million at the start of the year but could achieve $1.1 million today. If you bought it for $250,000 three decades ago, you might feel you have lost $100,000. In reality you are selling for $850,000 more than you paid, before allowing for inflation, improvements and ownership costs.



The old investment mantra “time in the market, not timing the market” is worth heeding. You will never pick the top or the bottom of a market – no one can. You only know the top has passed when prices fall, and the bottom was reached when prices start recovering. Editor's pick Opinion

Aged care How a rule change could save aged care users thousands Rachel Lane Money contributor The property market moves in cycles; “riding it out” could mean waiting years. Exactly how long depends on how much further prices fall and how quickly they recover. There is no guarantee the price you are chasing can be achieved again and it’s a very real risk that you end up selling for less than you could have today. What could your home buy you today? Every home costs money to hold, and rates, insurance and maintenance continue regardless of market changes. There is also an opportunity cost. The money tied up in your home could be released to invest, spend or buy a more suitable property (or a combination thereof).



If you are selling one home and buying another, your next home may also change in value, and not necessarily in the same direction or at the same rate. Changes in the property market don’t affect every property in the same way at the same time. What matters is not just what you sell your current home for but what it will cost to move and how much you will have left over. How do you want to spend the next chapter? The cost of waiting is not just financial. It can affect your health, happiness and independence. If staying means struggling with stairs, battling maintenance or becoming socially isolated, what is the price of holding on? Your home might be worth more in the future but that does not guarantee you will be better off. Where you live affects how you live, so your lifestyle deserves a place in the decision.



When it comes to downsizing decisions, sometimes the biggest loss is not the money you think you have missed out on but the time spent waiting for the perfect moment to begin your next chapter. Rachel Lane is the author of Downsizing Made Simple, a book and website aimed at demystifying downsizing. Advice given in this article is general in nature and not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.content:
NationalNSWSydney Metro Stations set for commuter surge along final stage of Sydney’s metro line Matt O'Sullivan October 28, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. As the long-awaited M1 extension to Bankstown opens on Friday, we take a look at how it happened and what it means for the city. See all stories .

The number of passengers forecast to board driverless trains has been increased at four stations along the final stretch of Sydney’s $30 billion M1 metro line during the morning peak hour, as expectations grow about the popularity of services from the south-west into the central city. The patronage forecast for the 8am to 9am peak on weekdays has been raised the most for Dulwich Hill station – up by 300 passengers to 1000 – followed by stations at Hurlstone Park, Canterbury and Belmore, which each have been increased by 200 commuters. Locals check out the renovated Dulwich Hill station on the M1 metro line during a community open day in August. Sitthixay Ditthavong The projections for Bankstown and Campsie have dropped by 100 passengers each to 2100 and 1400, respectively, from forecasts last year. The drop for Bankstown has been attributed to reductions in on-street parking spaces. Residential development is the main driver of changes to forecasts by Sydney Metro for stations along the south-west section, as well as the fact that there had been two years of growth since the T3 heavy rail line was closed to be converted to carry driverless trains. The M1 line’s final stage between Bankstown and Sydenham will open early on Friday.



Sydney Metro customer and planning executive director Samantha Phillips said the changes to the station patronage modelling primarily reflect residential development in areas along the corridor, and expected demand for high-frequency train services. “[The modelling is] showing a higher number of people using the metro than previously on the T3 [heavy rail line], and also people’s propensity to choose it because of the higher frequency and higher reliability,” she said. Phillips said she was curious to watch, once the line opens, the extent to which people walked further than usual or caught other public transport such as light rail to “travel back to go forward” on metro trains. “Our models suggest that some people will do that because it’s a faster trip,” she said. “Safety, reliability and frequency – they’re the three things that really drive customer satisfaction and keep people turning up.”



The modelling forecasts 9500 passengers will use the south-west section from 8am to 9am on weekdays, a 34 per cent rise on patronage on the T3 heavy rail line before it was closed in September 2024. The latest forecasts represent a 10 per cent increase in passengers in the hour-long period compared to Sydney Metro’s estimates in September last year of 8600 commuters when the line opens. Bankstown metro station is at the southern end of the M1 line. Sitthixay Ditthavong Sydney Metro is forecasting a 13 per cent surge to 300,000 passenger trips on weekdays along the M1 line when the final 13-kilometre south-west section opens and extends it to 66 kilometres of track between Tallawong and Bankstown via the central city. Phillips expects people to use cycling and pedestrian paths along the corridor to access metro stations and catch trains. “There’s going to be a lot of people wanting to cycle up or walk up and access the service,” she said.



Inner West Council Mayor Darcy Byrne said the easier transport access provided by the metro line from other parts of the city would be a shot in the arm for the local economy, especially nightlife and hospitality. Related Article Sydney Metro Why some train doors will not open when final section of Sydney’s metro line starts Byrne said significant increases in homes planned near the metro stations would also make residential developments more feasible. “Over the next decade, with the metro open and our housing plans approved, you’ll see significant increase in housing along the south-west line,” he said. “The point of the metro is that you’re providing a really good long-term public transport option that can support the increased housing that will come over time.” The $57 million GreenWay, which weaves north to south through five inner-west suburbs, was completed last year, while a 13.8-kilometre pathway dubbed the MetroWay will be built parallel to the Southwest Metro line. The two will intersect at Dulwich Hill.



Planning consent requires the MetroWay to be completed within two years of the opening of the metro train line between Bankstown and Sydenham. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: I have a very personal health condition. How much do I need to share at work?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? I have a very personal health condition. How much do I need to share at work? Kirstin Ferguson October 28, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Each week Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: a personal health condition, a nosy direction and feeling taken for granted. You don’t need to apologise for wanting the details of your condition to remain private. Dionne Gain I have been diagnosed with a medical condition of a very personal nature. I will need several scattered days off and possibly two weeks for an operation. My colleagues are extremely nosy, while my manager tells his EA everything, and she then circulates it around the office. I am angry at the thought of everyone knowing my business and continually questioning me. Should I invent a less personal procedure as a cover story, or am I legally required to tell my employer exactly what treatment I am having? Related Article Got a Minute? Can my boss really tell me what I can or can’t do on my lunch break? Do not invent a cover story. You don’t need to and doing so means you are being dishonest and will need to remember details which will ultimately undermine your credibility, right as you want your employer to respect your boundaries.



That said, you also don’t need to tell your employer your full medical history. They need to know you have to take medical leave and how long it will be, and you will need some paperwork from your doctor to show you are unfit for work. On your return, your employer will have to know whether you have any restrictions they should be aware of. The ins and outs of what you are having done are your business. I would put in writing to your manager a note to the effect that you will require leave for a medical procedure, and you will provide the necessary medical certificate and paperwork. I would also note in writing that you prefer to keep your medical information confidential and ask them to do the same. If anyone asks what your medical condition is, simply say, “I am just having a simple procedure which I prefer to keep private. Thanks for understanding.” Do not feel you need to apologise, and be consistent in your response. I am new to an HR manager role and struggling to protect staff confidentiality. Whenever an employee leaves my office after a private discussion, one director immediately demands all the details. He then appears to share them with other managers, who have mentioned matters they should not know. I told him some conversations were highly personal and should remain confidential, but he insists that, as a director, he is entitled to know about every staff issue. I am sure this is wrong, but how should I respond?



You are right to be concerned about this. If people feel they can’t confide in you, no one will be coming back to tell you issues that the business needs you to know. Related Article Got a Minute? My colleagues exclude me from conversations. Why are people so rude? Your director needs to understand that being in their role does not automatically entitle them to information. I think you need to set a clear guideline or policy with the chief executive or board governing confidential employee information. It could be something like a commitment from you to escalate any matters to them where it requires organisational action or a material risk. This could include disclosures around health and safety concerns, serious misconduct, legal obligations or key decisions the organisation must make. The guidelines or policy should then agree that everything else has to remain confidential to you to preserve the credibility of the HR role and to uphold individual privacy concerns. You might also want to try and move your office, so it is not so obvious who is coming in to meet you, and you don’t have every nosy parker on your doorstop the moment they leave. I work in distribution alongside a cleaner, a driver and an assistant stock manager. I reliably complete my duties, but two colleagues regularly tell management they have done work that I actually performed. They have now been recognised and rewarded for my contribution, while I feel as though I have been pushed aside and treated like nobody. I want to ask my manager for support, but I am unsure whether it is appropriate or how to explain what has been happening. What should I do?

World.title: RBNZ set to raise benchmark interest rate despite previously signalled pause
World.content:
Audio player for " Kiwibank economist Jarrod Kerr previews today's OCR decision " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2197473%2Frbnz-set-to-raise-benchmark-interest-rate-despite-previously-signalled-pause

Kiwibank economist Jarrod Kerr previews today's OCR decision Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Reserve Bank set to raise official cash rate for third consecutive meeting by 25 basis points to 3 percent

Surge in fuel prices, weak currency, stubborn core inflation make a pause risky

Recent slowing of inflation to 3.7 percent only temporary; to return above 4 pct next year

Nearness of a rise to next week's general election not an issue

A December rise currently 50-50, but further hikes to 3.5 pct expected next year

RBNZ statement due at 2pm, Governor's webcast at 3pm

The Reserve Bank (RBNZ) is set to raise its benchmark interest rate despite previously signalling a pause, as headline inflation has fallen, and just 10 days out from the general election.

The RBNZ is expected to raise the official cash rate (OCR) by 25 basis points to 3.0 percent, the third consecutive rate rise and the highest OCR level in a year.

Doug Steel. Supplied

BNZ senior economist Doug Steel said much has changed since the RBNZ's September decision.

"Oil prices are much higher, and the currency is materially lower than the Bank (RBNZ) assumed as it looks to get on top of stronger inflation."

He said the latest inflation numbers for the year ended September, although better than expected, showed stubborn core inflation, with signs the headline rate would surge back to 4.5 percent.

"It all adds to near term inflation looking materially higher than the RBNZ projected along with increasing risk that inflation becomes persistent without action from the central bank," Steele said.

"It would be a material shock to markets if the RBNZ did not lift the OCR."

Just do it!

ASB senior economist Mark Smith expected the monetary policy committee (MPC) to take the path of least resistance and hike, possibly in a split decision, but the upside risks were too high to ignore.

He said the timing of an OCR rise was unfortunate and might dampen economic activity and slow improvement in the labour market.

Mark Smith. Supplied

"The RBNZ in our view must address inflation risks as by not doing so it could end up with two problems, for example stagflation, rather than just a sluggish economy."

Smith said the RBNZ would likely be signalling that the anti-inflation fight was not yet over and that further rate rises were possible, depending on data and events.

"The message from the RBNZ, will likely be that more work will need to be done to ensure inflation settles around 2 percent. It will not be one of mission accomplished just yet. It is relatively easy to forecast 2 percent inflation, but it is much harder to deliver it."

More hikes coming

ANZ chief economist Sharon Zollner said the outlook for further rate moves was open and uncertain.

Sharon Zollner. RNZ / DOM THOMAS

"We've lightly pencilled in a pause in December in deference to the fact that the RBNZ has long said that their plan is to get to around neutral and then assess how the various upside and downside risks are playing out.

"Three percent is a slightly more comfortable fence to sit on."

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold forecast increases in December and February next year, taking the OCR into the RBNZ's neutral zone at 3.5 percent.

He said that would allow the RBNZ to be more gradual in assessing the effect of its hikes, and look at the state of the local and global economy, although he picked further hikes necessary in June and September to a high of 4 percent to make sure inflation was contained.

One potential complication of an OCR rise is the political fallout just ahead of the 7 November election.

Last month RBNZ Governor Anna Breman said the proximity of the decision to the election was not a factor.

"We focus on the mandate and the election does not come into that decision."

'Let the economy recover'

Kiwibank chief economist Jarrod Kerr argued against raising the OCR, and for leaving it as is until February.

"We need to let the economy recover before we worry about restraining it," he told Morning Report.

He said the Reserve Bank was being "cautious" about second-round effects of keeping the rate flat, which he said he did not anticipate.

He said inflationary pressures were from external factors such as the price of petrol and jet fuel, which were immediately passed on.

But Kerr said if rates were to rise, the Bank should "just get it over and done with" as businesses needed more certainty.

World.title: Why the Reserve Bank is about to do something relatively rare
World.content:
Audio player for " When does my property become relationship property? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2197863%2Fwhy-the-reserve-bank-is-about-to-do-something-relatively-rare

The Reserve Bank is probably about to do something that it doesn't often - hike interest rates during the final stages of an election campaign.

Economists expect the official cash rate to be increased by 25 basis points as the central bank leans against inflation being pushed up by higher fuel prices.

Commentators have often said that the Reserve Bank might avoid making a change close to the election, although it has no requirement to include any political consideration in its decision-making.

Gareth Kiernan. RNZ / Rebekah Parsons-King

Infometrics chief forecaster Gareth Kiernan said the most recent time it had made a change during an election campaign was in July 2014, when it raised the rate by 25 basis points ahead of a 20 September election.

In 2008, it cut the rate by 100 basis points a matter of weeks before the election.

Audio player for " Kiwibank economist Jarrod Kerr previews today's OCR decision " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2197863%2Fwhy-the-reserve-bank-is-about-to-do-something-relatively-rare

Kiwibank economist Jarrod Kerr previews today's OCR decision Morning Report Download MP3 6m

In 2002, it raised the rate by 25 basis points weeks before a July election and in 1999 it raised the rate by 50 basis points 10 days before the November election.

"I guess the difference between this time and previous occasions is that none of the elections have been close, so it was unlikely that interest rate changes would affect the result materially, whereas this time it's not at all clear what the election outcome might be," Kiernan said.

But he said the Reserve Bank was independent and needed to do its job of keeping inflation under control rather than worrying whether people would think its actions reflected the government's performance.

"If the government had been pursuing aggressively stimulatory monetary policy, then it would be more correct to draw a link between the government and the Reserve Bank's actions, but that is not the case this time. So I think most people will understand that any interest rate rise is a reflection of broader economic conditions than the government … Although National's eagerness to talk up their management and economic outcomes last year, and willingness to take credit for the interest rate cuts that had previously occurred, might make it harder for voters not to make some association between the government, the middling economic outcomes, and current interest rate rises."

Kelly Eckhold. Supplied / LinkedIn

Kelly Eckhold, chief economist at Westpac, said governments would always prefer interest rates were not rising.

"I think that's probably self-evident. Although I think every survey of what people seem to care about right now puts the cost of living right at the top of concerns beyond everything else.

"So I would have thought that it's probably not as big an issue compared to that, for example."

He said the need to tighten rates had been well signalled.

"I guess the Reserve Bank is weighing up the sort of the economy versus the cost of living in terms of what it's doing.

"It is probably relevant to note that we have actually had growth in the last year at 2.6 percent … which was actually probably an above trend growth rate for New Zealand. The challenge, I think, for people's perceptions is that the growth is coming from areas that don't necessarily touch them directly, unless you're involved in the tourism or perhaps in the centres that are more dominated by the agriculture sector. So hence you get this dissonance, I think, between people wondering why interest rates are going up when they don't think the economy is growing when in fact it is."

Ben Thomas. Supplied

Political commentator Ben Thomas said he thought the impact on voters would be limited. "I don't know how many voters are going for National or ACT because they genuinely believe the cost of living is under control."

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said the impact on voters would be limited because most mortgages were fixed.

"But the signal is mixed - interest rates are higher because the Reserve Bank reckons inflation is too high and economy is too strong. I obviously disagree with the Reserve Bank - but the signal to voters I think is pretty marginal. It is saying that the Reserve Bank is trying to control medium term inflation pressures. Many people will feel that the economy is not that strong and inflation is making them poorer."

Murat Ungor. Supplied

Otago University economist Murat Ungor said the governor had made it clear that the Reserve Bank would act in the run-up to the election if the inflation outlook required it.

"In practice, the election matters more for communication than for the decision itself. A move that markets have already priced in is far less politically charged than a surprise, so the bank's task is to signal clearly and then act on the data. Delaying a warranted increase because of the election calendar would itself be the more political choice, and it would risk a larger adjustment later."
