World.title: 'People are being hurt': West New Britain governor speaks out as 12 gunmen killed in Kimbe shootout
World.content:
Papua New Guinea's West New Britain province governor Sasindran Muthuvel says the public is deeply frustrated with repeated armed robberies and other violent crime.

Sasindran Muthuvel's comment comes after police confirmed the death of 12 men who they say staged an armed robbery at a tradestore in West New Britain's capital Kimbe on Monday.

Muthuvel told RNZ Pacific it was unfortunate that lives were lost, but noted the group fired on police while trying to flee the scene.

The governor said people of the province are frustrated at the surge in activity by criminal groups of so-called 'raskols'.

"A lot of genuine people are being hurt and killed also in these kind of holdups by these raskols because they don't know how to use firearms, or these are homemade guns.

"They just misfire and kill innocent people. We have lost mothers, young people, and all those things in these kind of holdups."

Police Commissioner David Manning said that while attempting to escape police, the armed group's vehicle rolled, resulting in the death of a number of passengers.

He said those not seriously injured in the vehicle roll-over subsequently drew weapons and chose to open fire on police.

"Police standing orders and the law are clear - when a criminal raises a weapon they will be stopped," Manning said in a statement.

"A total of 12 gunmen died in the incident, while one man, believed to be the ringleader of the group, survived and is in police custody."

Muthuvel said it was fortuitous that the Police Mobile Squad were already in the area attending to another incident.

Terrorising innocent communities

According to the governor, some members of the public have themselves attacked armed robbers in recent incidents, a reflection of the frustration in the community over the activities of criminal groups.

He said it was common for these groups to hold up PMVs (public motor vehicles) and rob the passengers.

PMVs are easy to hold up, Muthuvel said, because they frequently have to drive slowly to navigate the many potholes on local roads.

"When [the PMVs] slow down, they held them up. They get all the women to come outside. They remove, steal all their belongings and take their money and all those things.

"Most of the time, they physically abuse them, attack them, and all those things. This is where it's really frustrating for us.

"Many times, innocent people get attacked, businesses get robbed. And this police incident, it so happened that when they escaped, there was another police operation happening in that area, so Mobile Squad was already there."

Authorities cracking down

Muthuvel said he supports a call in parliament this month by Oro Province governor Gary Juffa for criminal groups to be officially categorised as terrorists.

"They're constantly going and terrorising innocent communities, publics, and all these people. So if it is not contained, then it will be a similar situation like what Governor Juffa is encountering in Popondetta."

Meanwhile, PNG's Police Minister John Pundari commended the swift intervention of police in the Kimbe robbery and other incidents.

"l commend those police officers on the front line in West New Britain who have confronted criminals involved in two armed robberies over the past four days.

"This follows an event last Friday when a group of gunmen robbed a PMV near Kimbe, and were confronted by a lone Police Officer. Following an exchange of gunfire, one gunman was killed while the remainder ran away into the bush.

"These incidents demonstrate that police will respond forcefully to remove firearms who elect to use illegal firearms," Pundari said.

World.title: 'Strengthening ties' or 'Shameful'?: Why Israel's new Pacific status is splitting the region
World.content:
Analysis - Israel's inclusion into the Pacific region's main political body has drawn sharply contrasting reactions across the region.

While the official diplomatic tone from Pacific leaders, including New Zealand, has been welcoming and focused on consensus, civil society groups have described the move as wrong and demanded a review.

Others, such as Kiwi media academic Professor David Robie, have called it "shameful", while veteran Solomon Islands diplomat Collin Beck said it puts into question the "credibility" of the Pacific Islands Forum's (PIF) partnership mechanism.

Israel announced its acceptance into the Forum via a news release last Wednesday, which swiftly attracted a range of reactions - both for and against the move.

The announcement coincided with Israel's Agency for International Development Cooperation (MASHAV) head Eynat Shlein's visit to the region.

PIF secretary-general Baron Waqa welcomed Israel’s Ambassador to Fiji and Pacific Island Countries Maya Yaron and Head of MASHAV Ambassador Eynat Shlein, who travelled from Israel to the Pacific for engagements across the region this week. Pacific Islands Forum

Fijian Deputy Prime Minister Viliame Gavoka offered a biblical justification for Israel's inclusion, speaking for the "entire Pacific Islands", while the Pacific Conference of Churches demanded the PIF review its decision.

The 18-member PIF has just over two dozen dialogue and development partners, which include countries such as the United States, China, the United Kingdom, France, Japan and Indonesia, that support the development priorities of the region.

Israel has been added to the list as a sectoral partner and will offer support in the areas of water management, desalination, agriculture and climate change adaptation.

"Strengthening ties with the Pacific Island nations is one of my objectives. Earlier this year, I opened Israel's Embassy in Fiji, which also serves nine other Pacific Island nations, all friendly to Israel," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar said.

"Under the current government, three of these countries, Papua New Guinea, Fiji and Nauru, have opened embassies in Jerusalem."

The PIF Secretariat, which is headed by former Nauru President Baron Waqa, has not publicly confirmed Israel's status yet. However, the New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters said the decision by PIF leaders should be respected and described criticism of Israel's inclusion as an "insult" to Pacific Island nations.

"Pacific support a rules-based international system, respect for international law," Beck, who is a Solomon Islands career diplomat and senior government official, said in a comment on a Facebook post on RNZ.

"We must engage with all peaceful countries," he wrote.

However, he added that the PIF's "mechanism on partnership now lacks credibility".

He said the review of how the PIF works with its partners "must come with criteria that [have] humanity at its centre, international law, respect for lives will surely place the Pacific on the right side of history".

He also noted that there should be respect for the Pacific Ocean of Peace Declaration adopted by Pacific leaders in September 2025.



Professor Robie, who has decades of experience researching and writing on the region, said the move undermines the Forum's founding commitment in 1971 to regional decolonisation.

"In what is probably one of its most shameful acts ever, the Pacific Islands Forum has betrayed one of its founding principles in admitting Israel - already a global rogue pariah state - as a development partner in the middle of the genocide of an Indigenous people, the Palestinians," he wrote as editor of Asia Pacific Report.

"As decisions of this nature are made by consensus, it means that all 18 member states of the region's main political body - including Australia and New Zealand - have given their blessing."

He pointed out that Israel, alongside the United States, had also voted against decolonisation at the UN Decolonisation Committee (C-24) meeting earlier this month.

"Six Pacific countries and territories - American Samoa, French Polynesia (Mā'ohi Nui), Guam (Guåhan), New Caledonia (Kanaky), Pitcairn and Tokelau - are still on the UN Decolonisation list," he wrote.

World.title: Katrina Jefferies cold case: Police investigating potential breakthrough
World.content:
Police are investigating a potential breakthrough in relation to the 21-year-old cold case killing of Auckland woman Katrina Jefferies, RNZ can reveal. A never-before-seen police report into her death reveals that about a decade ago police recommended a suspect be charged with murder, but the Crown later found there was "insufficient evidence" to support the charge. National Crime Correspondent Sam Sherwood reports.

For 21 years, Katrina Jefferies' family has waited.

They have waited for answers, for an arrest, and for the person responsible for killing the 22-year-old mother to be held accountable.

Twice police have offered rewards. Two years after her killing they offered $50,000 and then in 2019 police announced a $100,000 reward.

In 2018, Detective Inspector Paul Borrell completed a review of the case.

His report - obtained by RNZ - reveals police recommended a murder charge in 2015 and that a woman later made "completely fabricated and false" claims that she helped dispose of Jefferies' body.

The report says most homicides are "quickly solved with early breakthroughs".

"Regrettably [Jefferies' death] is not in this category and has involved a hard grind over the years to this point with a reality now being that it may well never be solved.

"This is a reality that needs to be seriously and realistically considered before there is any embarking on any further reviews or elements of work."

RNZ can now reveal police are investigating a new potential breakthrough in the case.

Detective Inspector Scott Beard says the investigation is open and being worked on "as a result of information only recently received by police".

All exhibits are also in the process of being reassessed, and it will be determined what if any further examination can be undertaken.

A photo of the scene where Katrina Jefferies was found, released by police. supplied

Operation Waikowhai

Katrina Jefferies was last seen by her mother Nicola as she left her Mt Roskill home alone about 8pm on 10 July 2005.

Two days later her body was found by a man walking his dog along Waikowhai Road in Hillsborough, near Waikowhai Park Reserve.

Her body was lying several metres down a steep downhill bank, off the side of the road.

Borrell's report said she was naked from the waist down, apart from wearing socks.

A number of items were found with her body that appeared "foreign to the scene", including a red tarpaulin, a yellow PVC raincoat and a black plastic bag which were all partially covering her body.

Police also found a wooden framed print and a piece of plywood board.

"Early reconstructions were that the body had been dumped at this location with the associated items at a time after her death and that this area was not therefore the actual murder scene."

The investigation - then dubbed Operation Waikowhai - was initially led by Detective Senior Sergeant Gerry Whitley. Borrell said someone, whose name was redacted, was nominated as a "principal suspect" early in the investigation.

"[Redacted] was a local drug dealer living in the same vicinity as the victim, had history of violence toward women and was profiled as being sexually predatory.

"Evidence would strongly infer that the victim was known to [redacted] even though he adamantly denied knowing her."

The yellow raincoat that was found with Katrina Jefferies' body. supplied

Operation Lyra

The initial investigation continued until 2006.

In 2014, police reopened the case under the name Operation Lyra.

Borrell said the investigation had a "strong focus" on one suspect whose name was redacted.

Borrell's review revealed that in August 2015 a 135-page report detailing the case was submitted to the Crown solicitor.

"It proposed that evidential sufficiency had been met and made recommendation that a charge of murder be preferred against [redacted]."

The Crown responded with a report to police in September 2016, advising there was insufficient evidence to support a murder charge.

In 2019 police announced a $100,000 reward in relation to the case. supplied

In 2017, the report was reviewed by another police officer, Detective Inspector Aaron Pascoe.

Pascoe said the report was "at times selective" in relation to information provided when compared to other accounts from either the same or other witnesses.

Borrell acknowledged "considerable time and effort" went into preparing the report for the Crown.

"On first read, the report is comprehensive and compelling. I have however, also formed a view that the evidential sufficiency of many strongly stated aspects that supported a murder charge are diluted upon closer analysis."

The 'witness'

Borrell's report revealed that in 2016 a "potentially critical witness" was identified and interviewed by the Operation Lyra team, after the report had been sent to the Crown recommending the murder charge.

The woman, whose name was redacted, made three statements to police over an 18-month period.

"She provided accounts of [redacted] making direct admissions of murder to her also describing being asked to dispose of the body and using her own vehicle to assist," Borrell said.

Borrell said "on the face of it" the woman's accounts were "potentially critical and powerful evidence well worth pursuing".

"It relayed an account of an eyewitness that could support existing circumstantial evidence gathered that implicated [redacted] and potentially connected the whole case together."

However, her statements contained a number of significant inconsistencies.

Katrina Jefferies. supplied

This included that she said she took her son to school on the morning of 12 July 2005 after she claimed she helped dispose of Jefferies' body in the early hours of that morning. Further inquiries established it was actually school holidays at the time.

The woman also gave "specific detail" about timings in the early hours of July 12 of being driven to Waikowhai Reserve in her car.

However, CCTV footage recovered by police revealed no car passed by the camera in the times she indicated. There were two vehicles, one entering the reserve about 3.30am and another leaving at 12.40am captured. However, neither vehicle resembled the make and model of her car.

The report noted that the CCTV "may not be conclusive due to the heavy rain that night also captured on CCTV".

Borrell also questioned why the woman had not mentioned the rain in her first two statements.

"Subjectively, it would seem very likely that a person involved in the disposal of a murdered body in the very early hours of the morning and in darkness in the company of an alleged murderer would remember that they had been drenched by heavy rain," Borrell said.

Borrell said Pascoe identified a number of examples where corroboration should exist, which would have added weight to her claims.

"Despite active and thorough investigation, no such corroborative evidence ever emerged."

In May 2017 the woman was interviewed again to clarify the "inconsistencies and ambiguities that had emerged".

Within 22 minutes of the interview, the woman asked for a break during which she recanted all her prior statements.

The woman said she had put together information by "listening to the gossip and from there, being able to inject her own information so as to construct a believable account", Borrell said.

"I knew that I may end up in prison for the story I told but I was just gonna end up telling the truth eventually because I had to," the woman said.

"I knew that you would eventually figure it out. I couldn't keep up the lie forever especially when I don't know certain points and especially if I had to go to court. I would be a blubbering mess because I don't know certain stuff."

Borrell said he was satisfied the woman had recanted because she realised she had been caught lying, rather than because she was being compelled to withdraw a true account.

Red tarpaulin found at the scene. Supplied

The forensics

A post-mortem revealed Jefferies had a blood alcohol level of 210mg per 100ml of blood (the current legal driving limit is 50 mg per 100ml of blood).

Borrell said vaginal and cervical swabs were taken from what was thought to be semen staining appearing on both.

He said "considerable and extensive" forensic analysis had occurred from 2005 through to the review dates with "no matches to any persons of interests".

"A cervical swab sample has been held back from testing and secured in the hope that DNA technology will advance in the future to a point where DNA profiles may be able to be raised from very low amounts of DNA material possibly present."

Borrell's report contained a subheading 'DNA D8 17 Allele'. The beginning of the section is redacted; however, it included an explanation from senior Environmental Science and Research (ESR) scientist Fiona Matheson.

She said D8 was one of the DNA sites used in forensic profiling, and that 17 referred to the number of times a particular DNA sequence was repeated at that site.

Matheson said ESR had generated a dataset which held over 20,000 profiles of people in New Zealand.

"For the case of the D8 17, the 17 allele in the dataset is at the large allele end of the spectrum for this locus and has been observed, relatively few times. This means that the expectation of finding a DNA profile with this allele present would be low in that very few individuals would have this component present as part of their DNA profile."

Borrell said this aspect of the investigation provided some avenues of inquiry involving profiling the 5600 people who appeared on the DNA database as having the D8 17 Allele in their DNA.

"Such a phase would involve geographic and behavioural profiling of each of the 5600 which theoretically would be able to reduce this number significantly after considerable work and time. The assumption with this approach is that the donor is actually on the DNA database."

He said an "integrated approach" of comparing the Mitochondrial DNA attained from the two hair samples against high scoring individuals identified through the D8 17 Allele profiling "may identify an individual who matches both these DNA samples".

"Such an outcome may add significant weight to the proposition that that person was involved in the death and/or disposal of Katrina Jefferies body.

"My view is that such a phase would be costly both in time and resource with any likelihood of success less probable than probable."

Detective Inspector Paul Borrell, pictured in 2016. RNZ / Tracy Neal

'Complex and challenging' investigation

Borrell said the investigations into Jefferies' killing had been "particularly complex and challenging enquiries".

"The sheer volume of information gathered, collated and effectively considered required effective and robust systems and processes to ensure correct priorities were set and that information relevant to take the enquiry forward was properly identified and prioritised, or rejected."

He said the first days of any homicide were "critical", and that it was key for "evidence sources to be quickly identified and prioritised at the earliest".

"Another critical discipline is that the direction of the enquiry must be driven by fact, and not assumptions or conjecture and that enquires are wrung out to their very natural end.

"An important aspect of this theme is toward corroboration and alibi (alibi the alibi), where suspects raised need to be properly worked through to a point where they are, or are unable to be properly and completely eliminated."

He also said that lines of inquiry followed at any particular time needed to be kept to a minimum to avoid an investigation becoming "overly complicated and confused".

"Effective tracking system to list, interpret and identify key findings are required and indicators are that they were not present."

Borrell said while the position of Jefferies' body suggested a sexual assault this was not supported by either the post-mortem findings or ESR's forensic analyses "which does not seem to infer that the motivation for the killing was sexual".

The investigation into her death was the fourth in quick succession in Auckland and "likely suffered from shortage of resource, experience and support", Borrell said.

He said the main focus of Op Lyra was on a suspect whose name was redacted, as well as the statement provided by the woman.

"I am completely satisfied that her account was completely fabricated and false. My view is that this current state as it stand at this point, further detracts from [redacted] being the offender than what had previously existed prior to [redacted] involvement in this inquiry."

New hope

In response to a series of questions from RNZ, Beard said the investigation into Jefferies' death was currently open and being worked on "as a result of information only recently received by Police".

"In 2021, police reassessed and reinvestigated the file. This has led to a recent review of all the exhibits, which is near completion.

"There is also new information recently received that police are currently working on."

The retained cervical swab had since been tested using newer technology without success.

Beard confirmed all exhibits including the hair samples were in the process of being reassessed.

"We are working with PHF Science as to what exhibits can be further tested. There is no guarantee an offender will be identified."

In relation to the D8-17 allele, Beard said significant amount of work had been conducted regarding forensic testing of exhibits.

"The D8-17 allele has identified numerous names due to the fact it is not a specific DNA sample. While it will be of assistance, it is yet to identify any potential suspects."

In relation to the criticisms of the 2015 report recommending the murder charge, Beard said it was accepted that a higher ranked investigator should review complex reports completed by investigators "to ensure a level of objectivity".

Beard was also asked about Borrell's comments that the case "may well never be solved".

"The word 'may' is used in terms of the homicide likely being solved. The comment is correct.

World.title: NZDF aims to fly drone swarms
World.content:
The Defence Force (NZDF) is aiming to experiment with flying drones in swarms.

Drone swarms are being used in surveillance, combat and logistics, including in Ukraine and Gaza, sparking global demand that is expected to quadruple in short order from over $1.5 billion last year.

The NZDF has put out a tender asking for a "limited quantity" of drones that can be coordinated by a single operator.

AI-powered swarm control systems allow a single operator to command dozens or hundreds of networked drones simultaneously.

The NZDF tender said it wanted the drones for assessment and experimenting with.

"It is not intended for operational use or large-scale fleet deployment."

Australia is aiming to launch swarms of aerial drones from its underwater Ghost Shark drone via a launcher it pokes above the sea surface.

Also, US company Shield AI has just done a deal to pair its swarming Hivemind mission autonomy software into "loitering" strike drones called OWLS and made in Perth.

World.title: Loyal back to reclaim Sydney to Hobart record
World.content:
A decade after his last appearance in the Sydney to Hobart Yacht Race, Anthony Bell has unveiled a new Loyal boat to challenge for line honours in this year's race.

But it's not a new boat — it's an old one.

Bell was first to Hobart in 2011 with Investec Loyal and in 2016 with Perpetual Loyal, setting a then-race record in the latter race of one day 13 hours, 31 minutes and 20 seconds.

On Tuesday in Sydney, Bell revealed his boat for this year's edition of the bluewater classic — the race record-holder and last year's winner, Comanche.

Comanche takes out line honours in Sydney to Hobart race Master Lock Comanche claims line honours in the 80th edition of the gruelling Sydney to Hobart yacht race, with a stunning daylight hours finish.

Bell spent up big to buy the five-time line honours-winning boat, which will race on Boxing Day as Tribeca Loyal.

Bell, the owner and skipper of the supermaxi, is aiming to lift the J.H. Illingworth Challenge Cup for a third time.

He has again recruited America's Cup and Olympic gold medallist Tom Slingsby to serve as the crew's sailing master.

The three-time world sailor of the year is delighted to be working on a yacht with the quality and power of Comanche.

"It's the most powerful supermaxi there is in the world," Slingsby said in Sydney.

"There's times there where we actually try to slow the boat down because it's got so much power and the waves could be too big that you're flying off the waves too fast.

"It averages really high speeds, it loves it when it's windy, so it's an exciting boat. You wouldn't want to choose any other boats to do the home run on.

"This boat already owns the Sydney Hobart race record, but … if we get the right conditions, we can break that record by a lot."

Master Lock Comanche took line honours in Hobart last year. (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

Despite his past success with Loyal, the 2012 Olympic gold medallist admits sailing on the open seas is a long way from his comfort zone.

"I'm not an ocean racer," Slingsby declared.

"I'm more of the short-course stuff.

"It's not something that I'm good at and really want to do, but I love coming back."

A major motivation for Slingsby and the crew is the continuing partnership with the Humpty Dumpty Foundation, which raises money for life-saving infant medical equipment for Australian hospitals.

The worthy cause is why Loyal will once again take on some celebrity deckhands to boost its fundraising profile.

Former Wallaby turned Rugby Australia chief executive Phil Waugh and Sydney Roosters great Anthony Minichello are among the famous names heading south.

"I certainly don't miss the contact of playing rugby league, but the camaraderie, and everyone being laser-focused on achieving a goal, that's the stuff you do miss when you retire from professional sport," Minichello said.

This year's star-studded crew continues the tradition for Loyal to rely on some unconventional athletes taking up a new sport.

"We've had 21 people who represented Australia, won world surfing titles, gold medals, played for the Wallabies, played rugby league, and we have two TV Week Gold Logie winners as well," Bell said.

AAP

World.title: Starc's ferocious late spell helps Australia recover from horror start
World.content:
Mitchell Starc has dragged Australia back into the third Test against South Africa after a stunning spell with the second new ball.

The home side mustered 329 after being sent in by Pat Cummins, but lost its last four wickets for just two runs as Starc found swing with the new ball to blow away the tail.

Starc finished with figures of 6-72 from 16.3 overs to allow Australia to share the spoils after a pulsating day of Test cricket.

Days of Test cricket are rarely split in half, but day one at Newlands could definitively split in two as South Africa handed Australia a lifeline after throwing away a promising position.

Throughout the opening session the Proteas were absolutely cruising, a morning's play that simply couldn't have gone worse for the tourists.

Steve Smith had been ruled out before play had even started, failing a fitness test on his troublesome neck.

Travis Head dropped a sitter to reprieve Aiden Markram off the bowling of a ropable Starc.

Marques Ackerman helped put South Africa in the driver's seat early on day one, but fell five runs short of his maiden Test century. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images)

The Proteas were scoring at over five runs per over, with openers Aiden Markram and Marques Ackerman powering their way to 0-158 not long after lunch.

Pat Cummins's decision to bowl first on a placid deck looked misguided.

But Nathan Lyon, preferred to Scott Boland in one of four changes made by the Aussies, made the breakthrough that precipitated a collapse of epic proportions.

Ackerman advanced down the pitch and was beaten by Lyon, with Alex Carey completing a regulation stumping.

Nathan Lyon (centre) picked up two first innings wickets on his return to the Test side. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images)

The collapse was not immediate, with Markham and David Bedingham combining for a 45-run partnership.

But Markram (75) was dismissed hooking Josh Hazlewood, superbly caught by Starc on the backward square leg boundary which started the South African's slide.

Skipper Temba Bavuma was bowled by Lyon for a two-ball duck, with Matthew Breetzke trapped LBW by Cooper Connolly for 2 as the Proteas lost 3-13 in the space of seven overs.

Starc then struck twice in the space of a single over, Bedingham (50) hooking to Hazlewood on the boundary before Wiaan Mulder (0) walked without waiting for a decision just two balls later after edging a hook to Carey.

Marco Jansen again threatened to take the Test away from Australia before his innings was ended by a searing Starc yorker. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman)

That left South Africa 6-232 just after tea and reeling.

South Africa's hero from Gqeberha, Marco Jansen, once again proved to be a thorn in Australia's side, and notched the fourth half-century of the innings in a valuable 95-run stand with Ryan Rickelton (42).

Jansen and Rickelton saw South Africa safely to the second new ball, but then ran head first into a rampant Starc, who wiped out the final four wickets in the space of six lethal deliveries.

Follow the live blog below for a recap of all the day one action as it happened.

World.title: Walsh back at fullback in Kangaroos team to face Cook Islands
World.content:
Reece Walsh appears to be the frontrunner to wear the number one jersey for the Rugby League World Cup knockout stages after being named to start against the Cook Islands.

The Brisbane game-breaker opened Australia's campaign against New Zealand before veteran James Tedesco had his turn in their win over Fiji.

Both were among their team's best players, giving Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters a selection headache.

Despite his impressive showing that included three try assists, it appears Sydney Roosters premiership captain Tedesco may have paid the price for the Kangaroos' below-par showing in their 36-22 win over Fiji last Sunday.

He has been named on the bench, with Walters turning back to Walsh for his side's final pool game.

With the unbeaten hosts needing to stiffen their defence across the park, Tom Dearden has won the race to partner Cameron Munster in a third halves pairing, with Sam Walker relegated to the reserves.

Walker has been in the headlines since the Fiji match, with his Roosters outfit withdrawing their contract offer.

Walters has recalled rested forwards including skipper Isaah Yeo and his battle-hardened Penrith teammate Liam Martin, who will line up in the second row alongside Jacob Preston, who came off the bench against Fiji.

After coming off the bench against Fiji, who made easy metres through the middle in a gallant defeat, Pat Carrigan and Tino Fa'asuamaleaui are back in the starting pack.

David Fifita and Keaon Koloamatangi have been demoted for the clash in Townsville.

Centre Bradman Best did enough in his first Kangaroos match to keep his spot ahead of Latrell Mitchell.

Ethan Strange, who replaced the injured Mitchell Moses in the squad, is set to make his Test debut after being named on the six-man bench in the number 14 jumper.

Kangaroos team (1-13):

1: Reece Walsh; 2: Jack Bostock; 3: Kotoni Staggs; 4: Bradman Best; 5: Tom Trbojevic; 6: Cameron Munster; 7: Tom Dearden; 8: Patrick Carrigan; 9: Harry Grantr; 10: Tino Fa'asuamaleauai; 11: Jacob Preston; 12: Liam Martin; 13: Isaah Yeo (C)

Reserves:

14: Ethan Strange; 15: Keaon Koloamatangi; 16: Cameron Murray; 17: Reuben Cotter; 18: Lindsay Smith; 19: James Tedesco; 20: Sam Walker; 21: Latrell Mitchell; 22: David Fifita; 23: Blayke Brailey

Robinson ruled out of tournament for Jillaroos

Julia Robinson scored one of Australia's 15 tries against England, but the Jillaroo will miss the rest of the tournament with a dislocated wrist. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

The Jillaroos also named their team for their next game at the Rugby League World Cup, with star centre Julia Robinson ruled out of the tournament.

Robinson dislocated her wrist in Saturday's 78-0 win over England. Scans ruled out a fracture, but confirmed ligament damage.

The Jillaroos will face Wales in Sydney on Sunday. Robinson was replaced in the extended squad by Canberra's Sheridan Gallagher.

Jess Sergis comes into the centres, while Jesse Southwell was named at five-eighth alongside Tarryn Aiken. Makenzie Weale and Sariah Paki move from the bench into the starting forward pack.

Reserves:

World.title: Tasmania Devils' inaugural VFL captain axed after pub incident
World.content:
The Tasmania Devils have axed VFL captain Robbie Fox, following an incident at a Hobart pub, the ABC understands.

Fox, 33, is understood to have been removed from the Granada Tavern, in Hobart's northern suburbs, after becoming drunk and disorderly at the venue two weeks ago.

It's understood Fox was abusive toward some staff at the venue, and at one point a bottle was thrown.

The Granada Tavern was contacted but declined to comment.

The ABC understands Fox was removed from the Granada Tavern following an incident two weeks ago. (ABC News: Owain Stia-James)

The incident has contributed to the Devils parting ways with their inaugural skipper, opting not to offer him a fresh contract for the 2027 season.

In a statement, Devils VFL boss Aaron Pidgeon said "the club's expectations regarding player behaviour, and adherence to our standards" were part of the decision not to offer him a new deal.

Fox is also employed by the Devils as the club's strategic projects and impact lead, and it's understood he will remain in the role.

Robbie Fox is a former Sydney Swans AFL player. (Facebook: Tasmania Football Club)

The veteran defender, who hails from Burnie, was recruited to the Devils after playing 105 games with the Sydney Swans, including the 2022 and 2024 AFL Grand Finals.

In an injury-affected season, he played 13 games this year for Tasmania in the VFL, leading the club to a top four finish and a home semi-final.

World.title: Music mogul Jay-Z picks himself to perform at next Super Bowl
World.content:
Jay-Z, the American music mogul behind Empire State of Mind, 99 Problems and entertainment company Roc Nation, that helps produce Super Bowl half-time shows, will himself be next year's featured performer at the NFL showpiece in California.

The NFL, Apple Music and Roc Nation announced Jay-Z will headline the 2027 Super Bowl half-time festivities on February 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.

Jay-Z attending a NFL game between Washington Commanders and the Dallas Cowboys at Northwest Stadium. (Reuters: Peter Casey-Imagn Images)

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said he had one request when the league first reached an agreement with Roc Nation: that Jay-Z take the stage himself "whenever the moment felt right to him".

"From Reasonable Doubt to standing on the Super Bowl half-time stage, this has been a journey," Jay-Z said in a statement.

"Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world's biggest stage.

"This run continues to be a dream come true."

After days of speculation, Jay-Z is set to return to the stadium where he closed his celebration of the 30th anniversary of Reasonable Doubt, the mogul's 1996 debut album.

The concerts included three sold-out shows at Yankee Stadium and sold-out performances in London and Paris ahead of a stop at SoFi Stadium over the weekend.

Jay-Z's Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL since 2019 to advise on and help produce the league's entertainment presentations, including the Super Bowl half-time show.

At the time, Jay-Z said he told Mr Goodell: "If this is about me performing at the Super Bowl, then we can just end this conversation now."

Inside SoFi Stadium at Inglewood, California, ahead of the Super Bowl 2022. (Getty Images: Gregory Shamus)

Seven years later, Jay-Z is ready to perform after all.

Jay-Z, born Shawn Carter, has won 25 Grammy Awards and received 89 nominations, the second-most in history behind his wife, Beyoncé — who has performed at two Super Bowls.

His catalogue also includes the albums The Blueprint and The Black Album, and hit songs such as Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem), 99 Problems and Empire State of Mind, his collaboration with Alicia Keys.

NFL half-time entertainment The NFL announces the Jonas Brothers will be the half-time entertainment when Melbourne hosts the Rams and 49ers to launch the season in September.

Last year, Reasonable Doubt was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.

His recent concerts brought out a rotating cast of guests.

At SoFi Stadium, his daughter Blue Ivy played piano on The Story of O.J. and Dead Presidents, while Scarface, John Legend and DJ Khaled joined him on opening night. Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg and Too $hort appeared during Saturday's finale.

Earlier in the run, Beyoncé, Rihanna, Eminem and Nas were among the guests at Yankee Stadium.

Bad Bunny and Lady Gaga perform during this year's Super Bowl half-time show at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images)

Jay-Z has built a career as an executive and entrepreneur. The Brooklyn rapper co-founded Roc-A-Fella Records and founded Roc Nation in 2008, building it into an entertainment company that works with artists and athletes.

He became the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017 and joined the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.

He is also a four-time Emmy winner.

Kendrick Lamar performs during the 2025 Super Bowl half-time show at Caesars Superdome in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Getty Images: Patrick Smith)

Roc Nation will executive produce the half-time show, with Hamish Hamilton directing.

The half-time show has collected Emmys in recent years. Bad Bunny's performance in February won a record seven, including best live variety special, while Kendrick Lamar's show last year won for music direction.

AP

World.title: AFL abandons Opening Round for season 2027
World.content:
The AFL has abandoned the Opening Round fixture from the past two seasons, with all 18 clubs now set to play in Round One in 2027.

The previous seasons saw the four teams based in New South Wales and Queensland play home games, while this year's draw also included one game at the MCG.

The split fixture meant each of the teams that played in the Opening Round — also referred to as round zero — subsequently had an early season bye.

Marcus Bontempelli of the Bulldogs during Opening Round in 2026 in Brisbane. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Russell Freeman)

Critics say the fixturing caused distortions in the draw, giving an advantage to the teams that played in Opening Round.

"We have listened to feedback and are pleased to be able to deliver a Round One for all our 18 clubs and fans as we bring back a traditional nine-game opening weekend across the country," AFL chief Andrew Dillon said in a statement.

Andrew Dillon announced the codes in-principle agreement to a new Illicit Drugs Policy in March. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Former premiership coach with West Coast and Collingwood and now ABC analyst, Mick Malthouse, said Opening Round compromised the fixture.

"We don't need it and it's a blessing now that we don't have it," he told ABC Sport.

"Let me say that 'zero round' was appropriately named.

"It had zero impact on the public; in fact, I'll go in the reverse and say it had a completely negative impact."

Malthouse said the early season byes caused by the Opening Round meant the ladder was not meaningful until all teams had played the same number of games, which in the season just passed did not happen until the end of Round 4.

"All round zero did was compromise the ability of sides to be ready for the next game," Malthouse said.

Mick Malthouse said Opening Round compromised the AFL draw. (Getty Images: Mark Dadswell)

"If you've got a game tucked under your belt, you're ready; you're miles in front of the next side.

"And don't worry about the results of those games; it's more important about the long-term effect on players.

The president of the AFL Fans' Association, Ron Issko, welcomed the move to reinstate a full Round One.

"Credit to the AFL for listening," he told ABC Sport.

"When you start a season after waiting six months for the season to start and not all teams are playing, it's sort of like a soft launch.

"It just didn't have that energy.

"We're a national competition and what's better than having all teams playing on Round One."

The AFL's move to highlight games in NSW and Queensland was seen as a response to the National Rugby League's move to stage that competition's opening games in Las Vegas.

Opening Round was seen as a response to the NRL starting its season in Las Vegas, in the United States. (AAP: Supplied/NRL Photos)

"We've looked over the border and so seeing that there's games played in Las Vegas, [said] 'Wow, if that's the way they operate, let us do something similar,'" Malthouse said.

"Forget about what's happening over the border and in fact embrace what's over the border and applaud them," he said.

Round One of the 2027 season will be played from March 17-21, with matches in NSW, Western Australia, South Australia and Victoria.

Hawthorn will play triple-premiers Brisbane in Round One of the 2027 AFL season. (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

It has been delayed one week from the usual season start time by the test cricket 150th anniversary match between Australia and England at the MCG.

The season will kick off with a match between the Sydney Swans and Geelong at the SCG on Wednesday, March 17.

The following night, losing grand finalist Fremantle will play the Western Bulldogs at home.

Three-time reigning premiers Brisbane will play on the Friday night against Hawthorn at the MCG.

Wednesday 17 March | Sydney Swans vs Geelong Cats, 7:30pm, SCG

Thursday 18 March | Fremantle vs Western Bulldogs, 5:10pm, Perth Stadium
