Tech.title: A 28-Year-Old DOGE Operative Gutted USAID. HR Had No Record of Him Working There
Tech.content:
On March 18, 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio handed the reins of the US Agency for International Development to Jeremy Lewin, a 28-year-old graduate of Harvard Law School, former investment banker, and affiliate of Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency. At the time, Lewin’s appointment drew criticism because of his lack of experience in government, diplomacy, or foreign assistance. But for career staff inside the agency, the issues surrounding Lewin’s new role were much more alarming than his thin résumé.

For at least two months, USAID senior staff had no knowledge of how Lewin, who appeared at the agency one day as a policymaker on an obscure detail from the General Services Administration, could have suddenly begun wielding the powers of the agency’s top official.

Internal USAID emails reviewed by WIRED reveal that during the three-week period of March 18 to April 4, during which Lewin began canceling lifesaving aid programs and personally signed off on the termination of thousands of USAID employees, he did not sign the paperwork typically required by law to begin work at the agency, despite repeated requests. In fact, his appointment was so mysterious that USAID security was unable to issue him an ID card because they had no records of his employment.

Lewin, currently director of policy planning at the State Department, tells WIRED that prior to Rubio delegating powers to him, he was “both detailed and dual appointed to work at USAID by Secretary Rubio according to well-established authorities and with the advice of State Department and White House counsel.”

Experts, though, say that while Lewin performed the duties of a top USAID leader under the title Rubio handed to him—deputy administrator of policy and programming and chief operating officer—it isn’t clear that he had the legal authority to do so. Questions about how DOGE affiliates like Lewin stepped into top roles at many federal agencies, including USAID, remain key to dozens of active lawsuits targeting DOGE and the Trump administration over federal workforce reductions, firings, and agency dismantlings.

Lewin has said, in a declaration submitted to the court in J. Doe 4 v. U.S. DOGE Service, that he began serving at USAID as a senior adviser as well as a director for strategy and programs on January 28, 2025. On March 18, according to court filings, Rubio, in his role as USAID’s acting administrator, delegated the authority of the deputy administrator of policy and programming and chief operating officer to Lewin, and also signed a document appointing Lewin an “officer of the United States.”

According to the emails reviewed by WIRED, on March 20, two days after Rubio placed Lewin atop the USAID hierarchy, White House liaison to USAID Adam Korzeniewski notified HR to begin the process of onboarding Lewin as a senior adviser performing duties as deputy administrator. Four days later, the emails reveal, after prompting from HR, Korzeniewski provided a proposed start date—March 18—and the next day, Lewin was sent a temporary job offer.

Tech.title: UK Home Office May Face Investigation Over Use of OpenAI Tech
Tech.content:
A UK government watchdog is considering an investigation into the Home Office’s use of generative AI tools to process asylum applications, WIRED has learned. The potential probe follows lawmakers and researchers publicly questioning the tools’ accuracy and the government’s secrecy around their use.

The Independent Chief Inspector of Borders and Immigration (ICIBI), which monitors the Home Office’s management of borders, immigration, and customs, has asked digital rights nonprofit Open Rights Group (ORG) to share more information on the tools as it draws up plans for the topics it will inspect next year, campaigner Sara Alsherif tells WIRED. ORG’s findings come from a six-month investigation into the tools, which involved 11 parliamentary questions, two ministerial letters, and 10 public records requests that attempt to pry details from the Home Office, which has withheld details on the tools.

The ICIBI tells WIRED it cannot confirm what topics are under active consideration before it publishes its annual inspection priorities, but it says it is aware of concerns about the use of AI tools and pointed to its findings last year that one of the tool’s “effectiveness and reliability were varied.”

“Asylum decisions are made by trained caseworkers, with AI tools used only to assist in navigating interview records and policy information. They cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims,” a Home Office spokesperson tells WIRED in an email. “We regularly monitor the performance of these tools alongside our established quality-assurance processes, and have already committed to publishing updated evaluations on their roll out.”

The Home Office uses the Asylum Case Summarisation (ACS) and Asylum Policy Search (APS) tools, built on OpenAI’s 2023 GPT-4 large language model and Microsoft Foundry, to summarize transcripts of interviews with asylum applicants and information about their countries of origin, according to documents obtained by ORG. The immigration and law enforcement authority started piloting these tools in late 2024 as the Labour government tried to clear a backlog of around 100,000 asylum cases, while staying on top of the tens of thousands of new applications the UK receives each year. While the department has made significant progress, halving the number of people waiting on an initial decision in the year through June, the number of appeals against decisions has ballooned.

Researchers are concerned about the accuracy of the AI tools–especially to decide something as high-stakes as whether to send someone back to a country where they fear persecution. ORG found that the percentage of summaries generated by the ACS deemed not fit for use—often because they contain factual errors or misrepresentations—is significantly higher than the published 9 percent error rate calculated in the pilot evaluation. There is no quality control for the summaries produced by the APS, it also found.

Asylum decision-makers use the tools to save time when reviewing asylum cases; when used together, the pilot showed the tools could save around an hour per case, according to government estimates. Caseworkers use the ACS to speed up their review of transcripts of interviews where asylum seekers explain how they were persecuted in their country and why they are afraid to return. They use the APS as a search assistant to find and summarize country policy information, which informs them whether the applicant faces a genuine risk of harm in their home country. In July, a UK judge accused the Home Office of citing an “AI hallucinated” document to refuse a Moroccan woman and her child’s asylum claim on the basis that her home country would be safe for her to return to.

Tech.title: UK Politician Jess Asato Got Deepfaked. Now She’s Taking xAI to Court
Tech.content:
Few people understand the current deepfake epidemic better than Jess Asato. The British Labour MP has spent years campaigning against the use of technology to abuse women and girls. Then, after calling out Elon Musk during the notorious Grok Deepfake Scandal of 2025, Asato found herself caught in the very crisis she had been trying to prevent.

Disturbing and degrading deepfake images of the MP circulated widely. One appeared to depict a sexual assault. When Asato reported them to X, the platform repeatedly dismissed her complaints. So she decided to take the fight somewhere else: the courts. She is now pursuing legal action against Musk’s xAI, arguing that it unlawfully used her image without her consent. The case could help establish a precedent for holding AI companies accountable when their products cause harm.

For Asato, this is personal, but it is hardly new territory. Before entering Parliament, she spent years working with charities supporting survivors of domestic abuse and vulnerable children. That experience has shaped her political career, informing her push for stronger protections for women and children online. Now, she is confronting more troubling questions: What happens when the technology enabling abuse becomes ubiquitous, the platforms hosting it refuse to intervene, and the people targeted are left to fight back on their own?

At stake for Asato is more than the misuse of a single image. It is whether consent still means anything when AI can manufacture almost anything, and whether the companies building these tools can be made to answer for what they do. Asato is betting that the law can catch up with the technology. And she is prepared to take on Musk to find out. (xAI did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)

Also, before you read on, be aware that this interview includes references to sexual assault and child sex abuse.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Tech.title: AI Agents Are Media’s New Favorite Audience
Tech.content:
Every morning, Michelle Seo receives a briefing from Chattiana, her Muse artificial intelligence agent.

Chattiana’s briefing lists Seo’s agenda and to-do list, and plucks water-cooler topics from the headlines in her various newsletters along with links to the sources.

“I’m kind of challenging myself as an introvert to start more conversations,” Seo, a San Diego-based public relations consultant, tells WIRED. The newsletter, she says, gives her a sense of the daily news and options for filling an awkward silence on a Zoom call.

Seo is far from the first person to consume her news with an AI assist. In fact, the trend has become so common that some news outlets are starting to produce content that treats AI agents—not human readers—as the intended audience. This can look like anything from feeds optimized for AI to pieces structured to allow agents to create personalized articles.

“We believe that the media ecosystem is changing,” says Axios chief revenue officer Jacquelyn Cameron. “We see this with open web deteriorating. We see that search is shrinking. We see that hyperpersonalization is surging, that LLMs are becoming more important in the way that people are consuming” their news.

Major publishers have responded to that change in a variety of ways. Many, including WIRED’s parent company Condé Nast, have signed deals to allow AI platforms to surface their content. Outlets are grappling with “generative engine optimization,” or GEO, strategies to ensure articles appear in responses to AI prompts. Last year, AIOSEO, a SEO plug-in for WordPress sites, launched a feature that provides websites with LLM.txt files, which help AI discover and interpret sites’ content.

Others have taken a more defensive posture: The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023 for copyright infringement, alleging that the companies illegally trained models on reporting. That case is still ongoing.

What Axios and a handful of others are trying, though, represents a more foundational shift in how the media operates—and who its stories are for.

“We have always said,” Cameron says, “that we want to be where the audience is.”

At the Digiday Publishing Summit in September, Axios announced the upcoming launch of Axios Direct: feeds designed for AI agents.

“We do believe that a significant portion of news consumption will move into AI systems, LLMs, and devices,” Cameron says. She describes the feeds as a more efficient way for agents to access Axios content, cutting back on narrative to prioritize structured data—more similar to a Bloomberg terminal than a series of articles.

Tech.title: NASA’s Oldest Martian Spacecraft Have Been Running for Decades. Here’s How
Tech.content:
NASA’s Mars Odyssey spacecraft has been operating for so long, it can rent a car without any fees. The spacecraft arrived at the Red Planet on October 24, 2001. It, along with its 20-year-old sibling, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), have operated longer than anyone watching their launches could have dreamed possible.

Having such a long record of observations from above the Martian surface has rewritten the story of water on the planet, past and present alike. Keeping the wizened orbiters going for so long has been possible only thanks to great engineering and constant problem solving—and a little luck. But scientists wonder whether, despite their storied legacies, Odyssey and MRO will be the last of their kind, at least for the Red Planet.

“Both Odyssey and MRO are some of the most productive spacecraft that have ever existed,” says Briony Horgan, a planetary scientist at Purdue University who isn’t affiliated with either mission, calling them “critical” to NASA’s overall Mars research program. Odyssey’s observations of the planet’s ice, for example, and MRO’s ability to see surface features change over time have each given scientists unprecedented insight into Mars as a vibrant planet rather than a lump of rock. Odyssey and MRO also connect humans to every NASA rover, which can’t communicate with Earth directly. It’s an impressive legacy for a pair of orbiters that were only meant to last just a few years.

Space is a notoriously harsh environment that takes luck and resilience to survive for decades. Particularly tricky is the barrage of high-energy particles hitting machinery; a powerful enough strike to a delicate enough apparatus can be fatal. And whereas engineers can keep constant tabs on satellites orbiting Earth, bandwidth to Mars is more limited—science spacecraft might only check in once or twice a week, says Rob Lillis, a planetary and space physicist at the University of California, Berkeley, who has worked on a range of more recent Mars orbiters.

“A Mars craft has to be able to manage by itself,” he says.

Tech.title: How CNET Makes Money: Content Labeling and Revenue Sources Explained
Tech.content:
At CNET, we don’t charge a subscription fee. All of our excellent, independent journalism is available free of charge for everyone. We pursue a variety of revenue sources to support our work, including selling space on our site to advertisers, licensing our content to partners and more.

We adhere to the strict standards of editorial integrity that have earned your trust throughout our 35-year history. In the spirit of transparency, here’s a guide to how we identify sources of revenue related to our content.

Key principles

CNET writers and editors follow a few core tenets that guide how we label our work. These are non-negotiable and spelled out below.

More from CNET

Independence: Editorial coverage, including stories, videos, product reviews, recommendations, and advice, is determined solely by our editorial organization for the benefit of the audience, without any advertising, marketing, or other business considerations.

Editorial coverage, including stories, videos, product reviews, recommendations, and advice, is determined solely by our editorial organization for the benefit of the audience, without any advertising, marketing, or other business considerations. Transparency: Disclosures are always clear, conspicuous and unambiguous to ensure that our audience understands when content is paid for by an advertiser, when independent content is made possible by an advertiser or when CNET earns a commission.

Disclosures are always clear, conspicuous and unambiguous to ensure that our audience understands when content is paid for by an advertiser, when independent content is made possible by an advertiser or when CNET earns a commission. Clear distinction: We maintain a clear boundary between independent editorial content and paid or branded content. When independent editorial content is made possible by a partner, we tell you.

Revenue sources and disclosures

The list below covers revenue sources disclosed on our site and platforms using specific language.

Affiliate links

CNET prides itself on independent, expert reviews and recommendations. Our writers and editors use their years of experience, along with lab-based testing, to recommend the best products and services available to our audience, along with the best deals on those products. We may earn a commission when you buy a product or service through a link on our platforms (e.g., in product reviews, “best lists,” or writing about deals). Not every product or service included on a best list or review will include buying links or buttons.

Disclosure: We include a prominent disclosure before or in sight of the first link. Standard disclosure language includes: “If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.”

‘Made Possible By’

CNET creates content using an organic process of ideation, collaboration and response to tech industry trends. Partners and advertisers can choose to support editorial production within a category or package in order to increase the breadth and depth of CNET’s independent, human-authored journalism.

In these cases, partners and advertisers do not have editorial control or pre-publishing approval, nor can they mandate inclusion of specific products or information not already chosen or planned by the editorial team. At no point do advertisers view this content before it is published. Advertisers or partners may provide support to broad topics, specific categories of coverage, or story types.

Disclosure: If a brand chooses to support our content on our site or on social media, we include a clear, visible disclosure near the content or pieces of content in a category with language explaining that the content was made possible by a partner.

Sponsored best list and gift guide placements, also known as Featured Deals

Some sponsors would like their product or service to be included in our best lists and gift guides, which gather our editors’ expert recommendations into lists. If the sponsor’s product is already independently recommended by our journalists, sponsors may pay a fee to be featured higher in that list or in a more visible spot. Such cases will be clearly labeled with a disclosure.

If the sponsor’s product is not already recommended by our journalists but aligns with our standards, sponsored placements sold by business teams appear outside the list itself on the same page. These are clearly labeled with a disclosure to prevent implication of editorial endorsement.

Tech.title: Trying an iPhone Duo at the Apple Store? Don’t Leave Without Testing These 6 Things
Tech.content:
The iPhone Duo went on sale Oct. 23, and anyone who didn’t preorder the device on Oct. 16 is now looking at a delivery date in late January. Apple stores have demo units on display, though, so you can spend time with Apple’s first foldable long before one could arrive at your door. A few minutes is enough to check what a spec sheet can’t tell you: how the hinge feels, how visible the crease is, how the phone sits in your hand folded and unfolded and how apps behave when you open it up. Here are six things worth testing on your next visit to an Apple store.

Here’s what should you be looking to do when you actually pick up the iPhone Duo. Because while the foldable phone might have a fun, unique design, you may run into things you’re unfamiliar with — or even dislike — when using it day to day. You’ll want to be confident that the device is a good fit for your needs before plunking down $2,000 or more for the folding phone.

We’re going to break down a series of things you should check out when you finally get to play with it at the Apple Store.

More from CNET

The opening animation

The iPhone Duo’s unfolding animation is neat. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

When the Duo was first revealed, Apple showed off a very intriguing animation when you unfold the it. Leave it to Apple to make a function so simple look so aesthetically pleasing.

It’ll likely be the first thing you notice when you first open the Duo up to see its inner display, and there’s a good chance you’ll continue to open and close the device to see the effect. At the end of the day, it’s a parlor trick — but a very good one, adding delight to ordinary use.

Admire the matte screen and minimal crease

Foldables, well, fold, and they typically come with creases. The Duo has a minimal crease and a matte display, both of which are wins. That said, even the most noticeable creases tend to “disappear” when you’re viewing content — you just get used to them while watching TV shows or YouTube videos. The Duo’s minimal crease should be even easier to ignore.

And let’s not forget about the matte screen. Several foldables ship with glossy displays, but the iPhone Duo will have a less shiny screen, making it easier to view in bright environments without annoying reflections.

Apple demonstrated how Netflix will be optimized for the Duo’s displays — from the cover screen to the main display to this half-open configuration with controls on the bottom half. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Watch videos

The outer passport-size display on the iPhone Duo may be a little awkward for watching videos because of how it crops content to fit the new aspect ratio. Still, it’s handy to prop the phone up in tent mode and watch shows that way. You also have a large inner display to work with, but because of its passport-style design, even that screen has a different aspect ratio than the widescreen format people are used to on regular phones, so there will likely be some letterboxing in videos.

Try watching something with the phone set up in both ways to see if it bothers you enough to dissuade you from buying the phone.

Again, it’s not an iPhone Duo issue but a foldable phone issue — the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the same size and format. The aspect ratio of the display might crop the top or sides of videos, so it’s worth trying out if you expect to watch a lot of full-screen videos.

The Duo supports drag-and-drop functionality when multitasking. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

See how apps act in different orientations

Like videos, apps on foldables can sometimes appear a little weird, and that could be the case with the iPhone Duo‘s aspect ratio. When you’re at the Apple Store, check out how your most-used apps look and feel on both the inner and outer displays, and make sure you rotate the inner screen to see how apps behave in this orientation, too — that wide screen could be great for watching vertical videos or scrolling through social media.

If some apps, such as Instagram, look a little different or are wonky, it’ll hopefully be just a matter of time until the developers make an update that optimizes the experience for this new design. Keep in mind that you can also have two apps open onscreen at once, making it easier to multitask.

Explore the cameras

The iPhone Duo has two 48-megapixel rear cameras. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

If you want the best camera experience on an iPhone right now, you should be looking at the iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max, but that doesn’t make the Duo a slouch for shooting photos, either.

Yes, the Duo is missing a third camera (telephoto), and if that’s important to you, then you probably shouldn’t even be considering Apple’s foldable. But still, if you’re going to shell out this much money for a new phone, test out those cameras — even if it’s in a controlled environment like an Apple Store.

Another thing to check out before you pull the trigger is your selfie shots with this new phone. There are two main ways to do this: with the phone closed, holding it up in the regular way you’d take a selfie using the outer screen’s 12-megapixel front-facing camera, or with the inner display open and shooting with the twin 48-megapixel rear cameras (the outer screen will show a preview of the shot).

There’s also a front-facing camera underneath the inner display, which is mostly for video calls — and which we suspect would produce the least-impressive shots from the device. Try them all and see what you think of the pics. And since you’re at an Apple Store, make sure you delete them afterward.

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Try typing on both displays

The odd but interesting aspect ratio of the front display on the iPhone Duo may be a little awkward for typing, so it’s best to do a typing test when you have one in front of you. While the inner display will provide a roomier and more comfortable typing experience, you probably won’t want to have to open up the Duo every time you want to shoot off a quick text to someone. If you have bigger hands, typing on the front screen could be a bit of a nightmare.

Typing one-handed on the small cover screen should be manageable, but try it out to see if it works for you. Some may find it convenient; others may find it cumbersome.

And when you’re typing on the inner display, try the Duo in both portrait and landscape orientations to see which feels better. You can also choose between a split keyboard and larger keys. It’s thoughtful of Apple to offer options that let you tailor the typing experience to your preferences, but you may find that none of them suit your style.

Tech.title: Microplastics Are Everywhere. Don’t Make It Worse
Tech.content:
Putting plastic in the microwave increases your risk of ingesting harmful microplastics. Kinga Krzeminska/Getty Images

Standing near your microwave almost certainly won’t give you cancer, but that doesn’t mean the popular kitchen appliance isn’t linked to health concerns. While glass, ceramic and porcelain are safe to use in a microwave, certain food storage vessels present a clear and present danger when nuked at such high temperatures.

The microwave is an undoubtedly handy tool for reheating leftovers — though better options exist — softening butter, or even quickly cooking meats with this surprisingly effective microwave grill plate, but what you put in the microwave matters to avoid the risk of ingesting microplastics.

Study after study has shown that the resulting chemical exposure from microplastics could pose significant health risks, and they have been linked to increases in medical issues like infertility and even cancer. Cheap plastic containers can leach microplastics into food, and that risk increases when you heat them in the microwave.

More from CNET



Here’s everything you need to know about microwaving plastic.

Most takeout containers are not microwave-safe

Most black plastic containers are not microwave-safe. Getty Images

“If you’re using takeout containers to reheat food, they need to be labeled as heat-safe,” advises Ricardo Jarquin, executive chef of Loews Coral Gables in Miami. “Most restaurants do not use them because they’re more expensive.”

Best Food Storage Containers for 2026 See at CNET

Aluminum, cardboard and paper-based containers are typically plastic-free and safe for storing and reheating food. Cheap plastic takeout containers are often unsafe and should never be used to reheat food. Styrofoam is even worse because it melts in the microwave, a clear sign it’s unsafe for reheating food.



What to use instead of plastic

It might sound like more work, but bringing your own food storage container for leftovers is the safest bet. FreshSplash/Getty Images

So what’s the best way to reheat that delicious meal? We chatted with Jarquin, who has overseen culinary operations and food safety protocols for major hotel chains including Four Seasons, Hilton, and Marriott, and Hope Montgomery, owner of Brick & Mortar in St. Petersburg, Florida, to get the skinny on safely using takeout containers.

Ideally, the restaurant is using compostable paper, aluminum or cardboard products, which can be found at Brick & Mortar and is Montgomery’s material of choice. A surefire way to ensure food is stored and reheated in a heat-safe container (whether by initial temperature or via microwave) is to use your own.

“The safest containers are BPA-free, or even better, glass ones like Pyrex,” recommends Jarquin. “Stainless steel and aluminum are great, too, just not for the microwave.”

One of our favorite options is this colorful 10-piece set that offers the convenience of multiple sizes. This means you can choose the right shape for what you plan to reheat or take home, from an entire entree to a few bites of dessert.

Beware of plastic containers marketed as microwave- and freezer-safe

Many plastic containers are marketed as “freezer- and microwave-safe,” but that’s not the case. Rubbermaid

Many plastic containers are marketed as “freezer- and microwave-safe,” but that’s mostly marketing jargon. Plastic containers should really never be frozen or microwaved. Ziploc and Rubbermaid both faced a 2025 class-action lawsuit for advertising their plastic containers as “microwave-safe” and “freezer-safe.” When heated, plastic containers can leach chemicals into food. When frozen, the plastic often breaks off, which can contaminate food.

How to reheat food safely

Deli containers may be considered food-safe, but glass and ceramic are safer options for reheating food in the microwave. Julien McRoberts/Getty Images

More important than reheating food so it tastes good is making sure it’s safe to eat. Never reheat your leftovers in a non-heat-safe vessel. That includes most cheap plastic containers restaurants use, such as plastic clamshells or black plastic containers. Deli containers like the ones you get your grocery store chicken salad in are considered “food safe” for storage, but it’s still not recommended to use them to reheat food at high temperatures.

When reheating food in the microwave, always use glass or ceramic. Keep any containers, lids or utensils that contain plastic or rubber out and use for serving only.

How to reheat food so it tastes good

An air fryer is one of our favorite ways to reheat leftovers. Thai Liang Lim/Getty Images

Beyond the risks of plastic exposure when hot food is stored in those containers, you’ll want to ensure reheating leftovers maintains overall quality.

“Though microwaving is quick and easy, better results can often be achieved by reheating on the stovetop,” says Montgomery. “A little extra fat like olive oil and butter, as well as seasoning, can also be helpful,” she adds, noting that this doesn’t pertain to some dishes like her restaurant’s famed beef tenderloin carpaccio, which should be consumed in its entirety on location.

Jarquin echoes these sentiments. “You get a much better result when reheating leftovers in a frying pan or in the oven,” he stresses, adding that some dishes may even taste better the next day. “At Americana Kitchen, the rigatoni with vodka sauce keeps getting tastier the next day. Also, our pizzas and mushroom pasta definitely get better the next day. The flavors soak in even more and the texture stays great when reheated slowly,” he says.

Jarquin also recommends enjoying at-home foods like “stews, curries, chili, and lasagna,” where flavors can keep developing overnight.

Concerns about bacterial growth

Food, including cooked rice, can develop bacteria quickly if not stored properly. Chris Monroe/CNET

Another risk with leftovers is the rapid growth of bacteria, which can cause brief but sometimes serious illnesses. In short, the longer food sits out, the quicker these bacteria grow.

“The general rule is that it takes about two hours at room temperature and one hour if it’s really hot out” (usually above 90 degrees Fahrenheit), said Jarquin. “After that, bacteria can grow quickly, and you don’t always see or smell it. That’s why it’s important to either serve food hot, chill it fast or keep it properly stored.”



At the end of the day, if you’re even slightly fearful of microplastics and/or foodborne illnesses, no leftover is worth the temporary satisfaction. Accept your losses and whip up your own homemade delicacy to ensure safe, plastic-free bites in the comfort of your own kitchen.

For a comprehensive guide to food safety protocols, check out the US Centers for Disease Control’s Four Steps to Food Safety.

Tech.title: Apple’s ‘Pro and Tell’ Event: Everything Announced So Far This Week
Tech.content:
Apple’s Pro and Tell experience week is here, and it’s off to a strong start, with the new iPad Mini unveiled on Monday morning and a new MacBook Pro and iMac on Tuesday. But there’s more to come: We’re also expecting a long-anticipated touchscreen laptop.

Apple’s had a busy few months, launching the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max in September alongside the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4 and the AirPods 5, followed by the iPhone Duo going on sale at the end of last week.

Apple’s refreshed smart home lineup, revealed during its recent Welcome Home event, is up next: the HomePod Mini 2 will launch on Friday; the Apple HomeView and Apple TV 4K on Nov. 13; and availability for the Home Collection products begins in December.

More from CNET

This week will culminate with Apple hosting a special event on Wednesday, and CNET will be on the ground capturing all the latest details. We’ll update this article as more details are revealed.

One of the two new iPad Mini colors: midnight. Apple

Apple’s new iPad Mini

Announced on Monday, Apple’s new iPad Mini is available to preorder on Wednesday and will go on sale Nov. 6. It starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, $799 for 256GB and $999 for 512GB.

Setting it apart from the last iPad Mini, which came out two years ago, the new tablet has an 8.5-inch OLED screen (versus an LCD), IP67 water and dust resistance, an Apple A20 processor, a repositioned front-facing camera and a through-screen speaker system called Acoustic Display, as well as being thinner and lighter than before.

Apple’s new iMac M6 comes in a choice of seven colors.

A new iMac

The latest iMac, announced Tuesday, features Apple’s M6 processor with a CPU and a GPU each having up to 12 cores, two more cores apiece than before, Apple said. A new dual 16-core Neural Engine delivers AI compute that’s up to twice as fast as the previous generation, the company said. The iMac also has a 24-inch 4.5K Retina display.

Preorders for the iMac M6 will begin Wednesday, Oct. 28, with availability to follow on Nov. 6. Pricing starts at $1,499 for an iMac with M6 featuring a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU. It’s available in seven colors: blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange and silver.

Apple

MacBook Pro refresh

The new 14-inch MacBook Pro, also announced Tuesday, similarly features the M6 processor with 12-core CPU and GPU and dual 16-core Neural Engine for AI tasks. Apple says the battery life runs up to 24 hours. The laptop features a Liquid Retina XDR display, a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera and a six-speaker sound system.

The MacBook Pro with M6 can be preordered starting Wednesday, Oct. 28, and will be in stores and delivered to customers starting Nov. 6. Pricing starts at $1,999.

Apple Creator Studio updates

Tuesday also brought updates to the Apple Creator Studio software suite. For instance, Final Cut Pro for Mac now includes built-in MotionVFX, a collection of visual effects, plug-ins, transitions, templates and motion graphics tools; the curated Content Hub now includes video assets and is available in Final Cut Pro; Pixelmator Pro introduces Generate Fill, which lets creators transform selected areas of an image using natural language; and Keynote, Pages and Numbers introduce new AI features in beta, including assistants that understand document contexts.

The Apple Creator Studio updates will be available in November to subscribers for free.

And as for the iPhone Duo launch last week, check out CNET’s ongoing folding test — you can watch the livestream here and tune in on Tuesday as we continue testing how many times the iPhone Duo can fold without cracking in the CNET lab.

Tech.title: 9 Out of 10 Coffee Experts Agreed, This Is the Best Way to Brew
Tech.content:
For experts, drip and espresso take a back seat to this brewing method. skaman306/Getty Images

Coffee inspires passionate debate among its drinkers, including the best way to brew and drink it. There are die-hard espresso devotees, cold brew enthusiasts, and those who prioritize push-button convenience above all.

Among the coffee intelligentsia, a few brewing methods rise to the top. Drip coffee isn’t maligned, but it isn’t how most of the professionals I spoke with make their morning cup, even if most Americans do. Even espresso, the method of choice for most of Europe, falls out of the top spot when asked about the best way to brew.

Nearly every coffee pro I consulted was aligned. Getty Images

So, then, what is the best process for brewing coffee? According to pros I spoke with, there is an answer, and it’s mostly unanimous. I asked 10 coffee experts — roasters, cafe owners, educators, barista champions, and one former president of the Specialty Coffee Association — to rank seven brewing methods: AeroPress, automatic drip machine, espresso, French press, K-Cup, moka pot and pour-over.

Here’s what they said.

The best way to brew coffee, according to experts

Pour-over earned the top spot by a healthy margin. Hario

While it wasn’t completely unanimous, pour-over was the clear winner for the overall average ranking. The good news is, pour-over is among the least expensive coffee-brewing methods available, requiring little more than a handheld kettle or other pouring device and a funnel dripper with a conical filter that sits on top of the cup or carafe to catch the coffee. (You can certainly spend more money for a serious pour-over kit.) On the other hand, well-executed pour-over coffee can be fussy and isn’t a set-it-and-forget-it kind of method.

Review: Oxo Good Grips Pour-Over Coffee Maker See at CNET

Naturally, pour-over is the kind of thing true coffee aficionados will happily subscribe to, requiring precise timing and temperature, not to mention the patience to watch the brew. This can, however, be complicated for those who need caffeine before they care about such details.

Ranked scores:

(1 = Best and 7 = Worst)

Pour-over : 1.625

: 1.625 AeroPress : 2.375

: 2.375 Espresso : 3.5

: 3.5 French press : 3.75

: 3.75 Moka pot : 4.625

: 4.625 Drip : 4.75

: 4.75 K-Cup: 6.625

Another method highly ranked by coffee pros

AeroPress got high marks from the coffee experts I spoke with. AeroPress

While pour-over had the highest overall ranking, it wasn’t the only method a pro ranked No. 1. AeroPress — an analog method that combines the agitation of pour-over, the immersion of French press and the pressure of espresso — had a couple of acolytes and came safely in second place in the overall ranking.

Marwyn Garcia, owner of Headcount Coffee, ranked it as number one among the available options (though noted that other, less common methods, such as an immersion brewer or coffee siphon, are also worthy adversaries). The AeroPress steep time is adjustable, allowing for personal preference in the brew, and he also emphasized bean quality, noting its importance in any method.

“Overall flavor is more dependent on how fresh your coffee is,” he says. “As well as the roast level, as it can require a longer brew time or steep to get the desired result.”

Among those who placed it second after pour-over, Howard also notes that AeroPress has definite upside: “It has great clarity and versatility,” he says, “especially for travel or a quick cup.”

Espresso and French press methods have merit

Espresso and French press tied for third. Corin Cesaric/CNET

Espresso and French press also received first-place rankings from certain coffee professionals, and effectively tied for third in terms of confidence among c.

Heather Perry, the CEO of Klatch Coffee, a two-time US barista champion and former president of the Specialty Coffee Association, notes that it’s espresso that is used to measure barista performance.

“It’s true that you need some specialized equipment and time to get the best results with espresso, but once you’ve got your machine dialed in, the characteristics of great espresso really shine through,” she says. “Wonderful, intense flavor, beautiful crema, and a great aroma too. Sweetness, acidity, and bitterness are all balanced in harmony.”

3 Best Espresso Makers of 2026 See at CNET

Those who favored the French press cited its ritualistic nature and its ability to easily make more than one cup.

“I’m a fan of the French press method because it really captures the relaxed, hands-on ritual of making coffee that I love,” says Bernadette Gerrity, vice president at Café Aroma. “I’ve always preferred old-school brewing methods to new gadgets because you can control everything, from the proportions to the flavor, without any waste,” she says. “It’s really easy to dial in your perfect cup with a French press. Plus, it’s quick, simple and satisfying — just coffee and water, no buttons or special pods needed.”

“It’s true that you need some specialized equipment and time to get the best results with espresso, but once you’ve got your machine dialed in, the characteristics of great espresso really shine through,” said Heather Perry. Pamela Vachon/CNET

“French press hits all of the marks, and it allows for several cups of coffee at a time, which allows the pot to be enjoyed by others,” says former professional coffee roaster Dave Linari of NewSylum Brewing. “I find the coarse grind of the bean and the coarse filter allow all of the flavors and aromas to come through as the bean intended,” he says. “The filter allows the coffee’s natural oils and fine particles to remain in the cup, which creates a richer texture and taste, and the whole system is a very simple and affordable piece of equipment, which you can use to froth milk as well.”

Why coffee pros love pour-over

Consistency

Pour-over brewing lets you control precise variables, including temperature, flow rate, and agitation. Chris Monroe/CNET

“With pour-over, a slow, deliberate pour allows control of precise variables including temperature, flow rate and agitation,” says Theo Chan, coffee reviewer and managing editor of Coffee Roast, “ensuring even extraction and revealing a coffee’s nuanced sweetness, acidity and aromatics.” (Agitation refers to the water’s ability to circulate among the coffee grounds during the brew.)

“Maximum control over variables equals consistency,” says James McCarthy, coffee roaster and head of education at Colombian coffee brand Devoción, who specifically recommends an origami pour-over dripper. “Since you’re using your own kettle, you can choose the water temperature and vary the flow rate according to preference.”

“For a cup of black coffee, I’d say pour-over is my go-to,” says Joe Howard, co-founder of YAWN Brew. “With a pour-over, you can really highlight the coffee’s unique characteristics of the origins. It’s a clean brew method that gives you good precision of the coffee.”

Suitability for roast preference

One coffee expert I spoke with lauded pour-over for its ability to tease out the delicate flavor of certain roasts. Basak Gurbuz Derman/Getty Images

Michael Cramer, founder of Lardera Coffee, notes that roast level is also an important factor in determining which method is favored. “I prefer light-roasted beans, and pouring water by hand produces a more uniform extraction, teasing out their intricate flavors and delicate aromas,” he says. “This requires more time and attention than other methods, but if you care about coffee, it’s a worthwhile investment. You’re giving up ease for the sake of consistency and flavor, which seems a trade-off worth making.”

Filter considerations

The ranking also considered the type of filter each method relies on. “Pour-overs use paper filters that remove oils, resulting in a cleaner and more delicate flavor profile highlighting the intricacies in a coffee while being able to represent any roast level well,” says Megan Biolsi, manager of coffee education and Training at Sightglass Coffee. “They typically require a little fine-tuning to achieve a great cup, but allow for intricate adjustments for those who want to experiment and perfect their morning brew.”

Lesser-favored methods: moka pot, drip machine and K-Cup

Moka pots have a certain charm, but coffee experts rank this brewing method lower on the list. Brian Bennett/CNET

While the moka pot, a stovetop espresso brewing method, and the automatic drip machine both received middle-of-the-pack votes, coffee professionals unanimously voted the K-Cup the least favored method. While Howard generously noted that it was “quick and tidy,” the consensus was that it “sacrifices flavor and texture,” allows no adjustment, and produces unnecessary waste with every cup.

Tech.title: Look Out for Political Deepfakes and Scams This Midterm Election Season
Tech.content:
You can’t automatically believe everything you see in the age of AI. Generative AI tools like chatbots, image and video generators make it easy for anyone to create realistic media. The capabilities of AI have improved so much that it’s nearly impossible to distinguish real from AI. That’s never been more frustrating or dangerous than it is now during election season.

The 2026 midterm election is on Nov. 3. All 435 House of Representatives seats are on the ballot, along with 33 Senate seats and many other state and local races across the country. Tech issues, such as data center construction, are popular topics among candidates and ballot measures across the country. You can check your voter registration and see who’s on your ballot now using Vote.org’s free tool.

This fall, we’ve seen a number of AI-edited political ads, with and without disclosures about their AI use. Unsurprisingly, we’ve seen AI used in some high-profile races, including to give Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff AI cosmetic procedures and to make it seem like Texas Senate candidate James Talarico had defaced a Bible. Political campaigns and groups have spent more than $16 million on these AI ads this year, a CNN analysis found.

More from CNET

We’ve seen how generative AI can wreak havoc during election season. During the 2024 presidential primary, many New Hampshire voters got phone calls from an AI voice replica of Joe Biden urging them not to vote. This wasn’t sanctioned by the Biden campaign, and AI robocalls are illegal, so the Democratic political consultant behind it was charged with voter suppression and fined $6 million.

Improvements to AI tech since 2024 only make for sharper swords in a bad actor’s arsenal. To protect yourself from being scammed or tricked by AI deepfakes, here are some tips.

Verify if those photos, videos and audio are AI

Obvious errors like seven-fingered hands in AI images are increasingly rare as AI tech improves. That’s bad news for people trying to visually determine whether something is AI or not.

Instead, it can be more accurate to use online verification websites. These are our top choices:

The Content Authenticity Initiative’s Inspect tool can identify many kinds of AI content.

OpenAI’s Verify tool can identify content made with ChatGPT.

Google’s SynthID Detector can identify Google-made AI content. You can also upload content to Gemini to scan for SynthIDs.

These websites work by scanning the metadata of an image, video or audio file for hidden signatures indicating it was made with AI. They aren’t foolproof, but they should catch some AI media.

Other services can also identify some AI content for a price, like Pangram’s $20 per month subscription for individual users. Apple is also adding a verification measure called Reference Images, but it’s limited to its newest iPhone 18 Pro models.

Be mindful that any AI detection service claiming a 100% success rate is lying. There are too many AI services available and too little standardization across the industry to get it right all the time.

Always double-check with official sources

We know from decades of cybersecurity research that attackers will try to prey on your emotions to get you to fall for a scam. The goal for these bad actors is to cloud your judgment. So one of the best ways to fight back is to arm yourself with knowledge.

For example, if you get a text saying your polling location has been changed with a link to the new one, don’t automatically click it. Go to your state’s board of elections website to verify whether a change has been made – it’s going to have the most official and up-to-date information on polling locations and times.

Check out this map from the US Election Assistance Commission to see the official election contact information for your state. You can also search for your state’s board of elections or check your governor’s website, which may also have voting info readily available. Nonprofit Vote.org can also help you track down your ballot information, no matter what state you’re voting in.

If you’re looking for official policy stances on a candidate rather than relying on potentially fake images or videos, your best bet is to start with their campaign website and platform. There’s no guarantee that the candidate is going to post entirely truthful information, but it should give you some insight into their beliefs on major issues.

Stay calm, be proactive and make a plan now

It’s cliché but true: Don’t believe everything you see online. Election season is a noisy time, and inevitably, you’re going to run across something that isn’t true. Use your gut and avoid panicking when possible. Fact-checking websites like Snopes.com can be useful resources.

The best way to avoid being scammed or tricked by a deepfake is to plan ahead and stay engaged: Make your voting plan now — many states offer an early voting period beginning in mid-October. Check your state’s voter ID laws. View your ballot in advance and research all the candidates on it, not just the headline races.

If you run into issues at your polling place, you can contact the Election Protection Hotline at 866-687-8683.

For more, check out our guide on what to do when you’ve been deepfaked.

Tech.title: The iPhone Duo Has Passed 75,000 Folds in Our Fold-a-Phone Testing Machine. Can It Beat the Galaxy Z Fold 8?
Tech.content:
Apple’s first-ever foldable phone — the iPhone Duo — launched Friday and was met with long lines and product sellouts. We braved three hours at the Apple Store on Friday to snag our own testing model for our lab in Louisville, Kentucky, where I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations.

Now the big question? How many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? As of 8:30 a.m. ET on Tuesday, we’ve passed 75,000 folds.

The goal is simple. On Friday afternoon, my team and I loaded the iPhone Duo into a proprietary machine we built to test foldable phones like Apple’s and Samsung’s rival Galaxy Z Fold 8, which we’ve also already started testing. I’ve overseen the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone. (Read on for how CNET tests foldable phones.)

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

How CNET’s Fold-a-Phone tests foldable phones like the iPhone Duo

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

Matthew Murray/CNET

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.
